# Start Here: Bitcoin Self-Custody

> New to Bitcoin self-custody? Start here. Learn what self-custody means, assess your needs, and find the right path for your situation.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Self-custody means holding the private keys to your own bitcoin, so that no exchange, bank or company can freeze it, lose it or spend it. This site shows how to do that safely: understanding what you are protecting against, making a seed phrase, setting up a hardware wallet, testing the backup, and then adding a passphrase, multisig or your own node when the amount justifies it. If your bitcoin is on an exchange today, the [hardware wallet setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/) is the step that matters most; if you are new to bitcoin, read the pages below in order.

## What is self-custody?

Self-custody is holding bitcoin by controlling its private keys yourself, instead of holding a claim on bitcoin that an exchange keeps for you. An exchange balance is the company's promise to pay you bitcoin when you ask. On the blockchain, the bitcoin belongs to whoever controls the keys, and on an exchange that is the exchange.

| | Exchange account | Self-custody |
|---|---|---|
| Who holds the keys | The exchange | You |
| Can the funds be frozen? | Yes, by the company or by a court order served on it | No |
| Withdrawing or sending | Needs the company's approval | Needs nobody's approval |
| If the company fails or is hacked | You become one of its creditors | Your bitcoin is unaffected |
| If you lose your password or backup | Support can reset the password | The bitcoin is gone |

The last row is the price of self-custody: there is no password reset and no way to reverse a payment. [What is self-custody?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/) covers it in full, including the exchange failures that made the case for it.

## What can go wrong with self-custody?

Self-custody moves the risk from a company to the way you handle your seed phrase, the 12 or 24 words that back up the wallet. The mistakes that lose bitcoin are permanent:

- Losing the seed phrase and the device together. Nobody can restore the wallet.
- Showing the seed phrase to anyone, including "support staff" or a website that asks for it. Whoever has the words can spend the bitcoin.
- Trusting a backup that was never tested. A miswritten word is discovered only when the device fails, which is too late.

The setup guides are written to prevent all three, and [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) exists for the last one.

## Where should you start?

| Your situation | Start with |
|---|---|
| New to bitcoin | [What is Bitcoin?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-bitcoin/) |
| Your bitcoin is on an exchange | [What is self-custody?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/), then [set up a hardware wallet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/) |
| You already use a hardware wallet | [Verify your backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/), then consider [running a node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) |
| You hold a life-changing amount | [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) and [air-gapped signing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) |
| You need privacy, or face a higher risk | [Why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) |

## How much security do you need?

The right setup depends on how much you hold, who might come after it, and how much technical work you are willing to do. Most people need one hardware wallet with a tested backup; the rest is for larger amounts or specific threats.

| If you are protecting | Start with |
|---|---|
| An amount you could lose without real harm | A software wallet on your phone |
| Savings you would miss | A hardware wallet |
| A life-changing amount | Multisig, with keys on two or three devices kept in different places |

| If the threat is | Add |
|---|---|
| Malware, phishing or an exchange failing | Nothing: a hardware wallet covers these |
| Someone targeting you personally | Air-gapped signing, multisig, and not telling people what you hold |
| A government or an attacker with similar resources | All of the above, plus [operational security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/operational-security/) |

If you are not technical, start with one hardware wallet and add layers as you learn; nothing on the advanced pages needs doing on the first day. [Assess your threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/) works through these questions in detail.

## Which reading path fits you?

Each path is a short list of pages in order. Pick the one that matches where you are now.

### Path 1: new to bitcoin

For someone who wants to understand bitcoin before holding any. About two to three hours of reading.

1. [What is Bitcoin?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-bitcoin/): what it is and why it works without a company behind it
2. [What is self-custody?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/): why the keys are what you own
3. [Why holding your own bitcoin matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/): the risks of leaving it on an exchange
4. [Private keys explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/intro/): the number that controls the bitcoin
5. [Seed phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/): how that number becomes words you can write down

### Path 2: your first wallet

For someone who understands the basics and is setting up a first wallet. Two to four hours, including the setup.

1. [Hardware wallets explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/): what the device protects you from
2. [Hardware wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/): the setup, step by step
3. [Backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/): prove the backup restores the wallet
4. [Before you deposit](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/): the checks to run before sending real money

### Path 3: stronger security

For someone already holding their own keys who wants to take more trust out of the setup. One to two days of projects.

1. [Seed generation with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/): make a seed whose randomness you can check
2. [Passphrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/): protect the seed phrase against being found
3. [Run your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/): check your own transactions instead of asking someone else's server
4. [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/): keep fees and address links under control

### Path 4: maximum security

For large holdings or a higher threat level. Several days to a few weeks.

1. [Why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/): what an observer can learn from the blockchain
2. [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/): remove the single point of failure
3. [Air-gapped wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/): sign on a device that never touches a network
4. [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/): break the link between your coins' past and present

## What principles hold across every guide?

### Verify instead of trusting

Check every receive address on the hardware wallet's own screen, not on the computer's. Check firmware signatures before installing. Compare what this site says with the vendor's documentation and other sources; we get things wrong too.

### Go slowly

Mistakes with bitcoin are usually permanent, and the deadlines that push people into them are usually invented. Read a guide through before starting it, send a small test amount first, and treat anyone hurrying you as a warning sign.

### Assume your computer is compromised

A hardware wallet is designed for the case where the computer or phone it connects to is controlled by an attacker: the device shows the transaction on its own screen and signs it there. That protection only holds if the seed phrase never touches a connected device, so never type it, photograph it or store it in a password manager.

### Avoid single points of failure

One backup in one place can burn, flood or be found. Backups in separate places, and for larger amounts [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/), mean that no single loss empties the wallet.

### Practise recovery

A backup you have never restored from is untested. Restore it once before depositing anything significant, using the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/).

## Where can you ask a question?

The [glossary](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/glossary/) defines the terms used across the site, and the [FAQ](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/) answers the common questions about seed phrases and recovery. If a guide is unclear or wrong, tell us on [Nostr](https://primal.net/p/nprofile1qqspxh8lqez8f9kt2cv7626rfax0phl8lu8tgt0jjjkwa6n8lhmt9qgxf4ey5) or [X](https://x.com/selfcustodylabs) and the page gets corrected.

# What is Bitcoin?

> Understand what Bitcoin is, how it works, and why it matters. A beginner's introduction to digital money that no one controls.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-bitcoin/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin is digital money that no person, company or government controls. It runs on a worldwide network of computers that anyone can join, its supply is capped at 21 million coins by rules every participant enforces, and a payment, once confirmed, cannot be reversed or blocked by anyone. It was launched in 2009 by someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto, whose identity has never been confirmed.

Irreversibility is the property that makes bitcoin feel strange at first. A payment that leaves your wallet is gone for good: there is no chargeback and no support line that can undo it. The same property means nobody else can undo or stop a payment either.

## How is bitcoin different from the money in a bank?

Bank money is created by central banks without a fixed ceiling, and banks and payment companies sit in the middle of every transfer. That is why a card can be declined, an account frozen and a wire clawed back days later.

| | Bank money | Bitcoin |
|---|---|---|
| Who issues it | Central banks and commercial banks | The network, on a fixed schedule written into the software |
| Supply | No fixed limit | 21 million, enforced by every node |
| Who approves a payment | The banks and payment networks involved | Nobody: a correctly signed transaction is valid |
| Can a payment be reversed? | Often, for days or weeks | No, once it is confirmed in a block |
| Can an account be frozen? | Yes | Not when you hold your own keys |

This is what "permissionless" means: you need nobody's approval to receive, hold or send bitcoin.

## How does a bitcoin transaction work?

Every participant keeps a copy of the same ledger, and every payment is added to all the copies. Nobody can quietly change an old entry, because everyone else's copy would stop matching. That shared ledger is the **blockchain**.

When Maya in Mexico City sends 0.1 BTC to her cousin Daniel in Buenos Aires, her wallet builds and signs the payment, the network passes it around, a miner includes it in a block, and Daniel's wallet checks it himself.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The path of a 0.1 BTC payment from Maya to Daniel: her wallet builds and signs the transaction, the network broadcasts it, miners verify every rule and include it in a block, and Daniel verifies his money himself](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/fundamentals/tx-path.svg)

</div>

No bank, card network, wire service or currency desk takes part. The network does the job those institutions normally do, and that is the core invention.

## What do miners do, and why can't the history be rewritten?

Miners are computers that compete to add the next block of transactions to the blockchain. To win, a miner has to find a solution to a puzzle that can only be found by trying enormous numbers of guesses, which costs real electricity. The winner publishes the block and receives newly created bitcoin plus the fees of the transactions in it; that reward is how new coins enter circulation.

That cost is what protects the history. To change an old block, an attacker would have to redo the work for that block and every block since, faster than the rest of the network adds new ones. It has never been done to bitcoin, and each new block makes the ones beneath it harder to change, which is why a transaction becomes more settled the deeper it sits.

## Why is the supply fixed at 21 million?

Bitcoin's rules allow at most 21 million coins, and every node on the network rejects a block that would create more, so the limit is not a policy anyone can quietly change. As of October 2026, a little over 20.1 million have been created. The amount created per block halves every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years (the last halving was in April 2024, the next is due around 2028), and the last fraction of a coin will be created around the year 2140.

A central bank that issues more money makes every existing unit a smaller share of the total. Bitcoin cannot do that, because the total is fixed and anyone can check it. That fixed, verifiable supply is why people call bitcoin "digital gold".

## Why does bitcoin matter to you?

- It moves money without permission. A payment to another country works the same as one next door, on any day of the week, without a bank on either side.
- Its supply cannot be inflated. The bitcoin you hold today is the same share of the total in ten years. In a country with a stable currency that may feel abstract; where inflation runs into double digits, it is not.
- It can be owned outright. Bank and brokerage accounts can be frozen or seized by anyone with enough authority over the institution. Bitcoin whose keys you hold has no such institution.

## What are the common misconceptions about bitcoin?

| Claim | What is actually true |
|---|---|
| Bitcoin is anonymous | Bitcoin is pseudonymous. Every transaction is public and permanent, and analysis firms can often trace coins between addresses. Privacy takes deliberate effort; see the [privacy section](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/). |
| Bitcoin is mainly for criminals | The public ledger is a poor hiding place: once one address is linked to a person, its whole history can be followed. Chainalysis, an analysis firm, has put illicit activity at under 1% of on-chain volume in its recent annual reports. |
| Bitcoin has no real value | Its value rests on what it does (moving money across borders without permission) and on its fixed supply. Whether that is worth something is a judgement each person makes. |
| Bitcoin is too volatile to be useful | Its price moves a lot over days and months. People who hold it as savings measure it over years; people who spend it often convert at the moment of payment. |

## What is a satoshi?

A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin (0.00000001 BTC), named after its creator and usually shortened to "sat". Because amounts are stored to eight decimal places, you never need to buy or send a whole coin.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Unit | Value in BTC | Symbol |
|------|--------------|--------|
| Bitcoin | 1 | BTC |
| Millibitcoin | 0.001 | mBTC |
| Microbitcoin | 0.000001 | μBTC |
| Satoshi | 0.00000001 | sat |

</div>

Most wallets today show amounts in bitcoin or in sats; millibitcoin and microbitcoin are rarely used.

## How do people get bitcoin?

1. Buying it on an exchange, a platform that trades ordinary currency for bitcoin. This is the usual starting point, and it works much like opening a brokerage account.
2. Being paid in it for goods or services, as many freelancers and small businesses are.
3. Trading peer to peer, with someone you know or through a peer-to-peer marketplace, which avoids an exchange at the cost of checking who you are dealing with.
4. Earning it as salary from an employer who pays in bitcoin.
5. Mining it with specialised hardware. Anyone can, but the hardware and electricity make it a business, not a hobby.

Bitcoin bought on an exchange stays in the exchange's custody until you withdraw it. If the exchange is hacked, goes bankrupt or freezes your account, you can lose access even though the balance is yours on paper; [why holding your own bitcoin matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/) covers the exchanges where that happened.

## Why is self-custody the point?

A bitcoin balance on an exchange is like a gift card: it shows a balance, but you are trusting the store to honour it. Self-custody means holding your own private keys, the secret that authorises spending. With the keys in your hands, no exchange failure can take your coins, no account freeze can stop you spending them, and nobody can refuse a payment on your behalf. The cost is that nobody can fix a mistake for you either, which is what the rest of this site is about. [What is self-custody?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/) is the next page.


---

# What is Bitcoin Self-Custody?

> Learn what Bitcoin self-custody means: controlling your own private keys, seed phrases, and taking full ownership of your Bitcoin without third parties.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin self-custody means holding the private keys to your own bitcoin yourself, so that no bank, exchange or company can freeze it, block a payment or lose it on your behalf. If you hold the keys, you hold the coins. If someone else holds the keys, what you hold is their promise to pay you, and "not your keys, not your coins" is a literal description of that arrangement rather than a slogan.

Most people who say they own bitcoin hold a balance on an exchange's website. That balance is a number on the exchange's computer, and it is worth what the company's promise is worth: if the company freezes the account, is hacked or goes bankrupt, the number becomes a claim in a bankruptcy. [Why holding your own bitcoin matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/) goes through the exchanges where that happened.

Self-custody also differs from a bank account. A bank legally controls the money in your account, so it can freeze it, delay a transfer, block a payment or comply with a court order without asking you. With self-custodied bitcoin there is nobody in the middle to ask: the network accepts a transaction signed with the right key and nothing else.

## What are private keys and seed phrases?

A private key is a very large random number that proves ownership of a particular amount of bitcoin. Anyone who knows the number can spend those coins, and nobody who lacks it can.

A seed phrase is a list of 12 or 24 ordinary words that encodes the number every private key in a wallet is derived from. Wallets use it because a raw key is too long to write down reliably, while words can be backed up with a pencil and paper. The seed phrase is the thing to protect: whoever holds it holds the bitcoin, losing it (along with the device) loses the bitcoin for good, and nobody runs a password reset or a support line that could undo either. [Private keys explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/intro/) and [seed phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/) cover how both work.

## What are the ways to self-custody bitcoin?

There are three common setups, and the right one depends on how much you hold and how much effort you will put into protecting it. Most people start with the first and move up as their holdings grow.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Setup | Best for | Protection | Cost (October 2026) |
|--------|----------|----------|------|
| Software wallet | Learning, small amounts, spending | Keys live on a phone or computer that also runs other software | Free |
| Hardware wallet | Savings you would miss | Keys stay on a dedicated device, which signs transactions itself | About $80 to $250 |
| Air-gapped setup | Large holdings | Keys stay on a device that never connects to a network | From about $50 for a DIY [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/) |

</div>

A **software wallet** is an app on your phone or computer. It is free and easy to use, and it is fine for learning or for holding what you would carry in a physical wallet. Its weakness is that the keys sit on a device that also runs a browser, email and every other app, so malware on that device can reach them.

A **hardware wallet** is a small device built for one job: holding keys and signing transactions with them. The keys never leave the device, and the device shows you what it is signing on its own screen, so an infected computer cannot change the payment without you seeing it. For any amount you would be upset to lose, a hardware wallet is the minimum we recommend. [Hardware wallets explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/) covers how they work and the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) covers which to buy.

An **air-gapped setup** keeps the keys on a device that has never been connected to the internet. Transactions move to and from it as QR codes or files on an SD card, so there is no cable or radio an attacker could use. It costs more effort than a USB hardware wallet, and it is a setup to grow into rather than start with; see [air-gapped wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/).

## What responsibility comes with self-custody?

**Danger: A lost seed phrase cannot be recovered**
If you lose your seed phrase and your wallet device fails, the bitcoin is gone. No support desk, password reset or court order can retrieve it, because the blockchain is not a company that can be asked or sued.

The features that stop anyone helping you recover lost bitcoin are the same features that stop anyone taking it without your consent. They come from the same design, so you cannot have one without the other. That is why backing up the seed phrase, storing the backup safely and testing a recovery matter as much as buying the bitcoin: the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) walks through the test.

## Do you need self-custody for a small amount?

Not immediately. Learning with a small amount on a well-known exchange is a reasonable start, and [why holding your own bitcoin matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/#when-should-you-move-bitcoin-off-an-exchange) sets out the amounts at which we would move it. The short rule: if losing the bitcoin would upset you, it belongs in a wallet whose keys you hold, and once it is more than the price of a hardware wallet, that wallet should be one.


---

# Why Holding Your Own Bitcoin Matters

> Understand the difference between holding Bitcoin yourself vs on an exchange. Learn why 'not your keys, not your coins' is essential for true ownership.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin left on an exchange belongs to the exchange in every way that counts: the exchange holds the private keys, so it decides when you can withdraw, and if it fails you become one of its creditors. Holding your own bitcoin, in a wallet whose keys only you control, is the only arrangement in which an exchange's freeze, hack or bankruptcy cannot touch your coins. Move bitcoin off the exchange once it is an amount you would be upset to lose, and into a hardware wallet once it is worth more than the device.

"Not your keys, not your coins" describes this exactly. An exchange balance is the company's promise to give you bitcoin when you ask. While the promise holds, a balance and real bitcoin look identical on screen; when it fails, the difference is the only thing that matters.

## What happens to bitcoin you leave on an exchange?

The exchange holds the keys, so the exchange signs every transaction that moves the coins, and nothing moves without it. That means:

- A withdrawal can be paused at any time, for any reason the exchange considers good enough.
- An account can be frozen by a compliance team, a court order or a fraud review that takes weeks to clear.
- A hack of the exchange takes customer coins with it, however careful the customer was.
- A bankruptcy turns every balance into a claim that takes years to settle and is usually paid in dollars.

None of this requires bad intent. It is how a custodial platform works.

## Which exchanges have failed with their customers' bitcoin?

These were large, well-known platforms, trusted by hundreds of thousands of customers or more on the day they stopped paying out.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Platform | Year | What happened | What customers lost |
|----------|------|---------------|-------------|
| Mt. Gox | 2014 | The largest bitcoin exchange of its time halted withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy after years of theft it had not detected | About 850,000 BTC reported missing; repayments began in 2024 |
| QuadrigaCX | 2019 | Canada's largest exchange collapsed after its founder died. The Ontario Securities Commission found in 2020 that he had run it as a fraud and that its wallets had been empty since April 2018 | At least C$169 million of the C$215 million owed to 76,000 clients |
| Celsius | 2022 | The lending platform froze withdrawals in June and filed for bankruptcy in July | About $4.7 billion owed to customers |
| FTX | 2022 | Customer deposits had been used by its sister trading firm, Alameda Research; its founder was convicted of fraud in 2023 | About $8 billion missing |
| BlockFi | 2022 | Paused withdrawals when FTX collapsed and filed for bankruptcy later that month | Liabilities of $1 billion to $10 billion, by its own filing |

</div>

Every customer of these platforms had one thing in common: none of them held their own keys. Bitcoin they had withdrawn to their own wallets was untouched by any of these collapses.

## What does a bankruptcy pay back?

Usually dollars, at the price on the day the company filed. The FTX bankruptcy valued customers' crypto at its price on 11 November 2022, when bitcoin traded at about $17,000, and paid those dollar amounts back from 2025, when bitcoin was worth several times as much. Celsius, BlockFi and Voyager used the same petition-date method. A customer who is "repaid in full" can still end up with a fraction of the bitcoin they had.

## Does exchange insurance protect your bitcoin?

Only partly, and rarely against the failures that have cost customers most. Where exchanges publish their insurance terms, the cover is a fraction of customer holdings and is typically for theft from the exchange's online wallets, not for internal fraud, mismanagement or bankruptcy. A successful claim is paid in money, at the price on the day of the incident, after a process that can take years. Insurance is a partial cushion for one kind of failure, not a replacement for holding the keys.

## Isn't losing your own keys a bigger risk?

It is the one objection to self-custody that deserves a serious answer. People do lose bitcoin they hold themselves, almost always by storing the seed phrase somewhere fragile and losing it, or by writing it down wrongly and never checking.

The answer is a handful of backup habits, not handing the keys to someone else:

1. Write the seed phrase down carefully, word by word, and copy it onto something durable; a stamped steel plate survives the fire and water that destroy paper.
2. Keep the backup where only you can reach it, and for larger amounts keep a second copy in a separate place, so a single fire or flood cannot take both.
3. Test the backup by restoring the wallet from it before putting in any significant amount. The [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) walks through it.

With those three in place, self-custody is safer than leaving bitcoin on even a well-run exchange, because the remaining risks are ones you control.

## Why does self-custody matter for bitcoin as a whole?

Bitcoin was designed to work without trusted intermediaries. The first sentence of the 2008 whitepaper says so:

> "A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution."
>
> Satoshi Nakamoto, *Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System*

When most bitcoin sits on exchanges, the system re-creates the structure it was built to avoid: a few companies between users and their money, each of which can be regulated, hacked or pressured like a bank. Every coin held in self-custody is one that no such company controls.

## When should you move bitcoin off an exchange?

There is no fixed threshold, but these are the points at which we would act:

| What you hold | What to do |
|---|---|
| A small amount, bought to learn how bitcoin works | Leaving it on a well-known exchange for a short time is a defensible start |
| A few hundred dollars or more | Learn self-custody now and move it to a wallet you control |
| An amount you would be upset to lose | Move it, and once it is worth more than the device, use a hardware wallet |
| A life-changing amount | A hardware wallet with a tested backup at minimum, and consider [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) |

Learn it before you need it. Waiting for an exchange to fail is the one way of learning this that costs money.

## How do you move bitcoin into self-custody?

1. [Assess your threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/) to decide how much security you need.
2. [Choose your setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/choosing-your-path/) to match it without overbuilding.
3. Follow the [hardware wallet setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/).
4. [Verify the backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) by restoring from it.
5. Run the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/), then withdraw a small test amount before the rest.


---

# Choose Your Self-Custody Setup

> Which Bitcoin self-custody setup fits what you hold: four tiers from a phone wallet to multisig, with the hardware, cost and effort each tier takes.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/choosing-your-path/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Choose the setup by how much bitcoin you hold now and expect to hold in the next year or two. Under about $1,000, a free wallet app on your phone is enough while you learn. From $1,000, use a hardware wallet with a metal backup. From $10,000, add a seed made with dice, a passphrase and your own node. Above $100,000, move to multisig, with keys on devices from different makers kept in different places. If you are unsure, the hardware wallet setup is right for most people, and the choice between reputable devices matters far less than getting off the exchange.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Tier | Holdings | Core setup | Hardware cost (October 2026) |
|------|----------|-----------|------------------|
| Starter | Under $1,000 | Phone wallet app | Free |
| Standard | $1,000 to $10,000 | Hardware wallet and metal backup | About $80 to $200 |
| Enhanced | $10,000 to $100,000 | Standard, plus a dice-generated seed, a passphrase and your own node | About $300 to $500 |
| Maximum | Over $100,000 | Multisig across devices from different vendors, in different places | $500 or more |

</div>

The bands are the same as on [assess your threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/), which also covers the factors that move you up a tier regardless of amount: being publicly known to hold bitcoin, living under capital controls or an unstable government, or facing someone who has singled you out. Your technical comfort matters less than you might expect. If you are new, start at a lower tier and move up; most of these setups take a weekend of careful work, and testing each step is worth the extra time.

## What is the starter setup, for under $1,000?

The starter setup is a wallet app on your phone, a paper copy of its seed phrase and the public servers the app uses by default. It is for learning with small amounts: moving bitcoin around is the fastest way to understand how wallets, addresses and backups behave, and a mistake at this size will not hurt.

Two free, bitcoin-focused apps that suit it are [BlueWallet](https://bluewallet.io/) and [Muun](https://muun.com/). Running your own node at this stage adds work without much benefit.

| Strengths | Limits |
|---|---|
| Free, and running in about ten minutes | The keys live on an internet-connected phone |
| Mistakes cost little | The public servers the app talks to can see your balance and addresses |
| Teaches the real mechanics | Not built to hold savings |

To set it up:

1. Install the app from the official app store listing, checking the developer's name.
2. Create a new wallet inside the app.
3. Write the seed phrase on paper, carefully, and store it somewhere only you can reach.
4. Send a small amount from an exchange and check it arrives.

Move to the standard setup once the balance passes about $1,000, or sooner if you want better security. [Software wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/software-wallets/) covers the category in more detail.

## What is the standard setup, for $1,000 to $10,000?

The standard setup is a hardware wallet, a metal copy of its seed phrase and a desktop app to drive it. A hardware wallet is a small device that keeps the private keys offline and signs transactions on the device itself, so malware on your computer cannot reach the keys or change a payment without the device's screen showing it.

Any of the devices the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) recommends works at this tier. As of October 2026 they cost from $79 (Blockstream Jade) to $249 (Trezor Safe 7), and a steel backup plate adds $20 to $50 so that the seed phrase survives a fire or flood. [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com/), free, runs the device from a computer; it can start on Sparrow's default public servers, and your own node can come later, because the hardware wallet does the security work either way.

| Strengths | Limits |
|---|---|
| Keys never leave the device | Costs the price of the device and plate |
| Every payment is checked on a screen you control | A short learning curve |
| Malware on the computer cannot sign anything | One device and one seed phrase are still a single point of failure |

To set it up:

1. Buy the device from the manufacturer's own store, not a marketplace, because tampered devices are sold.
2. Follow the [hardware wallet setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/).
3. Copy the seed phrase onto the metal plate.
4. Test the backup with [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/).
5. Run the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/) before moving a serious amount.

## What is the enhanced setup, for $10,000 to $100,000?

The enhanced setup is the standard setup plus three things: a seed made from your own dice rolls, a passphrase, and your own node. At this amount the work pays for itself in privacy and in a second secret protecting the seed phrase.

The seed comes from [dice rolls](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) rather than the device's random number generator alone; the [2026 Coldcard incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) showed what trusting a device's randomness can cost. A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/), sometimes called the "25th word", makes the seed phrase a two-part secret: whoever finds the words still cannot spend without the passphrase, which is stored separately. Your [own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), on a small dedicated computer (about $100 to $300 with a disk), answers your wallet's questions instead of a public server that could log them. And [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) lets you choose which coins each payment spends.

A device with a camera for QR codes, such as the Jade Plus ($149), suits this tier; any recommended device works.

| Strengths | Limits |
|---|---|
| Two separate secrets protect the keys | The passphrase is a second thing you can lose |
| Wallet queries go to your own node | The node is hardware you have to keep running |
| You check every rule of the network yourself | Coin control takes time to learn |

To set it up:

1. Complete the standard setup first, if you have not.
2. Make the seed with the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/).
3. Add a passphrase with the [passphrase guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/).
4. Set up a node with the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) and connect Sparrow to it.
5. Learn [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/), and read [why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) for the threats this setup is built against.

## What is the maximum setup, for over $100,000?

The maximum setup is multisig: a wallet that needs several independent keys to spend, typically any two of three (2-of-3), or three of five for larger holdings. It suits large amounts, public figures, anyone worried about their government and families planning to pass bitcoin on.

The parts are hardware wallets from different manufacturers, so one vendor's flaw cannot take everything; a metal backup of each seed phrase and copies of the wallet descriptor, the file that tells software how the multisig is built; and all of it spread across locations, so one fire, flood or burglary cannot reach every key. The node runs over [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/), the most sensitive signing happens on an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/), and [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) is part of the routine if privacy is part of your threat model. Expect $250 to $750 for the devices, $100 to $200 for backups and $100 to $300 for the node. Multisig transactions are larger on chain, so fees are somewhat higher.

| Strengths | Limits |
|---|---|
| A stolen device does not lose the coins | Every spend needs coordination between keys |
| A lost backup does not lose the coins | Recovery needs the descriptor as well as the seed phrases |
| One manufacturer's flaw does not lose the coins | You have to understand it, not only follow a checklist |

To set it up:

1. Be fully comfortable with the standard setup first; an advanced setup you do not understand is a risk.
2. Read [multisig explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/), then follow the [Sparrow multisig setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/sparrow-setup/).
3. Plan where each key and backup will live before you fund the wallet.
4. Consider an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) for signing and [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) for privacy.

Collaborative custody services such as Unchained and Casa hold one key of a multisig for you and help with recovery. Sharing the work with a professional this way is a legitimate choice, not a failure.

## Which hardware wallet should you buy?

For a first device, the BitBox02 Nova (Bitcoin-only edition) or the Trezor Safe 5 is the easiest to use safely. For the strongest practical security, a Jade Plus with a [dice-generated seed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/). To verify as much as possible yourself, the Trezor Safe 7 or a [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/) you build. Coldcard is not on the list: after the [2026 entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) we no longer recommend it for new purchases. The [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) has prices, features and the reasoning for each device, and [hardware wallets explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/) covers how the category works.

## Common questions

### Can you use more than one setup at once?

Yes, and many people do. A common pattern is a phone wallet for spending money and a hardware wallet for savings, which gives convenience where it is needed and security where it matters.

### Should you wait for a better wallet to come out?

No. Secure your bitcoin now with the best setup you can run today. Waiting leaves the coins exposed to exchange risk, and moving to a newer device later only takes a transaction to a fresh wallet.

### Is a wallet you have heard of safe?

The devices on the [comparison page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) are reputable, with the warnings it states. Among them, what decides your safety is whether you set the device up correctly and tested the backup, not which brand you chose.

### What about paper wallets?

We do not recommend them. A paper wallet, a single private key printed on paper, was an early answer to self-custody, but it adds more ways to fail than it removes: the key is exposed on the computer that generates it, spending part of the balance sends the change to an address the paper does not cover, and paper degrades. Hardware wallets have replaced them for every practical purpose.


---

# Assess Your Threat Model

> Determine what level of Bitcoin security you actually need. Match your setup to your real risks. Not everyone needs maximum security, but some people do.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A threat model is your answer to three questions: what you are protecting, who you are protecting it from, and how much effort you will put into the defence. For most people the answer is a hardware wallet with a tested backup, because the attackers they face are opportunistic: phishing, malware and failing exchanges. A passphrase and your own node suit someone who could be singled out; multisig with keys in separate places suits life-changing amounts and anyone who could face physical threats. Too little security loses bitcoin to an attacker, and too much loses it to a setup its owner cannot recover.

## What is a threat model?

A threat model is a short, honest assessment of what you hold, who might want it and what you are willing to do to keep it. The three answers decide the setup:

1. What you are protecting: how much bitcoin you hold now and expect to hold, and how much your privacy matters.
2. Who you are protecting it from: anyone from a phishing campaign sent to millions of addresses to someone who has decided they want your coins in particular.
3. What you will do about it: the time, money and ongoing attention you can give the setup.

When an answer changes, the model changes. Someone holding a few hundred dollars who tells nobody needs a very different setup from someone holding a large share of their net worth who posts about bitcoin under their own name.

## What kinds of attacker are there?

Most readers fit one of four levels. The table is the summary; each level is explained below it.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Level | Attacker | Typical defence |
|-------|----------|-----------------|
| 1. Opportunistic | Phishing, malware, exchange hacks | Hardware wallet and a tested backup |
| 2. Targeted, online | Someone who knows you hold bitcoin and will spend effort on you | Add a passphrase, your own node, coin control and silence about your holdings |
| 3. Physical | Criminals willing to use force or threats | Multisig with keys in separate places |
| 4. State-level | Governments and intelligence agencies | Beyond what a website can cover |

</div>

### Level 1: opportunistic attackers

An opportunistic attacker is not after you in particular. They run automated phishing campaigns, spread malware across millions of machines and pick through the wreckage of exchange hacks, and they move on as soon as a target takes effort.

The defence is a hardware wallet, which keeps keys away from the malware on your computer; a tested backup, which covers a lost or broken device; keeping bitcoin off exchanges; and never typing, pasting or photographing the seed phrase. Most bitcoin holders are at this level, and a hardware wallet with a tested backup is most of what they need.

### Level 2: targeted online attackers

A targeted attacker knows you hold bitcoin and has decided you are worth hours or days of effort. They research you, try to talk your phone carrier into moving your number to their SIM card (a SIM swap) so they can take over your accounts, and send phishing messages built from real details of your life.

The defence adds discipline to the level 1 setup:

- A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) on top of the seed phrase, so that a found or photographed seed phrase is not enough to spend.
- Your [own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), so balance checks and transactions do not pass through third-party servers that can tie your addresses to your IP address.
- [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) and coin control, so your transaction history does not map out your holdings.
- Not discussing your holdings. Every person who knows what you own is a possible leak.

### Level 3: physical threats

A physical attacker is willing to come to your door: a burglar who guessed right, someone tipped off by a person you trusted, or the "five-dollar wrench attack", in which perfect cryptography meets a threat of violence. The attacker does not need to hack anything, only to make you unlock the wallet yourself.

The defence is a setup that even you cannot empty in one sitting under duress. [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) does this because spending needs several keys, and keys stored in separate places cannot all be taken in one raid on your home. Backups spread across locations make it harder still. A small decoy wallet with a plausible balance, protected by a different passphrase, gives you something to hand over. At this level, not being publicly associated with bitcoin is essential, because public association is how attackers choose their targets.

### Level 4: state-level threats

A state-level attacker has legal power to compel you, surveillance resources to watch you and the means to seize any device you own. In some jurisdictions refusing to disclose a passphrase is itself a crime. The right defence depends on which state, under which laws and for what reason, so it is beyond what this site, or any static document, can responsibly cover. If this is your threat model, you need legal counsel and operational security advice from people who do this professionally.

## How much security does your amount need?

The amount at stake is the starting point, and the other factors below refine it. Plan for what the holdings may become, not only what they are today: a setup that suits a small amount should still make sense if it grows.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Amount | What we recommend |
|--------|--------------------|
| Under $1,000 | A software wallet is acceptable while you learn |
| $1,000 to $10,000 | A hardware wallet |
| $10,000 to $100,000 | A hardware wallet, with a passphrase |
| $100,000 to $1,000,000 | Multisig, strongly recommended |
| Over $1,000,000 | Multisig, and consider a professional security review |

</div>

Three other factors move you up or down a row:

| Factor | Lower risk | Higher risk |
|---|---|---|
| Who knows you hold bitcoin | Nobody | You post about it publicly, or you are a public figure |
| Where you live | A stable country with working property rights | Capital controls, an authoritarian government or an active conflict |
| Your technical comfort | Comfortable restoring a wallet from scratch | Unsure how your own backup works |

The last factor caps everything else: do not run security you do not understand. A setup you cannot recover is a risk, not a protection.

## Which setup fits your profile?

Four profiles cover most readers, each loosely matching one of the threat levels. Costs are hardware only, as of October 2026.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Profile | Fits | Core setup | Cost | Complexity |
|---------|------|------------|----------------|------------|
| A. Casual holder | Small amounts, learning, low profile | Hardware wallet and a tested backup | About $80 to $170 | Low |
| B. Serious holder | Savings you would miss, privacy matters | Hardware wallet, dice-generated seed, passphrase, own node | $200 to $400 | Medium |
| C. High-value holder | Significant holdings, some public exposure | 2-of-3 multisig across vendors and locations, node over Tor | $500 to $1,000 or more | High |
| D. Maximum security | Very large holdings, public figures, hostile jurisdictions | 3-of-5 multisig, air-gapped signing, legal and estate planning | $2,000 or more, plus professional services | Very high |

</div>

### Profile A: casual holder

Profile A fits someone holding a small amount, still learning and not publicly linked to bitcoin. The setup is one hardware wallet (a Trezor, BitBox02 or Jade is fine at this level; see the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/)), the seed phrase written on paper or stamped in metal, and one test restore to prove the backup works. A passphrase is optional here and often adds more risk of locking yourself out than it removes; your own node is useful but not required. It takes an afternoon.

### Profile B: serious holder

Profile B fits someone holding savings they would be upset to lose, who cares about privacy and whose friends may know they are interested in bitcoin. The setup is a bitcoin-only hardware wallet such as the BitBox02 Nova (Bitcoin-only edition) or the Jade Plus; a seed made with [your own dice rolls](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) rather than the device's random number generator alone, which the [2026 Coldcard incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) showed is worth doing; a metal backup, because paper is too fragile for this amount; a [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/); your [own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/); and coin control on every spend. CoinJoin is optional. Plan on a weekend of careful work.

### Profile C: high-value holder

Profile C fits someone with significant holdings who is at least partly known to hold bitcoin and has reason to expect targeted attacks. The setup is a 2-of-3 [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) built from hardware wallets by different manufacturers, so that one vendor's flaw cannot take everything, with the keys in different places so that one fire or burglary cannot reach them all. Metal backups are stored separately, the node runs over [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/), very few people know what you hold, and [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) is part of the setup rather than an extra. Expect it to take real, ongoing commitment.

### Profile D: maximum security

Profile D fits very large holdings, public figures and anyone in a hostile jurisdiction. The setup moves to a 3-of-5 multisig, signs on air-gapped devices, considers open-source firmware such as [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) for the signing computers, and spreads keys across jurisdictions so that no single legal system can reach them all. A professional security review is worth paying for, and [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) is essential. Collaborative custody services such as Unchained and Casa, which hold one key of a multisig for you, are worth considering for part of the holdings.

## What mistakes do people make at this stage?

| Mistake | What it looks like | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Over-engineering a small amount | A 3-of-5 multisig across three countries for $500 of bitcoin | Start simple and add layers as the holdings grow; every moving part is something that can fail |
| Under-engineering a large amount | $500,000 on one hardware wallet with the seed phrase in a desk drawer | Multisig with keys in separate places; at this amount it is no longer optional |
| Security theatre | Faraday bags and exotic hardware, with the seed phrase saved to iCloud | Get the basics right first, because the basics are what attackers go after |
| Complexity beyond competence | A multisig its owner could not restore from scratch | Rehearse a full recovery on paper before funding the setup |

The last mistake matters most. The day you need to recover is likely to be stressful and rushed, so if you cannot walk through a recovery now, the setup is a risk rather than a protection.

## When should you reassess your setup?

Reassess when your holdings grow significantly, when more people learn what you hold, when your country's situation changes, when your own skills grow, and after any security incident or close call. Most people move along the same path in the same order: a hardware wallet first, then a passphrase once the device is familiar, then their own node, then multisig when the amount justifies it, with privacy measures added along the way. Most people should not go all the way to the end of it.

To act on this page:

1. Pick the profile that matches your situation today, not the one that sounds most impressive.
2. Compare your current setup with that profile and note every gap.
3. Close the gaps one at a time, cheapest and highest-impact first, testing each change end to end before the next.
4. Put a reminder in your calendar to reassess in six months.


---

# Bitcoin Keys: Private Keys, Seeds, Derivation Paths

> Learn how Bitcoin keys work: private keys, seed phrases (BIP39), extended keys (xpub/xprv), and derivation paths. The foundation of Bitcoin ownership.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Owning bitcoin means controlling the private keys that can spend it: the network does not know your name, only whether a transaction is signed by the right key. In a modern wallet every key comes from one source, the seed phrase, which is turned into a master key and then, along a derivation path, into as many keys and addresses as the wallet needs. That is why the 12 or 24 words restore everything, why one backup covers unlimited addresses, and why anyone who sees them can take everything.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The key hierarchy: entropy becomes a 24-word BIP39 seed phrase, which derives the master private key, which the derivation path expands into unlimited child keys and addresses; the seed at the root restores everything](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/keys/key-hierarchy.svg)

</div>

## What does this section cover?

The pages build from the simplest idea to the most technical; read them in order, or go straight to the one you need.

| Page | What it explains |
|---|---|
| [Private keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/intro/) | The random number that controls bitcoin, and how public keys and addresses come from it |
| [Seed phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/) | How that randomness becomes 12 or 24 words under the BIP39 standard, and why their order matters |
| [Extended private keys (xprv)](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xprv/) | How one master key produces every key in the wallet |
| [Extended public keys (xpub)](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub/) | Watch-only wallets: seeing every address and balance without being able to spend |
| [Derivation paths](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path/) | The route from the master key to a particular address, and why it matters at recovery |
| [Passphrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) | An optional extra secret that turns the same seed phrase into a different wallet |
| [Seed generation with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) | Making the seed's randomness yourself, step by step |
| [Number systems](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/number-systems/) | Binary, decimal and hexadecimal, for the dice guide's arithmetic |

## Which principles matter most?

- **Keys are everything.** Your bitcoin is recorded on the blockchain; the private key is the only proof that you may move it. Without the key, there is no bitcoin.
- **The seed phrase is the key.** It is not a backup of your key but the same secret in another form: anyone who has it controls the bitcoin.
- **One seed, many keys.** A single seed phrase can produce billions of addresses, and the wallet uses a new one for each payment automatically.
- **Public is not harmless.** An extended public key (xpub) cannot spend, but it reveals every address and the whole transaction history of the account.

## How deep do you need to go?

| If you are | You need to know |
|---|---|
| Using a wallet | That the seed phrase is the bitcoin, that it restores the wallet anywhere, and how to back it up |
| Doing serious self-custody | Derivation paths (they matter at recovery), xpub versus xprv, and whether a passphrase suits you |
| Verifying everything yourself | How randomness affects security, how keys are derived, and how to generate and check a seed independently |


---

# Understanding Bitcoin Private Keys

> Learn what Bitcoin private keys are, how they work, and why they're essential for controlling your Bitcoin. The foundation of self-custody explained.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/intro/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A Bitcoin private key is a randomly chosen 256-bit number that authorises spending the bitcoin sent to the addresses derived from it. Whoever knows the number can spend those coins, and nobody who lacks it can, so keeping the private key secret and backed up is what self-custody consists of. Modern wallets do not make you handle private keys directly: they derive them all from a [seed phrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/), which is the thing you actually write down.

## How does a private key relate to a public key and an address?

| | What it is | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
| Private key | A secret number between 1 and about 1.16 × 10<sup>77</sup> | Nobody but you, ever |
| Public key | A point on the secp256k1 elliptic curve, computed from the private key | Revealed when you spend (or, for Taproot addresses, already part of the address) |
| Address | A short encoding of the public key, or of its hash, that people send bitcoin to | Anyone you give it to |

Each step goes one way only. Computing the public key from the private key, and the address from the public key, is quick; going backwards is not feasible with any known method, which is why an address and even a public key can be shared without exposing the private key.

## What does a private key do?

When you spend, your wallet uses the private key to sign the transaction: it produces a digital signature that anyone can check against the public key, but that only the holder of the private key could have made. Nodes accept the transaction only if the signature is valid. Nothing else (no account name, password or identity) is involved.

## Why is storing a private key hard?

A private key must be secret and must also survive. Stored on an online device, it can be copied by malware; stored offline, it can be lost, burned or misread. A raw key is also a 64-character hexadecimal string that is easy to copy wrongly by hand.

[Seed phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/) solve the copying problem: 12 or 24 words from a fixed list, with a built-in checksum, that regenerate every private key in the wallet. Hardware wallets solve the online problem by keeping the keys on a device that never exposes them. Losing the private keys, or the seed phrase they come from, loses the bitcoin; exposing them lets anyone take it.


---

# Bitcoin Seed Phrases Explained (BIP39)

> Understand how BIP39 seed phrases work: converting private keys to memorable words. Learn the 2048-word list and how seeds protect your Bitcoin.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A seed phrase is a list of 12 or 24 ordinary words that encodes every private key in your Bitcoin wallet, and it is the only thing you need to restore that wallet on any device, from any manufacturer, years later. The words come from a fixed list of 2048 defined by the BIP39 standard; they encode 128 or 256 bits of randomness plus a short checksum, and the wallet turns them into its master key. Whoever has the words controls the bitcoin, and whoever loses them (along with the device) loses it.

## What does a seed phrase look like?

A seed phrase (also called a recovery phrase or mnemonic) looks like this:

```text
reward symptom rude hamster wide weekend camera reward
pride roof weather keep ritual ocean rib wing
board potato whisper weasel chunk rival obvious clean
```

Each word stands for a number from 0 to 2047, its position in the [BIP39 word list](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/english.txt). This example is the one built step by step in the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/); never use a seed phrase you have seen published anywhere.

**Warning: The seed phrase is the bitcoin**
Anyone who sees these words can take everything. Never photograph them, type them into a computer or phone (anything but your hardware wallet), or store them digitally.

## Why use words instead of numbers?

The randomness behind a 24-word seed is 256 bits, plus 8 bits of checksum:

```text
101110001011101110010010111100111011010001011111101010111111001...
(264 bits in all)
```

Nobody can copy that reliably by hand, and even as 24 numbers between 0 and 2047 it is easy to get a digit wrong. Words are easier to write and read back accurately, and the BIP39 list was chosen to make mistakes visible: every word is identified by its first four letters, and words that look or sound alike were left out, so "reword" written for "reward" stands out.

## How is a seed phrase made, and how does it restore a wallet?

To create one, the wallet:

1. Generates random bits: 128 for 12 words, 256 for 24. This is the step you cannot watch, and when a Coldcard firmware bug quietly weakened it, [attackers brute-forced $116 million of seeds in 2026](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/). Generating the bits yourself [with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) removes that trust.
2. Appends a checksum: the first 4 bits (12 words) or 8 bits (24 words) of the SHA-256 hash of those random bits.
3. Splits the result into 11-bit chunks, 12 or 24 of them.
4. Looks up each chunk, a number from 0 to 2047, in the word list.

To restore, a wallet turns each word back into its number, checks the checksum, and then runs the phrase (with any [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/)) through PBKDF2 to produce the 512-bit seed that every key in the wallet is derived from. That is why word order matters: the same words in a different order encode a different number, which usually fails the checksum and otherwise opens a different, empty wallet.

![Lines 1470 to 1482 of the BIP39 English word list on GitHub, from "response" to "rice", with "reward" on line 1478](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/basics/words.webp)

## What does this mean in practice?

- **The seed phrase is the bitcoin.** The hardware wallet, the app and the computer can all be replaced. If your house burns down but your seed phrase is stored elsewhere, you have lost nothing.
- **It is not a password.** There is no "forgot my seed phrase" link and no company that can recover it. Complete control comes with complete responsibility.
- **It works across wallets.** Because BIP39 is a standard, the same seed phrase restores in almost any Bitcoin wallet (Trezor, BitBox, Jade, Sparrow and many others), so you are not locked into one vendor. A few products do not use BIP39 seed phrases, notably Electrum's own seed format and Bitkey, which shows no seed phrase at all.

## What does the checksum catch?

The last word is not fully random: part of it is the checksum, computed from the rest of the phrase. When you restore, a wallet that finds the checksum wrong tells you the phrase is invalid instead of opening an empty wallet. It catches most mistakes but not all: a wrong word still passes the 8-bit checksum of a 24-word phrase about 1 time in 256, and the 4-bit checksum of a 12-word phrase about 1 time in 16. That is why a backup is [tested by restoring it](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/), not just by checking it is accepted.

## How do bits become words, exactly?

This section shows the conversion for the example above. It is not needed to use bitcoin safely.

The 256 random bits plus 8 checksum bits make 264 bits, split into 24 chunks of 11:

```text
10111000101 11011100100 10111100111 01101000101 ...
```

Each 11-bit chunk is a number from 0 to 2047:

```text
1477, 1764, 1511, 837, 2005, 1992, 261, 1477, ...
```

and each number is a position in the word list, counting from 0:

| Number | Word |
|---------|------|
| 1477 | reward |
| 1764 | symptom |
| 1511 | rude |
| 837 | hamster |

The word list on GitHub numbers its lines from 1, so position 1477 is on line 1478. Because the list is alphabetical, words near "abandon" stand for small numbers and words near "zoo" for large ones. The [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) does the whole conversion by hand, from rolls to the 24th word.


---

# Extended Private Key (XPRV)

> What a Bitcoin extended private key (xprv) is, why it can spend from every address in a wallet, how to keep it offline, and what its prefix tells you.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xprv/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

An extended private key, or xprv, is a private key paired with a 32-byte chain code, which together can generate an unlimited tree of child private keys. The master xprv of a wallet is computed from the BIP39 seed (the seed phrase plus any passphrase), and every private key and address in the wallet descends from it, so whoever holds an xprv can spend from every address beneath it. It never needs to leave a hardware wallet, and it should not.

## How is the extended private key made?

Under BIP32, the wallet runs the 512-bit BIP39 seed through HMAC-SHA512 with the fixed key "Bitcoin seed". The first half of the result is the master private key and the second half is the chain code. Because a passphrase changes the BIP39 seed, it also changes the master xprv and every key below it; so does choosing a different [derivation path](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path/). Use your wallet's default path, and write down which one it is.

## What does the extended private key control?

From the master xprv, the wallet derives a child key for each step of the derivation path, ending in the account's extended private key and then in individual keys:

1. The account xprv produces individual private keys, one per address.
2. Each private key produces a public key.
3. Each public key produces an address.

The xprv also produces the matching [extended public key (xpub)](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub/), which can generate all the same addresses but cannot spend.

## Can one leaked private key expose the others?

Sometimes, and this is the subtle part. With ordinary (non-hardened) derivation, a single child private key combined with the parent's xpub is enough to compute the parent xprv, and with it every other key in that account. That is why the account levels of a derivation path use hardened derivation (the `'` in `m/84'/0'/0'`), which breaks that link, and why you should never export or share a single private key from an HD wallet whose xpub anyone else might have. A public key, on its own, reveals no private key at all.

## What does an xprv look like?

```text
xprv9yVYaFXM2uUDeaj3STkiHS8svtqoASkVZ8hdTYuBdgVQGKjr76ks922e4r6826YvdQtQdu71ZA2qK8fYE85jXvTPdBFwgQ2d8rk7hhXV5wu
```

[Ian Coleman's BIP39 tool](https://iancoleman.io/bip39/) shows the xprv and xpub for a seed phrase, which makes it useful for learning with a made-up test phrase. Never type a real seed phrase into it, or into any page, on a computer that is or has been online.

## What do the prefixes mean?

The first four letters record which kind of addresses the key was meant for. They come from the SLIP-132 convention, which wallets increasingly replace with [output descriptors](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/#the-wallet-descriptor) that state the script type explicitly.

| Prefix | Address type | Addresses start with |
|---|---|---|
| `xprv` | Legacy (BIP44), and also used for Taproot (BIP86) | `1`, or `bc1p` for Taproot |
| `yprv` | Nested segwit (BIP49) | `3` |
| `zprv` | Native segwit (BIP84) | `bc1q` |
| `Yprv`, `Zprv` | Multisig, nested or native segwit | `3`, `bc1q` |
| `tprv` | Any type, on testnet | Testnet addresses |


---

# Extended Public Key (XPUB)

> What a Bitcoin extended public key (xpub) is: it lets a watch-only wallet see every address and balance without spending, so it still needs protecting.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

An extended public key, or xpub, is the public counterpart of an extended private key: it generates every address in an account, in the same order, but cannot sign transactions. A wallet loaded with only the xpub shows the same addresses, balance and history as the real wallet and can produce new receive addresses, but cannot spend. That makes it safe for an online computer, and also sensitive: anyone with your xpub can see everything the account has ever done.

## What is a watch-only wallet?

A watch-only wallet is a wallet loaded with an xpub instead of private keys. You can run one on an everyday computer or phone to check your balance and generate receive addresses, while the private keys stay on a hardware wallet. Sparrow uses exactly this arrangement: it holds your hardware wallet's xpub and asks the device to sign.

| | Wallet from the xprv | Wallet from the xpub |
|---|---|---|
| Shows every address, in order | Yes | Yes |
| Shows balance and history | Yes | Yes |
| Generates new receive addresses | Yes | Yes |
| Can spend | Yes | No |

## Why should you keep your xpub private?

Anyone who has your xpub can see every address in the account, your current balance, your full transaction history and every future transaction. It is like handing someone your bank statements: they cannot take your money, but they know how much you have and where it goes. Share individual receive addresses, not the xpub, unless you are deliberately setting up a watch-only wallet or a multisig with someone you trust.

It also matters for safety. With ordinary (non-hardened) derivation, an xpub plus any single private key from the same account is enough to compute every private key in it; see [extended private keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xprv/#can-one-leaked-private-key-expose-the-others).

## What does an xpub look like?

```text
xpub6CUtym4EsH2Ws4oWYVHiea5cUvgHZuULvMdEFwJoC22P984zee57gpM7v9AhiLh3mVS4Ai5YTYxGibMUpZpdmpkrVAGjT9ydvurTtFm5Azy
```

The prefix records the intended address type:

| Prefix | Address type | Addresses start with |
|---|---|---|
| `xpub` | Legacy (BIP44), and also used for Taproot (BIP86) | `1`, or `bc1p` for Taproot |
| `ypub` | Nested segwit (BIP49) | `3` |
| `zpub` | Native segwit (BIP84) | `bc1q` |
| `Ypub`, `Zpub` | Multisig, nested or native segwit | `3`, `bc1q` |
| `tpub` | Any type, on testnet | Testnet addresses |

Newer wallets increasingly show an output descriptor instead, which wraps the xpub with the script type and derivation path so that nothing has to be inferred from the prefix.


---

# Derivation Path

> What a Bitcoin derivation path such as m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 means, how BIP32 grows a tree of keys from one seed, and which path each address type uses.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A derivation path is the route a wallet follows from its master key to a particular private key and address, written like `m/84'/0'/0'/0/0`. The same seed phrase gives different addresses on different paths, so restoring a wallet on the wrong path shows an empty wallet even though the funds are safe. Most single-signature wallets today use `m/84'/0'/0'` (native segwit, addresses starting `bc1q`); write down the path your wallet uses next to your backup.

## What is an HD wallet?

A hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet is one whose keys all descend from a single seed in a tree, as defined by the BIP32 standard. Every branch of the tree can produce new key pairs, so backing up the seed phrase once backs up every key the wallet will ever use. The derivation path names one branch of that tree.

## What does each part of a path mean?

```text
m / 84' / 0' / 0' / 0 / 0
```

| Part | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `m` | Master | The master key, made from the seed phrase (and any passphrase) |
| `84'` | Purpose | Which standard, and so which address type: 44 legacy, 49 nested segwit, 84 native segwit, 86 Taproot |
| `0'` | Coin type | 0 for bitcoin; testnet uses 1 |
| `0'` | Account | Separate accounts from one seed, each with its own addresses |
| `0` | Change | 0 for receive addresses, 1 for change addresses |
| `0` | Index | The address number: 0, 1, 2 and so on |

The apostrophe marks a hardened level. Hardened derivation means a leaked child private key cannot be combined with the parent's extended public key to recover the parent's keys, which is why the purpose, coin and account levels are hardened.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Anatomy of the derivation path m/44'/0'/0'/0/0: master seed, purpose, coin type where 0 means Bitcoin, account number, change flag where 0 is external and 1 is change, and the address index](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/keys/derivation-path-anatomy.svg)

</div>

## Which path does each address type use?

| Standard | Path (first receive address) | Address type | Example address |
|---|---|---|---|
| BIP44 | `m/44'/0'/0'/0/0` | Legacy (P2PKH) | `137oszRjc8tdUVWr5nSp6fzSND938PStMZ` |
| BIP49 | `m/49'/0'/0'/0/0` | Nested segwit (P2SH-P2WPKH) | `33S43b6qmVHVTjwp75M7XoTTPEvKVh8zqH` |
| BIP84 | `m/84'/0'/0'/0/0` | Native segwit (P2WPKH) | `bc1q6khgephuq2hyvrn49zrvsxztmtjg4ze7sxkpp4` |
| BIP86 | `m/86'/0'/0'/0/0` | Taproot (P2TR) | `bc1ps3yjzpnxeg9yx43f9zmrl9njhvlwh4pm5peuu5ucqqp7f4362cvqeesncf` |
| BIP48 | `m/48'/0'/0'/2'` | Multisig, native segwit (each key's path) | `bc1q...` (longer, script hash) |

BIP44 was written for wallets holding many coins and gives legacy addresses on bitcoin. BIP49 wraps segwit inside an older script type for compatibility. BIP84 native segwit is the common default and has lower fees than either. BIP86 Taproot uses Schnorr signatures and makes simple and complex spending conditions look alike on chain. BIP48 is the convention most wallets use for each key of a multisig. The [address types reference](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/address-types/) compares the address formats themselves.

## What if a restored wallet shows no balance?

The usual cause is a different path or script type from the original wallet, not lost funds. Check which address type your old wallet used (the first characters of its addresses tell you, as in the table above), set the restoring wallet to the same one, and look again. Sparrow and most hardware wallet apps let you choose the script type when importing.


---

# Bitcoin Passphrase (25th Word): Diceware Generation

> What a Bitcoin passphrase (the 25th word) is, when to use one, and how to make a strong one with dice and the EFF word list, then test and back it up.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A BIP39 passphrase is an extra secret, chosen by you, that is combined with your seed phrase to produce a different wallet. The seed phrase alone opens one wallet; the seed phrase plus the passphrase opens another, so someone who finds your 24 words but not the passphrase finds only the first. It is called the "25th word", but it is not a word from the BIP39 list: it can be any text, and the strongest kind is six words chosen with dice from the EFF word list. A passphrase also adds a way to lose everything, because it cannot be recovered and a single wrong character opens an empty wallet.

Time: 30 minutes. Cost: $5-10 (casino dice) or $0 (use any dice). Level: Beginner. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: 5 six-sided dice, pen and paper.

## How does a passphrase change the wallet?

BIP39 turns your seed phrase into the binary seed every key comes from by running PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 for 2048 rounds, with the seed phrase as the password and the text `mnemonic` followed by your passphrase as the salt. Without a passphrase the salt is just `mnemonic`.
