5. Move the rest, largest amounts last, using your own node if you have one. Don't consolidate everything into one giant transaction if privacy matters to you. See [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/).
6. Keep the old backup until the migration is confirmed and settled. An emptied wallet's seed can be destroyed later; a destroyed seed with funds still on it cannot.

If the amounts at stake are significant, consider landing the funds in a [multisig setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) rather than another single-signature wallet. This incident is the strongest argument for it to date.

## What does the incident teach?

**Entropy is a trust point.** Every "your keys are generated securely inside the device" claim rests on an RNG you cannot see working. It failed silently here for five years, on a device marketed to and trusted by the most security-conscious users in Bitcoin. The fix is not a better brand; it's [supplying entropy yourself](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and verifying what you can.

**Air-gap protects against exfiltration, not weak keys.** An air gap stops malware from reaching your device and your key from leaking out. It does nothing if the key was predictable the moment it was born. Victims' devices worked exactly as designed, offline, in safes, while their funds were swept remotely.

**Open source is necessary, not sufficient.** The bug sat in public code for over five years. What matters alongside source availability: reproducible builds, independent review of what the build *actually links*, how a vendor treats researcher warnings, and how it responds when things go wrong.

**Defense in depth works.** Every layer that operated independently of the broken RNG (dice entropy, passphrases, multisig) held. Nobody who used all three lost anything. Layer your security so that one silent failure is never enough.

For the fairness ledger: Coinkite shipped fixes within a day of the exploit, published a detailed advisory, and has since had independent reviewers validate the fixed RNG path. That's a competent crisis response, to a crisis a heeded warning could have prevented fourteen months earlier. Whether you continue using the brand is your call; our current device guidance is in the [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/).

## Common questions

### What was the 2026 Coldcard entropy incident?

From firmware 4.0.1 in March 2021, a build and link error made Coldcard devices generate seed phrases with Yasmarang, a software pseudo-random generator, instead of the hardware random number generator. The generator was seeded from almost nothing: a chip ID recoverable from the USB serial number, a millisecond counter, and a clock register that read zero on Mk2 and Mk3 devices. Attackers began draining wallets on 30 July 2026 and took roughly 1,816 BTC (about $116 million) from more than 5,200 addresses. The bug went undetected for 1,978 days.

### Is your Coldcard wallet affected by the entropy bug?

It depends on how and when the seed was created, not on the firmware the device runs today. At critical risk: seeds generated on a Mk2 or Mk3 with firmware 4.0.1 to 4.1.9. At risk: seeds generated on a Mk4 or Mk5 before 5.6.0, or a Q before 1.5.0Q. Not affected: seeds generated with 50 or more dice rolls, seeds imported from elsewhere, seeds generated before March 2021 or on fixed firmware, and TAPSIGNER, SATSCARD and OPENDIME devices.

### Does a BIP39 passphrase protect you from the Coldcard bug?

It helped, but it is not a pass. Wallets with a strong, unique passphrase were not drained, because the attacker would have to brute-force the passphrase on top of the recovered seed. The foundation is still a weak seed, so move to a newly generated one anyway: the passphrase bought time, not safety.

### Were Coldcard signatures affected, or only seed generation?

Only seed generation. Coldcard signs with deterministic nonces as specified in RFC 6979, so transactions signed by an affected device leaked nothing about the private key. The flaw lived entirely in the code that created the seed.

## Sources

- [Coinkite security advisory](https://blog.coinkite.com/coldcard-mk3-seed-generation-warning/): affected versions and required actions
- [Coinkite technical backgrounder](https://blog.coinkite.com/entropy-technical-backgrounder/): the vendor's own root-cause analysis
- [Wizardsardine: technical autopsy of an entropy failure](https://wizardsardine.com/blog/coldcard-vuln-deep-dive/): independent analysis, entropy math
- [TRM Labs: inside the $116M Coldcard hack](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/the-largest-hardware-wallet-exploit-of-2026-inside-the-usd-116-million-coldcard-hack): on-chain analysis of the attack waves

Figures on this page are as of mid-August 2026 and may be revised as investigations continue.


---

# Bitcoin Multisig: Complete Guide

> Understand and set up a Bitcoin multisig wallet. Concepts, 2-of-3 configurations, hardware devices, and a full step-by-step setup guide.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A **multisig** (multi-signature) wallet is a bitcoin wallet that needs more than one key to spend, written as M-of-N: M signatures out of N keys. For an individual the usual choice is 2-of-3, where any two of three keys can move the funds, so losing one key does not lose your bitcoin and stealing one key does not steal it. Each key lives on a separate hardware wallet, ideally from a different manufacturer and in a different place. The cost is complexity: besides the seed phrases you must back up the wallet descriptor, and recovery has to be rehearsed before the wallet holds anything significant.

Time: 2-3 hours. Cost: $200-450 (3 hardware wallets) + $30-60 (metal seed backups). Level: Intermediate to advanced. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

An ordinary wallet has a single point of failure: one seed phrase controls everything, so if it is stolen or lost, so is the bitcoin. Multisig removes that by spreading control across several keys, none of which can spend alone.

## How does M-of-N work?

N is the total number of keys in the wallet and M is the number of signatures needed to spend.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A 2-of-3 multisig: three keys exist at home, office and safe, and any two signatures spend; no single key ever can, so one key can be lost or stolen without losing the funds](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallets/multisig-quorum.svg)

</div>

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Setup | Signatures needed | Keys | Use |
|-------|----------|-------|----------|
| 2-of-3 | 2 | 3 | Individual self-custody, the most common choice |
| 3-of-5 | 3 | 5 | Very large holdings, organisations, families |
| 2-of-2 | 2 | 2 | Shared control, with no room for losing a key |
| 1-of-2 | 1 | 2 | Easy access from two places, with no theft protection |

</div>

## How is a multisig wallet created and spent from?

To create one:

1. Generate three separate seeds, usually one on each of three hardware wallets.
2. Export the extended public key (xpub) from each device.
3. Combine the three xpubs in coordinator software such as Sparrow, which creates the multisig wallet and its descriptor.
4. Register the wallet on each hardware wallet, so each device can check addresses and change itself.

To spend:

1. The coordinator creates an unsigned transaction, a PSBT (partially signed bitcoin transaction).
2. Device 1 signs it; the transaction is still incomplete.
3. Device 2 signs it; it now has the two signatures it needs.
4. The coordinator broadcasts the complete transaction.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Multisig signing flow: an unsigned PSBT goes to device 1 and device 2, each signs independently, the signatures combine into a fully signed transaction and it is broadcast; no single machine ever holds two keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallets/multisig-signing.svg)

</div>

## What does multisig protect against?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| What happens | Single-signature wallet | 2-of-3 multisig |
|----------|------------|-----------------|
| One key is stolen | Funds lost | Safe: the thief needs a second key |
| One key is lost | Funds lost for good | Safe: the other two keys still spend |
| A fire destroys one backup | Funds lost, if it was the only backup | Safe: the other keys are elsewhere |
| You are forced to hand over a key | Funds lost | Safe: one key cannot spend, and the others are not in the room |
| One hardware wallet's firmware is flawed | Funds at risk | Safe: the other vendors' keys still hold |

</div>

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Single-sig puts full control on one seed phrase, one point of failure; a 2-of-3 multisig spreads control over three keys where any two spend, so one key compromised or lost leaves the funds safe](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallets/multisig-vs-single.svg)

</div>

The last row stopped being hypothetical in July 2026. The [Coldcard entropy flaw](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) made single-signature Coldcard wallets brute-forceable and about $116 million was drained, while multisig wallets with one weak Coldcard key lost nothing, because the other vendors' keys held.

## What does multisig cost you?

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| A thief needs more than one key | More to back up and look after: several seeds plus the descriptor |
| One key can be lost without losing the funds | Larger transactions, so higher fees |
| Keys can be placed for inheritance | Spending needs two devices, so it is slower |
| Several people can be required to agree on a spend | Recovery needs the descriptor as well as the seeds |

**Danger: Multisig can lose funds if it is mismanaged**
Back up the wallet descriptor, not only the seed phrases, and test a full recovery before depositing anything significant. If you are not yet comfortable with a single-signature hardware wallet, master that first.

## When is multisig worth it?

Multisig suits significant holdings you would be devastated to lose, long-term storage you rarely spend from, business funds that need several approvals, and inheritance planning, and it assumes you have several secure places to keep keys. It is unnecessary for amounts under roughly $10,000, for spending money, and for anyone still learning basic self-custody, where the added complexity is itself a risk. [Choose your setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/choosing-your-path/) puts the threshold for recommending it at about $100,000.

## What are the parts of a multisig setup?

### Hardware wallets

Each key lives on its own hardware wallet. Use devices from different manufacturers (for example Jade Plus, Keystone 3 Pro and Trezor Safe 5) so that one vendor's flaw cannot reach the funds; the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) covers which devices suit multisig.

### Coordinator software

Coordinator software, such as [Sparrow](https://sparrowwallet.com/) or Nunchuk, holds no private keys. It creates the multisig wallet from the devices' xpubs, generates receive addresses, builds unsigned transactions and combines the signatures.

### The wallet descriptor

The **wallet descriptor** is a line of text that defines the multisig wallet: every key's xpub and fingerprint, the M-of-N rule, the script type and the derivation paths. Without it, recovering from two of the three seeds is impossible, because the third key's xpub is recorded in the descriptor and nowhere else; even with all three seeds you would need to know the threshold, script type and paths it records. Store a copy of the descriptor with each seed backup; it is not secret enough to spend with, but it does reveal your balance and history to whoever reads it.

## Which configuration should you choose?

For most individuals, 2-of-3 is the right balance: any one key can be lost or stolen without losing the funds, there are three devices and three backups to manage, and fees are lower than for larger quorums.

3-of-5 suits very large holdings, organisations and families spread across places. Two keys can be lost or stolen without losing the funds, but there are five devices to buy, five seed phrases to secure, higher fees and more coordination for every spend.

2-of-2 is not recommended for most people. It has no redundancy: lose one key and the funds are gone. Use it only for specific shared-control arrangements where both parties will always be available.

## Should you run multisig yourself or use collaborative custody?

Collaborative custody services hold one key of a multisig for you, while you hold the others, so they cannot spend without you but can help you recover or pass the funds on.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Service | Model | You hold | They hold |
|---------|-------|----------|-----------|
| Unchained | 2-of-3 | 2 keys | 1 key |
| Casa | 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 | 2 or more keys | 1 key |
| Nunchuk | Flexible | Your choice | Optional |

</div>

All three charge for their services; check their current pricing.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| | Running it yourself | Collaborative custody |
|--------|--------------|----------------------|
| Technical skill needed | High | Low to medium |
| Privacy | Full | The provider sees your balances |
| Help available | Community forums | Professional support |
| Cost | The hardware, once | A subscription |
| Recovery | Entirely on you | The provider can help |
| Suits | Technical users | Beginners and busy people |

</div>

If you are new to multisig, collaborative custody is a reasonable way to learn it. If you are technical and value privacy, run it yourself with Sparrow. If the holdings are significant and you are not technical, collaborative custody is worth what it costs.

## What mistakes do people make with multisig?

| Mistake | What goes wrong | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Not backing up the wallet descriptor | Two seed phrases survive, but without the third key's xpub the wallet cannot be rebuilt | Keep a copy of the descriptor, printed or on a file, with each seed backup |
| Storing several seeds together | One theft or fire reaches two keys | Keep each seed in a different place |
| Using one hardware wallet brand for every key | One firmware flaw affects every key | Mix manufacturers, for example Jade, Trezor and Keystone |
| Not testing recovery | The backup turns out to be incomplete when it is needed | Rehearse a full recovery with a small amount first |
| Overcomplicating it | A 5-of-7 across three continents with timelocks that nobody can operate | Start with 2-of-3 |
| Not checking addresses on the devices | Malware shows a fake address on the computer | Check every receive address on at least two hardware wallets' screens |

## What should you check before depositing?

- Each hardware wallet is from a different manufacturer (recommended).
- Each seed phrase is backed up on metal.
- The seed phrases are stored in separate places.
- The wallet descriptor is backed up, with copies in different places.
- A receive address has been checked on at least two of the hardware wallets.
- A test transaction has been received and sent.
- A full recovery from the backups has been rehearsed.
- Every hardware wallet has the multisig wallet registered.

The setup itself is covered in three guides: [hardware setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/), [the Sparrow setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/sparrow-setup/) and [backup and recovery](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/backup-recovery/).

## Common questions

### What is a Bitcoin multisig wallet?

A multisig wallet requires more than one key to spend, written as M-of-N: M signatures out of N total keys. A 2-of-3 wallet has three keys and any two can authorise a spend, so losing one key does not lose the funds and stealing one key does not steal them. Each key normally lives on a separate hardware wallet in a separate location.

### Do you need multisig for your bitcoin?

Not for everything. Multisig suits significant holdings you would be devastated to lose, long-term storage, business funds needing several approvals and inheritance planning, and it assumes you have several secure storage locations. It is unnecessary for amounts under roughly $10,000, for spending money and for anyone still learning basic self-custody, where the added complexity is itself a risk of loss.

### What multisig configuration should you use?

2-of-3 is the most popular choice for individual self-custody: it tolerates the loss of any single key while requiring an attacker to compromise two. 3-of-5 suits very large holdings and organisations. 2-of-2 gives shared control with no fault tolerance, so a single lost key is fatal. Use hardware wallets from different manufacturers so that no single vendor's mistake can reach your funds.

### Does multisig protect against a hardware wallet vulnerability?

Yes, and the 2026 Coldcard entropy incident demonstrated it. Where one key in a 2-of-3 wallet was a weak Coldcard seed, the attacker still could not spend, because a second signature was needed. This is the failure multisig exists for. The weak key should still be replaced, but the funds were never at risk.


---

# Multisig Hardware Setup

> Prepare your hardware wallets for multisig. Learn how to initialize signing devices from different manufacturers for maximum security.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Before building a multisig wallet, each of its hardware wallets is set up on its own, as if it were a single-signature wallet: three devices, ideally from three manufacturers, each with current firmware, its own PIN and its own seed made with dice. For each one you record the master fingerprint, back the seed up on metal, store that backup somewhere different from the other two, and test it. Only then do the devices go into [the Sparrow setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/sparrow-setup/).

## Step 1: Choose three devices from different makers

Step 1 picks the devices. Mixing manufacturers means one vendor's firmware flaw, like the [2026 Coldcard entropy bug](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/), reaches only one key, which a 2-of-3 wallet survives.

| Combination | Key 1 | Key 2 | Key 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Most isolated | Jade Plus (QR) | Keystone 3 Pro (QR) | Trezor Safe 5 or 7 (USB) |
| Easiest to use | Trezor Safe 5 (USB) | BitBox02 Nova (USB) | Blockstream Jade (USB or QR) |
| Lowest cost | Blockstream Jade (USB or QR) | Trezor Safe 3 (USB) | [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/), built yourself (QR) |

As of October 2026 three devices cost about $200 to $750 depending on the combination; the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) has current prices. A Coldcard you already own can still serve as one key, after you [check whether its seed needs replacing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/#am-i-affected) and make a new one with dice on fixed firmware; we just do not recommend buying one new.

## Step 2: Check each device and update its firmware

Step 2 makes sure each device is genuine and current before any seed exists on it. Buy from the manufacturer or a reseller it lists, check the packaging for tampering, run the maker's authenticity check, update to the latest firmware, and read the vendor's security advisories. A seed generated on flawed firmware stays weak after the firmware is updated, so update first.

## Step 3: Create a separate seed on each device, with dice

Step 3 gives every device its own key. Each device gets a fresh seed that has never existed anywhere else: never reuse a seed from another wallet, never put the same seed on two devices. Make each seed with dice: [by hand](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/), then restore it onto the device, or with the device's own dice entry where it has one (the Keystone 3 Pro and SeedSigner; 99 rolls for 24 words). Independent entropy for each key is what keeps one vendor's silent failure from mattering. Choose 24 words, and give each device its own PIN of at least 6 to 8 digits, with no obvious patterns and none reused between devices.

## Step 4: Record each device

Step 4 writes down what you will need to identify each key later. For every device, record:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Label | Device 1 |
| Make and model | Jade Plus |
| Master fingerprint (8 characters) | `7c8a9b2d` |
| Firmware version | As shown on the device |
| Seed length | 24 words |
| Where the device is kept | Home safe |
| Where its seed backup is kept | Bank safe deposit box |

The master fingerprint identifies the key without revealing it; Sparrow shows it when the device connects, and it appears in the wallet descriptor. Store these records separately from the seed phrases, and label each device (1, 2, 3). The [multisig record sheet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/worksheets/multisig-record/) has these fields for all three keys, plus the wallet details Sparrow gives you later.

## Step 5: Back up each seed on metal, in separate places

Step 5 makes each seed survive fire, water and time. Paper burns, gets wet, fades and gets thrown away by mistake, so stamp or engrave each seed onto a metal backup (Blockplate, Cryptosteel, Seedplate and Billfodl are common makes), read it back against the paper, and destroy the paper.

Then spread the backups out so that no single place holds two keys, and no seed is stored with its own device:

| | Device | Seed backup |
|---|---|---|
| Key 1 | Home safe | Bank safe deposit box |
| Key 2 | Home, somewhere separate from key 1 | A trusted family member's home |
| Key 3 | A different city: a second property, an office or a trusted person | A third location, such as a second deposit box |

With this layout a burglary at home reaches devices but no seed; a lost deposit box costs one seed, and the other two keys still spend.

## Step 6: Test each seed backup

Step 6 proves each backup restores its device before the multisig depends on it. For each device in turn: reset it, restore it from its metal backup, and check the master fingerprint matches your record. The [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) covers the method.

Before going on to [Sparrow](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/sparrow-setup/), check that all three devices have unique seeds backed up on metal in different places, recorded fingerprints, unique PINs, current firmware and labels.

## How do you set up each device?

The menus differ by maker. These notes cover what matters for multisig; follow the maker's own guide for the rest.

### Trezor

Connect by USB and set the device up in Trezor Suite. Trezor has no dice entry on the device as of October 2026, so choose to recover a wallet and enter the 24 words you made with dice, rather than letting it create one. Trezor PINs can be up to 50 digits. For multisig, Sparrow reads the key directly from the device over USB; no export file is needed.

### BitBox02

Connect by USB and set the wallet up in the BitBoxApp: restore the 24 words you made with dice, or follow BitBox's own diceware procedure, then set the device password. For multisig, Sparrow reads the key directly over USB and shows the fingerprint.

### Jade and Jade Plus

The Jade has no dice entry on the device: restore the 24 words you made with dice, or choose 23 words with Blockstream's dice method and let the Jade calculate the last, then choose QR mode for air-gapped use. For multisig, export the key to Sparrow by scanning the QR code the Jade displays.

### Keystone

Create the wallet on the device with a password and 24 words, using its dice roll option (firmware 1.2.6 or later). For multisig, export the extended public key from the device's multisig menu as a QR code or to a microSD card.

### Coldcard (existing owners)

Update first (Mk4 and Mk5 to 5.6.0 or later, Q to 1.5.0Q or later). Power the device from a battery pack or USB power adapter rather than a computer, set the prefix and main PIN, and create new seed words with the dice option (99 rolls), 24 words. For multisig, insert a microSD card and export the key from `Advanced/Tools`, `Export Wallet`, `Generic JSON`.


---

# Multisig in Sparrow Wallet

> Step-by-step guide to creating a 2-of-3 multisig wallet in Sparrow. Learn to configure your multisig, verify addresses, and make transactions.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/sparrow-setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A 2-of-3 multisig is created in Sparrow by making a new wallet with the Multi Signature policy, adding each of the three hardware wallets as a keystore, saving it, registering the wallet on each device, checking that every device shows the same first receive address, and backing up the wallet descriptor. Sparrow is free, works with every major hardware wallet over USB, QR codes or microSD, and holds no private keys: it coordinates, and the devices sign.

Before starting, you need [Sparrow](https://sparrowwallet.com/download/) installed (with its download signature checked), three hardware wallets [set up with their own seeds](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/) and the master fingerprint of each recorded, and ideally your own [Bitcoin node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/).

## Step 1: Connect Sparrow to a server

Step 1 decides who Sparrow asks about your wallet's addresses. Your own node keeps that private; a public server works for a first test, but it sees your addresses, so plan to move to your own.

1. Open Sparrow Wallet
2. Go to `File` → `Preferences` → `Server`
3. Choose your connection type:
   - Bitcoin Core, if you run your own node
   - Private Electrum, for your own Electrum server
   - Public Server, acceptable for testing but less private
4. Click `Test Connection` then `Close`

## Step 2: Create a new wallet

Step 2 creates the empty wallet.

1. Go to `File` → `New Wallet`
2. Enter a name, for example "Vault"
3. Click `Create Wallet`

You'll see the **Settings** screen with configuration options.

## Step 3: Set the multisig policy

Step 3 makes the wallet a 2-of-3 multisig:

1. Change `Policy Type` from Single Signature to Multi Signature.
2. Set the cosigners required (M) to 2 and the total cosigners (N) to 3.
3. Leave the script type as Native Segwit (P2WSH), the most efficient and the usual choice.

Your settings should show: `2 of 3 Multi Signature (Sorted Multi, Native Segwit)`

## Step 4: Add the first hardware wallet

Step 4 adds keystore 1. Below the settings are tabs for `Keystore 1`, `Keystore 2` and `Keystore 3`.

### USB devices (Trezor, BitBox02)

1. Click on `Keystore 1` tab
2. Click `Connected Hardware Wallet`
3. Connect your first hardware wallet via USB
4. Click `Scan...` in the dialog
5. Click your device when it appears
6. Unlock the device with your PIN
7. Click `Import Keystore`

Sparrow fills in the keystore: rename its label to identify the device (for example "Trezor, key 1"), and check that the master fingerprint matches your record. The derivation path is `m/48'/0'/0'/2'`, the usual one for each key of a native segwit multisig, and the xpub is the device's extended public key for it.

### Air-gapped devices (Jade, Keystone, SeedSigner, Coldcard)

1. Click the `Keystore 1` tab
2. Click `Airgapped Hardware Wallet`
3. Select your device type
4. Import the key from the device's microSD export file, or scan the QR code it displays
5. Rename the label to identify the device, and check the fingerprint

## Step 5: Add the second hardware wallet

Step 5 repeats step 4 on the `Keystore 2` tab with the second device, by USB or air-gapped as it requires. Label it (for example "Keystone, key 2") and check its fingerprint against your record.

## Step 6: Add the third hardware wallet

Step 6 does the same on the `Keystore 3` tab with the third device. Label it (for example "BitBox02, key 3") and check its fingerprint.

## Step 7: Apply and save

Step 7 creates the wallet. Check that the three keystores have different fingerprints and clear labels, click `Apply`, set a password for the wallet file when asked (optional, but recommended), and save.

## Step 8: Register the multisig on each hardware wallet

Step 8 tells each device which wallet it belongs to. A device that knows the other keys and the 2-of-3 rule can check receive and change addresses itself; one that does not would have to trust the computer.

### Coldcard

1. In Sparrow, go to `Settings` tab
2. Click `Export...` at the bottom
3. Select Coldcard Multisig and save it to a microSD card
4. Insert MicroSD into Coldcard
5. On the Coldcard: `Settings`, `Multisig Wallets`, `Import from SD`
6. Review and confirm the wallet details
7. Coldcard will now verify multisig addresses

### Keystone

1. In Sparrow, click `Export...`
2. Select Keystone Multisig and choose Show QR
3. On the Keystone, open the multisig wallet menu and choose to import a multisig wallet
4. Scan the QR code displayed by Sparrow
5. Confirm the wallet details

### Trezor, BitBox02 and Jade over USB

These devices receive the multisig details from Sparrow when you display an address over USB, and show them for you to confirm:
1. Go to `Receive` tab in Sparrow
2. Click `Display Address` on the hardware wallet
3. The device will show the multisig configuration for confirmation
4. Verify and confirm

## Step 9: Check the first address on every device

Step 9 proves Sparrow and all three devices agree on the wallet before any money goes in.

1. Go to the `Receive` tab, which shows the first multisig receive address
2. Click `Display Address` for each hardware wallet in turn
3. Check that every device shows exactly the same address, and confirm on each

If any device shows a different address, stop: something is wrong, and nothing should be deposited until you find it.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Multisig address verification: Sparrow, Coldcard, Keystone and Trezor each display the receive address, and all four must show the identical bc1q string; any mismatch means stop immediately](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallets/address-verification.svg)

</div>

## Step 10: Back up the wallet descriptor

Step 10 saves the one thing, besides the seeds, that recovery needs. Without the wallet descriptor you cannot rebuild the multisig from two of its three seed phrases, because the third key's xpub is recorded only there.

### Export as PDF
1. Go to `Settings` tab
2. Click the QR code icon (top right of settings)
3. Click `Save PDF...`
4. Save and print this document
5. Store copies with each seed phrase backup

### Export as File
1. Click `Export...` at bottom of Settings
2. Select Sparrow to export the wallet file
3. Save the `.json` file to multiple locations

The PDF contains the descriptor as a QR code, all three xpubs with their fingerprints, the derivation paths and the script type. Store a copy with each seed backup.

## How do you receive and send from the multisig?

### Receiving

1. Go to `Receive` tab
2. Click `Get Next Address` for a new address
3. Check it on at least two of the hardware wallets
4. Send a small test amount first
5. Wait for confirmation

### Sending

1. Go to `Send` tab
2. Enter recipient address
3. Enter amount
4. Set fee (check [mempool.space](https://mempool.space) for current rates)
5. Click `Create Transaction`
6. Click `Finalize Transaction for Signing`

### Signing

The transaction needs two of the three signatures.

With USB devices:
1. Connect first hardware wallet
2. Click `Sign`
3. Verify transaction details on device
4. Confirm on device
5. Disconnect, connect second device
6. Click `Sign` again
7. Verify and confirm on second device

With air-gapped devices:

1. Click `Save PSBT` to a microSD card, or show it as a QR code
2. Load PSBT on first device and sign
3. Export signed PSBT back to computer
4. Load into Sparrow
5. Repeat with second device

When it has two signatures, click `Broadcast Transaction`.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Signing a 2-of-3 multisig spend in Sparrow: Sparrow creates the unsigned PSBT, device 1 signs for one of two needed signatures, device 2 completes the quorum, and Sparrow broadcasts; the PSBT moves between devices, the keys never do](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallets/sparrow-signing-steps.svg)

</div>

## What habits keep it safe?

- Check addresses on the devices before the first deposit, after software updates, and from time to time afterwards.
- Before depositing a large amount, send a small test amount in, then send it back out, which proves the wallet can spend.
- Keep Sparrow updated, checking each download's signature.

## What if something does not work?

| Problem | What to check |
|---|---|
| The device is not detected | Try another USB cable and port, and make sure the device is unlocked |
| The addresses do not match | That you imported the right xpubs, that the derivation paths are `m/48'/0'/0'/2'`, and that every device is registered with the same multisig; re-export and re-import the wallet to the devices if needed |
| The transaction will not sign | That the PSBT belongs to this wallet, that the device has the multisig registered, and that it holds one of this wallet's keys |

The next guide, [backup and recovery](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/backup-recovery/), covers storing the backups and rehearsing a recovery.


---

# Multisig Backup & Recovery

> How to properly backup your multisig wallet and recover it if needed. Critical information for protecting your bitcoin long-term.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/backup-recovery/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A 2-of-3 multisig is recoverable from any two of its three seed phrases plus the wallet descriptor, so the backup plan is: each seed phrase on metal in its own location, never stored with its own device, and a copy of the descriptor with every seed. Then rehearse the recovery before the wallet holds anything significant: restore a device from its seed, rebuild the wallet in Sparrow from the descriptor alone, and sign a test transaction. The same complexity that protects a multisig loses it if the backups are wrong.

## What do you have to back up?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Item | Copies | What it is for |
|------|--------|---------|
| Seed phrase 1 | 1, on metal | Restores key 1 |
| Seed phrase 2 | 1, on metal | Restores key 2 |
| Seed phrase 3 | 1, on metal | Restores key 3 |
| Wallet descriptor | 3 or more | Rebuilds the multisig from its keys |
| Device PINs | 3 | Unlock the hardware wallets |

</div>

**Danger: Back up the wallet descriptor as carefully as the seeds**
Recovery usually means rebuilding the wallet from two of the three seeds. Two seeds do not reveal the third key's xpub, so without the descriptor, which contains it, the wallet cannot be rebuilt.

## What is in the wallet descriptor?

A **wallet descriptor** is the text that defines a multisig wallet:

```text
wsh(sortedmulti(2,
  [73c5da0a/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6...ABC,
  [8f3a2b1c/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6...DEF,
  [a2c4e6f8/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6...GHI
))#checksum
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `wsh` | Native segwit script type |
| `sortedmulti(2, ...)` | Two signatures needed, with the keys sorted |
| `[73c5da0a/48h/0h/0h/2h]` | Each key's master fingerprint and derivation path |
| `xpub...` | Each signer's extended public key |
| `#checksum` | A check that the descriptor was copied correctly |

The seed phrases alone do not say which keys belong together, how many signatures are needed, which paths were used or which script type. With all three seeds and those facts you could rebuild the wallet; with two seeds, the descriptor is the only place the third key's xpub exists. It cannot spend anything, but it reveals the wallet's balance and history to whoever reads it, so store it as privately as the seeds.

## Where should the backups be kept?

Four rules:

1. Never store two seed phrases together.
2. Never store a seed phrase with its own device.
3. Store a copy of the descriptor with each seed backup.
4. Use different buildings, and ideally different cities.

A layout that follows them, the same as in [hardware setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/#step-5-back-up-each-seed-on-metal-in-separate-places):

| | Device kept at | Seed backup kept at |
|---|---|---|
| Key 1 | Home safe | Bank safe deposit box |
| Key 2 | Home, separately from key 1 | A trusted family member's home |
| Key 3 | Another city: a second property or an office | A third location, such as a second deposit box |

A descriptor copy goes with each seed backup. A burglary at home finds two PIN-protected devices but no seed; losing any one seed location costs one key, which a 2-of-3 wallet survives; and any two seed locations, with their descriptor copies, are enough to recover.

## How do you make the backups?

### Seed phrases on metal

Metal survives the fires, floods and fading that destroy paper. For each seed: after confirming it restores its device, stamp or engrave it onto a metal plate, read the plate back letter by letter against the seed, and store it in its own location. One wrong letter is a wrong seed.

### The wallet descriptor

In Sparrow, open the `Settings` tab, click the QR code icon at the top right, click `Save PDF...` and print several copies. The PDF holds the descriptor as a QR code for recovery, every xpub as text, and the fingerprints and derivation paths. Print on acid-free paper and keep one copy with each seed backup. An encrypted copy on a USB stick in a safe is a reasonable extra.

## What do you do if something is lost?

### One device is lost or broken

If device 2 is lost but you have its seed backup: buy a new hardware wallet, restore seed 2 onto it, register the multisig on it, and check its addresses match the other devices. The wallet never stopped working, since two keys remained. Moving the funds to a fresh multisig afterwards is optional.

### One seed backup is lost

If seed backup 1 is destroyed but device 1 still works, the wallet still spends, but key 1 now exists only on one device. Act promptly: use device 1 and one other device to move the funds to a new multisig with three new seeds, and back those up properly.

### One device is stolen

If device 3 is stolen, the thief has one key and needs two. Use devices 1 and 2 to move the funds to a new multisig straight away, before the thief can try for another key; the stolen device is then worthless.

### Every device is destroyed

If all three devices are gone but you have two seed backups and the descriptor:

1. Get two new hardware wallets.
2. Restore seed 1 onto one and seed 2 onto the other.
3. In Sparrow, create a new wallet and import the descriptor, by scanning the QR code on the PDF (the scan icon next to the wallet name) or with `File`, `Import Wallet`.
4. Check that the fingerprints match your records and that the expected addresses and balance appear.
5. Sign a small test transaction with the two restored devices.
6. Then move everything to a new multisig with three new seeds on three new devices, and back that up.

## How do you test the recovery before relying on it?

Run these before depositing a significant amount:

1. Single device: wipe device 1, restore seed 1 onto it, register the multisig again, and check the fingerprint and addresses match. Sign a small test transaction.
2. Whole wallet: delete the wallet from Sparrow, import it again from the descriptor alone, check the addresses and balance, and sign a transaction with the devices.
3. Disaster: pretend every device is lost. Using only two seed backups and the descriptor, restore onto other devices, import the descriptor, and sign and broadcast a transaction.

If all three work, the backup plan works.

## Recovery checklist

- Each seed phrase is on metal, in its own location, not with its device, and has passed a restore test.
- The descriptor is exported as a PDF with a QR code, printed, stored with each seed backup, and has passed an import test.
- Every device has its own PIN, recorded away from the seeds, and has the multisig registered.
- Addresses have been checked on every device.
- Each device's fingerprint is recorded, the locations of everything are written down, and someone you trust knows where to find that record.

## How does multisig affect inheritance?

Your heirs need to know the multisig exists, to reach two of the three seed backups and the descriptor, and to have instructions for recovering it. You can do this yourself, with written instructions held by a lawyer or in a safe place; through a collaborative custody service (Unchained, Casa and Nunchuk offer inheritance features and help heirs recover); or by giving one key to a trusted person or lawyer, who can then help your heirs without being able to spend alone. [Inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) covers the options in detail.

## What mistakes do people make with multisig backups?

| Mistake | What goes wrong | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Storing seeds digitally | Screenshots, cloud storage and email can be breached | Metal only for seed phrases |
| Keeping all backups in one place | One fire, flood or theft takes everything | Spread them across locations |
| No descriptor backup | Two seeds cannot rebuild the wallet | Printed copies with each seed |
| Never testing recovery | The backup fails when it is needed | Rehearse recovery before depositing |
| Forgetting PINs | A device has to be restored from its seed before you can sign | Write PINs down, away from the seeds |


---

# Bitcoin Transactions: UTXOs, Signing and Fees

> How Bitcoin transactions work end to end: UTXOs, transaction creation, signing, broadcasting, fees, and the transaction types you will actually encounter.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A bitcoin transaction is not a debit from an account. It spends specific unspent outputs (UTXOs) that you prove you control, destroys them, and creates new outputs locked to whoever you are paying, with any remainder returned to you as change and the difference left as the miner's fee. That model explains why fees depend on size rather than amount, why change addresses exist, and why combining coins can reveal what you own.

## What does this section cover?

| Page | What it explains |

# UTXOs Explained

> Understand Bitcoin's UTXO model. Learn how Unspent Transaction Outputs work, why Bitcoin isn't an account balance, and how UTXOs affect fees and privacy.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A **UTXO** (unspent transaction output) is a separate amount of bitcoin, created by an earlier transaction and locked to one of your addresses, that has not been spent yet. A bitcoin wallet has no single balance: it holds a collection of UTXOs and shows you their total, and every payment spends whole UTXOs and creates new ones. That is why fees depend on how many coins a payment uses, why change comes back to you, and why spending coins together can reveal that they belong to the same person.

## How is a wallet like a purse full of notes?

A purse holding one $50 note, two $20 notes and three $5 notes contains six notes worth $105, not "$105 of balance". A bitcoin wallet works the same way:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| UTXOs | Value |
|-------|-------|
| One UTXO | 0.05 BTC |
| One UTXO | 0.02 BTC |
| One UTXO | 0.02 BTC |
| One UTXO | 0.005 BTC |
| One UTXO | 0.005 BTC |
| **Total** | **0.1 BTC** |

</div>

That is five UTXOs that add up to 0.1 BTC.

## How are UTXOs created and destroyed?

A UTXO is created when someone sends you bitcoin, locked so that only your key can spend it, and destroyed when you spend it, at which point new UTXOs are created from its value. Every transaction does both. Its inputs are existing UTXOs you own, which it consumes; its outputs are new UTXOs, for the recipient and as change for you.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Paying 0.04 BTC from a wallet holding 0.05, 0.03 and 0.02 BTC UTXOs: the 0.05 is destroyed whole and becomes 0.04 for the recipient, a new 0.0099 change UTXO and a 0.0001 mining fee, while the other two UTXOs stay untouched](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/utxo-lifecycle.svg)

</div>

## What are the properties of a UTXO?

### A UTXO is spent whole

A UTXO cannot be partly spent: used as an input, the whole of it is consumed. To pay 0.03 BTC from a 0.1 BTC UTXO, the transaction spends all 0.1 BTC, sends 0.03 BTC to the recipient, and returns about 0.07 BTC to you as a new change UTXO, less the fee.

### UTXOs can be combined

One transaction can spend several UTXOs. They are all consumed, and their combined value funds the new outputs.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Combining UTXOs: three 0.02 BTC coins are consumed together to pay 0.05 BTC, produce 0.0099 BTC change and leave 0.0001 BTC as fee; all three inputs are destroyed in one spend](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/utxo-combining.svg)

</div>

### Every UTXO has a history

Every UTXO can be traced back through the blockchain, transaction by transaction, to the block reward that first created its coins. The history is permanent and public.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A 0.05 BTC UTXO traced back through its history: a payment from Alice, before that an exchange withdrawal, a mining pool payout, and finally the coinbase mining reward; every hop is permanent and public](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/utxo-history.svg)

</div>

This traceable history has important implications for [privacy](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters).

### Every UTXO is locked to an address

Each UTXO is locked to a bitcoin address, and only the holder of that address's private key can spend it. Your wallet manages many addresses and their UTXOs, and the balance it shows is the sum of every UTXO locked to an address it controls.

## Why does the UTXO model matter?

### Fees depend on how many UTXOs you spend

Bitcoin fees are based on a transaction's size in bytes, not the amount sent, and each input adds bytes:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Input Type | Size |
|------------|------|
| Legacy (P2PKH) | ~148 bytes |
| SegWit (P2WPKH) | ~68 vbytes |
| Taproot (P2TR) | ~57 vbytes |

</div>

More inputs make a larger transaction, and a larger transaction costs more:

```
SAME VALUE, DIFFERENT FEES:
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Sending 0.1 BTC using 1 UTXO:
  ~140 vbytes → Low fee

Sending 0.1 BTC using 10 UTXOs:
  ~680 vbytes → ~5x higher fee

Sending 0.1 BTC using 50 UTXOs:
  ~3,400 vbytes → ~25x higher fee
```

### Privacy depends on which UTXOs you combine

Spending UTXOs from different sources together reveals that they belong to the same owner:

```
PRIVACY LEAK:
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
INPUTS:                       OUTPUT:
  From Exchange A  ─┐
  From Exchange B  ─┼──→     0.15 BTC (payment)
  From friend      ─┘

Chain analysis conclusion:
  "All three inputs belong to the same person"
```

This is the **common-input-ownership heuristic**, the most important rule chain analysis uses; see [chain analysis](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/).

### Small UTXOs can become unspendable

A UTXO worth less than the fee needed to spend it is **economic dust**: it costs more to move than it is worth. At 100 sat/vB, spending one native segwit input costs about 6,800 sats, so a 5,000-sat UTXO is worthless until fees fall.

## How does your wallet handle UTXOs?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Function | What Your Wallet Does |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Balance** | Sums all UTXOs you control |
| **Receiving** | Generates new addresses to receive new UTXOs |
| **Sending** | Selects which UTXOs to spend (coin selection) |
| **Change** | Creates change outputs back to addresses you control |

</div>

### What is coin selection?

**Coin selection** is how a wallet chooses which UTXOs to spend for a payment. Wallets use different strategies:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Strategy | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| **Largest first** | Uses biggest UTXOs first |
| **Smallest first** | Uses smallest UTXOs first |
| **Random** | Selects randomly |
| **Branch and bound** | Tries to find exact match (no change) |

</div>

Choosing the UTXOs yourself is called coin control, and it matters for both privacy and fees; see [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/).

## What does a wallet balance really contain?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A wallet showing a 0.088 BTC balance actually holds five separate UTXOs of 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005 and 0.003 BTC, each locked to its own address with its own history, and each spent whole or not at all](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/wallet-utxos.svg)

</div>

Each UTXO has its own value, address and history, and is spent whole or not at all.

## What do people get wrong about UTXOs?

| Belief | What actually happens |
|---|---|
| "I can send part of my balance" | Only whole UTXOs are spent; the wallet creates change so it looks like part of a balance |
| "Fees depend on how much I send" | Fees depend on size in bytes, which depends on how many UTXOs are spent, not on their value |
| "All my bitcoin is the same" | Each UTXO has its own history and sources, with different privacy consequences |
| "My balance is one number" | It is the sum of separate UTXOs, and knowing which you hold matters for fees and privacy |


---

# How Bitcoin Transactions Work

> Understand how Bitcoin transactions work: inputs, outputs, change, fees, and the complete lifecycle from creation to confirmation.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/understanding/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A bitcoin transaction spends earlier outputs you control (its inputs) and creates new ones (its outputs): usually one for the person you pay and one returning the remainder to you as change. Whatever the inputs add up to beyond the outputs is the fee, which goes to the miner who includes the transaction in a block. Once signed, the transaction is broadcast to the network, waits in the mempool, and is confirmed when a miner puts it in a block; every block after that adds a confirmation and makes it harder to reverse.

## What are inputs and outputs?

Bitcoin does not keep account balances. It keeps unspent transaction outputs, or [UTXOs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos/), and a transaction consumes some and creates others:

- An input is a UTXO you previously received, which the transaction spends.
- An output is a new UTXO the transaction creates, for the recipient or as change for you.

In effect a transaction says: "consume these outputs I received earlier, and create these new ones."

## Why does change come back to you?

Because an input is always spent whole. If you need only part of it, the rest returns to you as change, usually to a new address your wallet controls:

- You have an input worth 0.01 BTC.
- You send 0.008 BTC to a friend.
- 0.0019 BTC comes back to you as change, on a new address.

Your wallet does this automatically.

## How is the fee paid?

The fee is not a separate line: it is the difference between what the inputs are worth and what the outputs pay. In the example, 0.01 BTC goes in, 0.008 BTC plus 0.0019 BTC comes out, and the missing 0.0001 BTC is the fee.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Anatomy of a transaction: a 0.01 BTC input becomes 0.008 BTC to a friend and 0.0019 BTC change to a new address you control; the missing 0.0001 BTC is the fee, which is just the difference between inputs and outputs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/tx-anatomy.svg)

</div>

Fees depend on a transaction's size in bytes, not on the amount sent, and each extra input adds size. [Transaction fees](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/fees/) covers how to set them.

## What happens after you press send?

### Creating and signing

You enter the recipient's address and the amount. The wallet chooses which UTXOs to spend, adds the outputs including change, sets a fee for current conditions, and signs the transaction with your private key, which proves you are allowed to spend those inputs.

### Broadcasting

The wallet sends the signed transaction to one or more Bitcoin nodes. Each checks it against the rules and relays it to its peers, and within seconds it has spread across the network.

### Waiting in the mempool

Every node keeps a mempool, a holding area for valid transactions not yet in a block. Miners choose from it, mostly by fee rate (satoshis per virtual byte). A transaction with too low a fee can wait for a long time; [creating transactions](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/create/#what-if-a-transaction-is-stuck) covers how to speed one up.

### Confirmation

About every ten minutes a miner finds a new block and includes a set of transactions from the mempool. Once yours is in a block it has one confirmation, and each later block adds another.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Confirmations | Status | Typical use |
|---------------|--------|-------------|
| 0 | Unconfirmed: broadcast, not yet in a block | Do not treat as paid |
| 1 | In a block | Small payments |
| 3 | Harder to reverse | Medium amounts |
| 6 | Very hard to reverse | Large amounts; the common standard |

</div>

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The transaction pipeline: the wallet creates it, the key signs it, nodes relay the broadcast, it waits in the mempool until a miner includes it in a block, and every following block adds a confirmation](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/tx-pipeline.svg)

</div>


---

# How Bitcoin Transactions Are Created

> How a Bitcoin transaction is put together: choosing UTXOs as inputs, setting outputs and change, and unsticking a slow payment with RBF or CPFP.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/create/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Creating a bitcoin transaction means choosing which UTXOs to spend as inputs, the outputs (the recipient's address and amount, plus a change address for the remainder), and a fee rate. Most wallets do all of this when you enter an address and an amount. Doing it yourself, called coin control, lets you avoid spending coins that would link your identity to a payment and keep fees down. If a transaction sits unconfirmed because its fee was too low, it can be replaced with a higher-fee version (RBF) or pulled through by a high-fee transaction that spends its output (CPFP).

## How does a wallet build a transaction for you?

You enter the recipient's address and the amount, and the wallet selects inputs, adds the outputs and change, calculates the fee and, once you approve, signs and broadcasts. Many wallets let you pick a fee rate or a priority level. For everyday payments this is convenient and leaves little room for mistakes.

## What is coin control?

**Coin control** is choosing yourself which UTXOs a transaction spends, instead of leaving it to the wallet. With it you also choose the change address and set the fee exactly. [Sparrow](https://sparrowwallet.com/), [Electrum](https://electrum.org/) and [Bitcoin Core](https://bitcoincore.org/) all support it. It matters for privacy, because spending coins from different sources together tells observers they belong to the same person, and for fees, because every input adds size; [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) covers how to use it.

## What if a transaction is stuck?

A transaction stays in the mempool while its fee rate is below what miners are currently taking. Two methods speed it up.

### Replace-by-fee (RBF)

**Replace-by-fee** sends a new version of the transaction, spending the same inputs, with a higher fee; miners take the better-paying version and the original is dropped. Wallets used to have to mark a transaction as replaceable when it was created, but since Bitcoin Core 28.0 (October 2024) nodes accept a replacement for any unconfirmed transaction by default, and Bitcoin Core 29.0 removed the option to refuse. In practice you use the wallet's "bump fee" or "increase fee" action; Sparrow has one on every unconfirmed transaction it sent. Only the sender can do this, since only the sender can sign the inputs again.

### Child pays for parent (CPFP)

**Child pays for parent** is the receiver's option, and the sender's when RBF is not available. You create a second transaction, the child, that spends an output of the stuck transaction, the parent, with a fee high enough to cover both. Miners can only collect the child's fee by including the parent too, so they take both together.


---

# How Bitcoin Transaction Signing Works

> How Bitcoin transaction signing works: what signing means, online vs offline signing flows, and single-sig versus multisig signing.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/sign/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Signing a bitcoin transaction means using the private key for each input to produce a digital signature, which proves to every node that the holder of that key authorised this exact spend; change anything in the transaction and the signature no longer matches. Signing can happen on the same online device that builds the transaction, or on an offline device that receives the unsigned transaction as a PSBT file or QR code, which keeps the private key away from the internet entirely.

## What does a signature prove?

A signature shows that whoever made it holds the private key matching the input's public key, without revealing the key. Anyone can check it; nobody without the key can produce it. That is the whole of bitcoin's permission system: no account, password or identity, only a valid signature. Anyone who gets the private key can therefore sign, and spend.

## What is the difference between online and offline signing?

| | Online signing | Offline signing |
|---|---|---|
| Where the key is | On the internet-connected device that builds the transaction | On a separate device that never connects |
| How the transaction moves | It does not; build and sign happen in one place | As a PSBT, by USB, QR code or SD card |
| Risk | Malware on the device can reach the key | Malware on the online device cannot reach the key |
| Suits | Small spending wallets | Savings, cold storage, multisig |

In offline signing, a watch-only wallet on the online computer (which has no private keys) builds the transaction, the offline device signs it, and the signed transaction comes back for broadcast. A hardware wallet connected by USB is in between: the transaction travels over the cable, but the key never leaves the device.

## How does multisig signing differ?

A single-signature wallet needs one signature per input. A multisig wallet needs several: in a 2-of-3 wallet, two of the three keys must sign before the transaction is valid. Multisig is common in business wallets, collaborative custody and personal setups for larger amounts, and it relies on PSBTs to carry the transaction from one signer to the next.

## What is a PSBT?

A **PSBT** (partially signed bitcoin transaction, defined in BIP174) is a standard file format for a transaction that is not yet fully signed, along with the information each signer needs to check and sign it. It lets a transaction be built on one device and signed on others, one signature at a time, until it is complete. PSBTs are what make air-gapped signing and multisig work across devices from different makers.

## What does air-gapped signing look like?

1. Build the transaction on an online, watch-only wallet.
2. Export it as a PSBT.
3. Carry it to the offline device by QR code or SD card (or USB, with care).
4. Check and sign it on the offline device.
5. Carry the signed transaction back to the online device.
6. Broadcast it.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Air-gapped signing: an online watch-only wallet builds the transaction and exports a PSBT, the file crosses the gap by USB, QR or SD card, an offline device holding the private key signs it, and the signed PSBT returns for broadcast; the key never crosses](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/airgap-signing.svg)

</div>

The private key stays on the offline device throughout.


---

# How to Broadcast a Bitcoin Transaction

> How a signed Bitcoin transaction reaches the network, and why broadcasting through your own node instead of a public server keeps your IP and addresses private.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/broadcast/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Broadcasting is sending a fully signed transaction to the bitcoin network: the first node to receive it checks it and relays it to its peers, and within seconds it sits in nodes' mempools, where miners pick it up. Broadcasting through your own node reveals nothing to anyone else; broadcasting through a wallet company's or a public server tells that server your IP address and the transaction, and lets it log, delay or refuse to relay it. Your own node, ideally over Tor, is the private choice.

## Should you broadcast through your own node or a third-party server?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Two ways to broadcast a transaction: through your own node it reaches the peer-to-peer network with no intermediary, while a third-party server sees your IP address and can log, delay or censor the transaction before relaying it](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/broadcast-paths.svg)

</div>

| | Your own node | Third-party server |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | Bitcoin Core, or a node package such as Umbrel or Parmanode | Public Electrum servers, a block explorer, the wallet company's servers |
| Who sees the transaction first | Only your node | The server operator, with your IP address |
| Can it be delayed or refused? | No | Yes, by the operator |
| Setup | A node to run and maintain; see the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) | None |

Many phone wallets broadcast through their developer's servers by default. That is convenient, but it is a trade of privacy and control for no setup.

## How do you broadcast more privately?

- Route the wallet's connection through Tor, whether it talks to your own node or a public server, so the IP address it reveals is not yours.
- Know what your phone wallet connects to by default, and point it at your own server if it allows.
- Run your own node: it is the one arrangement in which nobody else sees your transaction before the network does.


---

# Bitcoin Transaction Fees Explained

> Understand how Bitcoin transaction fees work, why they vary, and how to minimize costs. Learn fee estimation, RBF, CPFP, and fee optimization strategies.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/fees/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A bitcoin transaction fee is the amount a transaction leaves unclaimed between its inputs and outputs, which the miner who includes it in a block collects. It is set by size, not value: the fee is the transaction's size in virtual bytes (vB) times a fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB), so sending 0.001 BTC costs the same as sending 100 BTC in a transaction of the same size. Rates rise and fall with demand for block space; check a mempool viewer before sending, use native segwit or Taproot addresses, and if a transaction gets stuck, bump its fee.

## How is the fee calculated?

```text
fee = transaction size (vB) × fee rate (sat/vB)
```

So the amount sent does not matter; the number of inputs and outputs does, because each adds size.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Bitcoin fees follow transaction size, not value: sending 0.001 BTC and sending 100 BTC in the same 140 vB transaction both cost 1,400 sats at 10 sat/vB, while a 10-input transaction of 1,100 vB costs 11,000 sats](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/fee-size-not-value.svg)

</div>

A **satoshi** (sat) is 0.00000001 BTC, and a **virtual byte** (vB) is the unit of transaction size the fee market uses, which counts segwit signature data at a discount. A typical payment from one native segwit input to two outputs (the recipient and your change) is about 140 vB.

| Transaction | Size | Fee at 2 sat/vB | Fee at 10 sat/vB | Fee at 50 sat/vB |
|------------------|------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 input, 2 outputs | About 140 vB | 280 sats | 1,400 sats | 7,000 sats |
| 3 inputs, 2 outputs | About 380 vB | 760 sats | 3,800 sats | 19,000 sats |
| 10 inputs, 2 outputs | About 1,100 vB | 2,200 sats | 11,000 sats | 55,000 sats |

To turn sats into money: 1,000 sats is $1 when bitcoin is worth $100,000, and twice that when it is worth $200,000.

## Why do fees change?

Each block has room for a limited amount of data (4 million weight units, in practice a few thousand transactions), and a new block comes about every ten minutes. When more people want to transact than the next blocks can hold, they bid against each other with higher fee rates, and miners take the highest-paying transactions first.

| Demand | Typical fee rate | Typical wait |
|--------|------------------|-------------------|
| Low | Under 1 to 5 sat/vB | The next block, or a few hours at the very lowest rates |
| Normal | 5 to 20 sat/vB | 10 minutes to an hour |
| High | 20 to 100 sat/vB | 10 to 30 minutes |
| Extreme | 100 sat/vB and more | Priority inclusion |

The floor has moved. Since Bitcoin Core 30.0 (October 2025), nodes by default relay transactions paying as little as 0.1 sat/vB, down from 1 sat/vB, though such transactions confirm only when miners have room for them.

## How does address type affect size?

| Address type | Input size | Output size | Addresses start with |
|--------------|------------|-------------|-------|
| Legacy (P2PKH) | About 148 vB | About 34 vB | `1` |
| Nested segwit (P2SH-P2WPKH) | About 91 vB | About 32 vB | `3` |
| Native segwit (P2WPKH) | About 68 vB | About 31 vB | `bc1q` |
| Taproot (P2TR) | About 57 vB | About 43 vB | `bc1p` |

Spending from native segwit or Taproot addresses costs much less than from legacy ones; moving from legacy to segwit cuts the fee for a typical payment by roughly 30 to 40%.

## How do you choose a fee?

Look at what the mempool, the queue of unconfirmed transactions, is currently accepting: [mempool.space](https://mempool.space) shows it, as do Sparrow's fee estimates and your own node. Then decide how urgent the payment is, and allow for spikes, which can come suddenly.

| What you need | What to pay |
|-----------|---------------------|
| Confirmation in the next block | The current high-priority rate |
| Confirmation within a few hours | The medium-priority rate |
| Confirmation within a day | The low-priority rate |
| Consolidating UTXOs | Wait for rates under 5 sat/vB |

The common mistakes are overpaying when demand is low because nobody checked, underpaying when demand is high so the transaction sticks, and trusting wallet defaults, which are often set high.

## What if a transaction is stuck?

### Replace-by-fee (RBF)

**Replace-by-fee** broadcasts a new version of your transaction, spending the same inputs, with a higher fee. Since Bitcoin Core 28.0 (October 2024) nodes accept a replacement for any unconfirmed transaction by default, whether or not the original was marked replaceable, so only the sender's wallet needs to support it. In Sparrow: find the unconfirmed transaction, right-click it, choose to increase the fee, set the new rate, and broadcast the replacement.

### Child pays for parent (CPFP)

**Child pays for parent** creates a new transaction that spends an output of the stuck one, with a fee high enough to make the pair worth mining together. It is the receiver's option, since the receiver cannot replace a transaction the sender signed. The child's fee has to cover the parent's shortfall as well as its own size.

## How can you pay less in fees?

### Consolidate when fees are low

Combining many small UTXOs into one, at a time when fees are 1 to 5 sat/vB, means future payments need one input instead of many.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Consolidation: one low-fee transaction turns 50 small UTXOs into a single large one, so the next payment needs 1 input instead of 50; do it at 1-5 sat/vB and only with same-source coins, because consolidation links histories](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/consolidation-payoff.svg)

</div>

Consolidation links the histories of the coins combined, so only consolidate coins from the same source; [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) covers when it is safe.

### Batch payments

Paying several people in one transaction costs far less than separate transactions, because the inputs and change are shared.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Batching: three separate 140 vB payments to Alice, Bob and Charlie total 420 vB, while one transaction paying all three is about 200 vB, 52% smaller and cheaper at any fee rate](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/transactions/batching.svg)

</div>

### Send when demand is low

Fees are often lower at weekends and higher during US business hours, though there is no reliable schedule.

### Use modern address types

Receive to native segwit (`bc1q`) or Taproot (`bc1p`) addresses, so the coins are cheaper to spend later.

## Where does Lightning fit?

For small, frequent payments, the [Lightning Network](https://lightning.network) settles almost instantly for fees often of a few sats, with no on-chain transaction per payment. It needs payment channels, which have their own on-chain costs to open and close, and it is a spending tool, not cold storage.


---

# Bitcoin Transaction Types Explained

> Bitcoin transaction types explained: pre-signed, fully signed, and partially signed (PSBT). When each type is used and how they differ.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/types/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A bitcoin transaction goes through up to three states: unsigned (built, but not yet authorised), partially signed (some but not all of the needed signatures added, as in multisig), and fully signed (valid to broadcast). The standard file format for the first two is the PSBT. A pre-signed transaction is a fully signed one kept to broadcast later, for example as part of an inheritance plan.

## What is an unsigned transaction?

An unsigned transaction is one that has been built (inputs, outputs and fee chosen) but not signed. It is usually made on an internet-connected computer by a watch-only wallet, ideally connected to your own node; since that wallet has no private keys, building the transaction there puts nothing at risk. The unsigned transaction, in PSBT format, is then carried to the device that holds the keys, such as an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) or a hardware wallet.

## What is a partially signed transaction?

A partially signed transaction has some of its required signatures but not all, the normal state of a [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) spend in progress:

1. A watch-only wallet builds the transaction and exports it as a PSBT.
2. The first signing device adds its signature.
3. The PSBT goes to the next device, which adds another, until the required number is reached.
4. The complete transaction returns to the online computer for broadcast.

The PSBT format (BIP174) carries the transaction and everything each signer needs through all of these steps; a PSBT with no signatures yet is still a PSBT.

## What is a fully signed transaction?

A fully signed transaction has every signature it needs and is valid to broadcast. After an offline device signs, the transaction comes back to the online computer, which broadcasts it; the offline device has no connection to do so itself.

## What is a pre-signed transaction?

A pre-signed transaction is a fully signed transaction saved to broadcast later, without needing the keys again. It stays valid until any of its inputs is spent by another transaction. Pre-signed transactions combined with a timelock, which makes a transaction invalid before a set date or block height, are one way to build inheritance and recovery plans; [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) covers the options.


---

# Bitcoin Privacy: Chain Analysis, CoinJoin, UTXO Control

> Bitcoin privacy fundamentals: what is exposed on the public blockchain, how chain analysis works, and how CoinJoin and UTXO control protect you.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin's blockchain is public: every transaction, address and amount is permanently visible to anyone who looks, so privacy is something you design for rather than something you get by default. This section covers what the blockchain reveals, how surveillance firms link addresses to people, and the habits and tools that keep your finances your own: your own node, UTXO management, CoinJoin and PayJoin.

## What does this section cover?

| Page | What it explains |
|---|---|
