# Why Bitcoin Privacy Matters

> Why financial privacy matters for Bitcoin users. What information is exposed on the public blockchain and how it affects your security.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Every bitcoin transaction is public and permanent: the addresses, the amounts and the time are readable by anyone, forever. Bitcoin is pseudonymous rather than anonymous, so the moment one of your addresses is linked to your name (through an exchange, a payment or a public post) your balance, income and spending history can be read and followed. That matters for security, because known holders become targets, as well as for freedom from surveillance and discrimination. Privacy is achievable, with your own node, careful handling of coins and, where needed, CoinJoin, but it takes deliberate effort.

## What does the blockchain record?

When you make a Bitcoin transaction, more information is recorded than most people realize. The sending address, the receiving address, the exact amount, the precise time: all of it goes on a permanent public ledger that will exist as long as Bitcoin exists.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A transaction from address A worth 1.80 BTC paying 1.50 BTC to B with 0.30 BTC change: the blockchain publishes both addresses, both amounts and the time at block 812,345, readable by anyone forever, with no names attached](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/blockchain-shows.svg)

</div>

Now, the blockchain doesn't contain names, only addresses. This is called **pseudonymity**. You're identified by a string of characters rather than your legal name. At first glance, this seems private enough. But here's the problem: pseudonymity is fragile. Once your identity connects to any address, the veil starts to unravel.

## How does a pseudonym become a name?

The moment your real identity touches any Bitcoin address, your privacy begins to erode. And in the modern Bitcoin ecosystem, these connections happen constantly, often without you realizing it.

Think about how most people acquire Bitcoin. They sign up for an exchange, submit identification documents, and buy their first coins. When they withdraw those coins, the exchange records exactly which address belongs to which verified customer. That single withdrawal creates a permanent link between your legal identity and your Bitcoin activity.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Action | What Gets Exposed |
|--------|-------------------|
| Buy from KYC exchange | Your name linked to withdrawal address |
| Pay a merchant | Merchant knows your address |
| Post address online | Anyone can search and find it |
| Send to a friend | Friend knows your address |
| Receive salary in BTC | Employer knows your address |

</div>

Once that first link exists, blockchain analysis can follow the trail. Your coins move from address to address, and each hop is publicly recorded.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A KYC exchange records that John Smith withdrew to address A; the public chain shows A paying B, then C, then D, so an analyst attributes all four addresses, the total balance and the merchant payments to John Smith](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/privacy-exposure.svg)

</div>

What started as "just one withdrawal" becomes a comprehensive financial profile.

## Why should you care?

"I have nothing to hide" is a common response, but financial privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing. It protects four things: your physical safety, your access to financial services, your freedom from surveillance and your dignity.

### Security

The most immediate danger is physical. If people know how much Bitcoin you hold, you become a target.

Consider the "$5 wrench attack." Someone doesn't need to hack your wallet if they can threaten you or your family. Bitcoin's pseudonymity only protects you until someone connects your identity to your holdings. Then you have a physical security problem that no amount of technical security can solve.

Beyond physical threats, known Bitcoin holders face an onslaught of sophisticated social engineering. Scammers research wealthy targets and craft personalized attacks. If they know you're worth targeting, they'll invest the time to find your vulnerabilities.

### Financial discrimination

Your transaction history is more revealing than you might think. Merchants could theoretically charge you more if they see you're wealthy. Services might deny you based on where your coins have been, even if you had nothing to do with their prior history. Insurance companies and lenders increasingly factor financial profiles into their decisions.

This isn't science fiction. Chain analysis companies already offer "risk scoring" services that flag addresses based on transaction history. Your coins might be marked as "high risk" because of where they passed through before reaching you.

### Surveillance and control

Governments and corporations have always sought to monitor financial activity. Bitcoin's transparent ledger makes this easier, not harder. Tax authorities can trace your entire transaction history without requesting records from a bank. Data brokers can build and sell your financial profile. In more hostile jurisdictions, authoritarian regimes can identify and target people based on their financial behavior.

### Dignity

Perhaps the most fundamental argument: financial privacy is a reasonable expectation. You don't share your bank statements on social media. You don't announce your purchases to strangers. You don't invite the world to scrutinize your spending habits.

You shouldn't have to justify every purchase. Your wealth shouldn't be visible to anyone curious enough to look. Your financial decisions are your own business. Privacy isn't about having something to hide; it's about having something to protect.

## Is bitcoin anonymous?

No, and believing it is has led to serious mistakes. In some ways bitcoin is less private than cash or a bank account:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Cash | Bitcoin |
|------|---------|
| No permanent record | Permanent public record |
| Physical transfer leaves no trail | Every transfer is logged forever |
| Difficult to trace at scale | Entire history traceable by anyone |

</div>

Bitcoin may actually be **less private** than traditional banking in some important ways. Your bank doesn't publish your transactions publicly; they're visible to the bank and to law enforcement with appropriate legal process, but not to the general public. Bank records can eventually be deleted; blockchain records cannot. Bank surveillance requires legal authorization; blockchain surveillance requires only an internet connection.

## Who is watching?

What started as academic research has become a multi-billion dollar industry. Chain analysis companies employ hundreds of specialists to study blockchain data, and they've gotten remarkably good at what they do.

These companies don't just look at the blockchain in isolation. They build comprehensive databases linking addresses to identities, analyzing transaction patterns, and flagging suspicious activity. They've tagged millions of addresses as belonging to exchanges, mixing services, ransomware operators, and individual users.

Their capabilities include:

- Clustering addresses they believe belong to the same entity
- Identifying which addresses belong to major exchanges
- Tracking behavioral patterns that reveal user identities
- Building probabilistic models to link addresses to real-world identities

Their clients include:

- Law enforcement agencies investigating crimes
- Tax authorities ensuring compliance
- Banks conducting due diligence
- Cryptocurrency exchanges screening transactions

To be clear: some of this activity is legitimate. Tracking ransomware payments and recovering stolen funds are valuable services. But the same tools that trace criminals can trace anyone, and the surveillance infrastructure, once built, doesn't distinguish between legitimate privacy and criminal evasion.

## What can you do about it?

Privacy takes effort, but it is achievable, and understanding the problem is the first step. [Chain analysis explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/) breaks down the techniques surveillance companies use, which also shows where they fail. Then each privacy tool addresses specific weaknesses: [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) and coin control, [your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/), and [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/). Habits matter as much: not posting addresses publicly, using a new address for every payment, and not discussing what you hold. [Protecting your privacy](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/protecting-privacy/) puts it together.


---

# Chain Analysis Explained

> Learn how blockchain surveillance works. Understand the heuristics and techniques used to track Bitcoin transactions and link addresses to identities.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

**Chain analysis** is the practice of studying the public bitcoin blockchain to group addresses by owner, follow coins from one transaction to the next, and attach those groups to real people, mostly using data from exchanges. It is an industry selling to governments, exchanges and banks. It works from heuristics, which are rules of thumb about how people usually spend, and from outside data, so it produces probabilities rather than proof, and each heuristic has known weaknesses that privacy tools such as coin control and CoinJoin exploit.

## What does chain analysis try to do?

At its core, chain analysis is pattern recognition on a massive scale. Analysts study blockchain data to achieve several goals:

**Clustering addresses:** Determining which addresses belong to the same person or entity. If they can prove that addresses A, B, and C all belong to you, they've dramatically expanded what they know about your activity.

**Tracking fund flows:** Following bitcoin as it moves through the network. Where did your coins come from? Where did they go? Who else handled them along the way?

**Identifying entities:** Linking address clusters to real-world identities. This is where the blockchain's pseudonymity breaks down entirely.

**Flagging transactions:** Marking certain coins as "tainted" or suspicious based on their history. Yes, your coins can be flagged for something a previous owner did.

This intelligence is valuable. Law enforcement uses it to track criminals. Exchanges use it to comply with regulations. Tax authorities use it to ensure compliance. And increasingly, ordinary financial institutions use it to make decisions about which customers to serve.

## Which techniques does chain analysis use?

Chain analysis isn't black magic. It's a set of logical inferences applied at scale. The industry relies on **heuristics**: rules of thumb that are usually (but not always) true. Understanding these heuristics reveals both their power and their limitations.

### The common-input-ownership heuristic

This is the most powerful tool in the analyst's arsenal, and it's deceptively simple.

**The assumption:** If multiple addresses are used as inputs in the same transaction, they all belong to the same owner.

**Why it usually works:** To spend bitcoin from multiple addresses in one transaction, you need the private keys for all of them. Typically, only one person has those keys.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The common input ownership heuristic: addresses A, B and C worth 0.5, 0.3 and 0.4 BTC are spent together into outputs of 0.7 and 0.5 BTC, so an analyst concludes one entity controls all three inputs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/chain-common-input.svg)

</div>

**When it breaks down:**
- CoinJoin transactions intentionally combine inputs from multiple people
- PayJoin transactions mix buyer and seller inputs

### Change address detection

When you spend bitcoin, you rarely have the exact amount needed. If you have a 1 BTC UTXO and want to pay someone 0.7 BTC, the remaining 0.3 BTC comes back to you as change, sent to a new address your wallet controls.

Analysts exploit this pattern. In any transaction with two outputs, they ask: which one is the payment, and which one is change returning to the sender?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Change detection: a 1.00 BTC input pays 0.70 BTC to a round-number payment output and 0.29 BTC to a new address of the same script type; the odd remainder marks it as change returning to the sender, with 0.01 BTC as fee](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/chain-change-detection.svg)

</div>

Several indicators help analysts make this determination:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Indicator | Why It Suggests Change |
|-----------|----------------------|
| New address | Wallets generate fresh change addresses |
| Odd decimal places | Payments tend to be round numbers |
| Same script type | Wallet uses consistent address format |
| Smaller amount | Change is often the remainder |

</div>

The real power comes from combining heuristics. Once analysts identify a change address, they can link it to your other addresses via common input ownership when you spend from it later. Your change address becomes another piece of your financial profile.

### Address reuse

Using the same address twice is a privacy catastrophe. It creates an undeniable link between transactions.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Address reuse: a payment received at address A, a payment sent from A and a second payment received at A are all permanently linked; knowing one transaction reveals the others, which is why wallets rotate addresses](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/chain-address-reuse.svg)

</div>

Modern wallets generate new addresses automatically for this reason, but address reuse still happens, especially when people share a single "donation" address publicly or when merchants use static payment addresses.

### Timing analysis

Time leaves fingerprints. Transactions close together in time are often related, and regular patterns reveal behavioral information.

If you deposit to an exchange and withdraw minutes later, those transactions are likely related. If you receive payment and immediately forward it to another address, the connection is obvious. If you make transactions at the same time every day or week, you're creating a pattern that can be correlated with real-world activity.

### Amount correlation

Numbers tell stories. Payments are often round numbers (0.1 BTC, 0.01 BTC), while change addresses tend to have irregular amounts. If 0.5 BTC enters a mixer and 0.5 BTC exits somewhere else, they might be connected, though sophisticated mixers work hard to break this correlation.

## How do analysts build a profile of you?

The real power of chain analysis comes from combining these techniques. Individually, each heuristic provides a piece of the puzzle. Together, they build comprehensive profiles.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Cluster building: addresses A, B and C spent together are one owner, change detection adds D, a later co-spend adds E, and the analyst ends up holding a map of every address you control](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/chain-analysis-cluster.svg)

</div>

## Where does the identity data come from?

Blockchain analysis is powerful, but it becomes devastating when combined with off-chain data. The blockchain tells analysts where coins move; external data tells them who's moving them.

### Exchange records

Here's the uncomfortable truth: when you use a KYC (Know Your Customer) exchange, you're creating a permanent link between your legal identity and your Bitcoin addresses. The exchange knows who you are. They know which addresses you've deposited to and withdrawn from. And they share this information with chain analysis companies, sometimes directly, sometimes through regulatory requirements.

This is often the starting point for tracing. An analyst might not know who controls a random address on the blockchain, but once that address receives funds from a known exchange withdrawal, the connection is made.

### Web scraping

Chain analysis companies don't just watch the blockchain; they scour the internet. They search for Bitcoin addresses posted in forums, donation addresses on websites, addresses in leaked databases, and social media posts where people mention their addresses. Every public mention of a Bitcoin address is potential data.

That donation address on your blog? It's been catalogued. That transaction ID you shared to prove a payment? It's been noted. The internet never forgets, and neither do surveillance companies.

### Network metadata

Even beyond blockchain and web data, your transactions leak information. If you're not using Tor, your IP address may be associated with your transactions. Browser fingerprints, transaction timing patterns, and unique wallet behaviors all create signatures that can be correlated with other data.

## How certain are the attributions?

There's an important distinction between clustering and attribution. Clustering means determining that addresses A, B, and C belong to the same entity. Attribution means determining that entity is you.

**Strong attribution** comes from direct evidence: your exchange account withdrew to that address, you posted that address publicly, or that address appears in a law enforcement database linked to your identity.

**Weak attribution** comes from inference: the address transacted with someone identified, the behavioral pattern matches expectations, or statistical analysis suggests a likely owner.

Chain analysis companies often have high confidence in their clusters but varying confidence in attribution. They know addresses belong together; they're less certain about who controls them. This matters because weak attribution can be challenged, and because it creates false positive risk.

## What does this mean for you?

Let's make this concrete. If an analyst has identified even one address you control, here's what they can potentially learn:

**Your transaction history is visible.** Every transaction from identified addresses is recorded permanently. Where you sent coins, when you sent them, how much you sent: all of it.

**Past actions affect future privacy.** Those coins you bought years ago still carry their history. Address reuse from the past still creates links. Your entire financial history can be reconstructed retroactively if the starting point is identified.

**Exchanges are key vulnerability points.** KYC exchanges create the identity links that make everything else possible. Even using an exchange once, years ago, creates a permanent record that can anchor future analysis.

## What are the limits of chain analysis?

Chain analysis is powerful, but it's not omniscient. Every technique has limitations, and understanding them reveals opportunities for protection.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Technique | Limitation |
|-----------|------------|
| Common input ownership | Broken by CoinJoin and PayJoin |
| Change detection | Multiple conflicting indicators |
| Timing analysis | Users can deliberately delay transactions |
| Amount correlation | Equal-output transactions obscure amounts |

</div>

**CoinJoin and similar techniques** specifically target these heuristics. When multiple people combine their transactions, the common input ownership assumption breaks down completely. When outputs are all equal amounts, change detection becomes impossible. When timing is randomized, temporal analysis loses power.

This is the key insight: chain analysis relies on assumptions about how people typically use Bitcoin. Use Bitcoin atypically, intentionally, and those assumptions fail.


---

# Protecting Your Privacy

> Overview of Bitcoin privacy techniques. Learn the principles and methods for protecting your financial privacy when using Bitcoin.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/protecting-privacy/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Protecting bitcoin privacy comes down to a few habits and three tools. The habits: never reuse an address, keep coins from different sources apart, do not post addresses or discuss your holdings, and think before each transaction about what it links. The tools: your own node, so no server learns your addresses; UTXO management and coin control, so payments do not tie your coins together; and CoinJoin or PayJoin, which break the links chain analysis relies on. Start with the habits and your own node, and add the rest as your [threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/) requires.

This page is the overview; [why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) and [chain analysis explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/) cover the problem.

## Which principles come first?

- Think before you act. Every transaction leaves a permanent trace, so ask whether it links your identity to an address, reveals more than it needs to, or could be done more privately.
- Keep identities separate. Do not mix KYC bitcoin (bought with ID) with non-KYC bitcoin, work payments with personal ones, or public donation addresses with private savings.
- Leak as little as possible. Use a new address for every payment, do not post addresses publicly unless you must, and consider who can see each transaction.

## Which techniques help, and how hard are they?

| Technique | What it does | Effort | Guide |
|-----------|--------------|------------|---|
| Never reuse addresses | Stops payments being linked through one address | Easy | |
| Keep coin sources separate | Keeps identities apart | Easy | [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) |
| Do not post addresses | Prevents scraping | Easy | |
| Run your own node | Stops your addresses leaking to servers | Medium | [Node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) |
| Coin control and labels | Decide which coins each payment spends | Medium | [Coin control](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/#what-is-coin-control) |
| CoinJoin | Mixes coins with others to cut their history | Harder | [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) |
| PayJoin | Hides a payment inside an ordinary-looking transaction | Medium | [PayJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/payjoin/) |

## Why run your own node?

A wallet that uses someone else's node or a public server reveals all your addresses, your transaction history and possibly your IP address to whoever runs it. With your own node the wallet's questions stay on your hardware, nobody else sees your addresses, and you verify everything yourself. [What is a Bitcoin node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/what-is-node/) and [why run your own](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/why-run-node/) explain it, and the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) sets one up.

## Why manage your UTXOs?

Your bitcoin is a set of separate coins, and how you spend them decides what observers can link. Combining coins from different sources ties them together, more coins mean higher fees, and careless spending reveals your activity. Label where every coin came from, never combine KYC and non-KYC coins, choose inputs with coin control, and consolidate only coins from the same source. The [UTXO management guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) covers it.

## What does CoinJoin add?

CoinJoin combines inputs from several people into equal outputs, which defeats the common-input-ownership heuristic and hides which output belongs to whom. After a good CoinJoin, analysts cannot tell which output is yours, and the coins' history is cut: they gain forward privacy. The mixed coins then need careful handling, and some exchanges flag CoinJoin history. The [CoinJoin page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) covers both.

## How can you acquire bitcoin more privately?

Bitcoin bought on a KYC exchange is linked to your identity from the start, and no later technique fully undoes that. Other ways to acquire it:

| Method | Privacy | Trade-offs |
|--------|---------------|-----------|
| Peer to peer | Higher | More effort, and a risk of scams |
| Some bitcoin ATMs | Medium | Often filmed, and many now require ID |
| Being paid in bitcoin | Higher | The payer knows your address |
| Mining | Highest | Expensive equipment and technical knowledge |

## What about privacy at the network level?

A transaction that looks private on chain can still leak your IP address when it is broadcast, when you come online, and who you connect to.

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| Tor | Hides your IP address |
| A VPN | Hides your IP address from everyone except the VPN provider |
| Your own node | Broadcasts your transactions without a third-party server |
| Your own node over Tor | The best combination |

The [Tor guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/) sets it up.

## What can't be fixed afterwards?

| Situation | Why it cannot be undone |
|-----------|----------------------|
| A withdrawal from a KYC exchange | The exchange keeps your identity on record |
| An address posted online | It may be archived, scraped or saved |
| A payment to an identified address | The transaction is permanent |
| Blockchain history in general | The past cannot be changed |

What you can do is start fresh with new coins, CoinJoin existing coins for forward privacy, and be more careful from now on.

## What does each technique cost?

| Technique | Privacy benefit | Cost or risk |
|-----------|----------------|-----------|
| Your own node | No address leakage | Disk space and setup time |
| CoinJoin | Cuts transaction links | Fees, time, and possible questions from exchanges |
| Buying peer to peer | No KYC link | A price premium and counterparty risk |
| Coin control | Better privacy for each payment | Manual effort and a learning curve |

## Where should you start?

1. Run your own node, with the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/).
2. Learn [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/).
3. Use [coin control](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/#what-is-coin-control) on every payment.
4. Consider [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) for coins you already hold.

And keep the habits: a new address every time, labels on every incoming payment, sources kept apart, and a moment's thought before each transaction.


---

# Bitcoin UTXO Management: Coin Control & Consolidation Guide

> Bitcoin UTXO management for lower fees and better privacy. Coin control in Sparrow, consolidation strategies, dusting attacks, and source separation rules.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

UTXO management means deciding which of your coins (UTXOs) each transaction spends, instead of leaving it to the wallet: keeping coins from different sources apart, labelling where each came from, merging small coins from the same source when fees are low, and freezing unexpected tiny deposits. Done well, it keeps fees down, stops payments from revealing your whole balance, and avoids linking your KYC coins to your private ones. The tool for it is coin control, which Sparrow and Electrum both offer.

Time: 40 minutes. Level: Intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

[UTXOs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos/), [how transactions work](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/understanding/) and [why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) are useful background.

## What goes wrong without UTXO management?

Leaving coin selection to the wallet leads to fees higher than they need be, privacy leaks that tie coins from different sources together (see [chain analysis](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/)), small coins that cost more to spend than they are worth, and exposure to tracking attacks that rely on you spending what you were sent.

| UTXO property | What it means for management |
|----------|------------------------|
| A UTXO is spent whole | Payments create change |
| Each UTXO spent adds bytes | More inputs mean higher fees |
| Each UTXO has a public history | Spending UTXOs together links their histories |
| Each UTXO is locked to an address | Labels are how you remember where it came from |

## Why do many small UTXOs cost more?

Fees depend on a transaction's size, not its value, and each input adds 57 to 148 vB depending on address type, against 31 to 43 vB per output. Sending 0.1 BTC at 50 sat/vB:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Coins spent | Inputs | Size | Fee |
|----------|--------|--------------|-----|
| One 0.1 BTC UTXO | 1 | About 140 vB | About 7,000 sats |
| Ten 0.01 BTC UTXOs | 10 | About 750 vB | About 37,500 sats |
| A hundred 0.001 BTC UTXOs | 100 | About 6,900 vB | About 345,000 sats |

</div>

The same amount sent, at fees that differ fiftyfold.

## How does spending coins together hurt privacy?

Spending several UTXOs in one transaction tells everyone they belong to the same person. Analysts call this the **common-input-ownership heuristic**, and it is one of their main tools.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Coins from a KYC exchange, a peer-to-peer trade and mining kept in three separate compartments stay unlinked, while spending 0.05, 0.07 and 0.03 BTC from all three in one 0.15 BTC transaction links every history under the common-input-ownership heuristic](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/utxo-source-separation.svg)

</div>

## When does a small UTXO become dust?

A UTXO worth less than the fee to spend it is economic **dust**. At 100 sat/vB one native segwit input costs about 6,800 sats to spend, so a 5,000-sat UTXO costs more to move than it holds, and the higher fees go, the more small coins fall below the line.

## What are the rules of UTXO management?

### Keep UTXOs above about 0.01 BTC

A coin of 0.01 BTC (1,000,000 sats) or more stays worth spending across most fee conditions. The cost of spending one native segwit input, as a share of the coin:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Fee rate | 0.001 BTC coin | 0.01 BTC coin | 0.1 BTC coin |
|-----------------|----------------|---------------|--------------|
| Low (10 sat/vB) | 0.7% | 0.07% | 0.007% |
| Medium (50 sat/vB) | 3.4% | 0.34% | 0.03% |
| High (200 sat/vB) | 13.6% | 1.4% | 0.14% |
| Extreme (500 sat/vB) | 34% | 3.4% | 0.34% |

</div>

### Do not put everything in one UTXO

With all your bitcoin in one coin, every payment shows the recipient your whole holding through the change.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Paying 0.01 BTC from a single 1.00 BTC UTXO creates a 0.99 BTC change output, so the recipient can see the sender held at least 1.00 BTC](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/utxo-change-reveal.svg)

</div>

### Keep coins from different sources apart

Never spend together coins from an exchange that has your ID (KYC coins) and coins without it, coins from different exchanges, or [mixed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) and unmixed coins. Each combination creates a link that stays on the blockchain for good.

### Label everything

Without labels you will forget which coins came from where, which carry your identity and which have been mixed. Label each one when it arrives, for example "Exchange withdrawal, January 2026", "Repayment from a friend, no KYC", "Mixed with Jam, round 3".

## What is coin control?

**Coin control** is choosing exactly which UTXOs a transaction spends. Without it the wallet decides, often badly.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Without coin control the wallet auto-selects a 0.03 BTC KYC coin and a 0.025 BTC non-KYC coin for a 0.05 BTC payment, linking the sources; with coin control you spend a single 0.05 BTC KYC coin and the non-KYC coin stays separate](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/utxo-coin-control.svg)

</div>

### How do you use coin control in Sparrow?

Sparrow's coin control is the most complete:

- To see your coins, open the wallet's `UTXOs` tab, which lists every UTXO with its amount, address, label, date and transaction.
- To spend particular coins, tick them in the `UTXOs` tab, click `Send Selected`, and enter the destination and amount.
- To label a coin, double-click it and type the label; labels are kept between sessions.
- To freeze a coin, such as unexpected dust, right-click it and choose `Freeze UTXO`; it is then left out of every transaction until you unfreeze it.

### How do you use coin control in Electrum?

Choose `View`, `Show Coins` to add a `Coins` tab. In it, right-click a coin and choose `Spend From` to build a transaction from that coin only, or `Freeze` to exclude it.

### How do you choose which coins to spend?

- Match the amount: pick a coin close to the payment so that little change is created. For a 0.048 BTC payment from coins of 0.1, 0.05 and 0.02 BTC, the 0.05 BTC coin leaves only 0.002 BTC of change.
- Combine only coins from one source: for a 0.15 BTC payment, two coins of 0.1 and 0.08 BTC from the same exchange are better than any combination that mixes in a coin from another exchange or a non-KYC coin.
- Spend older coins first: they are less likely to be linked by timing to your recent activity.

## How do you consolidate UTXOs without losing privacy?

**Consolidation** is combining several UTXOs into one larger one, so future payments need fewer inputs. Done well it saves fees; done badly it ties your coins' histories together for good.

**Danger: Consolidate coins from one source at a time**
A consolidation tells the world that every coin in it belongs to the same person. Never combine KYC with non-KYC coins, coins from different exchanges, or mixed with unmixed coins.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Consolidating 0.01, 0.02 and 0.03 BTC that all came from Coinbase into 0.06 BTC reveals nothing new; consolidating the same amounts from Coinbase, Kraken and a non-KYC trade fuses three separate histories forever](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/utxo-consolidation-rule.svg)

</div>

Consolidate when you have many coins under 0.01 BTC, when recent payments have needed five or more inputs, when simple payments cost more than they should, or after months of small regular purchases. Check the fee rate at [mempool.space](https://mempool.space) first:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Fee rate | Consolidate? |
|----------|----------------|
| 1 to 10 sat/vB | Yes: an ideal time |
| 10 to 30 sat/vB | If you need to |
| 30 to 100 sat/vB | Wait if you can |
| Over 100 sat/vB | No |

</div>

## Step 1: Sort your UTXOs by source

Step 1 groups every coin by where it came from: each exchange, each non-KYC source, mixed coins. Labels make this quick; without them, go through your transaction history and label as you go.

## Step 2: Plan one consolidation per source

Step 2 decides which coins go together. Make a separate transaction for each source, for example:

```text
Transaction 1, coins from exchange A: 0.005 + 0.003 + 0.007 + 0.002 → 0.017 BTC, less the fee
Transaction 2, coins from exchange B: 0.008 + 0.012 + 0.004 → 0.024 BTC, less the fee
Transaction 3, non-KYC coins: 0.05 + 0.02 → 0.07 BTC, less the fee
```

## Step 3: Send each consolidation when fees are low

Step 3 makes the transactions. Wait for a low fee rate, select the coins of one source with coin control, send them to a new address in your own wallet, and set a low fee, since there is no hurry.

## Step 4: Check and label the result

Step 4 confirms the new coin arrived and the old ones are gone, and labels the new coin with its source so it is not mixed with others later.

## Is consolidation worth the fee?

Consolidating ten native segwit coins now, at 10 sat/vB:

```text
Inputs:   10 × 68 vB = 680 vB
Output:    1 × 31 vB =  31 vB
Overhead:              ~11 vB
Total:                ~722 vB  →  about 7,200 sats
```

Spending the same ten coins later at 100 sat/vB would cost about 72,200 sats, so consolidating saves about 65,000 sats. The bigger the gap between today's fees and future fees, the more it pays.

It is not worth it when the coins come from different sources, when they are already large (combining 0.5 BTC coins gains little), when fees are high, or when you are about to mix them anyway; [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) does its own combining.

## What sizes should your UTXOs be?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Purpose | Target size | Why |
|---------|-------------|-----------|
| Long-term holding | 0.1 to 1 BTC | Cheap to spend later, even in large payments |
| Regular spending | 0.01 to 0.1 BTC | Flexible, without showing your whole holding |
| Smallest worth keeping | 0.01 BTC | Stays economical in most fee conditions |

</div>

A mix of sizes, for example one coin of 0.5 BTC, three of 0.1 BTC and five of 0.02 BTC, lets you pay most amounts without large change or revealing everything.

When withdrawing from an exchange, withdraw at least 0.01 BTC at a time, and ideally 0.05 to 0.1 BTC; many tiny withdrawals become expensive to spend. Balance that against how long coins sit on the exchange, which carries its own [risk](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/holding-bitcoin/).

## Which wallets support UTXO management?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Wallet | Coin control | Labels | UTXO list | Platform |
|--------|--------------|----------|-----------|----------|
| Sparrow | Yes, the most complete | Yes | Yes, detailed | Desktop |
| Electrum | Yes | Yes | Yes | Desktop |
| Wasabi | Yes | Yes | Yes | Desktop |
| BlueWallet | Yes | Yes | Yes | Mobile |

</div>

Avoid wallets that show only a balance and hide the coins behind it; they make UTXO management impossible.

## What mistakes do people make with UTXOs?

| Mistake | What goes wrong | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Letting the wallet choose coins | It combines sources | Use coin control every time |
| Receiving many small payments | Each becomes a small coin that is costly to spend | Use Lightning for small amounts, and consolidate when fees are low |
| Consolidating KYC with non-KYC coins | Your private coins become linked to your identity | Keep separate wallets for each kind |
| Ignoring change | Change carries part of the payment's privacy loss | Minimise change, and label it |
| Buying tiny amounts every week and withdrawing each | Dozens of small coins | Withdraw less often, in larger amounts, and consolidate when fees are low |

## What is a dusting attack?

A **dusting attack** is sending tiny amounts of bitcoin to many addresses in the hope that recipients later spend them alongside their other coins, revealing which addresses belong together:

1. The attacker sends a few hundred sats (546 is the smallest standard amount for a legacy address, 294 for a native segwit one) to thousands of addresses.
2. A recipient later spends the dust together with their other coins.
3. The attacker sees which coins moved with the dust, and links them to one owner.
4. Combined with other analysis, that can identify the owner.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A dusting attack in three steps: the attacker sends 546 sats to thousands of addresses, the victim co-spends the dust with a real 0.4 BTC coin, and the movement of the dust links the victim's addresses into one cluster](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/utxo-dusting-attack.svg)

</div>

Protect yourself by freezing small coins you did not expect, never consolidating unknown dust, using coin control, and labelling incoming transactions so that unexpected tiny amounts stand out.

## What should you check before every transaction?

- You chose the coins yourself.
- Every input comes from the same kind of source: KYC, non-KYC or mixed.
- The change goes to an address in the right wallet.
- The transaction and its outputs are labelled.
- You are not consolidating coins from different sources.
- The selection is the cheapest that meets the rules above.


---

# Bitcoin CoinJoin: How It Works & Best Practices

> How Bitcoin CoinJoin works: equal outputs, anonymity sets, the 2026 tools (JoinMarket NG, Jam, Ashigaru Whirlpool, Wasabi), and post-mix rules.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A **CoinJoin** is a single bitcoin transaction in which several people combine their coins and each receives back outputs of the same size, so that nobody watching the blockchain can tell which output belongs to whom. It is non-custodial (each person signs only their own input) and it cuts the link between a coin's past and its future, which is bitcoin's most important on-chain privacy tool. As of October 2026 we recommend JoinMarket NG with the Jam interface, which has no coordinator to seize; and the privacy only survives if you follow the post-mix rules below.

Time: 30 minutes. Level: Intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

This page is the theory; the hands-on guide is the [CoinJoin tutorial with JoinMarket NG and Jam](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin-tutorial/). [UTXOs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos/), [chain analysis](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/) and [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) are useful background.

## What does a CoinJoin look like?

Ten people each drop an identical banknote into a hat, shake it and each take one back: everyone leaves with what they put in, and nobody watching can say which note went where. A CoinJoin does this in one bitcoin transaction: several users contribute inputs and receive equal-sized outputs, so an observer cannot match inputs to outputs.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A normal payment of 1.00 BTC from Alice to Bob leaves one traceable link, while a CoinJoin where Alice, Bob and Carol each contribute 1.00 BTC and each receive 1.00 BTC back gives every output three equally likely owners](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-vs-normal.svg)

</div>

Two properties make it safe. Nobody ever holds your coins: you sign only your own input, and only after checking the transaction pays you back. And there is nothing to confiscate, because the privacy comes from the structure of the transaction, not from trusting a company.

## Why does CoinJoin exist?

Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous: every transaction is public forever, and [chain analysis](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/chain-analysis/) firms are good at attaching names to addresses. Without countermeasures, the exchange you bought from can follow your coins for years, anyone you pay can look up your balance and income, analytics companies sell profiles of your finances, and thieves can pick out wealthy targets.

CoinJoin attacks the tracing directly. It breaks the **common-input-ownership heuristic**, the assumption that all inputs of a transaction belong to one person, and the output matching that chain analysis depends on. After a good CoinJoin your coins have forward privacy: their future movements can no longer be confidently tied to their past.

## How does CoinJoin work?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Five unequal inputs of 0.82, 0.31, 0.55, 0.24 and 0.47 BTC each produce one identical 0.20 BTC mixed output plus their own change of 0.62, 0.11, 0.35, 0.04 and 0.27 BTC; the mixed outputs cannot be told apart, but change stays linkable by amount](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-equal-outputs.svg)

</div>

### Why do the outputs have to be equal?

If the outputs had different sizes, an analyst could trace them by matching amounts. Equal outputs remove that signal.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![With unequal outputs an analyst matches the 0.5, 0.8 and 0.3 BTC inputs to their outputs by amount; with three equal 0.30 BTC outputs plus change of 0.20 and 0.50, the amounts carry no signal](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-equal-vs-unequal.svg)

</div>

### What is an anonymity set?

The **anonymity set** is the number of equally plausible owners each output has; bigger is better.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![One coin entering three successive CoinJoin rounds of five participants each: candidate owners grow from 5 after one round to 25 after two and up to 125 after three, multiplying with every remix](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-anonymity-rounds.svg)

</div>

After one 100-person round, an analyst picking an output has a 1% chance of naming the right owner.

### Why do several rounds help?

Each extra round multiplies the possibilities an analyst has to consider, and remixing with new participants compounds the ambiguity. That is why every serious tool supports remixing, and why a single round is a half-measure.

### Why can nobody steal the coins?

A CoinJoin is one transaction that everyone must sign. Each participant:

1. Contributes an input they control
2. Checks the draft transaction pays them back in full
3. Signs only their own input, and only if step 2 checks out

If anyone, including a coordinator, tampers with the outputs, the signatures never arrive and the transaction fails. The worst a malicious party can do is waste your time.

## What does it look like in practice?

Three people each hold 0.1 BTC with a history they would rather not carry: Alice was paid by her employer, who knows her address; Bob withdrew from an exchange that keeps records under his name; Carol received coins whose past is publicly known. They join one CoinJoin:

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Alice's employer, Bob's exchange and anyone watching Carol each follow a 0.1 BTC coin into the same CoinJoin and out to three identical 0.1 BTC outputs; every watcher's trail dead-ends into a one-in-three guess](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-dead-ends.svg)

</div>

Afterwards, Alice's employer sees her 0.1 BTC enter a CoinJoin and become one of three identical outputs. It cannot tell which one is hers, and neither can Bob's exchange or anyone watching Carol's coins. Each history now dead-ends into ambiguity, and with bigger rounds and more remixes the ambiguity grows from "one in three" to "one in hundreds".

## What can CoinJoin do, and what can't it?

| CoinJoin does | CoinJoin does not |
|---|---|
| Cut the link between your coins' past and future | Hide that you took part: CoinJoins are recognisable on chain, and the transaction into one is visible to whoever knew your coins |
| Give analysts probabilities instead of proof | Make you anonymous: amounts, timing and your later behaviour still leak information |
| Give mixed coins a fresh start | Survive bad habits: one careless transaction afterwards can undo it (see the rules below) |
| | Work at any amount: equal outputs limit how much can be mixed at once |

## Which CoinJoin tools work in 2026?

Law enforcement and burnout reshaped CoinJoin between 2024 and 2026, and older guides recommend setups that no longer exist:

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| April 2024 | US authorities seize Samourai Wallet's servers and the original Whirlpool coordinator goes dark. The founders later plead guilty and in November 2025 are sentenced to five and four years in prison |
| June 2024 | zkSNACKs shuts down the original Wasabi coordinator; Sparrow Wallet removes its Whirlpool integration |
| June 2025 | Ashigaru, a community fork of Samourai, launches a new Whirlpool coordinator, reachable only over Tor |
| April 2026 | The original JoinMarket repository is archived after a long quiet period; development continues in JoinMarket NG |

### JoinMarket NG and Jam (our recommendation)

[JoinMarket NG](https://github.com/joinmarket-ng/joinmarket-ng) is the actively developed implementation of the JoinMarket protocol, wire-compatible with the original client whose repository was archived in April 2026. There is **no coordinator at all**: it is a peer-to-peer market with two roles.

Takers pay a small fee to mix on demand, at any time and any amount; makers provide the liquidity and earn those fees, with their own coins mixed as a side effect. Because no company sits in the middle, there is nothing to seize and nobody to subpoena, so the Samourai story cannot repeat. JoinMarket's old weakness was that it lived on the command line; [Jam](https://github.com/joinmarket-webui/jam) is a web interface for JoinMarket NG that makes wallet creation, single CoinJoins, scheduled mixing and maker mode point-and-click, and it ships as an app on most node-in-a-box platforms.

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| No coordinator to trust, seize or overcharge | Needs your own Bitcoin node and some setup |
| Any amount, mixed immediately as a taker | Smaller rounds (typically 4 to 20 participants), so plan several |
| You can earn fees as a maker instead of paying them | |
| Market-set fees, typically fractions of a percent | |

It suits self-custody users who run their own node. The [tutorial](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin-tutorial/) walks through the setup.

### Whirlpool: gone, then back (Ashigaru)

The original Whirlpool is gone; a revival exists under new management.

The original Whirlpool depended on Samourai Wallet's central coordinator. When the servers were seized in April 2024 every Whirlpool client stopped mixing the same day, which is the textbook demonstration of coordinator risk. Sparrow Wallet removed its integration shortly after; old guides pointing at "Whirlpool via Sparrow" are obsolete.

In June 2025, [Ashigaru](https://ashigaru.rs/), an open-source fork of Samourai run by anonymous maintainers, launched a new, independent Whirlpool coordinator. It is reachable only over Tor and uses the Zerolink fixed-pool model, with two pools of 0.025 BTC and 0.25 BTC and a flat 5% fee per pool entry (0.00125 and 0.0125 BTC), after which remixing is free. It needs Ashigaru's own software (Ashigaru Terminal on desktop, Ashigaru Mobile) and does not work with Sparrow or the old Samourai apps.

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Zerolink pools with free remixes, a proven design | Still a central coordinator, the weakness that ended the original |
| Strictly Tor-only | A 5% entry fee, against a fraction of a percent for JoinMarket |
| | Fixed pool sizes only |

It suits people who specifically want the Zerolink model and accept the fee and the coordinator risk.

### Wasabi Wallet

[Wasabi](https://wasabiwallet.io/) survived its own coordinator shutdown. zkSNACKs, the company behind it, left in June 2024, but the wallet is maintained by its community and, since version 2.2, has no built-in coordinator fee: you choose an independent coordinator, several of which charge nothing, so the cost can be just mining fees.

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| The easiest: install, pick a coordinator, turn on CoinJoin | You trust your chosen coordinator to be honest about who is in a round |
| Large rounds (often 100 or more) and variable amounts that reduce leftover change | Coordinators are central parties that can disappear or be pressured |
| Free or nearly free, depending on the coordinator | |

It suits desktop users who want mixing to run on its own and accept choosing a coordinator.

### How do they compare?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| | JoinMarket NG and Jam | Ashigaru Whirlpool | Wasabi |
|--------|--------------------|--------------------|--------|
| Coordinator | None (peer-to-peer) | Centralized (Ashigaru) | Centralized (third-party) |
| Amounts | Flexible | Fixed pools (0.025 / 0.25 BTC) | Variable |
| Cost | Maker fees, well under 1% | 5% pool entry, free remixes | Often free, plus mining fees |
| Anonymity set per round | 4 to 20 | Grows with remixes | 100 or more |
| Own node | Required | Recommended | Recommended |
| Can earn fees | Yes (maker) | No | No |

</div>

We recommend JoinMarket NG with Jam. It is the only option with no central point of failure, it fits everything else this site teaches (your node, your keys), and 2024 showed that coordinator-based services can vanish overnight. Wasabi is a reasonable simpler alternative; Ashigaru's Whirlpool is for committed Zerolink users.

## Why does CoinJoin need your own node?

Whichever tool you use, connect it to your own Bitcoin node. A wallet that talks to someone else's server tells that server all your addresses, including the freshly mixed ones, and the CoinJoin protects nothing. JoinMarket NG requires your own node; treat it as required everywhere. See the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/).

## What should you do after a CoinJoin?

Mixing is half the work; what you do afterwards decides whether the privacy holds.

**Danger: Mixed coins lose their privacy in one careless transaction**
Never spend mixed coins together with KYC or unmixed coins, never consolidate several mixed coins into one, always use your own node, and choose the inputs by hand for every transaction that touches mixed coins.

### Why must mixed and unmixed coins never be combined?

It is the most common way people undo their own CoinJoin:

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Two transactions that undo a mix: merging a 0.10 BTC mixed coin with a 0.15 BTC KYC coin into one 0.25 BTC payment re-attaches your identity, and consolidating three 0.10 BTC mixed coins from different rounds into a single 0.30 BTC output proves one owner ran all three rounds](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/coinjoin-postmix-rules.svg)

</div>

The KYC coin carries your name. Spending both in one transaction attaches your name to the mixed coin too, and the mixing bought nothing. Keep mixed and unmixed funds in separate wallets so the software cannot combine them by accident.

### Why not consolidate mixed coins?

Before such a consolidation, each mixed output could have belonged to anyone in its round. After it, all three provably share an owner, which collapses their anonymity sets at once. Spend mixed UTXOs individually. If a payment truly requires combining, understand you are spending privacy to make it.

### What do you do with change from a mixed coin?

Spending a mixed coin usually produces change, which is linked to the payment you just made. Treat it as partly exposed: remix it through another round, spend it somewhere privacy does not matter, or combine it only with other change, never with fresh mixed coins.

### Why use coin control?

Without [coin control](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/), your wallet picks UTXOs itself and will eventually pair a mixed coin with a labelled one. Choose the inputs by hand for every transaction that touches mixed funds.

### How long should mixed coins wait?

If you mix at 14:00 and spend at 14:15, the timing alone links the two. Let mixed outputs sit for days or weeks, and avoid being the first or last participant to move after a round.

### Where does Lightning fit?

Opening a [Lightning](https://lightning.network/) channel with a mixed UTXO adds another layer: the channel opening is visible, the payments inside it are not, and the eventual closing produces coins with still more distance from their origin.

### What should you check before spending mixed coins?

- The wallet is connected to your own node.
- You chose the inputs yourself.
- Every input comes from your mixed coins, with no KYC coins among them.
- You are spending one mixed coin, not consolidating several.
- Enough time has passed since the mix.

### What mistakes undo a CoinJoin?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Mistake | Why it matters | How to avoid it |
|---------|--------------|--------------|
| Merging mixed and unmixed coins | Re-links the coins to your identity | Separate wallets |
| Consolidating mixed UTXOs | Proves common ownership | Spend individually |
| Using a public server | Operator learns your addresses | Run your own node |
| Auto coin selection | Wallet pairs the wrong UTXOs | Coin control |
| Spending immediately | Timing correlation | Be patient |
| Ignoring change | Change is semi-exposed | Remix or quarantine it |

</div>

## Common questions

### What is a Bitcoin CoinJoin?

A CoinJoin is a single bitcoin transaction in which several users combine their inputs and each receives an equal-sized output, so an outside observer cannot match inputs to outputs. Everyone leaves with what they put in, but nobody watching can say which output belongs to whom.

### Does Whirlpool still work in 2026?

The original Whirlpool is gone, and a revival exists under new management. US authorities seized Samourai Wallet's coordinator in April 2024 and every Whirlpool client stopped mixing the same day; Sparrow Wallet removed its integration shortly after. In June 2025 Ashigaru, an open-source fork run by anonymous maintainers, launched an independent Whirlpool coordinator reachable over Tor. We cover it but do not recommend it, because it brings back the coordinator risk that ended the original.

### Which CoinJoin implementation should you use in 2026?

We recommend JoinMarket NG with the Jam web interface. JoinMarket NG has no coordinator at all: it is a peer-to-peer market where takers pay a fee to mix on demand and makers earn those fees, so there is nothing to seize and nobody to subpoena. Jam makes it a point-and-click app that ships on most node-in-a-box platforms. It needs your own Bitcoin node, and rounds typically have 4 to 20 participants, so plan on several.

### Is CoinJoin legal?

In most jurisdictions, yes: it is a privacy technique, comparable to keeping your bank statements out of public view. The 2024 to 2025 Samourai prosecutions targeted the operators, who ran a central coordinator business and were convicted of operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business; no CoinJoin user was charged. Some exchanges flag CoinJoin history and may freeze deposits or ask questions, so do not send freshly mixed coins straight to a KYC exchange, and know the rules where you live. None of this is legal advice.

### Do you need CoinJoin?

It is most valuable if you hold KYC coins and want forward privacy, if you spend bitcoin and do not want every counterparty to see your net worth, if you are a journalist, activist or otherwise a target, or if you hold enough that being identifiable is a physical risk. It may be unnecessary if your coins were acquired without your identity attached, or you only move small amounts. Match the effort to your [threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/).


---

# CoinJoin Tutorial: JoinMarket NG and Jam Step by Step

> Step-by-step Bitcoin coinjoin with JoinMarket NG and Jam: your own node, a dedicated hot wallet, funding, mixing rounds, and sweeping out cleanly.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin-tutorial/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To run a CoinJoin without trusting a coordinator, use JoinMarket NG, a peer-to-peer CoinJoin engine, through Jam, its web interface, on top of your own Bitcoin node: install Jam (most node-in-a-box platforms offer it as an app), create a separate hot wallet for mixing, fund it with the amount to mix, run collaborative transactions or Jam's scheduler, and sweep the mixed coins to fresh addresses in your cold storage. It takes one to two hours to set up, then the mixing runs on its own, and costs maker fees of a fraction of a percent plus mining fees. The [theory page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) explains why it works.

Time: 1-2 hours of setup, then mixing runs on its own. Cost: Maker fees (a small fraction of a percent) plus mining fees. Level: Advanced. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

You need a [Bitcoin node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), or the time to set one up in step 1. The setup has four parts, built in this order:

1. Your own Bitcoin node, which everything else talks to.
2. A separate hot wallet, which exists only to run CoinJoin rounds.
3. [JoinMarket NG](https://github.com/joinmarket-ng/joinmarket-ng), the engine that finds counterparties and builds the CoinJoins.
4. [Jam](https://github.com/joinmarket-webui/jam), the web interface for it.

## What are you building?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The JoinMarket stack: Jam in your browser drives the JoinMarket NG daemon, which signs coinjoins and talks to makers over Tor, while your own Bitcoin Core node verifies the chain and your balance](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/joinmarket-stack.svg)

</div>

Jam is the control panel, JoinMarket NG does the mixing, and your node keeps everything private and verified. Counterparty traffic runs over Tor.

## Why is the mixing wallet a hot wallet?

**Danger: The mixing wallet's keys are online**
Running CoinJoin rounds needs keys that stay online while the rounds run, so the mixing wallet is a hot wallet, less secure than your hardware wallet by design. Treat it as a temporary working wallet, not savings: fund it only with the amount you are mixing (start with an amount you could bear to lose while learning), give it its own new seed, and never import your cold storage or hardware wallet seed into it.

The separation also makes the privacy rules easy to follow. With mixing funds in their own wallet, your KYC coins and your mixed coins physically cannot end up in the same transaction by accident.

## Step 1: Run your own Bitcoin node

Step 1 gives JoinMarket NG a backend to check balances and broadcast transactions, and for privacy that backend must be your own node. If your setup asked someone else's server, that server would see every address you are trying to unlink, before, during, and after the mix.

Two ways to get there:

- A node-in-a-box platform, the easiest: Umbrel, Start9 and RaspiBlitz run Bitcoin Core for you and offer Jam as an app, so step 2 takes five minutes.
- Your own Bitcoin Core on your own hardware: follow the [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) first, then come back.

Either way, wait until the node is fully synced before mixing.

## Step 2: Install JoinMarket NG and Jam

Step 2 installs the mixing software.

### On a node-in-a-box

If you run Umbrel, Start9 or RaspiBlitz, open its app store and install Jam. The app bundles the JoinMarket backend and wires it to your node automatically. When Jam opens in your browser, skip to Step 3.

### On your own Linux server

On your own Linux machine, install JoinMarket NG with its installer:

```bash
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joinmarket-ng/joinmarket-ng/main/install.sh | bash
source ~/.joinmarket-ng/activate.sh
```

Piping a script from the internet into your shell deserves a look first: download `install.sh`, read it, then run it.

Then point it at your node. The configuration lives in `~/.joinmarket-ng/config.toml`; set the backend to Bitcoin Core and fill in your node's RPC credentials:

```toml
backend_type = "descriptor_wallet"   # use Bitcoin Core as the backend
# plus your Bitcoin Core RPC host, port, user, and password
```

Start the wallet daemon (`jmwalletd`), which exposes the API that Jam connects to. Finally install Jam itself and point it at the daemon; the [Jam installation docs](https://jamdocs.org/software/installation/) cover the supported setups, including Docker.

Installer options and daemon names change faster than guides do. If anything here disagrees with the [JoinMarket NG documentation](https://joinmarket-ng.github.io/joinmarket-ng/) or the [Jam documentation](https://jamdocs.org/), follow theirs.

## Step 3: Create the mixing wallet

Step 3 creates the temporary hot wallet in Jam.

1. Give it an obvious name, such as `mixing`, so it is never mistaken for anything long-term.
2. Set a strong password. Jam encrypts the wallet with it, and anyone with the machine and the password can spend the funds.
3. Write down the seed phrase, even for a temporary wallet: coins may sit here for days while rounds run, and a failed disk should not cost them. If Jam offers an extra passphrase on top of the seed (a mnemonic extension), you can add one; write it down too, because the seed alone will not restore the wallet without it.
4. Never put your cold storage seed here.

When the wallet opens, Jam shows a receive address. That is where your coins to be mixed will go.

## Step 4: Fund the wallet

Step 4 moves the coins to be mixed into the mixing wallet's receive address, from an exchange withdrawal or your existing wallet. For a first session, 0.001 to 0.01 BTC is enough to watch full rounds complete without meaningful risk. The funding transaction is visible to whoever knew your coins before, such as the exchange, and they can see the coins went to a wallet that then joins CoinJoins; that is expected, since CoinJoin gives coins a private future, not a hidden past. Wait for a confirmation before mixing.

## Step 5: Mix

Step 5 runs the CoinJoins. Jam offers two ways, both available once the wallet is funded.

A single collaborative transaction: in the send screen, toggle the collaborative option, pick the number of counterparties, and send, either to one of your own fresh addresses or straight to a payment destination. You pay each maker its advertised fee plus mining fees; even with many counterparties the total is normally a small fraction of one percent. This is the taker role: your mix happens on your schedule, usually within minutes.

The scheduler: Jam's main feature runs a full mixing session for you: it splits your balance and executes a sequence of collaborative transactions over several hours or days with randomized timing, ending by sweeping the wallet. This is the closest thing to "press play, come back to mixed coins". Use it when you are mixing a meaningful amount rather than experimenting.

While rounds run, keep the machine on, since rounds cannot complete with the daemon offline (always-on node-in-a-box setups suit this). If nothing seems to happen, check the order book Jam shows, which lists the makers offering liquidity and their fees. And remember that rounds compound: one join gives one round's anonymity set, and the scheduler's chain of joins is what builds real privacy, as the [theory page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/#how-coinjoin-works) explains.

## Step 6: Sweep out and wind down

Step 6 moves the mixed coins to long-term storage; the mixing wallet is a waypoint, not a destination.

1. Send the mixed coins to fresh addresses of your long-term wallet (your hardware wallet or cold storage), one UTXO per address, never to an address that has been used before. If you used the scheduler, you can give it destination addresses so the final sweep lands there directly.
2. Follow the post-mix rules from the theory page: [never merge with KYC coins, never consolidate, coin control always](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/#best-practices-after-coinjoin). The mixing is the cheap part; the discipline afterwards is what keeps the privacy.
3. Once the wallet is swept, the wallet can sit empty until your next batch, or be retired entirely. Keep the seed backup until the balance is zero and confirmed elsewhere.

## Should you stay on as a maker?

So far you have been a taker, paying small fees to mix on demand. Jam's earn tab lets you switch sides and run as a maker: your wallet offers liquidity, other people's coinjoins include your coins, and you collect fees while your coins get remixed over and over for free.

- Your keys stay online the whole time; this is a long-running hot wallet by design, so size the balance accordingly.
- Earnings are modest; think of them as offsetting your costs while your privacy keeps compounding.
- Committed makers can lock a fidelity bond (timelocked coins) to rank higher in taker selections; read the [JoinMarket NG docs](https://joinmarket-ng.github.io/joinmarket-ng/) before locking anything.

## What if something does not work?

- Jam cannot reach the backend: the wallet daemon is not running, or (manual path) Jam is pointed at the wrong host or port.
- The backend cannot reach the node: RPC credentials in `config.toml` do not match your Bitcoin Core settings, or the node is still syncing.
- No collaborative transaction starts: check the orderbook. If you see no offers, your Tor connection is likely down; if you see offers but joins fail, retry, since individual makers do drop out mid-round.
- Everything is slow: that is normal. Tor adds latency and the scheduler adds deliberate random delays. Slow is part of the privacy.

## What should you check?

- The mixing wallet has its own new seed, written down.
- It has a strong password.
- The first session uses a small amount you could bear to lose.
- The node is fully synced, and the daemon talks only to your own node.
- The mixed coins were swept to fresh cold storage addresses.
- The post-mix rules are followed: no merging, no consolidation, coin control on every spend.

Afterwards, manage the mixed coins with [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/), and consider [PayJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/payjoin/) for the payments themselves.


---

# Bitcoin PayJoin (BIP78): Stealth Privacy for Payments

> Learn how PayJoin (BIP78) enhances Bitcoin privacy by breaking the common-input-ownership assumption. Set up PayJoin with Sparrow Wallet and BTCPay Server.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/payjoin/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

**PayJoin** (BIP78, also called pay-to-endpoint) is a way of paying in bitcoin in which the receiver adds one of their own inputs to the sender's transaction. The result looks like an ordinary payment, but it breaks the assumption chain analysis relies on most, that all of a transaction's inputs belong to the sender, and it hides the real amount paid. It costs no more than a normal payment; it needs a receiver that supports it, such as a merchant using BTCPay Server, and a sending wallet that does, such as Sparrow.

Time: 30 minutes. Cost: Free (just transaction fees). Level: Intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

[UTXOs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos/) are useful background.

In a normal payment the sender provides every input, the receiver gets one output and the sender gets change. In a PayJoin the receiver contributes an input too, so the transaction on chain looks normal while the analyst's reading of it is wrong.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![In a normal payment Alice's 1.0 BTC input pays Bob 0.7 with 0.3 change; in a PayJoin Bob adds his own 0.5 BTC input and receives 1.2, so the analyst reads the payment as 1.2 and wrongly assumes every input is Alice's](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/privacy/payjoin-vs-normal.svg)

</div>

## Why does PayJoin matter?

Chain analysis assumes that all inputs in a transaction belong to one owner. The assumption is right most of the time, which is what makes it useful for surveillance. PayJoin breaks it, and because a PayJoin looks like any other payment, analysts can no longer be sure of the assumption even for transactions that are not PayJoins. Every PayJoin adds that doubt across the whole transaction graph, so wider use helps everyone's privacy, including people who never use it.

## How does a PayJoin work?

1. Alice wants to pay Bob 0.7 BTC.
2. Her wallet builds a normal transaction: a 1 BTC input, 0.7 BTC to Bob, 0.3 BTC change to Alice.
3. Instead of broadcasting it, the wallet sends it as a PSBT to Bob's PayJoin endpoint.
4. Bob adds an input of his own, 0.5 BTC, and raises his output to 1.2 BTC.
5. Bob sends the modified transaction back.
6. Alice's wallet checks that it still pays what she intended, and she signs her input.
7. The final transaction is broadcast: inputs of 1 BTC (Alice) and 0.5 BTC (Bob); outputs of 1.2 BTC (Bob) and 0.3 BTC (Alice).

| What an analyst assumes | What actually happened |
|----------------------|---------|
| The sender owned 1.5 BTC of inputs | The sender owned 1 BTC and the receiver 0.5 BTC |
| The payment was about 1.2 BTC | The payment was 0.7 BTC |
| The change was 0.3 BTC | Correct, by coincidence |

## How does PayJoin compare with CoinJoin?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| | PayJoin | CoinJoin |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Participants | Two: sender and receiver | Many: from 4 to over 100 |
| Coordination | Directly between the two, during the payment | A coordinator, or a peer-to-peer market |
| How it looks | Like a normal transaction | Recognisable as a CoinJoin |
| Purpose | Privacy for a payment | Cutting a coin's history |
| Fees | A normal transaction fee | Mixing fees and a larger transaction |

</div>

PayJoin is stealth privacy: it does not look like a privacy transaction. CoinJoin is explicit privacy: anyone can see it is a CoinJoin, though they cannot trace through it. The two complement each other.

## Which wallets support PayJoin?

### Sending

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Wallet | Platform | Can send PayJoins |
|--------|----------|-----------------|
| Sparrow | Desktop | Yes |
| BTCPay Server | Web | Yes |
| Wasabi | Desktop | Yes |
| BlueWallet | Mobile | Yes |
| JoinMarket | Desktop | Yes |

</div>

### Receiving

Receiving under BIP78 needs a wallet that supports it and an endpoint, a web address the sender's wallet can reach. BTCPay Server is the easiest way, and handles it automatically for customers whose wallets support it. A newer version, BIP77 ("Payjoin v2"), lets a receiver accept PayJoins without running a server, and some wallets have begun to adopt it; check your wallet's documentation.

## Step 1: Get the recipient's PayJoin request

Step 1 starts from the recipient. A PayJoin-capable recipient gives you a BIP21 payment request (a `bitcoin:` link or QR code) that includes a PayJoin endpoint, an address such as `https://btcpay.example.com/BTC/pj`.

## Step 2: Paste the request into Sparrow

Step 2 builds the payment. In Sparrow, open the `Send` tab and paste the BIP21 request. Sparrow recognises the PayJoin endpoint itself.

## Step 3: Review and send

Step 3 completes it. Sparrow negotiates with the recipient's endpoint, shows that the transaction is a PayJoin, and checks that the payment still goes where you intended. Confirm and broadcast.

## How do you accept PayJoins with BTCPay Server?

1. Open the store's checkout settings.
2. Enable PayJoin (BIP78).
3. Set up a hot wallet for the store, since PayJoin needs the server to contribute and sign an input.

When a customer pays an invoice, a wallet that supports PayJoin negotiates it automatically; one that does not simply pays normally, with no error. The customer does nothing different.

## How do you use PayJoin well?

Use it whenever a recipient offers it, since every PayJoin helps network privacy, and run BTCPay Server if you accept payments, to offer it to your customers. Combine it with coin control and your own node.

Do not expect anonymity from PayJoin alone: it defeats one heuristic, not all of them. Using it with KYC coins does not hide them from the exchange that knows them. And you cannot control the receiver's side; a receiver with poor practices can leak information about the payment.

## What are PayJoin's limits?

- Amounts are still visible on chain.
- It defeats the common-input-ownership heuristic, not the others.
- It protects new transactions, not past ones.
- Both sides need compatible software.

Use [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) instead when you need to cut links to a coin's past, want a larger anonymity set, or cannot count on the receiver's cooperation. Use PayJoin when paying a recipient that supports it, when you want privacy that does not look like privacy, or simply to add doubt to the network's transaction graph.

## Where does PayJoin fit among privacy tools?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| [Your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) | Keeps your addresses from third parties |
| [Coin control](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/) | Stops your coins being linked together |
| PayJoin | Defeats the common-input-ownership heuristic |
| [CoinJoin](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) | Cuts the traceability of a coin's history |
| [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/) | Hides your IP address when transacting |

</div>

The strongest privacy uses several layers together.

## Where can you read more?

- [BIP78](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0078.mediawiki), the PayJoin specification
- [BTCPay Server's PayJoin documentation](https://docs.btcpayserver.org/Payjoin/), for merchants
- [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com), which sends PayJoins

# Bitcoin Nodes: What They Are and Why They Matter

> What Bitcoin nodes do, why running your own matters for self-custody, and how a personal node verifies every transaction without trusting third parties.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A Bitcoin node is software that downloads the blockchain, checks every block and transaction against the consensus rules, and answers wallets' questions. Running your own means you stop trusting someone else's view of the chain and verify it yourself. For self-custody it matters more than most people realise: without your own node, your wallet asks a stranger's server about your balance and transactions, revealing your addresses and trusting the answers.

## What does this section cover?

| Page | What it explains |
|---|---|
| [What is a Bitcoin node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/what-is-node/) | What a node does, the kinds of node, and how a node differs from a wallet |
| [Why run your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/why-run-node/) | The privacy and verification you gain, and the common objections |

The [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) sets one up.


---

# What is a Bitcoin Node

> Understand what a Bitcoin node does, how it differs from a wallet, and its role in the network. Essential knowledge before running your own node.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/what-is-node/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A **Bitcoin node** is a computer running software, usually Bitcoin Core, that keeps a copy of the blockchain, checks every block and transaction against bitcoin's rules, relays them to other nodes, and answers wallets' questions. Every wallet depends on a node to see its balance and send transactions; the only question is whose. With someone else's node, its operator learns your addresses and you trust its answers. With your own, you verify everything yourself and your queries go nowhere.

## What does a node do?
