### It stores the blockchain

A full node downloads and keeps the complete blockchain: every transaction since the first block was mined in January 2009. That was about 770 GB in September 2026, growing by roughly 75 GB a year.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A full node stores the complete chain of blocks from block 1 in January 2009 to block 970,000 and beyond, about 770 GB in September 2026, so it can verify any claim about any transaction locally](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nodes/block-chain-copy.svg)

</div>

Having the complete history means the node can verify any claim about any transaction itself, without trusting anyone.

### It verifies everything

A node believes nothing it is told. For every new block and transaction it checks every rule itself: whether the signatures are valid, whether the coins being spent exist and are unspent, whether the block follows the consensus rules. A block that breaks any rule, even by one satoshi, is rejected, whatever other nodes do. Your node enforces the rules you chose to run.

### It relays transactions and blocks

Nodes communicate with each other in a peer-to-peer mesh, sharing new transactions as they're created, propagating new blocks as they're mined, and helping new nodes synchronize with the current state. When you broadcast a transaction, your node sends it to its peers, who send it to their peers, until it reaches miners who can include it in a block.

### It keeps a mempool

Before transactions are confirmed in blocks, they wait in the **mempool**, a holding area of pending transactions. Each node keeps its own, deciding which unconfirmed transactions to hold on the basis of validity and fee rate.

### It answers wallets

When your wallet needs to check your balance, see if a payment arrived, or broadcast a transaction you've signed, it asks a node. That node sees exactly what your wallet is asking about: your addresses, your transactions, your financial activity.

## How is a node different from a wallet?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Node | Wallet |
|------|--------|
| Stores the full blockchain | Stores only your keys |
| Verifies every transaction | Creates your transactions |
| Serves data to wallets | Needs a node to function |
| No private keys | Contains private keys |
| Anyone can run one | Personal to you |

</div>

A wallet cannot work without a node; the question is whose.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A wallet holds keys but must ask a node for balances, incoming payments and broadcasting; every question reveals the wallet's addresses to whichever node answers](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nodes/wallet-asks-node.svg)

</div>

## Why does it matter whose node your wallet uses?

A wallet's questions reveal your addresses, your transaction history, your balance and when you are online to whichever node answers them. Someone else's node learns all of it, and "someone else" could be a careful volunteer, a chain analysis company or anything in between.

### Random public nodes

Many wallets connect to public servers by default. It works without any setup, but every query tells an unknown operator which addresses belong to your wallet:

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A wallet's queries can go to a random public node, whose unknown operator logs the addresses and builds a profile, or to your own node, where the queries never leave your home](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nodes/who-answers.svg)

</div>

Combined with timing and transaction patterns, that builds a detailed profile.

### Your own node

With your own node, the leak disappears: the wallet asks your node, and the questions never leave your control. That makes running a node a basic privacy measure, not a hobby for enthusiasts.

## What kinds of node are there?

### Full node

A **full node** downloads and verifies the whole blockchain, every block and transaction from the first to the latest, and is what people usually mean by running a node. It gives full verification and the best privacy, since queries stay local. The cost is storage (about 770 GB as of September 2026, growing by roughly 75 GB a year) plus an initial sync that can take hours to days depending on your hardware.

### Pruned node

A **pruned node** is a full node that deletes old block data once it has verified it. It still checks everything, but needs only about 10 GB of storage; in exchange it cannot serve old blocks to other nodes or run an Electrum server, which needs the full history.

### Light client (SPV)

A **light client** downloads only block headers, small summaries that show whether a transaction is in a block, and asks full nodes for everything else. It is fast and needs almost no storage, but it trusts the nodes it asks, which is acceptable for small amounts and not for serious holdings or privacy.

### Bitcoin Core

Bitcoin Core is the reference implementation, the original Bitcoin software maintained by the community since Satoshi's initial release. When people say "run a node," they usually mean running Bitcoin Core.

Alternatives such as Bitcoin Knots exist, but Bitcoin Core is the most widely used and the usual choice.

## What does "don't trust, verify" mean?

"Don't trust, verify" is the design principle that separates bitcoin from earlier financial systems. Traditional finance requires trust at every layer: trust that banks are solvent, trust that ledgers are accurate, trust that institutions follow the rules. Bitcoin replaces that trust with verification.

Without your own node, you're reintroducing trust. You trust someone else to tell you your correct balance. You trust them to accurately report whether transactions are valid. You trust them not to lie about the blockchain state.

With your own node, that trust becomes unnecessary. You verify everything yourself. You can't be deceived about your balance because you've independently confirmed it. You enforce Bitcoin's rules directly because you check every rule on every transaction.

## What does running your own node give you?

**Privacy.** When your wallet talks to your node, no third party learns which addresses belong to you, what your balance is, or what transactions you're making. This is the single biggest privacy upgrade most Bitcoiners can make.

**Security.** You verify your own transactions against your own copy of the blockchain. No one can fool you with fake confirmations or misleading balance information. What your node says is what's true, because your node has verified it independently.

**Sovereignty.** You're not just using Bitcoin. You're participating in it. Your node validates the consensus rules, and by running it, you're part of the decentralized enforcement mechanism that keeps Bitcoin working.

**Network health.** Every node makes Bitcoin stronger. The more nodes exist, the more copies of the blockchain exist, the harder it becomes to attack or censor the network. Running a node isn't just self-interested: it's a contribution to Bitcoin's resilience.

## What do people get wrong about nodes?

### Do you need a node to hold bitcoin?

No. Your wallet holds bitcoin via private keys. A node is for verification and privacy. You can absolutely hold bitcoin without running a node; you'll just be trusting someone else's node for information about your holdings.

### Does running a node earn bitcoin?

No. Nodes don't earn rewards. Mining earns rewards. Nodes verify transactions and propagate blocks, but this service is provided for free. The reward is the security and privacy benefits to the node operator.

### Do you need technical skills to run a node?

Much less than you used to. Modern node software (especially user-friendly distributions like Umbrel or RaspiBlitz) has made running a node accessible to anyone who can follow basic instructions. If you can set up a Raspberry Pi or install software on a computer, you can run a node.

### Is your hardware wallet a node?

No. Hardware wallets store keys and sign transactions. That's it. They have no blockchain data and can't verify anything independently. When you check your balance on a hardware wallet setup, that information is coming from a node somewhere, either yours or someone else's.


---

# Why Run Your Own Node

> Understand why running your own Bitcoin node matters for privacy, security, and true self-custody. Learn the risks of using third-party nodes.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/why-run-node/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Running your own Bitcoin node is not required to hold bitcoin, but it completes self-custody: your keys sign, and your own node verifies. Without one, your wallet tells someone else's server all your addresses, balances and history, and trusts that server to tell the truth about payments and confirmations. With one, nobody learns what you own and nobody can fool you about whether you were paid. It costs a small computer, a 2 TB SSD and a few days of syncing.

## What does a third-party node learn about you?

Every time your wallet connects to someone else's node or server, it reveals:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| What is revealed | What the operator can do with it |
|---------------------|------|
| All your addresses | Map your whole wallet |
| Your balances | Know how much bitcoin you have |
| Your transaction history | Build a financial profile |
| Your IP address | Link your addresses to your location |
| When you are online | Learn your patterns of activity |
| Addresses you have not used yet | Wallets often ask about these in advance |

</div>

Public servers can be run by anyone: analysis companies building databases of who owns which address, exchanges following what customers do after withdrawing, governments monitoring finances, or thieves looking for targets. You cannot know who runs the ones your wallet connects to.

## Can someone else's node lie to you?

Yes. Without your own node, you trust others to tell you the truth about the blockchain.

### Fake confirmations

A skilled attacker who can control which node your wallet talks to can show it a payment that does not exist on the real blockchain, and the wallet will display it as confirmed.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The fake confirmation attack: an attacker's node tells your wallet a 10 BTC payment is confirmed while no such transaction exists on the real chain, and the loss surfaces later; your own node verifies blocks itself, making the lie impossible](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nodes/fake-confirmation.svg)

</div>

It is difficult to pull off, but not impossible in a targeted attack.

### The wrong chain

If bitcoin splits into competing versions, as Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash did in 2017, a wallet can end up connected to a node following the other one, and you may believe you received bitcoin when you received a different coin with different rules and value. Your own node follows the rules you chose to run.

## What does your own node verify?

Your node checks for itself that every transaction is valid, that every block follows every rule, and that your balance is real. Your security then rests on your wallet and your own verification, instead of your wallet and a node of unknown honesty, and a payment counts as confirmed only when your node has verified the block it is in.

## How does a node complete self-custody?

Self-custody has three parts: you control the keys (a hardware wallet), you verify the transactions (your own node), and you depend on no third party. A hardware wallet alone covers the first; the node covers the other two.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Complete self-custody stands on three legs: a hardware wallet that signs, your own node that verifies, and your own connection that broadcasts; together they give full control with no third party in the loop](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nodes/self-custody-trio.svg)

</div>

## What else does a node give you?

- It strengthens the network: more nodes make bitcoin harder to attack and more decentralised, and running one is taking part in enforcing its rules.
- It teaches you how bitcoin works: how transactions spread, how blocks are checked, how the mempool fills and empties.
- It powers other services: your own Electrum server, a Lightning node, a block explorer or payment processing.

## What are the common objections?

### Isn't it too technical?

Not any more. If you can install an app and wait for it to sync, you can run a node, and packages such as Umbrel and RaspiBlitz make it easier still.

### Isn't the storage too much?

A pruned node needs only about 10 GB. A full node needs about 770 GB as of September 2026, and a 2 TB SSD costs far less than the bitcoin it protects.

### What if you don't leave your computer on?

A node only needs to be running when you use your wallet, and it catches up when switched on. A dedicated small computer or old laptop left running is more convenient.

### What if you're not a target?

You may not be today. But privacy is easier to keep than to recover, and you cannot know who is logging data for later use.

## Who should run a node?

| | Who |
|---|---|
| Strongly recommended | Anyone holding significant bitcoin, valuing financial privacy, regularly receiving bitcoin, or using self-custodial Lightning |
| Worth doing | Anyone who wants to learn how bitcoin works, support the network, or depend less on others |
| Can wait | Complete beginners, people holding very small amounts, and people who only use custodial services |

The [node guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) sets one up.


---

# Bitcoin Wallet Setup: Hardware Wallet & Backup Guides

> Step-by-step Bitcoin wallet setup guides. Learn to configure hardware wallets, verify backups, and complete the pre-deposit security checklist.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Setting up self-custody takes three guides, done in order: [set up a hardware wallet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/), [verify that the backup restores it](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/), then work through the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/). Together they take two to three hours, and nothing significant should go into the wallet until all three are done. If bitcoin itself is new to you, read [Start here](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/) first.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The wallet setup path in order: configure the hardware wallet, verify the backup actually restores it, then run the final pre-deposit checks; nothing gets funded until all three steps pass](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallet-setup/setup-path.svg)

</div>

## What does each guide cover?

| Guide | Time | What it covers | Do it after |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Hardware wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/) | 1-2 hours | Buying and checking the device, firmware and PIN, a seed made with your own dice, wallet software (Sparrow), checking a receive address | Nothing: most people start here |
| [Backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) | 30-60 minutes | Restoring the wallet from the written backup alone and comparing addresses, testing a passphrase, what to do if it fails | Hardware wallet setup |
| [Before you deposit](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/) | 15-30 minutes | The final checks: seed, recovery test, passphrase, address on the device, genuine software, a test transaction | Backup verification |

If you already have a hardware wallet, start with [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/).

## Which hardware wallet should you use?

| Situation | Recommendation (prices October 2026) |
|-----------|----------------|
| Budget | Blockstream Jade ($79) |
| Simplicity | BitBox02 Nova, Bitcoin-only edition (€175) or Trezor Safe 5 ($129) |
| Verifiable security | Jade Plus ($149) with a [dice-generated seed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) |
| Full transparency | Trezor Safe 7 ($249, with an auditable secure element) |

The [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) covers every device and why Coldcard, Ledger and Bitkey are not on this list, and [choose your setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/choosing-your-path/) matches a setup to how much you hold.

## When is a software wallet enough?

A [software wallet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/software-wallets/) keeps the keys on your phone or computer. It is free and convenient, and acceptable for amounts under about $1,000, for learning, and as a spending wallet alongside a hardware wallet for savings. It is not the place for significant savings or long-term holdings, because the keys sit on a device that also runs everything else.

## What comes after setup?

1. [Run your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), so your wallet checks transactions itself.
2. Learn [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/), for privacy and lower fees.
3. [Add a passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/), as a second secret protecting the seed phrase.
4. Move to [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) for larger holdings.

## Common questions

### Do you need to buy a hardware wallet?

For anything more than pocket money, yes. A hardware wallet is the minimum we recommend for any amount you would be upset to lose, because it keeps the keys off the computer and phone that malware can reach.

### Which is better: Trezor, Ledger or Coldcard?

As of October 2026, Trezor is the one of the three we recommend: open source, with a long security record. Coldcard is not currently recommended, because its [2026 entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) cost users about $116 million after a warning about the flaw had been dismissed. Ledger's secure element firmware is closed source, which means trusting what you cannot verify. Jade, BitBox02 Nova and Passport are also worth considering; the [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) covers them all.

### Can you use the same seed on several devices?

You can, but it is rarely a good idea: every device holding the seed is another place it can be stolen from, and none of them adds protection against losing it. If you want redundancy, [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) gives it without copying one seed around.

### What if you already have a hardware wallet set up?

Start with [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) to confirm your existing backup restores the wallet, then work through the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/).


---

# Hardware Wallet Setup: Step-by-Step Bitcoin Security Guide

> Step-by-step guide to setting up your first hardware wallet. Learn how to initialize, secure, and use a hardware wallet for Bitcoin self-custody.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Setting up a hardware wallet takes one to two hours: buy the device from its maker, check it is genuine, update the firmware, set a PIN, create the seed phrase (ideally with your own dice rolls), write it down, test the backup, then connect the device to wallet software such as Sparrow and confirm a receive address on the device's own screen. Done this way, your private keys are created on the device and never leave it, so malware on your computer cannot reach them or change a payment without the device showing you.

Time: 1-2 hours. Cost: $80-250 (hardware wallet). Level: Beginner to intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

## What is a hardware wallet?

A hardware wallet is a small dedicated device that creates and stores your bitcoin private keys and signs transactions with them, without the keys ever leaving it. It does four things an online phone or computer wallet cannot:

- It generates the seed phrase inside the device, offline.
- It keeps the keys in isolated storage that the computer cannot read.
- It signs transactions internally; the computer only ever sees the signed result.
- It shows the address and amount on its own screen, which malware on the computer cannot redraw.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Sending from a hardware wallet: the software creates the transaction, the device screen shows the real recipient and the 1,500 sat fee, you press confirm on the device and it signs, then the software broadcasts; malware can redraw a monitor but not the device screen](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallet-setup/hw-signing.svg)

</div>

You do not need a hardware wallet to hold bitcoin yourself. It is a facilitator: a transaction can be built on an online computer, signed by hand on a computer that never goes online, and broadcast from any node, as [do you need a hardware wallet?](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/#do-you-need-a-hardware-wallet-to-hold-bitcoin) shows step by step. A hardware wallet makes that offline signing quick and hard to get wrong, which is why this guide uses one.

## Which hardware wallet should you buy?

For a first device, we recommend the BitBox02 Nova (Bitcoin-only edition) or the Trezor Safe 5: both are easy to use, and both restore a seed you made yourself with dice. For security you can verify more of yourself, the Jade Plus or Passport Prime, which sign over QR codes without a cable. If you want to build your own, a [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/) (our favourite, though not for beginners; see the [build guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/)) or a Krux, which keep no seed in memory, so every bit of entropy is yours. The [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) has current prices and the reasoning for each, and three of them have step-by-step guides of their own: the [Trezor Safe 5](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/trezor-safe-5/), the [BitBox02 Nova](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/bitbox02-nova/) and the [Jade Plus](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/jade-plus/), each set up on a seed made with dice.

Two familiar names are missing. Coldcard was our security pick for years, until the [2026 entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/): a firmware flaw present since 2021 made device-generated seeds guessable, and about $116 million was stolen. The flaw is fixed and dice-generated seeds were never affected, but a warning about that exact code was dismissed in 2025, so we do not recommend new purchases until trust is rebuilt; if you own one, [check whether you are affected](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/#am-i-affected). Ledger devices run closed-source secure-element firmware that nobody outside Ledger can audit, which after 2026 is more trust than we are willing to recommend.

## What do you need before you start?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Item | Why |
|------|---------|
| The hardware wallet, bought from its maker | Devices from marketplaces and resellers can be tampered with |
| A computer or phone | Runs the wallet software |
| The USB cable (or a microSD card, for air-gapped devices) | Connects the device; most come with one |
| A metal backup plate, or paper for now | Holds the seed phrase; metal survives fire and water |
| A pen, not a pencil | Pencil smudges and fades |
| Six dice, ideally casino dice | For your own entropy in step 3 |
| An hour in a private room | No cameras, no visitors, no rush |

</div>

## Step 1: Verify the device is genuine

Step 1 checks the device was not opened or swapped before it reached you. Before powering it on, look for signs that the packaging was opened or resealed and that any tamper seals are intact. Then, once it is on, run the maker's authenticity check; Trezor Suite and the BitBoxApp, for example, check the device's attestation during first setup. If anything fails or looks wrong, stop and contact the maker; do not set the device up.

## Step 2: Update the firmware and set a PIN

Step 2 prepares the device. Power it on and follow its prompts:

1. Choose language and region.
2. Update to the latest firmware, and read the vendor's security advisories page. The 2026 Coldcard incident hit seeds generated on old, flawed firmware.
3. Set a PIN. Avoid 1234, 0000, repeated digits and birthdays; pick a random PIN you can remember, or write it down separately from the seed phrase.
4. Choose to create a new wallet.

## Step 3: Create the seed phrase with your own entropy

Step 3 decides how much you are trusting the manufacturer. A device that generates the seed by itself is trusted completely to produce good randomness, and in 2026 [that trust failed in public](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) at nine-figure scale.

The recommended way is a seed made from your own dice rolls. On a device that takes dice rolls during setup (the Keystone 3 Pro, SeedSigner or Krux), 99 rolls of a six-sided die cover a 24-word seed even if the device's own generator is broken. The Trezor Safe 5 has no dice entry as of October 2026, so with it you [make the seed yourself](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and restore it onto the device, which also makes every step checkable; BitBox and Blockstream document their own procedures, in which dice choose the words and the BitBox02 or Jade supplies a valid last word. A seed the device makes on its own is acceptable only for starter amounts, and then with a [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) added, so the funds do not rest on the device's randomness alone.

The device shows the 12 or 24 words one at a time. Write each one in order, numbered and spelled exactly. Never photograph the words or type them into anything but the hardware wallet itself.

**Warning: A firmware update cannot fix a weak seed**
A seed made by flawed firmware stays weak after the firmware is updated, which is why affected Coldcard owners had to move their funds to new wallets. Make the seed on current firmware, with your own entropy, and that migration never arises.

## Step 4: Check the backup

Step 4 confirms what you wrote down. Most devices quiz you on a few words from the seed phrase before finishing setup. That check catches a missed word, but not a misspelled word the device never asked about, and it does not prove the backup restores your wallet. Do the full test in the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) before you deposit more than a small amount.

## Step 5: Set up wallet software

Step 5 installs the software that shows your balance, builds transactions and keeps track of addresses; the hardware wallet only signs.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Software | Platform | Works with |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com/) | Desktop | Any hardware wallet |
| Nunchuk | Desktop and mobile | Any hardware wallet, including multisig |
| Trezor Suite | Desktop and web | Trezor devices |
| BitBoxApp | Desktop and mobile | BitBox02 |
| BlueWallet | Mobile | Air-gapped devices and watch-only wallets |

</div>

We recommend Sparrow for most people: it works with every major hardware wallet, connects to your own node when you have one, and gives you coin control.

## Step 6: Connect and verify a receive address

Step 6 proves the software and the device agree on the wallet.

1. Connect the hardware wallet and open the wallet software.
2. Add the hardware wallet as a new wallet or keystore.
3. Show a receive address in the software, then display it on the device.
4. Check that the two match, character by character.

Malware can show a fake address on a computer screen, so the device's screen is the one to believe, every time you receive and every time you send.

## How do you send and receive the first time?

To receive:

1. Click Receive in the wallet software to show a new address.
2. Display the same address on the hardware wallet and check it matches.
3. Give the address to the sender, and send a small amount first.
4. Wait for at least one confirmation.

To send:

1. Create the transaction in the software, with the recipient's address and the amount.
2. Check the recipient, the amount and the fee on the hardware wallet's screen.
3. Approve it on the device.
4. Let the software broadcast the signed transaction.

## What mistakes should you avoid?

| Mistake | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Storing the seed phrase digitally: a photo, notes app, cloud drive, password manager or email | Anything stored on a connected device can be copied by malware or a breached account |
| A weak PIN | A stolen device with a guessable PIN is a stolen wallet |
| Not testing the backup | A wrong word is discovered only when the device fails, which is too late |
| Trusting the computer screen | Malware can replace an address on the computer; it cannot on the device |
| Buying from marketplaces | Tampered and pre-seeded devices have been sold on eBay and Amazon |

## Should you add a passphrase?

A passphrase, sometimes called the "25th word", is an extra secret that turns your seed phrase into a different wallet, so that someone who finds the words alone finds nothing. It also adds a way to lose everything: forgetting it, or getting one character wrong, opens an empty wallet, and it must be backed up separately from the seed phrase. Add one once you are comfortable with the device; the [passphrase guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) covers when it is worth it and how to make a strong one.

## What should you do after setup?

1. [Verify the backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) by restoring from it.
2. Receive a small amount first, and send it once, before moving the rest.
3. Connect the wallet to [your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) for privacy.
4. Learn [UTXO management](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/utxo-management/).
5. Consider [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) once the holdings are significant.


---

# How to Set Up a Trezor Safe 5 With a Dice Seed

> Set up a Trezor Safe 5 on 24 words you made with dice: Bitcoin-only firmware, recovery on the touchscreen, PIN, passphrase and Sparrow, from Trezor's guides.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/trezor-safe-5/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To set up a Trezor Safe 5 on randomness you control, make a 24-word seed with dice first, then let Trezor Suite install the firmware and check the device is genuine, choose Recover instead of creating a wallet, and type the 24 words on the device's touchscreen. As of October 2026 the Safe 5 cannot take dice rolls itself, so restoring a seed you made is the only way to supply your own entropy; it also gives you a standard BIP39 seed that almost every wallet can restore. Then set a PIN, test the backup, add a passphrase if you want one, and connect Sparrow, checking every address on the Trezor's own screen.

Time: 1-2 hours, plus the dice. Cost: $129 (device). Level: Beginner. Reviewed: 26 Oct 2026. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: A Trezor Safe 5, a 24-word seed made with dice, a computer with Trezor Suite and Sparrow.

Every step below follows Trezor's own guides as of October 2026, linked at the end. We have reviewed them against Trezor's documentation; we have not yet done this setup on a Safe 5 ourselves.

## What do you need before you start?

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| A Trezor Safe 5, bought from trezor.io or an authorised reseller | A device from a marketplace may have been tampered with |
| A computer with [Trezor Suite](https://trezor.io/start) | Installs the firmware and runs the authenticity check. Trezor's guide says iPhone users must use the desktop app |
| 24 words made with dice, on paper | The seed you will restore; the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and the [dice worksheet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/worksheets/dice-seed/) make it |
| [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com/) | The wallet software we recommend once setup is done |
| An hour in a private room | No cameras, no visitors |

## Why restore a seed instead of letting the Trezor create one?

A Trezor Safe 5 that creates a wallet itself makes a 20-word backup in Trezor's SLIP39 format from the device's own randomness mixed with randomness from the computer. Trezor Suite's entropy check, run automatically on firmware 2.8.7 or later, confirms the device really mixed in the computer's part, and Trezor said in August 2026 that its devices were not affected by the [Coldcard entropy flaw](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/). A seed you make with dice does not depend on either generator, and you can check every step of it yourself. Trezor's own backup page lists BIP39 backups of 12 and 24 words as supported on the Safe 5, so a dice seed restores normally.

## Step 1: Make the 24 words with dice

Step 1 creates the seed before the Trezor is involved. Follow the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/): 99 rolls of a six-sided die give the 256 bits of a 24-word seed, and the guide calculates the last word, which carries the checksum, on an offline computer. Write the 24 words on paper, numbered, and check the spelling against the BIP39 word list. Trezor has no dice method of its own as of October 2026; on 5 August 2026 it said it was considering user-supplied entropy, without committing to it.

## Step 2: Install Trezor Suite and the firmware

Step 2 puts current firmware on the device. Download Trezor Suite for desktop from [trezor.io/start](https://trezor.io/start), connect the Safe 5 with its USB-C cable, and click **Set up my Trezor** after the device security check. Trezor Suite offers two firmware types: choose **Bitcoin-only**, which leaves out the code for other coins, then click **Install firmware**. The device restarts by itself when the install finishes.

## Step 3: Pass the authenticity check

Step 3 confirms the device is a genuine Trezor. Click **Start** in Trezor Suite and follow the prompts on the device. If the check fails, stop: do not set the device up, and contact Trezor support. You can skip the optional "Know your Trezor" tutorial that follows.

## Step 4: Recover the dice seed on the touchscreen

Step 4 loads your 24 words onto the device. When Trezor Suite offers to create a new wallet or recover one, choose **Recover**, then:

1. Click **Start Recovery** and confirm on the device.
2. Accept the terms on the touchscreen.
3. Select the number of words on the device: 24. Trezor's default is 20, so change it.
4. Enter each word on the touchscreen in order. The keyboard is T9-style: tap the tile holding each letter once, and the device suggests matching words.
5. Tap the green checkmark to confirm each word.

When all 24 are accepted, the device shows "Wallet recovery completed". Type the words only on the Trezor, never into Trezor Suite, a website or any other app.

## Step 5: Set a PIN

Step 5 locks the device. Set a PIN on the device when Trezor Suite asks, or later under **Settings**, then **Device**. Trezor accepts 4 to 50 digits; avoid sequences and dates. After 16 wrong PIN attempts the Safe 5 erases the wallet, which you can then recover only from your 24 words.

## Step 6: Check the backup

Step 6 proves the paper matches the device. Trezor Suite's recovery check has you enter the backup words on the device and confirms they match the wallet it holds, without wiping anything. That catches a miswritten word, but the full test is restoring from the paper alone and comparing addresses, as the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) describes. Do it before you deposit more than a small amount.

## Step 7: Add a passphrase if you want one

Step 7 is optional. A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) turns the same 24 words into a separate hidden wallet, so the words alone open nothing of value. Turn it on in Trezor Suite under **Settings**, **Device**, **Passphrase**, then open the hidden wallet from the wallet menu at the top left with **+ Passphrase wallet**, and type the passphrase on the Safe 5 rather than in Trezor Suite. Trezor passphrases are case-sensitive and up to 50 ASCII characters.

**Warning: A mistyped passphrase opens an empty wallet, not an error**
Trezor does not store the passphrase and cannot recover it. Any other string, including one with a single wrong character, opens a different and empty wallet. Write the passphrase down, keep it apart from the 24 words, and test opening the hidden wallet before you put funds in it.

## Step 8: Connect Sparrow and check a receive address

Step 8 moves daily use to Sparrow, which works with every major hardware wallet and with [your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/). Close Trezor Suite first: only one application can talk to the device at a time. Then, following Sparrow's guide:

1. In Sparrow, choose **File**, **New Wallet**, name it, and select **Connected Hardware Wallet**.
2. Click **Scan…** with the Trezor connected and unlocked. On Linux, if nothing is found, install the device rules with **Tools**, **Install Udev Rules**.
3. If you use a passphrase, switch on the passphrase toggle Sparrow shows for the Trezor, and enter it on the device.
4. Click **Import Keystore**, then **Apply**, and set a password for the wallet file.
5. Open **Receive**, click **Display Address**, and check that the address on the Trezor's screen matches Sparrow's, character by character.

The Trezor's screen is the one to believe, every time you receive and every time you send, because malware can change what a computer shows but not what the device shows.

## Common questions

### Can the Trezor Safe 5 take dice rolls?

No. As of October 2026 the Trezor Safe 5 has no way to enter dice rolls during setup and Trezor documents no dice procedure. The way to supply your own entropy is to make the seed with dice and restore it, as this guide does.

### Should I choose Bitcoin-only or Standard firmware?

Choose Bitcoin-only if you hold only bitcoin. It leaves out the code for other coins, so less code runs next to your keys, and Trezor Suite installs either type in the same step.

### What if Trezor Suite shows a zero balance after I restore?

A zero balance after a restore usually means a different wallet was opened, not that funds are gone. Check each of the 24 words against your paper, check that a passphrase was entered exactly, and check that the wallet software uses the same address type as before, usually native segwit with addresses starting `bc1q`.

## Where do these steps come from?

These steps follow Trezor's and Sparrow's documentation as read on 26 October 2026: [Get started with the Trezor Safe 5](https://trezor.io/guides/trezor-devices/trezor-safe-5/get-started-with-the-trezor-safe-5), [Recover wallet on Trezor Safe 5](https://trezor.io/guides/backups-recovery/general-standards/recover-wallet-on-trezor-safe-5), [Understanding Trezor wallet backups](https://trezor.io/learn/security-privacy/how-trezor-keeps-you-safe/understanding-trezor-wallet-backups-12-20-or-24-words), [Entropy check](https://trezor.io/learn/security-privacy/how-trezor-keeps-you-safe/entropy-check-how-trezor-suite-verifies-wallet-generation), [What is a passphrase?](https://trezor.io/guides/backups-recovery/advanced-wallets/what-is-a-passphrase), Trezor's [statement on the Coldcard vulnerability](https://trezor.io/blog/news/coldcard-vulnerability-trezor-devices-are-not-affected), and Sparrow's [connected wallet guide](https://sparrowwallet.com/docs/connected-wallet.html). Menu labels change between versions of Trezor Suite; if a label differs, the vendor's current guide is the authority.


---

# How to Set Up a BitBox02 Nova With a Dice Seed

> Set up a BitBox02 Nova on 24 words chosen with dice: pairing, the genuine check, restoring the words on the device, passphrase and Sparrow, from BitBox's docs.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/bitbox02-nova/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To set up a BitBox02 Nova on randomness you control, choose the 24 words with dice first, then pair the Nova with the BitBoxApp, let the app check the device is genuine, and pick **Restore from recovery words** instead of creating a wallet, entering each word on the Nova itself. As of October 2026 the Nova does not take dice rolls on the device, but BitBox documents its own dice procedure, written for the BitBox02, in which you pick 23 words from a printed table and the device offers the valid last words. Then set the device password, test the backup, add a passphrase if you want one, and connect Sparrow or keep using the BitBoxApp, checking every address on the Nova's screen.

Time: 1-2 hours, plus the dice. Cost: About €175 (device). Level: Beginner. Reviewed: 26 Oct 2026. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: A BitBox02 Nova, five dice and a coin, the BitBoxApp, and optionally Sparrow.

Every step below follows BitBox's own guides as of October 2026, linked at the end. We have reviewed them against BitBox's documentation; we have not yet done this setup on a Nova ourselves.

## What do you need before you start?

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| A BitBox02 Nova, bought from bitbox.swiss or an authorised reseller | A device from a marketplace may have been tampered with |
| The [BitBoxApp](https://bitbox.swiss/download/) on a computer, Android phone, iPhone or iPad | Installs the firmware, checks the device and runs setup |
| Five dice (or one die rolled five times) and a coin, or six dice for the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) | Your own entropy for the 24 words |
| BitBox's [diceware instructions](https://bitbox.swiss/bitbox02/BitBox_Diceware_HowTo.pdf) and [lookup table](https://bitbox.swiss/bitbox02/BitBox_Diceware_LookupTable.pdf), printed | Only for BitBox's own dice procedure |
| [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com/), optionally | The wallet software we recommend for daily use |
| An hour in a private room | No cameras, no visitors |

## Why restore a seed instead of letting the Nova create one?

A BitBox02 Nova that creates a wallet itself generates the seed from its own randomness, and BitBox's default setup saves that seed to a microSD card, which BitBox's Nova guide notes is unencrypted by default. A seed whose words you chose with dice does not depend on the device's random number generator, the failure behind the [Coldcard entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/), and 24 words on paper or metal do not depend on a memory card staying readable.

## Step 1: Choose the words with dice

Step 1 creates the seed before the Nova is involved, in one of two ways that both give 24 BIP39 words.

BitBox's diceware procedure uses five dice and a coin for each word. Reroll any die showing 5 or 6 until all five show 1 to 4, keeping the dice in their positions, then flip the coin. In BitBox's printed lookup table the first die picks the page, the first four dice pick the row, and the fifth die with the coin picks the column. Write words 1 to 23 and leave word 24 blank: the device supplies it in step 4. BitBox's page describes this for the BitBox02 and, as of October 2026, does not name the Nova; it uses the same **Restore from recovery words** option the Nova's setup offers.

The other way is our [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/): 99 rolls of a six-sided die make all 24 words, and an offline computer calculates the last one, so the device does not choose any part of the seed.

Either way, record rolls only on paper, and never type the words into a computer, phone or website.

## Step 2: Install the BitBoxApp and pair the Nova

Step 2 connects the device. Install the BitBoxApp from [bitbox.swiss/download](https://bitbox.swiss/download/); on an iPhone or iPad, install it from the App Store and check the publisher is Shift Crypto AG, since similarly named apps from other publishers are not BitBox's. Then:

1. Connect the Nova by USB-C to a computer or Android phone. An iPhone or iPad has no USB data connection for it, so there the Nova pairs over Bluetooth: tap the Bluetooth ID the Nova shows, and check that the code iOS displays matches the one on the Nova.
2. Choose the screen orientation on the Nova.
3. Compare the pairing code in the app with the one on the Nova, and confirm on the device.
4. On a new device, tap **Install firmware** and wait without closing the app or unplugging the Nova.

## Step 3: Check the Nova is genuine

Step 3 confirms the device came from BitBox. The BitBoxApp checks this automatically every time the device connects: it sends a random challenge that the device must sign with a key created in its secure chip and certified by BitBox at the factory. If the check fails, the app shows a large red warning that the device is not authentic; stop there and contact BitBox. The sealed bag and seal pattern on the packaging are a rough first check only, because packaging can be copied.

## Step 4: Restore the dice words on the device

Step 4 loads your seed onto the Nova. In the **Set up your wallet** screen:

1. Select **Restore from recovery words**, even though the wallet is new.
2. Name the device, click **Continue**, and confirm the name on the Nova.
3. Check and confirm the date on the device.
4. Choose 24 words.
5. Enter each word letter by letter on the Nova, in order. With BitBox's diceware procedure, enter words 1 to 23; the device then offers eight valid last words. Flip a coin three times (heads-heads-heads for the first, tails-tails-tails for the eighth), select that word, and write it on your paper as word 24.
6. Set the device password on the Nova and enter it again to confirm.

The BitBoxApp then synchronises, and the wallet is ready. The words go into the Nova only, never into the BitBoxApp.

## Step 5: Test the backup

Step 5 proves the paper restores the wallet. Restoring from your own words already shows that they load, but not that the paper you will keep is correct: a word copied wrong after setup would surface only on the day you need it. Test the written copy as the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) describes before you deposit more than a small amount.

## Step 6: Add a passphrase if you want one

Step 6 is optional. A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) turns the same words into a separate hidden wallet. In the BitBoxApp, open **Settings**, **Manage device**, and under **Expert settings** select **Passphrase**, then **Enable passphrase**, and confirm on the Nova. From then on, after the device password the Nova asks for the passphrase, which you enter on the device and check character by character on its display before confirming. BitBox accepts up to 149 characters: letters, digits, spaces and standard ASCII symbols, all of which count. A typo opens a different, empty wallet without any error, and BitBox cannot recover a lost passphrase, so note the wallet's root fingerprint and send a small test amount first.

## Step 7: Connect Sparrow and check a receive address

Step 7 is optional: the BitBoxApp is BitBox's own wallet software and covers daily use. To use [Sparrow](https://sparrowwallet.com/), which connects to [your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/), follow BitBox's Sparrow guide:

1. Update the Nova's firmware in the BitBoxApp, then close the BitBoxApp completely; while it is open, Sparrow cannot connect.
2. In Sparrow, click **New Wallet**, name it, click **Create Wallet**, and select **Connect Hardware Wallet**.
3. With the Nova connected, click **Scan**, and enter the device password on the Nova. The first time, confirm that the pairing code matches in Sparrow and on the Nova.
4. Choose **Keystore #0** from the arrow beside **Import Keystore**, then click **Import Keystore**.
5. Set **Policy Type** to Single Signature and **Script Type** to Native Segwit (P2WPKH), click **Apply**, and set a password for the wallet file.
6. Open **Receive**, click **Display Address**, and check that the address on the Nova matches Sparrow's, character by character.

BitBox's Sparrow guide, last updated in August 2025, is written for the BitBox02 and does not name the Nova. If Sparrow does not find the Nova, use the BitBoxApp.

## Common questions

### Can the BitBox02 Nova take dice rolls?

Not on the device. As of October 2026 the way to use dice with a BitBox is BitBox's diceware procedure, in which dice choose 23 words from a printed table and the device offers eight valid last words, or a seed made with the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and restored. BitBox documents its procedure for the BitBox02 without naming the Nova.

### Should I keep a microSD backup as well?

A BitBox microSD backup is not needed when you restore from words, and BitBox's Nova guide notes that such backups are unencrypted by default, so a card is as sensitive as the words themselves. Keep the 24 words on paper or metal and, if you also make a card, store it as carefully as the words.

### What if the BitBoxApp shows a zero balance after I restore?

BitBox's own guide says a zero balance after a restore usually means a different wallet was opened, not that coins are lost. Check the words, check the passphrase if you use one, and let the app finish synchronising. The BitBox02 supports only SegWit and native SegWit accounts, so coins on legacy addresses starting with 1 do not appear in the BitBoxApp.

## Where do these steps come from?

These steps follow BitBox's and Sparrow's documentation as read on 26 October 2026: [How to set up the BitBox02 Nova on iOS](https://support.bitbox.swiss/nova/how-to-set-up-bitbox02-nova-ios), [How to restore from recovery words](https://support.bitbox.swiss/en_US/how-to-restore-from-recovery-words), [Create a Bitcoin wallet with your own entropy](https://support.bitbox.swiss/en_US/wallet-foundations-recovery/create-bitcoin-wallet-own-entropy), [Set up the optional passphrase](https://support.bitbox.swiss/en_US/set-up-bitbox02-optional-passphrase), [Verifying the BitBox02 packaging](https://support.bitbox.swiss/verifying-the-bitbox02-packaging), [Connect the BitBox02 to Sparrow](https://support.bitbox.swiss/en_US/connect-bitbox02-sparrow) and Sparrow's [connected wallet guide](https://sparrowwallet.com/docs/connected-wallet.html). Menu labels change between versions of the BitBoxApp; if a label differs, BitBox's current guide is the authority.


---

# How to Set Up a Jade Plus Air-Gapped With Dice

> Set up a Jade Plus over QR codes on words chosen with dice: firmware, genuine check, final-word calculation, QR PIN Unlock and Sparrow, from Blockstream's docs.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/jade-plus/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To set up a Blockstream Jade Plus air-gapped on randomness you control, update its firmware and run the Genuine Check over USB first, choose 23 words with dice, then pick **Restore Wallet** on the device, enter those words and let the Jade Plus calculate a valid last word. After that, choose QR mode, unlock it with QR PIN Unlock, and add it to Sparrow by scanning QR codes, so the Jade never connects to a computer again for daily use. As of October 2026 the Jade has no dice entry on the device, but Blockstream documents dice methods for choosing the words and the final-word calculation that turns them into a valid seed.

Time: 1-2 hours, plus the dice. Cost: $149 (device). Level: Intermediate. Reviewed: 26 Oct 2026. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: A Jade Plus, dice, a USB cable for the first firmware update, a phone or computer with a camera, and Sparrow.

Every step below follows Blockstream's own help pages as of October 2026, linked at the end. We have reviewed them against Blockstream's documentation; we have not yet done this setup on a Jade Plus ourselves.

## What do you need before you start?

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| A Jade Plus, bought from Blockstream or an authorised reseller | A device from a marketplace may have been tampered with |
| A USB-C cable and a computer with Chrome or another WebSerial browser | The first firmware update and the Genuine Check |
| Dice: one six-sided die is enough | Your own entropy for the words |
| Blockstream's [binary words table](https://help.blockstream.com/generate-recovery-phrase-offline-binary-table), printed | Turns each 11 bits from the dice into a word |
| A phone or computer with a camera | Carries the QR PIN Unlock exchange and talks to Sparrow by QR |
| [Sparrow Wallet](https://sparrowwallet.com/) on a computer with a webcam | The wallet software that builds transactions for the Jade to sign |
| An hour in a private room | No cameras, no visitors |

## How does an air-gapped Jade Plus work?

An air-gapped Jade Plus is a Jade Plus that exchanges data with your wallet software only through QR codes shown on one screen and read by the other's camera, never through a cable or Bluetooth. Sparrow shows the unsigned transaction as an animated QR code, the Jade Plus reads it with its camera, shows the amount and address for you to approve, and displays the signed transaction as a QR code for Sparrow to read back. Nothing but those codes crosses between the two, so malware on the computer can neither reach the keys nor change what the Jade's screen asks you to approve.

## Step 1: Update the firmware and run the Genuine Check

Step 1 is the only part done over a cable. Blockstream recommends updating the firmware before setting the device up. Connect the Jade Plus by USB to a computer, open Blockstream's upgrade web portal in a WebSerial browser such as Chrome, and click **Update your Jade**; the Blockstream app and a command-line script can do the same. A Jade that shipped with firmware older than 1.0.38 should be factory reset before or after its first upgrade.

Then check the device is genuine at [verify.blockstream.com](https://verify.blockstream.com), the web Genuine Check for devices not being set up in the Blockstream app, and select **Yes** on the Jade to sign the challenge. If the check reports that the device is not genuine, stop, do not use it, and contact Blockstream support.

## Step 2: Choose 23 words with dice

Step 2 makes your entropy. Blockstream's six-sided-die method turns each roll into bits: 1 is `00`, 2 is `01`, 3 is `10`, 4 is `11`, 5 is `0` and 6 is `1`. Roll until you have 11 bits (if the last roll gives one bit too many, keep only the leftmost one you need), read the 11 bits left to right, and look the word up in Blockstream's binary words table. Repeat for words 1 to 23, on paper only. Blockstream also documents methods with eight- and sixteen-sided dice that take fewer rolls per word.

You can instead make all 24 words with our [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and enter them in full in step 3, choosing **Existing** for the last word.

## Step 3: Restore the words and let the Jade Plus calculate the last one

Step 3 loads the seed. On the Jade Plus:

1. Select **Set Up Jade**, then **Advanced Setup**, then **Restore Wallet**, and choose 24 words.
2. Enter your 23 words on the Jade's keyboard, in order.
3. Select **Calculate**. The keyboard for the 24th word now accepts only words that make a valid seed.
4. Choose one of the valid words, or click through the calculation and the Jade picks one at random.
5. Write the final word on your paper as word 24.

If the Jade Plus offers to make a SeedQR (a QR code of your seed that you draw by hand on Blockstream's template), you can skip it unless you plan to unlock with a SeedQR instead of a PIN. Test the paper before funding the wallet, as the [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) describes: entering the words once proves they load, not that the copy you keep is correct.

## Step 4: Choose QR mode and set up QR PIN Unlock

Step 4 makes the device air-gapped. Choose **QR** as the connection method, and complete QR PIN Unlock with a six-digit PIN. The Jade has no secure element: its PIN works with Blockstream's PIN server, the "blind oracle" described in the [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/), and QR PIN Unlock relays that exchange through QR codes and a web page on your phone, so the Jade Plus itself never goes online. Each session:

1. On the Jade Plus, select **QR Mode**, then **QR PIN Unlock**.
2. On your phone or computer, open Blockstream's companion page at [blkstrm.com/pn](https://blkstrm.com/pn) and select **Continue**.
3. Enter your PIN on the Jade Plus, then tap **Done** on the page.
4. Scan the Jade's animated QR code with the phone's camera until the progress bar is full, then press the checkmark on the Jade Plus.
5. Point the Jade's camera at the page's animated QR code until its progress bar fills. The Jade Plus unlocks.

If scanning stalls, set **QR Density** to Low in the Jade's **Options**. Blockstream says that after three wrong PIN entries you must restore the wallet from your recovery phrase. With a SeedQR you can skip the PIN and scan the SeedQR each session instead, which makes the drawn code exactly as sensitive as the 24 words.

**Warning: Three wrong PINs and the words are the only way back**
On the Jade, three wrong PIN entries mean restoring from the recovery phrase. Before funding the wallet, make sure the 24 words, including the last word the Jade chose, are on paper and tested.

## Step 5: Add a passphrase if you want one

Step 5 is optional. A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) turns the same words into a separate hidden wallet. Before unlocking, open **Options** on the Jade's main menu and select **BIP39 Passphrase**. Set **Frequency** to **Always Ask** (asked at every login) or **Next Login Only** (asked once, which also hides that you use one), and **Method** to **Manual** for any characters or **WordList** to build it from BIP39 words. Passphrases are case-sensitive and spaces count. A typo opens a different, empty wallet without any error, so note the fingerprint the Jade shows at the lower right when you open the passphrase wallet, and compare it every time. Set this before step 6: the passphrase wallet has its own key for Sparrow.

## Step 6: Add the Jade Plus to Sparrow by QR

Step 6 gives Sparrow the public key, so it can show balances and build transactions while the private keys stay on the Jade.

1. On the unlocked Jade Plus, select **Options**, **Wallet**, **Export Xpub**. The default is single-signature native segwit, `m/84'/0'/0'`; keep it unless you know you need another.
2. In Sparrow, choose **File**, **New Wallet**, name it, and select **Airgapped Hardware Wallet**.
3. Find the Jade in the list, click **Scan…**, and hold the Jade's animated QR code up to the webcam until Sparrow has read it.
4. Click **Apply** and set a password for the wallet file.

Blockstream warns that the script type in Sparrow must match the one exported, or the wallet shows the wrong addresses and no balance.

## Step 7: Check a receive address and sign by QR

Step 7 proves the Jade and Sparrow agree, before any money moves. To check an address, open **Receive** in Sparrow, select **Scan QR** on the Jade Plus and point it at the address's QR code; the Jade searches its wallet and confirms the address is its own. It checks the first 500 addresses and then offers **Skip** to search further.

To send:

1. In Sparrow, enter the address and amount, click **Create Transaction**, then **Finalize Transaction for Signing**, then **Show QR**.
2. On the Jade Plus, select **Scan QR** and read Sparrow's animated code.
3. Check the address and amount on the Jade's screen, not only in Sparrow, and confirm.
4. In Sparrow, click **Scan QR** and hold up the signed transaction the Jade now shows.
5. Click **Broadcast Transaction**.

Send a small amount out and back first. QR mode handles bitcoin only; Liquid needs USB or Bluetooth and the Blockstream app.

## Common questions

### Can the Jade Plus take dice rolls?

Not on the device. As of October 2026 you roll dice off the device with one of Blockstream's documented methods, enter the first 23 words, and the Jade Plus calculates a valid 24th word. You can also enter a full 24-word seed made with the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/).

### Do I need the Blockstream app?

No. This guide uses a web browser for the firmware update and the Genuine Check, Blockstream's QR PIN Unlock page, and Sparrow. The Blockstream app is needed only for Liquid, or if you prefer to connect by USB or Bluetooth.

### Is a SeedQR safer than QR PIN Unlock?

A SeedQR keeps nothing on the device: the Jade Plus forgets the seed when it powers off, and you scan the drawn code to sign. That removes the PIN server from the picture, but the drawn code is your full seed, so it needs the same protection as the 24 words, and anyone who sees it can copy the wallet. QR PIN Unlock keeps the seed on the device behind a PIN and the blind oracle.

## Where do these steps come from?

These steps follow Blockstream's and Sparrow's documentation as read on 26 October 2026: [Set up Jade](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/set-up-transact-recover-your-wallet/set-up-jade), [Air-gapped Jade Plus setup](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/use-jade-air-gapped/air-gapped-jade-plus-setup), [Update Jade firmware](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/set-up-transact-recover-your-wallet/update-jade-firmware), [Perform a Genuine Check with Jade](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/set-up-transact-recover-your-wallet/perform-a-genuine-check-with-jade), [Generate a recovery phrase offline](https://help.blockstream.com/generate-recovery-phrase-offline) and its [six-sided-die method](https://help.blockstream.com/generate-recovery-phrase-offline-d6), [Create a recovery phrase using dice](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/add-more-security-functionality/create-a-recovery-phrase-using-dice), [Access Jade air-gapped with QR PIN Unlock](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/use-jade-air-gapped/access-jade-air-gapped-with-qr-pin-unlock), [Connect Jade to a companion app](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/set-up-transact-recover-your-wallet/connect-jade-to-a-companion-app), [Add a BIP39 passphrase for Jade](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/add-more-security-functionality/add-a-bip39-passphrase-for-jade), [Add Jade Plus to an air-gap supported app](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/use-jade-air-gapped/add-jade-plus-to-an-air-gap-supported-app), [Verify receive addresses with an air-gapped Jade Plus](https://help.blockstream.com/blockstream-jade/use-jade-air-gapped/verify-receive-addresses-with-an-air-gapped-jade-plus), and Sparrow's [QR air-gapped wallet guide](https://sparrowwallet.com/docs/airgapped-wallet-qr.html). Menu labels differ slightly between Blockstream's articles and change between firmware versions; if a label differs, Blockstream's current guide is the authority.


---

# How to Test Your Bitcoin Seed Backup (Before You Need It)

> Learn how to properly verify your Bitcoin seed backup works before trusting it with significant funds. Step-by-step guide to testing your recovery process.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To know your seed phrase backup works, restore a wallet from it and check that it produces the same addresses as your real wallet. Write down the wallet's first receive address, enter the seed phrase (and passphrase, if you use one) from your written backup into a wiped or second device, and compare the first addresses character by character. If they match, the backup restores your wallet; if not, find the error while the original device still works. Do it before you deposit anything significant, again after making a metal copy, and every year or so after that.

Time: 30-60 minutes. Cost: Free. Level: Beginner. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: A seed phrase backup to test.

## Why isn't the device's word check enough?

Most hardware wallets quiz you on a few words at the end of setup, and that is where most people stop. The quiz catches a missing word. It does not catch a misspelled word it never asked about, handwriting you will misread in five years, words in the wrong order, a passphrase you have forgotten, or a metal plate stamped from a copy with a mistake in it. Each of these surfaces only when the device has failed and the backup is all that is left, which is too late to fix.

## Which test should you use?

| Test | When it suits | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| Wipe and restore the same device | The wallet is new and empty | The backup restores the wallet on this device |
| Restore on a second device | The wallet already holds funds, or you want independent confirmation | The backup restores the wallet on different hardware or software |
| The device's own backup check (for example Trezor's Check backup) | Any time, without wiping anything | The words match the seed stored on the device |
| An offline BIP39 tool on an air-gapped computer | You are technical and want to see the derivation yourself | The words derive the addresses you expect |

The first two are the full test, because they recover the wallet from the backup alone. The device's own check is a good periodic test: it compares what you type with the seed it holds, without wiping anything.

## Step 1: Record what the wallet should look like

Step 1 notes the values the restored wallet must reproduce. In your wallet software (Sparrow, for example), write down the wallet's first receive address and, ideally, its account xpub, the [extended public key](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub/) that covers every address in the account. Note also the derivation path and script type the wallet uses, usually `m/84'/0'/0'` and native segwit (addresses starting `bc1q`), and whether you use a passphrase.

The [backup verification worksheet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/worksheets/backup-check/) has boxes for these values and for what the restored wallet shows, so the comparison in step 3 is side by side on one sheet.

## Step 2: Restore the wallet from the backup

Step 2 rebuilds the wallet using only what is written on the backup.

If the wallet is new and empty, wipe the device using its factory reset (Trezor Suite calls it Wipe device; check your device's manual for the exact menu), then choose to recover a wallet and enter the words from the backup.

If the wallet holds funds, do not wipe it. Restore on a second device instead: a second hardware wallet, of the same or another brand, or a wallet app on an air-gapped computer used for this test only. Never type the seed phrase into a computer or phone that is or has been online.

In both cases, enter the words exactly as they are written on the backup, not as you remember them, and add the passphrase if you use one.

## Step 3: Compare the addresses

Step 3 is the actual test. Connect the restored wallet to wallet software set to the same derivation path and script type, and compare its first receive address with the one you recorded in step 1, character by character; if you recorded the xpub, compare that too, which covers every address at once.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Backup verification: restore the written seed on a second device and compare first addresses; identical addresses prove the paper backup restores the wallet, any difference means stop and find the error before funding](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallet-setup/backup-check.svg)

</div>

If they match, the backup restores your wallet. If they do not, stop and work through [what to do if verification fails](#what-if-verification-fails) before putting any more money in.

## Step 4: Check the passphrase wallet separately

Step 4 matters only if you use a passphrase. A passphrase turns the same seed phrase into a completely different wallet, so it has to be tested as part of the backup:

1. Restore with the seed phrase only, with no passphrase, and note the first address. This is the wallet the words alone open.
2. Add your passphrase and note the first address again. This should be your real wallet.
3. Check the second address matches your real wallet.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A passphrase splits one seed into two wallets: the 24 words alone derive the decoy wallet at one address, and the words plus your passphrase derive your real wallet at a different address; the passphrase is part of the backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/wallet-setup/passphrase-wallets.svg)

</div>

The usual passphrase mistakes are capital letters (`Bitcoin` is not `bitcoin`), a stray space at the end, look-alike characters such as zero and the letter O, and forgetting that you set one at all. The [passphrase guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/#what-exactly-counts-as-a-different-passphrase) lists what counts as a different passphrase.

## Step 5: Clean up the test

Step 5 removes the extra copy of your keys. If you restored on a second device, wipe it with its factory reset, or delete the test wallet and its files from the air-gapped computer. Put the backup back where it lives.

## How do you use an offline BIP39 tool safely?

Ian Coleman's BIP39 tool is a single HTML page that shows the keys and addresses a seed phrase derives, which makes the derivation visible. It is only safe offline:

**Warning: Only on a computer that will never go online**
Typing your real seed phrase into any page on an internet-connected computer exposes it. Use this tool only on an air-gapped computer, from a copy downloaded and checked beforehand.

1. Download the standalone HTML file from the releases page of [github.com/iancoleman/bip39](https://github.com/iancoleman/bip39) on an online computer.
2. Move it to the air-gapped computer on a USB stick.
3. Open it in a browser there, with no network connection.
4. Enter the seed phrase (and passphrase), choose the same derivation path as your wallet, and compare the first few addresses with your wallet's.

## How often should you verify the backup?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| When | What to do |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Setting up a new wallet | A full test before the first significant deposit |
| After making a metal backup | Test the metal copy itself, not the paper it was copied from |
| Every 6 to 12 months | Check the backup is still readable, or run the device's own backup check |
| Before major life changes | A full test |
| After any change to the backup | A full test |

</div>

Run a full test straight away if the backup has been exposed to water, fire or heat, if paper is yellowing or ink fading, if you cannot read your handwriting clearly, if stamped metal is unclear or corroded, or if someone may have seen it.

## What if verification fails?

First, do not panic: your original wallet still works. The error is in the backup, and you have found it while you can still fix it.

If the addresses do not match, check in this order:

1. The words: all present, spelled correctly, in the right order, from the English BIP39 list.
2. The passphrase: exactly right, including capitals and spaces, or absent if you do not use one.
3. The derivation path and script type, which differ between address types:

| Addresses start with | Script type | Derivation path |
|---|---|---|
| `bc1q` | Native segwit (BIP84) | `m/84'/0'/0'` |
| `3` | Nested segwit (BIP49) | `m/49'/0'/0'` |
| `1` | Legacy (BIP44) | `m/44'/0'/0'` |
| `bc1p` | Taproot (BIP86) | `m/86'/0'/0'` |

If the backup itself is wrong, make a new one while the wallet is still accessible. Some devices can show the seed phrase again on their own screen (check the manual; many, including Trezor, cannot). If yours cannot, or if you think the faulty backup may have been seen by someone, create a new wallet with a new seed, back it up and test it, and move the funds to it.

## Backup verification checklist

- The seed phrase is legible, and all 12 or 24 words are present, spelled correctly and in order.
- A wallet restored from the backup alone shows the same first receive address (and xpub) as the original.
- The passphrase wallet has been tested, if you use one.
- The metal copy has been tested, not only the paper.
- Any test device has been wiped.
- The backup is back in its secure place.


---

# Before You Deposit: Critical Checklist

> Essential verification steps before sending Bitcoin to any new wallet. This checklist can save you from catastrophic, irreversible mistakes.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Before sending a significant amount of bitcoin to a new wallet, check six things: the seed phrase was made safely and is written down correctly; a recovery from the written backup alone has been tested; the passphrase, if you use one, is backed up and tested; receive addresses are checked on the hardware wallet's own screen; the device and software came from their makers and are up to date; and a small test amount has gone in and come back out. A payment into a wallet cannot be undone, so a mistake found after the deposit is found too late. If any item below is not true yet, wait.

The same checks are a [printable checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/worksheets/before-you-deposit/) to tick off at your desk.

## What can go wrong if you skip a check?

| Skipped check | What can happen |
|---|---|
| The seed phrase was copied wrongly | The backup restores a different, empty wallet, and the funds are lost when the device fails |
| The device or software was tampered with | The funds are stolen |
| The backup was never tested | You believe you have a backup when you do not |
| The address was not checked on the device | Malware sends the deposit to an attacker's address |

## Is the seed phrase safe and correct?

- You know how the seed was made: from your own dice rolls, or by the device on current firmware. If it came from a [Coldcard on 2021 to 2026 firmware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/), move to a new seed before depositing anything.
- It is written down physically, on paper or metal.
- Every word is spelled as in the [BIP39 word list](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/english.txt), and the words are numbered and in order.
- It has never been photographed, typed into a computer or phone, stored in a notes app, cloud service or password manager, spoken aloud, sent in a message or shown to anyone.

## Has the backup been tested?

**Danger: Do not skip the recovery test**
An untested backup fails silently: you find out it is wrong only when the device has failed and the backup is all you have. Restore the wallet from the written backup alone before depositing.

- You have restored the wallet from your written backup, by wiping the device or on a second device, using nothing but what is written down.
- The restored wallet's first receive address matches the original's.

The [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) walks through it.

## If you use a passphrase, is it backed up and tested?

- You understand that a passphrase creates a completely different wallet, and that forgetting it loses the bitcoin.
- It is backed up separately from the seed phrase.
- You have restored with the seed phrase and passphrase together, and seen that the passphrase wallet shows different addresses from the seed-only wallet.

## Have you checked the receive address on the device?

- You generated a receive address in your wallet software and displayed the same address on the hardware wallet.
- The two match, checked character by character (at least the first and last eight characters).

This matters because malware can change the address shown on a computer, but not the one the hardware wallet shows on its own screen.

## Are the device and software genuine and up to date?

- The hardware wallet was bought from its manufacturer, not a marketplace such as Amazon or eBay.
- The packaging showed no signs of tampering, and the maker's authenticity check passed, where the device has one.
- The firmware is the latest version, checked against the manufacturer's website.
- The PIN is not guessable: not a birthday, sequence or repeated digit.
- Wallet software came from its official site ([Sparrow](https://sparrowwallet.com), [Electrum](https://electrum.org), or the manufacturer's own app), and you checked the download's signature if you know how.
- The computer is your own, up to date and free of software you do not recognise.

## Has a test transaction worked both ways?

- A small amount, enough to check and not enough to hurt, has arrived in the wallet.
- You have sent a transaction out of the wallet successfully.
- You understand how fees are set and how to choose one; see [transaction fees](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/fees/).

## Are you ready for the responsibility?

- You can explain in your own words what a seed phrase is, and that the seed phrase, not the device, is what holds the bitcoin.
- You know that nobody can help if the seed phrase is lost, and that anyone who sees it can take everything.
- You know where the backup will be stored, and have thought about fire, flood and theft.
- You have thought about what happens to the bitcoin if you die; see [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/).
- You are not rushing. At least a day between setup and a significant deposit is a good rule, and a rising price is not a reason to hurry.

## When should you not deposit?

Do not deposit if you are not certain the seed phrase is written correctly, if you have not tested recovery, if the hardware wallet came from an unofficial source, if anyone has seen your seed phrase, if you are using a computer you do not trust, or if you feel rushed or something about the setup seems wrong. Delaying costs nothing; a mistake can cost everything.

## What should you do after depositing?

1. Wait for the transaction to confirm: one confirmation for small amounts, six for large ones.
2. Keep a private record of it.
