3. Do not publish your receive addresses, screenshots of your balance or the fact that you own bitcoin. Reused addresses leak your history, and known holders become targets.

## What if something goes wrong?

### What if you sent bitcoin to the wrong address?

Bitcoin transactions cannot be reversed. If the address belongs to nobody you know, the funds are almost certainly gone, which is why every address is checked on the device first.

### What if you cannot remember your passphrase?

Without the exact passphrase, the seed phrase opens a different, empty wallet, and there is no recovery mechanism. This is why the passphrase is tested before depositing.

### What if you lost your seed phrase?

If the device still works, create a new wallet with a new seed, back it up and test it, then move the funds to it. If the device is lost or broken too, the funds cannot be recovered.

### What if someone saw your seed phrase?

Assume it is compromised. Create a new wallet with a new seed straight away, move all the funds to it, and never use the old seed again.


---

# Bitcoin Security: DIY Seed Generation & Advanced Protection

> Advanced Bitcoin security: generate seeds with dice, add passphrase protection, and apply operational and physical security best practices.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin security works in layers, added in order as your holdings and threats grow: a hardware wallet with a tested backup first, then a seed you made with dice, a passphrase, operational security (how you behave and what you say), physical security (where things are kept and what happens under threat), and finally multisig. Most people need only the first few; match the layers to your [threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/). These guides assume you already have a working hardware wallet; if not, start with [wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/).

## What are the layers?

| Layer | What it adds | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Hardware wallet | Keys stay on a device that signs; most people stop here | [Hardware wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/) |
| 2. A seed made with dice | Randomness you can verify instead of trusting the device | [Seed generation with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) |
| 3. Passphrase | A second secret, so a found seed phrase is not enough | [Passphrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) |
| 4. Operational security | Habits that stop you giving yourself away | [Operational security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/operational-security/) |
| 5. Physical security | Protection against theft, disaster and threats to you | [Physical security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/physical-security/) |
| 6. Multisig | No single key, device or place can lose or spend everything | [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) |

## What does each guide cover?

| Guide | Time | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| [Seed generation with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) | 2-4 hours | Rolling dice for entropy, converting rolls to bits, calculating the BIP39 checksum, backing up on metal. Why: a device's random number generator can fail silently, as Coldcard's did until 2026, and dice-generated seeds were untouched |
| [Passphrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) | 30 minutes | How a passphrase changes the wallet, making a strong one with dice, testing and backing it up. A forgotten passphrase cannot be reset |
| [Operational security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/operational-security/) | 30 minutes to read | Not discussing holdings, verifying before trusting, assuming devices are compromised, safe communication, social engineering |
| [Physical security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/physical-security/) | 30 minutes to read | The "$5 wrench attack", home security, backup locations, travelling with bitcoin, decoy wallets |

## In what order should you add them?

| Stage | What to do | Who |
|-------|------------|------|
| 1 | A hardware wallet with a proper backup | Everyone |
| 2 | Test the backup by restoring from it | Everyone |
| 3 | Stop discussing your holdings publicly | Everyone |
| 4 | Add a passphrase | Meaningful holdings |
| 5 | Make your own seed with dice | High security needs |
| 6 | Secure storage and home security | Significant holdings |
| 7 | Multisig | Large holdings |

## What mistakes undermine security?

| Mistake | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Security theatre | Worrying about exotic threats while ignoring the real ones, which are phishing, malware and social engineering |
| Complexity beyond competence | A setup you could not recover yourself, which is a trap rather than security |
| Single points of failure | One seed, one place, one device |
| Trusting without verifying | Believing a website instead of checking the address on your device and the signature on the software |
| Talking too much | Every person who knows you hold bitcoin widens your exposure |

Related reading: [what happens if you lose your seed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/lost-seed/), [recovery scams](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/), and the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/).


---

# Operational Security for Bitcoiners

> Essential operational security practices for Bitcoin holders. Learn how your behavior affects your security and how to minimize your attack surface.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/operational-security/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

**Operational security** (opsec) is protecting your bitcoin through behaviour rather than technology: not telling people what you own, checking everything yourself before acting on it, assuming any device may be compromised, keeping your bitcoin life separate from the rest, and treating every unexpected contact as a possible scam. Bitcoin's cryptography has never been broken; people lose bitcoin through phishing links, oversharing, misplaced trust and manipulation, and the best hardware wallet cannot stop someone from talking themselves out of it.

## What are the principles?

### Don't talk about your holdings

**Danger: Telling people you own bitcoin is the most common way to become a target**
Everyone who knows is a possible route for social engineering, a possible physical threat and the start of a chain of gossip you cannot control.

Avoid posting about bitcoin under your real name, telling colleagues, acquaintances or extended family, wearing bitcoin merchandise or putting stickers on your laptop or car, and mentioning amounts to anyone. Discussing bitcoin as an idea without revealing ownership is fine, as is telling close family who need to know for inheritance, and taking part in bitcoin communities without your real identity.

### Verify everything

| Situation | What to check |
|----------|----------------|
| A receive address | That it matches on the hardware wallet's own screen |
| A software download | That it came from the official website, and that its signature verifies |
| A firmware update | That the manufacturer's website announces it |
| A "support" message | Nothing: real companies never message you first |
| An investment opportunity | If it sounds too good to be true, it is a scam |

The usual failures are trusting an address shown only on a computer, downloading wallet software from a search advert, answering "support" messages on social media, and clicking links in emails that claim to be from an exchange.

### Assume any device can be compromised

Act as if your computer could be showing fake addresses, your phone could be SIM-swapped or carry spyware, your email could be read by an attacker, public Wi-Fi could be monitored and cloud storage could be breached. So: check addresses on the hardware wallet, protect important accounts with hardware security keys, never store a seed phrase digitally, use a VPN on public networks, and turn on two-factor authentication everywhere, hardware-based where possible.

### Keep things separate

Use different wallets for different purposes, a separate email address for bitcoin accounts, separate identities for bitcoin and personal life, backups in different places, and ideally a dedicated computer for bitcoin.

### Keep your exposure small

Fewer accounts mean fewer breaches, fewer people who know mean fewer routes for social engineering, fewer devices mean fewer to compromise, and less public presence means less reason to be targeted.

## What habits does good opsec need?

| Area | Habits |
|---|---|
| Daily | Never discuss amounts; check addresses on the device before sending; go to websites directly instead of clicking email links; use a unique password everywhere; distrust unexpected contact |
| Communication | Use encrypted messaging such as Signal for anything sensitive; keep bitcoin off SMS and ordinary email; stay vague when asked about bitcoin; never share your seed phrase with anyone, for any reason |
| Devices | Keep operating systems updated; install nothing unnecessary; consider a dedicated bitcoin-only computer; use hardware security keys |
| Accounts | Two-factor authentication everywhere (hardware key first, then an authenticator app, SMS last); unique strong passwords in a password manager; a separate email for financial accounts, ideally with a privacy-focused provider; watch for logins you did not make |

## How does social engineering work?

**Social engineering** is manipulating people into handing over information or access, and it is the most common way in.

| Attack | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Phishing | Fake emails, websites, wallet apps and browser extensions: "your account has been compromised, click here" |
| Impersonation | "Tech support" offering help, someone claiming to be from your exchange, "moderators" in Telegram or Discord groups |
| Romance and trust scams | A relationship built over weeks that ends in a request for funds, an "investment opportunity" from a new friend, a fake job that involves bitcoin transfers |
| Urgency and fear | "Act now or lose your funds", "your account will be locked", pressure to decide quickly |

The defence: slow down, because urgency is the warning sign; check independently, using your own route to the company rather than any link you were sent; ask why they are contacting you at all; and never share a seed phrase, which no legitimate person or company ever needs.

## How much opsec do you need?

| Profile | Practices |
|---|---|
| Casual holder | Do not discuss holdings publicly; use a hardware wallet; strong passwords and two-factor authentication; basic checking habits |
| Serious holder | All of the above, plus a dedicated email for bitcoin, more care about who knows, your own node, and a VPN where useful |
| High-value holder | All of the above, plus a dedicated bitcoin computer, strict separation, backups spread across places, legal structures where appropriate, and a professional security review |

## Which warning signs mean stop?

Stop immediately if anyone asks for your seed phrase, if "support" contacts you first, if you are pressed to act now, if someone asks for remote access to your computer, if an investment seems too good, if you are sent a link in an email or direct message, if you are asked to "verify" your wallet, or if anyone claims they can recover lost bitcoin. The [recovery scams](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/) page covers the last one in detail.


---

# Physical Security for Bitcoin Holders

> Protect your Bitcoin from real-world threats. Home security, backup storage, travel considerations, and defense against physical attacks.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/physical-security/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Physical security is protecting your bitcoin, and yourself, from threats in the real world: burglary, fire, theft of a backup, and someone forcing you to hand over your coins. Cryptography cannot help against a person who threatens you until you transfer the funds, the so-called "$5 wrench attack", and kidnappings aimed at bitcoin holders, such as the January 2025 abduction of Ledger co-founder David Balland in France, show it is not theoretical. The defences, in order, are not letting anyone know you are worth targeting, secure storage spread across places, and a setup that you cannot empty alone under duress.

## How do you avoid becoming a target?

The best physical security is never being identified as worth attacking.

| Avoid | Examples |
|---|---|
| Advertising | Bitcoin clothing, stickers on a laptop or car, hardware wallets on display, branded packaging on deliveries (ask for plain boxes) |
| Discussing | Mentioning that you own bitcoin to acquaintances, at meetups or under your real name online; "I don't own any" is an acceptable answer |
| Displaying | Checking your balance in public, wallet apps on your home screen, bitcoin tabs open where others can see |

## What home security makes sense?

For significant holdings, ordinary home security matters:

- Barriers: good locks on every entrance, reinforced door frames (kicked doors break at the frame, not the lock), window locks or film, motion-activated outside lights, and no bushes hiding doors and windows.
- Monitoring: visible cameras, a monitored alarm, smart locks that tell you when doors open, and neighbours who look out for each other.
- Storage: a fire-rated safe bolted down, somewhere other than the main bedroom (the first place burglars search), some ordinary valuables a burglar can take instead, and nothing irreplaceable stored only at home.

## Where should seed backups be kept?

The seed backup is the most sensitive object you own.

| Location | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|----------|------|------|
| A safe at home | Accessible, under your control | A known location; fire and flood |
| A bank safe deposit box | Secure and fire-protected | Bank hours and rules; not private from the bank |
| Buried or hidden | Very hard to find | You may forget where; damp and corrosion |
| A trusted relative's home | Another location | Needs trust, and depends on their security |
| Several locations | Survives losing one | More places that could be found |

Keep backups on metal, since paper burns; keep two or three copies in different places, in different cities if you can; use tamper-evident bags so you would know if one were opened; and keep a secure record of where each one is. A single backup, a paper-only backup, a bank box as the only copy, a backup loose in a drawer and a hiding place you might forget are all ways to lose everything.

## How can you prepare for coercion?

### A decoy wallet

A [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) lets one seed phrase open two wallets: without the passphrase it opens a decoy holding a small, believable amount; with it, the real wallet. Under threat you reveal only the decoy, and the attacker cannot tell the passphrase wallet exists.

**Warning: A decoy only works if the attacker believes it**
It fails if the attacker knows about passphrases and suspects one, if the decoy's balance is implausible, or if they have researched you first. Never put your life at risk for it.

### Multisig

With [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/), you genuinely cannot spend alone: the other keys are in other places, or with other people. That is not a bluff, and it makes you a less attractive target.

### Timelocks

Some setups delay transactions, so that funds are not available immediately even under coercion, which buys time. They are more complex to set up.

## How should you travel with bitcoin?

Carry only what you need, keep a separate travel wallet away from your main holdings, advertise nothing, and know the local laws, which vary.

For a hardware wallet, there are three options: leave it at home, take an empty device and create a wallet at your destination if needed, or take a loaded device, which you need for spending but which raises the risk. If you take one, keep it in your hand luggage, know how to explain it at security, consider keeping only a small amount on it, and memorise the PIN rather than writing it down.

At borders, some countries require crypto holdings to be declared and some can compel you to unlock devices; research before you travel. A hotel safe is better than nothing but not secure, so do not leave devices unattended in the room.

## What do you do if something happens?

| Event | What to do |
|---|---|
| Your home is burgled | Check whether a backup was touched; if so, move the funds to a new wallet straight away; report it to the police; improve your security |
| You are physically threatened | Comply if you must, since no amount of bitcoin is worth injury; give up the decoy wallet if you have one; report it when safe; move the remaining funds to a new setup |
| A seed backup is stolen | Move the funds immediately while you still have the device, to a new wallet with a new seed, and work out what else was exposed |
| A hardware wallet is stolen | The PIN and its limited attempts give you time; restore from your backup onto a new device and move the funds to a new seed, treating the old one as compromised |

## How much is enough?

Security that fits your real threat, does not take over your life, can be kept up consistently and still lets you use your bitcoin is right. Security that exceeds your risk, causes constant stress, or is so complex you lock yourself out is paranoia, and it has its own risks. Most people need basic discretion, a hardware wallet, backups in more than one place and ordinary home security; few need elaborate decoys or professional protection. The aim is to be a harder target than the alternatives, not to be invulnerable. Match the effort to your [threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/).


---

# Advanced Bitcoin Security: Multisig & Air-Gapped Setups

> Advanced Bitcoin self-custody: 2-of-3 multisig setup, inheritance planning for heirs, air-gapped signing computers, and open-source firmware guides.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The advanced guides address specific threats that a single, well-kept hardware wallet does not: multisig removes single points of failure, inheritance planning makes sure your bitcoin outlives you, an air-gapped computer signs and generates seeds with no network at all, a dedicated bitcoin computer keeps wallet software away from your everyday browsing, and open-source firmware replaces the code that runs before the operating system. Most people do not need them; they assume you already have a working hardware wallet, a tested backup and the basics from [Learn](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/) and [wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/). Match them to your [threat model](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/threat-models/).

## Which advanced setup protects against what?

| Setup | Protects against | Effort | Who needs it |
|-------|------------------|------------|--------------|
| [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) | Single points of failure, a compromised device | High | Large holdings, inheritance plans |
| [Inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) | Your bitcoin being lost when you die | Medium | Anyone with bitcoin to pass on |
| [Air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) | Network attacks and malware reaching your keys | Medium | Dice seed generation, offline signing |
| [Bitcoin computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/) | Compromise through everyday devices | Medium | Privacy-minded users |
| [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) or [coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/) | Proprietary firmware, including Intel's Management Engine | Very high | The highest security requirements |

## What does each guide involve?

| Guide | Time | Cost | What it covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) | 4-8 hours | About $200-750 | Choosing a quorum, preparing three hardware wallets, building the wallet in Sparrow, backup and recovery |
| [Inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) | 2-4 hours | Varies | Why bitcoin inheritance differs, approaches from simple to multisig, legal points, common mistakes |
| [Air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) | 2-4 hours | $50-200, or free with an old laptop | Choosing hardware, removing network cards, Libreboot, an encrypted Linux install, offline software |
| [Bitcoin computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/) | 1-2 hours | $50-150, or free with repurposed hardware | A computer used only for bitcoin; unlike an air-gapped one it connects, to run a node or broadcast |
| [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) | 3-5 hours | $15-30 of flashing hardware | Open-source firmware on supported ThinkPads, with the Intel ME stripped and disabled |
| [Coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/) | 2-4 hours | $0-30 | Open-source firmware on more machines, with some proprietary code retained |

## In what order should you build them?

| Stage | Steps |
|---|---|
| 1. Foundation | A [hardware wallet](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/), a [verified backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/), [your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) |
| 2. Stronger security | A [dedicated bitcoin computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/), [operational and physical security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/), [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/) |
| 3. Advanced protection | An [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/), a [seed made with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) |
| 4. Maximum security | [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/), [open firmware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) |

If you want to remove single points of failure, start with a 2-of-3 [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/). If you want your family to inherit your bitcoin, start with [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/). To generate your own seed securely, combine an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) with the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/).

## Common questions

### Is multisig worth the complexity?

For life-changing amounts, yes: removing single points of failure is worth the extra work. For smaller amounts, a well-kept single-signature setup is enough.

### Can you use an old laptop as an air-gapped computer?

Yes; old laptops are ideal. Remove the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth cards rather than only disabling them in software. See [removing the network hardware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/#step-1-remove-the-network-hardware).

### Do you need open-source firmware?

Most people do not: a good hardware wallet used well is strong security. Open firmware suits extreme threat models and people who want to be able to inspect everything. Open source is not a guarantee, though: in the 2026 Coldcard incident the bug sat in public code for five years. Openness makes verification possible; someone still has to do it.

### Should you choose a secure element or open source?

You no longer have to choose. Secure elements resist physical extraction and open source allows auditing, and the Trezor Safe 7 pairs open firmware with an auditable secure element, while the BitBox02 Nova and Passport Prime combine certified chips with fully open code. See the [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/).


---

# Dedicated Bitcoin Computer Guide

> Build a dedicated Bitcoin computer for secure transactions. Learn why using a regular computer is dangerous and how to protect your Bitcoin.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A dedicated Bitcoin computer is a laptop used for nothing but bitcoin: it runs your wallet software, builds and broadcasts transactions, and never browses the web, opens email or installs anything else. Keeping wallet software off your everyday machine means malware picked up from websites, downloads and attachments cannot watch your balance or swap the addresses you paste. It still connects to the internet, unlike an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/), and the signing stays on your hardware wallet. Setting one up takes one to two hours on a second-hand ThinkPad.

Time: 1-2 hours. Cost: $50-150 (used laptop) or $0 (repurpose old computer). Level: Beginner to intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: Spare laptop or desktop, USB drive.

[Hardware wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/) and [why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) are useful background.

## Why not use your everyday computer?

An everyday computer is exposed to websites, downloads, email attachments, browser extensions and all the software you install, and a hardware wallet protects the keys but not everything else. Malware on that computer can:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Risk | What it leads to |
|------|--------|
| Reading your balances | The attacker learns how much you hold, and may target you |
| Changing the clipboard | Addresses you paste are swapped for the attacker's |
| Watching your activity | The attacker learns when you transact |

</div>

A hardware wallet's screen still protects each payment, as long as you check the address on it. A dedicated computer removes these risks at the source and keeps your bitcoin activity apart from the rest of your digital life, which is worth it once the amounts justify a second machine.

## What are the steps?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Step | What you do |
|------|----------------|
| 1. [Choose the hardware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/choice/) | Pick a laptop, ideally one Libreboot supports |
| 2. [Set it up](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/setup/) | Libreboot, Linux Mint, full-disk encryption and Tor |

</div>

For the most protection, sign on an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/), which never connects at all. For the firmware, see [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/), the most open option for supported ThinkPads, or [coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/), which supports more models.


---

# Choose Your Bitcoin Computer

> How to choose the right laptop for Bitcoin self-custody. Hardware recommendations and security precautions for your dedicated Bitcoin machine.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/choice/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Any modest laptop is powerful enough to be a Bitcoin computer, so choose by firmware rather than speed: we recommend a ThinkPad that [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) supports, so that the proprietary BIOS can be replaced with open-source firmware. The ThinkPad X230 or T430 suits a small budget, and the T480s a medium one. Second-hand is fine, with a new SSD and new USB sticks.

## Why choose a laptop Libreboot supports?

Some people suggest buying a brand-new laptop for security, but a new laptop still ships with proprietary firmware that you cannot inspect. That is why we recommend a laptop on which you can install open-source firmware, and our choice is [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/). Flashing it is not the easiest process, but it is worth the effort.

## Which laptop fits your budget?

- Low budget: the Lenovo ThinkPad [X230](https://psref.lenovo.com/syspool/Sys/PDF/withdrawnbook/ThinkPad_X230.pdf) or [T430](https://psref.lenovo.com/syspool/sys/pdf/withdrawnbook/thinkpad_t430.pdf). Both are cheap second-hand, sturdy and easy to work on.
- Medium budget: the Lenovo ThinkPad [T480s](https://psref.lenovo.com/syspool/Sys/PDF/ThinkPad/ThinkPad_T480s/ThinkPad_T480s_Spec.pdf). Supported by Libreboot since its December 2024 release, it takes NVMe SSDs and up to 24 GB of memory, and is fast enough for other bitcoin work too. It needs Lenovo's firmware updated before flashing; see the [requirements](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/requirements/).

## What precautions does a second-hand laptop need?

These laptops are usually bought second-hand, so before turning one into a Bitcoin computer:

- Fit a new SSD. If you cannot, at least wipe the existing drive and encrypt it with LUKS during installation.
- Use new USB sticks for installation and backups, not old or unknown ones.


---

# Bitcoin Computer Setup Guide

> Set up your dedicated Bitcoin computer with Libreboot BIOS, Linux Mint, and LUKS encryption for maximum security and privacy.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Setting up a Bitcoin computer takes four steps: replace the BIOS with Libreboot, install Linux Mint, encrypt the whole disk with LUKS during installation, and route the computer's bitcoin traffic through Tor. Then install only the wallet software you need, such as Sparrow, and nothing else.

## Step 1: Replace the BIOS with Libreboot

Step 1 replaces the firmware. 
[Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/) replaces the laptop's proprietary BIOS with open-source firmware built on coreboot. On the ThinkPads it supports, it strips the Intel Management Engine down with me_cleaner and disables it, and keeps the remaining vendor code to what the board needs to boot. That does not make the machine free of closed code, but it removes most of the proprietary software that runs before your operating system, and what is left of the firmware is source you can read and rebuild. For a Bitcoin computer, whose job is to create and broadcast transactions in an environment you trust, that is a much smaller base to trust.

## Step 2: Install Linux Mint

Step 2 installs the operating system. Linux Mint balances ease of use and stability: it is light, runs few unnecessary services, inherits Ubuntu's broad hardware support, and its desktop is easy to find your way around even if you are new to Linux. Check the installer's checksum and signature before writing it to a USB stick.

## Step 3: Encrypt the disk with LUKS

Step 3 protects what is stored on the laptop if it is stolen. During installation, choose to encrypt the whole drive; Linux Mint uses LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup), which keeps everything encrypted at rest behind a passphrase you type at start-up and supports several passphrases in separate key slots. Encryption protects the data when the laptop is off or stolen; it does not protect a running system from malware, which is what the rest of this setup is for.

## Step 4: Route bitcoin traffic through Tor

Step 4 hides where your bitcoin activity comes from. Tor encrypts your internet traffic and routes it through several relays, so nobody watching can tie your IP address to what you do. If your [node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/) already runs over [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/) on a separate device, the laptop does not strictly need to send everything through Tor, but because it is online, routing its bitcoin activity through Tor gives the most privacy. It hides your IP address from anyone trying to link your wallet or node to your location, gets around ISPs or governments that block bitcoin traffic, and keeps your connections private even when you run your own node.


---

# Bitcoin Inheritance Planning: Pass Bitcoin to Heirs

> Plan Bitcoin inheritance for your heirs. Approaches from sealed instructions to family multisig, plus how to write recovery instructions.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin has no beneficiary forms, no account a court can order opened and no password reset, so bitcoin whose owner dies without a plan is lost for good. An inheritance plan gives your heirs what they need to recover it (the keys, or enough of them, plus written instructions) without making it easier for anyone to steal while you are alive. For significant holdings, the best balance is a 2-of-3 multisig in which an heir holds one key from the start; for smaller amounts, a passphrase-protected seed with the two parts stored apart, or a sealed letter, can be enough. Whatever you choose, write instructions a non-technical person can follow, test the plan with your heir, and review it every year.

## Why is bitcoin inheritance different?

| Traditional assets | Bitcoin |
|-------------------|---------|
| Banks verify the heir's identity | Only the keys prove ownership |
| Courts can order access | No authority can recover keys |
| Forgotten passwords can be reset | A lost seed phrase is lost for good |
| Institutions keep records | Only you know what you hold and where the keys are |

The underlying tension is that security needs secrecy, because the fewer people who can reach your keys the safer they are, while inheritance needs sharing, because someone must be able to reach them after you are gone. Every approach is a balance between the two.

## Which approach suits you?

| Approach | Best for | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|----------|----------|------------|----------------|
| A sealed letter | Small amounts, high trust | Simple; heirs need no technical knowledge | A single point of failure; whoever finds it can take the bitcoin |
| A lawyer or executor | Moderate amounts, an existing estate plan | Fits existing planning; can include conditions | Trusts a third party; probate takes months or years; the lawyer may not understand bitcoin security |
| Split shares (SLIP39) | Moderate to significant amounts, technical heirs | No single person or place holds everything; survives losing a share | Recombining needs technical understanding; not every wallet supports it |
| Multisig, with an heir holding a key | Significant amounts, long-term planning | No single point of failure; heirs recover without rebuilding anything; you spend normally meanwhile | Complex to set up; needs several hardware wallets; every holder must keep the descriptor |
| Collaborative custody (Unchained, Casa) | Very large holdings | A professional holds one key and helps heirs recover | Fees; the company could fail; less privacy |

**Warning: Never split a seed phrase by giving people different words**
Giving words 1 to 12 to one person and 13 to 24 to another adds no redundancy, since losing either half loses the bitcoin, and it weakens the seed: half of a 12-word seed leaves only about 62 bits to guess, within reach of a determined attacker. Use SLIP39 shares or multisig instead.

## How does a family multisig work?

A family multisig is a 2-of-3 multisig wallet in which you hold one key, an heir holds a second, and the third is kept in a vault or by a lawyer.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![An inheritance 2-of-3 multisig: you hold key 1 for daily use, your heir keeps key 2, and key 3 sits in a vault or with an attorney; while you live you spend with key 1 plus another, and after your death the heir recovers everything with keys 2 and 3](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/advanced/inheritance-multisig.svg)

</div>

While you are alive, you spend with key 1 plus key 2 or key 3. After your death, your heir uses keys 2 and 3. Nobody, including the heir, can spend alone.

## Step 1: Set up the multisig

Step 1 builds the wallet. Follow the [multisig guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) to create a 2-of-3 multisig, assigning the keys with inheritance in mind: key 1 on your own device (a Jade Plus, for example), key 2 on a device your heir keeps (a Trezor Safe 5, say), and key 3 on a backup device (such as a Keystone 3 Pro) in secure storage.

## Step 2: Let each key holder back up their own seed

Step 2 keeps each seed with its holder. Each holder backs up their own seed phrase; you do not need to know theirs, and they do not need to know yours.

| Key | Held by | Seed stored |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| Key 1 | You | Your secure location |
| Key 2 | Your main heir | Their secure location |
| Key 3 | Backup | A safe deposit box or with your lawyer |

## Step 3: Give every key holder the wallet descriptor

Step 3 makes the wallet recoverable from any two keys.

**Danger: Every key holder needs a copy of the wallet descriptor**
Recovering with two of the three seeds is impossible without it, because the third key's xpub is recorded in the descriptor and nowhere else.

The **wallet descriptor** (also called the wallet configuration or multisig file) records every key's xpub, the 2-of-3 rule, the derivation paths and the address format. In Sparrow, export it as a PDF from the wallet's `Settings` tab, and store copies with each hardware wallet's backup, with your estate documents and with your instructions.

## Step 4: Write instructions your heirs can follow

Step 4 writes down what to do, for someone who may know nothing about bitcoin. For example:

```markdown
## Bitcoin inheritance instructions

### What you are inheriting
A 2-of-3 multisig bitcoin wallet. Any two of its three keys can move the funds.

### What you need
1. Two of the hardware wallets, or their seed phrases
2. The wallet descriptor (attached, or kept at ___)
3. Sparrow Wallet (https://sparrowwallet.com)

### How to reach the funds
1. Download Sparrow Wallet and check its signature
2. Choose File, Import Wallet, and load the wallet descriptor
3. Connect the first hardware wallet and check Sparrow recognises it
4. Connect the second hardware wallet
5. You can now see the balance and send transactions

### Contacts
- Lawyer: [name, phone]
- Technical helper, if needed: [name, phone]
- Where key 3 is: [details]

### If something goes wrong
- Never give seed phrases to "recovery services": they are scams
- Contact [trusted technical person] before doing anything
- Bitcoin cannot be "hacked": if the seeds are safe, the funds are safe
```

The [inheritance letter template](https://selfcustodylabs.com/worksheets/inheritance-letter/) is this letter as a printable form to fill in by hand, with the step 6 table at the end.

## Step 5: Test the plan

Step 5 proves it works before anyone depends on it:

1. Spend a small amount with keys 1 and 2, then 1 and 3, then 2 and 3.
2. Have your heir restore their key on a fresh device.
3. Check that every holder's copy of the descriptor produces the same addresses.
4. Walk your heir through the whole recovery with a test amount.

## Step 6: Record where everything is

Step 6 writes down who holds what, kept with the estate documents:

| Item | Where | Who knows |
|------|----------|-----------|
| Key 1 device | Your home | You |
| Key 1 seed | Your secure location | Only you |
| Key 2 device | With your heir | Your heir |
| Key 2 seed | Your heir's secure location | Only your heir |
| Key 3 device | The backup location | You, and your executor |
| Key 3 seed | Kept separately from the key 3 device | You, and your executor |
| Wallet descriptor | Several places | Every key holder |
| Instructions | With the estate documents | Your executor |

## What if you use a single-signature wallet?

### A seed phrase and a passphrase, stored apart

Store the seed phrase in one secure place, put a strong [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) on the wallet, and store the passphrase somewhere else, for example with your lawyer. Leave instructions explaining that both are needed. Neither place alone gives access, though the plan still depends on both surviving and being found.

### An automated check-in service

Some services send pre-written messages if you stop checking in for a set time. They need nobody to know in advance, but they depend on the service continuing to exist, and the message should only say where to find the instructions, never contain a seed phrase or passphrase.

### SLIP39 shares

Some wallets, including Trezor's, can split a backup into SLIP39 shares, any set number of which rebuild the wallet. A 3-of-5 split might give shares to your main heir, a second heir, your lawyer, a safe deposit box and a trusted friend; any three recover it. Not every wallet supports SLIP39, and recovery is more complex.

## What mistakes lose an inheritance?

| Mistake | Why it matters | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| "I'll set it up later" | The most common failure: death does not wait | Set up a basic plan now, and improve it later |
| Keeping seeds and instructions together | Whoever finds both can take everything | Store them apart |
| Assuming heirs will work it out | They may never find the wallet, fall for scams or give up | Write clear instructions |
| Forgetting the multisig descriptor | Two seeds cannot rebuild the wallet without it | Store it with every seed |
| Never testing | An untested plan is a guess | Walk through it with your heirs |
| A single point of failure | One lost document, place or person ends the plan | Build in redundancy |
| Over-engineering | Heirs cannot carry out a plan they do not understand | Match the complexity to their skills |
| Trusting recovery services | They are scams aimed at grieving families | Warn your heirs explicitly |

## What legal steps should you take?

This is general information, not legal advice; consult an estate lawyer who knows digital assets in your jurisdiction.

- Mention your bitcoin in your will, even though the keys are handled separately, so that its existence and your wishes are documented. For example: "I own bitcoin. Instructions for accessing it are stored separately and have been provided to [person or place]. I direct that it pass to [beneficiary]."
- Consider a trust, which can keep the estate private, set conditions on distribution and manage the transition.
- Keep tax records: purchase dates and prices, which wallets you control, and any taxable events, which can save your heirs money and disputes.
- If your heirs live in other countries, the laws differ, and where keys are stored can have legal consequences; take advice in each jurisdiction.

## How often should you review the plan?

Once a year, check that you can still reach every key, that the backups still work, that contacts for your lawyer, heirs and executor are current, that the instructions are still accurate, and whether the wallet software has changed. Update the plan after a large change in value, marriage, divorce, a birth or death, a move abroad, a change of lawyer or executor, a hardware wallet reaching the end of its life, or any security concern.

## What should you do today?

If nothing else, take these five steps; they take about half an hour:

1. Write down which wallets hold your bitcoin.
2. Check that your seed phrase backups exist and are readable.
3. Tell one trusted person that you own bitcoin and where the instructions are.
4. Write basic instructions for reaching it.
5. Store the instructions separately from the seed phrases.

The best plan is one that actually gets set up, that your heirs can carry out, that does not weaken your security, and that you review.


---

# Frequently Asked Questions

> Common questions about Bitcoin self-custody, seed phrases, recovery, and security. Get answers to the questions that could save your Bitcoin.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

These are short answers to the questions people ask most about bitcoin self-custody, each linking to the page that covers it in full. The most urgent: if you lose your seed phrase and your device, the bitcoin is almost certainly gone; anyone offering to recover it for a fee is almost certainly a scammer; and a restored wallet showing zero is usually a settings problem, not lost funds.

## Common questions

### What happens if you lose your seed phrase?

If you lose your seed phrase and your hardware wallet is also lost, broken or wiped, your bitcoin is lost for good: there is no recovery mechanism. If the device still works, move the funds to a new wallet with a new seed straight away. That is why a backup is tested before money goes in; see [what if you lose your seed phrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/lost-seed/).

### Are bitcoin recovery services legitimate?

Almost never. Services that promise to recover lost or stolen bitcoin for a fee target people who have just lost money, and they take an upfront payment, or your seed phrase, and disappear. Legitimate help never needs your seed phrase. See [recovery scams](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/).

### Why does a restored wallet show a zero balance?

Usually because the restoring wallet uses a different derivation path, address type or passphrase from the original, not because the bitcoin is gone. Check those settings first; [recovery troubleshooting](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-troubleshooting/) goes through them in order.

### Is your Coldcard seed affected by the 2026 entropy flaw?

If a Coldcard generated your seed between March 2021 and July 2026 without dice, treat it as compromised and move the funds to a new seed; updating the firmware does not fix an existing seed. Seeds made with 50 or more dice rolls, and seeds imported from elsewhere, were not affected. The [incident page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) has the full table.

### Can someone steal your bitcoin if they know your address?

No. An address only lets people send you bitcoin; spending needs the private key, which comes from your seed phrase. An address does reveal its balance and history, though, which is why a new one is used for every payment.

### Do you need to run your own Bitcoin node?

It is not required, but it is recommended for privacy and verification. Without your own node, your wallet trusts a third-party server for blockchain data and tells it your addresses. See [why run your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/why-run-node/).

### What is a passphrase, and should you use one?

A passphrase, sometimes called the 25th word, is an optional extra secret combined with your seed phrase that opens a completely different wallet, so someone who finds the words alone finds nothing. If you forget it, the funds behind it are unrecoverable. It suits holdings of roughly $10,000 and more, once you are comfortable with your device; see the [passphrase guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/).

### Which hardware wallet should you buy?

For a first device, the BitBox02 Nova or the Trezor Safe 5, which are the easiest to use safely. For security you can verify more of, the Jade Plus or Passport Prime, with a seed made from dice. Coldcard is not currently recommended after the 2026 entropy incident. Any of them is far safer than leaving bitcoin on an exchange; see the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/).

### Is it safe to buy a hardware wallet on Amazon?

Buy from the manufacturer, or a reseller listed on the manufacturer's site. Tampered devices have been sold through marketplaces. If you bought elsewhere, run the maker's authenticity check, look for signs of tampering, and never accept a device that arrives with a seed phrase already set up.

### How do you know your hardware wallet is genuine?

Check the packaging for signs of opening and run the manufacturer's authenticity check during setup; Trezor Suite and the BitBoxApp, for example, check the device's attestation. A device that fails the check, or arrives already set up, should not be used. See [hardware wallet setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/#step-1-verify-the-device-is-genuine).

### How much bitcoin justifies self-custody?

Any amount you would be upset to lose. A hardware wallet costs about $80 to $250, which is worth it for holdings above roughly $1,000; below that, a phone wallet is fine while you learn. See [choose your setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/choosing-your-path/).

### What is multisig, and do you need it?

Multisig requires several keys to spend, such as any two of three, which removes single points of failure but adds complexity. We recommend it for holdings over about $100,000 or for people with higher security concerns; see [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/).

### What if you sent bitcoin to the wrong address?

Bitcoin transactions cannot be reversed. If the address belongs to someone you know, ask them to send it back; otherwise the funds are almost certainly gone. That is why every address is checked on the hardware wallet's screen before sending.

### How often should you verify your backup?

Fully when you set up a wallet, again after making a metal copy, after any change to the backup, and before major life changes; check it is still readable every 6 to 12 months. See [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/).

### How do you pass bitcoin on to your family?

With a plan your heirs can follow: where the backups are, what is needed to recover (including any passphrase or multisig descriptor), and instructions written for someone who is not technical. Bitcoin whose owner dies without sharing access is lost for good. See [inheritance planning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/).


---

# What Happens If You Lose Your Seed Phrase?

> The hard truth about losing your Bitcoin seed phrase. What you can do, what you can't do, and how to prevent this from happening to you.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/lost-seed/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

If you lose your seed phrase but your wallet device still works, nothing is lost yet: create a new wallet with a new seed, back it up properly, and move everything to it now. If you have lost the seed phrase and the device is also lost, broken or wiped, the bitcoin is almost certainly gone for good. There is no backdoor, support line or recovery service that can bring it back, and anyone who offers to is very likely a scammer. A few words missing from a seed you still mostly have is the one case that can sometimes be recovered, with open-source tools on your own computer.

## Why can't a lost seed phrase be recovered?

A seed phrase is not a password to an account held somewhere; it is the source of the private keys themselves. Those keys are the only thing that can sign a transaction moving your bitcoin, and nobody else has them: not Trezor, not Ledger, not an exchange. The network does not know who you are, only whether a signature is valid. The property that stops anyone taking your bitcoin without your keys is the same one that stops anyone recovering it for you.

## What can you do in each situation?

### The seed is lost, but the device still works

1. Create a new wallet with a new seed phrase straight away.
2. Back the new seed up properly, and test it.
3. Move all the bitcoin from the old wallet to the new one.
4. Never use the old seed again, even if you find it later; while it was lost, someone else may have found it.

Do it now, because the device could fail at any time.

### The seed and the device are both lost

The bitcoin is almost certainly unrecoverable. Before accepting that:

1. Search thoroughly: other copies you may have made, a safe deposit box, family, another property.
2. Look for partial backups: do you have some of the words (see below)? Did you ever type the seed somewhere you should not have, on an old device or in notes?
3. Check software wallet backups: some software wallets keep encrypted backups, sometimes in cloud storage. This does not apply to hardware wallets.

If none of that works, the loss is permanent.

### Some words are missing or unreadable

A partly remembered seed can sometimes be recovered by trying every possible word in the gaps. How feasible that is depends on how many words are missing, whether you know their positions, and whether you know one of the wallet's addresses to test candidates against:

| Missing words (positions known) | Candidates | Realistic? |
|---------------|------------|------------|
| 1 | 2,048 | Yes, in seconds |
| 2 | About 4.2 million | Yes, in minutes to hours on a home computer |
| 3 | About 8.6 billion | Possibly, with days of graphics-card time |
| 4 or more | 17.6 trillion and up | Not for most people |

The checksum cuts the candidates that need full testing by 16 times for a 12-word phrase and 256 times for a 24-word one. Unknown positions, or no known address to test against, make each row much harder. BTCRecover is an open-source tool for this, run on your own computer. Never give a partial seed to anyone offering to do it for you.

### You forgot the passphrase

A passphrase opens a completely different wallet, and one wrong character gives a different one. If you remember roughly what it was, trying variations (with BTCRecover, for example) can work; if you have no idea, recovery is effectively impossible, for the same reason guessing missing words is.

## How do recovery scams work?

**Danger: Almost every bitcoin "recovery service" is a scam**
They ask for your partial seed phrase and take whatever is left, or ask for a fee up front and vanish. They claim special technology they do not have and show testimonials they invented. No service can recover a fully lost seed phrase.

If someone contacts you offering recovery, they found you because you posted about your loss, which scammers watch for, and they will sound professional and sympathetic. Legitimate help looks different: open-source tools that you run yourself, honesty about the limits, and no request for your seed phrase. [Recovery scams](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/) covers the tactics.

## How do people lose seed phrases?

| Cause | Examples |
|---|---|
| Poor backups | Paper that was damaged or thrown away, a single copy, a backup never tested, a photo on a phone that was later lost |
| Life events | A fire or flood, theft, moving house and losing track, the death of a relative who held a copy |
| Habits of mind | "I'll remember where I put it", "I'll make a proper backup later", too many wallets to keep track of |

## What should you do now to avoid it?

1. Find your seed backup today, check it is complete and legible, and [test a recovery](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) on a separate device.
2. Make copies, on [metal](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/#step-6-back-up-on-metal), and keep them in separate places.
3. Keep a secure record of where the backups are, plan for [inheritance](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/inheritance-planning/), and do not hide them so well that you forget them.
4. Keep the setup simple enough to manage; complexity creates its own ways to fail.

If you have already lost bitcoin, do not chase it through "recovery" services. Many early bitcoiners lost coins to poor backups; it is a hard lesson, and the practices above stop it happening again.

## Common questions

### Can you recover your bitcoin if you lost your seed phrase?

If your seed phrase is lost and your hardware wallet is also lost, broken or wiped, your bitcoin is permanently inaccessible. There is no backdoor, no customer support and no recovery service that can recover funds without the seed phrase. The only routes are finding the original backup, or an unwiped device that still holds the keys.

### Why is it impossible to guess a lost seed phrase?

A 24-word BIP39 seed holds 256 bits of entropy, so guessing it means trying up to 2^256 combinations, more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. No computer can do that in any practical time, and quantum computers would at best halve the effective bits, which still leaves an impossible search.

### Are seed phrase recovery services legitimate?

No. Any service claiming to recover a lost seed phrase from a hardware wallet, an exchange or an address is a scam, because recovery without the seed is impossible. Legitimate help is limited to cases such as finding a few missing words or a partly remembered passphrase with open-source tools you run yourself, or repairing a damaged device that still holds the keys.

### What should you do now to avoid losing your seed phrase?

Write it on metal rather than paper, keep copies in at least two separate places, test a recovery before depositing significant funds, and never store it digitally. If you cannot afford to lose access through a single lost backup, consider a 2-of-3 multisig.


---

# Bitcoin Recovery Scams: How to Protect Yourself

> Why almost every 'Bitcoin recovery service' is a scam. Learn to recognize fraud and understand what legitimate recovery actually looks like.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A bitcoin recovery scam is an offer, usually unsolicited, to recover lost or stolen bitcoin for a fee or in exchange for your seed phrase. Nobody can recover bitcoin from a lost seed phrase, reverse a confirmed transaction or take coins back from a thief's address, so the offer is a fraud: the scammer takes the fee and disappears, or takes the seed phrase and empties whatever is left. If someone contacts you about recovering bitcoin, treat them as a scammer, do not send money or information, and block them.

## Why are recovery scams so common?

People who have just lost bitcoin are distressed and want to believe it can be undone, and scammers look for them deliberately: they watch social media, Reddit and bitcoin forums for posts about lost coins, run advertisements for "recovery services", build convincing websites, and impersonate real companies. Their approach is professional, sympathetic and full of false hope.

## What forms do recovery scams take?

| Scam | How it works | Warning signs |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront payment | They claim they can recover your bitcoin, take a fee (often in crypto or gift cards), show fake "progress", then disappear or demand more | Any payment before recovery; vague explanations of their "technology"; pressure to act quickly; untraceable payment methods |
| Seed phrase theft | They say they need your partial seed phrase "to help", then take any funds they can reach, or brute-force the gaps faster than you | Any request for your seed phrase or part of it; offers to "check whether your seed is valid"; requests for remote access |
| Fake software or websites | A "recovery tool" or site asks you to enter your seed phrase, sends it to the scammer and sweeps the wallet | Any website asking for a seed phrase; downloads from unofficial sources; promises of "instant recovery" |
| Impersonation | Someone posing as Ledger, Trezor or another company reports a "security breach" and asks you to "verify" your seed | Unexpected contact from a wallet company; urgent security warnings; any request for a seed phrase, which real companies never make |

Common stories follow these patterns: a victim shown screenshots of other "recovered" wallets pays a fee and hears nothing more; another is told twelve of their twenty-four words are needed "to verify the format" and finds the wallet empty the next day; another receives an email that looks exactly like their wallet maker's and enters the seed phrase to "protect" it; another pays a first fee, then a second, then a third for "mining fees", and loses everything.

## Why is recovery impossible?

A 24-word seed phrase holds 256 bits of randomness, about 10^77 possible seeds, more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Guessing one with no information would take longer than the age of the universe on any computer, and no technique for "hacking the blockchain" exists.

What is possible is narrower, and you can do it yourself with open-source tools: finding a few missing words from a seed you mostly have (one or two easily, three with days of graphics-card time when the positions are known), or a partly remembered passphrase. [What if you lose your seed phrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/lost-seed/#some-words-are-missing-or-unreadable) sets out the limits.

## What does legitimate help look like?

| Legitimate | Fraudulent |
|---|---|
| Open-source tools you download and run yourself, such as [BTCRecover](https://github.com/3rdIteration/btcrecover); nobody else sees your seed | Claims to recover any seed phrase |
| Clear about the limits: a fully lost seed cannot be recovered | Asks for payment up front |
| Free, or paid only for a defined result | Needs your seed phrase or part of it |
| Explains the process so you understand it | Vague "proprietary technology" |
| You go to it | It contacts you first, often with urgency |

## What should you do if you have lost access?

If you are thinking about using a recovery service: stop, and do not act while upset. A fully lost seed cannot be recovered; use only open-source tools that you run yourself; never share your seed phrase; and accept that some losses are permanent.

If you have part of the seed: write down everything you remember, including possible variations; download BTCRecover from its official GitHub page; run it on an offline computer if you can; be patient; and never share the partial seed with "helpers".

If someone has contacted you: assume they are a scammer, do not engage, send nothing, and block and report them.

## What if you have already been scammed?

1. Stop all contact, and send no more money, even if they promise to return the first payment.
2. Record everything: messages, addresses, amounts.
3. Report it to your local police, and in the US to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center ([ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/)), or your country's fraud reporting body.
4. Report the scammer on the platform where you found them, and warn others.

Recovering money lost to scammers is rare; reporting helps stop them reaching others. Do not hire a second "recovery" service to get back what the first one took: those are scams too.

## How do you protect yourself in future?

Keep proper backups, with several copies and a tested recovery; never share your seed phrase with anyone, for any reason; distrust anything that sounds too good; check official sources rather than search adverts; and know what is and is not possible. The [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) and the [before you deposit checklist](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/before-you-deposit/) cover the practice.

| Claim | Reality |
|-------|---------|
| "We can recover any lost bitcoin" | Impossible |
| "We have special technology" | No such technology exists |
| "Send us your seed to verify it" | They will empty the wallet |
| "Pay up front and we will recover it" | You will lose the fee too |
| "We have recovered millions for clients" | Invented testimonials |

## Common questions

### How do bitcoin recovery scams work?

Scammers reach victims through search adverts, social media and forums, claiming they can recover lost or stolen bitcoin. They charge fees up front, or ask for sensitive information such as seed phrases or wallet files, then disappear or demand more. No legitimate service can recover bitcoin from a lost seed phrase.

### Can a hacker recover your stolen bitcoin?

No. Once bitcoin has moved to an address a thief controls, only the thief's private key can move it again. No hacker, government agency or recovery service can reverse a confirmed transaction or extract keys from an address.

### Are there any legitimate bitcoin recovery services?

A few help with narrow problems: guessing a forgotten passphrase you partly remember, brute-forcing a weak password on an encrypted wallet file, or repairing a physically damaged device that still holds the keys. They never claim to recover funds from a lost seed phrase, and they work openly, with references you can check.

### What should you do if a recovery service has scammed you?

Stop all contact, pay nothing more, record everything, and report it to your local cybercrime authority and the platform where you found the scammer. Do not hire a second recovery service to get back what the first took; those are scams too.


---

# Wallet Recovery Troubleshooting

> Common problems when recovering a Bitcoin wallet and how to solve them. Empty wallet after recovery, wrong addresses, and other troubleshooting steps.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-troubleshooting/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

When a wallet restored from a seed phrase shows a zero balance or unfamiliar addresses, the bitcoin is almost always still there: the restoring wallet is looking in the wrong place. Check, in this order, that it uses the same script type and derivation path as the original (the first characters of your old addresses tell you which), the same passphrase if you used one, the same account number, and a large enough gap limit, and that the seed is a BIP39 seed rather than Electrum's own format. Only if all of that fails is the seed itself likely to be wrong.

## Why does a restored wallet show a zero balance?

### The derivation path or script type is different

Wallets derive addresses along a [derivation path](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path/), and the path depends on the address type. Restoring with a different one shows a different, empty set of addresses.

| Your old addresses started with | Script type to choose | Derivation path |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|---|
| `1` | Legacy (P2PKH, BIP44) | `m/44'/0'/0'` |
| `3` | Nested segwit (P2SH-P2WPKH, BIP49) | `m/49'/0'/0'` |
| `bc1q` | Native segwit (P2WPKH, BIP84) | `m/84'/0'/0'` |
| `bc1p` | Taproot (P2TR, BIP86) | `m/86'/0'/0'` |

In Sparrow, create a new wallet, enter the seed, and choose the script type that matches; if it is still empty, try the others. Most current wallets, including Trezor Suite and Electrum (for BIP39 seeds), default to native segwit (`bc1q`); older wallets often used legacy.

### A passphrase was used

If you set a passphrase, the seed phrase alone opens a different, empty wallet. Restore again with the passphrase enabled (in Sparrow, tick the passphrase option when entering the seed). Passphrases are case-sensitive and every space counts: `MyPassphrase` and `mypassphrase` open different wallets. See [what counts as a different passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/#what-exactly-counts-as-a-different-passphrase).

### A word is wrong

One wrong word gives a completely different wallet, and occasionally a wrong word still passes the checksum. Check each word against the [BIP39 word list](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/english.txt). Misspellings such as "advise" for "advice" or "latter" for "letter" are easy to spot, because every word on the list is identified by its first four letters and the near-misses are not on it.

### The wallet has not looked far enough

Wallets stop scanning after a run of unused addresses, usually 20, called the gap limit. If you generated many addresses without using them, later funds may not be found. Raise the gap limit (in Sparrow, in the wallet's settings under Advanced) to 100 or more and rescan.

### The seed is an Electrum seed

Electrum creates its own kind of seed by default, from the same word list but with a different checksum, and it does not restore in BIP39 wallets (they reject it as invalid, or the result is empty). If the seed came from Electrum, restore it in Electrum, choosing its own seed type rather than BIP39.

## Why are the addresses different from the ones you expected?

Check the script type first, using the table above. Then check the account number: some wallets use several accounts under one seed, at `m/84'/0'/0'`, `m/84'/0'/1'`, `m/84'/0'/2'` and so on, and restoring account 0 shows none of account 1's addresses. When importing, set the account number (the third number in the path) to the one you used.

## Why does the wallet reject the seed phrase?

A rejected seed has failed its checksum, which means at least one word is wrong or in the wrong place. Check each word against the list, check the order, and check the number of words, which must be 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24. Check the language too: BIP39 has word lists in several languages, and a seed made in a Spanish or Japanese wallet needs the same language to restore. An Electrum seed is also rejected by BIP39 wallets (see above).

## Why were only some of the funds found?

You may have received bitcoin to more than one address type, for example some to legacy addresses and some to native segwit ones, or used more than one account. In Sparrow, create a wallet for each script type, and for accounts 0, 1 and 2, from the same seed, and check each balance. Funds from transactions that have not confirmed appear only once they confirm; check their status on [mempool.space](https://mempool.space).

## What if the hardware wallet shows a different address from the software?

Treat it as a security problem until proven otherwise, and never send to an address the hardware wallet does not display. The cause may be malware altering the address on the computer, a different derivation path in the software, or a hardware wallet holding a different seed from the one you expect. Check you have the right wallet file, check the paths match, and pair the device with the software again. If the addresses still differ, do not transact.

## How do you recover a multisig wallet?

A multisig needs more than seed phrases: the wallet descriptor (or configuration file), which records every key's xpub and the M-of-N rule. Find your descriptor backup and import it; in Sparrow, use `File`, `Import Wallet`. The order of keys matters in older multisig setups, so rebuild from the original descriptor rather than by hand. [Multisig backup and recovery](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/backup-recovery/) covers the whole process.

## What should you check, in order?

1. Every word against the BIP39 list, and the word count.
2. Whether a passphrase was used.
3. Each script type: legacy, nested segwit, native segwit, Taproot.
4. Account numbers 0, 1 and 2.
5. A gap limit of 100 or more.
6. Whether the seed is an Electrum seed.
7. A second wallet program, to rule out the first.
8. For multisig, the wallet descriptor.

## When should you get help?

Ask for help only after working through the checklist, and only from people and tools that never need your seed phrase: open-source tools you run yourself, or the community forums of your wallet. Most "bitcoin recovery services" are scams; read [recovery scams](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-scams/) before contacting anyone.

To avoid all of this next time, write down which wallet software you used, which script type and derivation path, and whether you used a passphrase, keep that note with your backup, and [test the backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) before relying on it.

## Common questions

### Why does a recovered wallet show a zero balance?

The usual cause is a different derivation path or address type from the original wallet. Restore with the path and script type that match your old addresses (legacy, nested segwit, native segwit or Taproot). If you used a passphrase, you must enter exactly the same one to reach the original wallet.

### Why does a recovered wallet show different addresses than expected?

Different wallets use different default derivation paths, so restoring a seed in another wallet can produce valid addresses you do not recognise. Check the derivation path and script type, and match them to what your original wallet used.

### What if a recovery finds only some of your funds?

The rest may be under a different account number, derivation path or passphrase. Check every standard path, raise the gap limit above the default of 20, and make sure you have not used more than one passphrase with the same seed.

### When should you get professional help with wallet recovery?

Only after checking derivation paths, address types, gap limits and passphrases yourself. Use reputable open-source tools, and avoid any service that asks for your seed phrase. For a multisig, use the original wallet software and your own backups before contacting anyone.


---

# Bitcoin Glossary: 100+ Terms Explained

> Complete glossary of Bitcoin and self-custody terminology. Definitions for UTXO, seed phrase, hardware wallet, multisig, and 100+ other terms.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/glossary/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Plain-language definitions of the Bitcoin and self-custody terms used across this site, from address types and air-gapping through to UTXOs, xpubs, and derivation paths. Over 100 entries, listed alphabetically. If a term you need is missing, [email us](mailto:selfcustodylabs@proton.me) and we will add it.

---

## Jump to a letter

[A](#a) · [B](#b) · [C](#c) · [D](#d) · [E](#e) · [F](#f) · [G](#g) · [H](#h) · [I](#i) · [J](#j) · [K](#k) · [L](#l) · [M](#m) · [N](#n) · [O](#o) · [P](#p) · [Q](#q) · [R](#r) · [S](#s) · [T](#t) · [U](#u) · [V](#v) · [W](#w) · [X](#x)

---

## A

### Address
A string of characters representing a destination for Bitcoin payments. Similar to an email address, but for receiving Bitcoin. Modern addresses typically start with `bc1q` (SegWit) or `bc1p` (Taproot). See [Address Types](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/address-types).

### Air-Gapped
A security measure where a device is completely isolated from the internet and other networks. Air-gapped computers communicate only through QR codes, SD cards, or manual data entry. See [Air-Gapped Computer Guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets).

### Altcoin
Any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin. Examples include Ethereum, Litecoin, and thousands of others.

---

## B

### Bech32
The encoding format for Native SegWit addresses (starting with `bc1q`). Uses only lowercase letters and numbers, avoiding confusing characters like `0/O` and `1/l`.

### Bech32m
An updated version of Bech32 used for Taproot addresses (starting with `bc1p`).

### BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal)
A design document for introducing new features or information to Bitcoin. Important BIPs include BIP39 (seed phrases), BIP32 (HD wallets), and BIP44/49/84/86 (derivation paths).

### BIP39
The standard for mnemonic seed phrases. Defines the 2048-word list used to encode wallet seeds as human-readable words. See [Seed Phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed).

### Bitcoin Core
The reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. A full node software that validates all transactions and blocks. See [Bitcoin Node Guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node).

### Block
A collection of Bitcoin transactions bundled together and added to the blockchain. New blocks are created approximately every 10 minutes.

### Blockchain
A distributed ledger containing all Bitcoin transactions ever made. Each block links to the previous one, forming a chain.

### Block Explorer
A web tool that lets you view transactions, addresses, and blocks on the blockchain. Examples: Mempool.space, Blockstream.info.

### Block Height
The number of blocks in the blockchain since the genesis block (block 0). Used to identify specific points in Bitcoin's history.

### Block Reward
The amount of new bitcoin created with each block, paid to the miner who finds the block. Currently 3.125 BTC, halving approximately every 4 years.

---

## C

### Change Address
When you spend a UTXO but don't use the full amount, the remainder is sent to a change address in your own wallet. Like getting change when you pay with a $20 bill.

### Change Output
The transaction output that returns excess funds to the sender's wallet after a payment.

### Checksum
A small piece of data used to verify integrity. In seed phrases, the final word(s) include checksum data to detect errors.

### Coinjoin
A privacy technique that combines multiple users' transactions into a single transaction, making it difficult to trace which inputs correspond to which outputs. See [CoinJoin Guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin).

### Cold Storage
Keeping Bitcoin private keys on a device that never connects to the internet. The most secure form of storage.

### Cold Wallet
A wallet that stores private keys offline. Hardware wallets and air-gapped computers are cold wallets.

### Confirmation
Each new block added after a transaction is included counts as one confirmation. More confirmations = higher certainty the transaction is permanent. 6 confirmations is traditionally considered final.

### Consensus
The agreement among Bitcoin nodes about the current state of the blockchain. Bitcoin's proof-of-work consensus ensures all honest nodes agree.

### CPFP (Child Pays for Parent)
A technique to speed up an unconfirmed transaction by creating a new transaction that spends its output with a higher fee.

### Custodial
A service where a third party holds your private keys (and thus your Bitcoin) on your behalf. Exchanges are custodial. Opposite of self-custody.

---

## D

### Derivation Path
The hierarchical path used to derive specific keys from a master seed. Example: `m/84'/0'/0'/0/0`. Different paths generate different addresses. See [Derivation Paths](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path).

### Descriptor
A standardized way to describe how addresses are generated from keys. Used for wallet backup and recovery, especially in multisig setups.

### Difficulty
A measure of how hard it is to mine a new block. Adjusts every 2016 blocks (~2 weeks) to maintain the 10-minute block target.

### Dusting Attack
A privacy attack where tiny amounts of Bitcoin are sent to many addresses to track their future spending patterns.

---

## E

### Electrum Server
