Software that indexes the Bitcoin blockchain to allow lightweight wallets to query transaction data efficiently. Examples: Electrs, Fulcrum.

### Entropy
Randomness used to generate private keys and seed phrases. High-quality entropy is essential for security: the [2026 Coldcard incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/), where weak entropy let attackers brute-force seeds and steal ~$116M, is the canonical example of what happens without it. See [Why Randomness Matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random).

---

## F

### Fee
The amount paid to miners to include a transaction in a block. Measured in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB).

### Fee Rate
The fee density of a transaction, typically measured in sat/vB. Higher fee rates result in faster confirmation.

### Full Node
Software that independently validates all Bitcoin transactions and blocks against consensus rules. See [What is a Bitcoin Node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/what-is-node).

---

## G

### Genesis Block
The first block in the Bitcoin blockchain, mined by Satoshi Nakamoto on January 3, 2009.

---

## H

### Halving
The event where the block reward is cut in half, occurring approximately every 4 years (210,000 blocks). Reduces Bitcoin's inflation rate.

### Hardware Wallet
A dedicated physical device designed to securely store Bitcoin private keys offline. Examples: Trezor, BitBox02, Jade, Passport, Keystone. See [Hardware Wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets).

### Hash
A fixed-length output produced by running data through a cryptographic hash function. Used extensively in Bitcoin for security and verification.

### Hash Rate
The total computational power being used to mine Bitcoin, measured in hashes per second.

### HD Wallet (Hierarchical Deterministic)
A wallet that generates all addresses from a single seed phrase, allowing complete wallet recovery from just the seed words.

### Hot Wallet
A wallet connected to the internet. More convenient but less secure than cold storage. See [Software Wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/software-wallets).

---

## I

### Input
A reference to a previous transaction output being spent in a new transaction. Transactions consume inputs and create outputs.

### Intel ME (Management Engine)
The Intel Management Engine is a separate processor in Intel chipsets that runs its own closed firmware, with access to memory and the network, independently of the operating system. On most Intel machines it cannot be removed, only cut down and disabled, as Libreboot and coreboot do with me_cleaner. See the [Libreboot guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/).

---

## J

### JSON-RPC
A protocol used to communicate with Bitcoin Core. Many wallet applications use JSON-RPC to interact with a node.

---

## K

### KYC (Know Your Customer)
Identity verification requirements imposed by exchanges and financial services. Links your identity to your Bitcoin purchases, reducing privacy.

---

## L

### Legacy Address
The original Bitcoin address format, starting with `1`. Higher transaction fees than newer formats. See [Address Types](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/address-types).

### Lightning Network
A "Layer 2" payment network built on top of Bitcoin, enabling fast, low-fee transactions.

### Libreboot
Libreboot is an open-source replacement for a computer's BIOS or UEFI firmware, built on coreboot, that keeps proprietary vendor code to the minimum a board needs and disables the Intel ME where it can. See the [Libreboot guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/).

---

## M

### Mempool
The collection of unconfirmed transactions waiting to be included in a block. Each node maintains its own mempool.

### Mining
The process of using computational power to validate transactions and create new blocks. Miners compete to solve a proof-of-work puzzle.

### Mnemonic
The human-readable word sequence (seed phrase) used to encode a wallet's seed. See [Seed Phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed).

### Multisig (Multisignature)
A security setup requiring multiple private keys to authorize a transaction. Example: 2-of-3 multisig needs any 2 of 3 keys to spend. See [Multisig Setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig).

---

## N

### Native SegWit
The most efficient address format for standard transactions, starting with `bc1q`. Lower fees than Legacy or Nested SegWit. See [Address Types](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/address-types).

### Nested SegWit
A backwards-compatible SegWit format using addresses starting with `3`. A bridge between Legacy and Native SegWit.

### Node
A computer running Bitcoin software that validates and relays transactions. See [Bitcoin Node Guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node).

### Non-Custodial
A wallet or service where you control your own private keys. Self-custody is non-custodial.

---

## O

### OP_RETURN
A Bitcoin script opcode that allows storing small amounts of data in a transaction without creating spendable outputs.

### Orphan Block
A valid block that is not part of the main chain, usually because another block at the same height was propagated first.

### Output
The destination(s) of a Bitcoin transaction. Each output specifies an amount and the conditions for spending it.

---

## P

### P2PKH (Pay to Public Key Hash)
The technical name for Legacy addresses (starting with `1`).

### P2SH (Pay to Script Hash)
The technical name for Script addresses (starting with `3`). Used for complex scripts including Nested SegWit.

### P2TR (Pay to Taproot)
The technical name for Taproot addresses (starting with `bc1p`).

### P2WPKH (Pay to Witness Public Key Hash)
The technical name for Native SegWit addresses (starting with `bc1q`).

### Passphrase
An optional extra secret, which can be any text, combined with a seed phrase to open a separate wallet. Sometimes called the "25th word", though it is not a word from the BIP39 list. See [Passphrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/).

### PayJoin
A privacy-enhancing transaction where both sender and receiver contribute inputs, breaking blockchain analysis heuristics.

### Private Key
A secret number that controls Bitcoin at a specific address. Must be kept secret. See [Private Keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/intro).

### Proof of Work (PoW)
The consensus mechanism Bitcoin uses to secure the network. Miners must perform computational work to create new blocks.

### PSBT (Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction)
A format for passing unsigned or partially signed transactions between devices or parties. Essential for hardware wallets and multisig.

### Public Key
A number derived from a private key that can be shared publicly. Used to generate addresses and verify signatures.

---

## Q

### QR Code
A two-dimensional barcode often used to encode Bitcoin addresses for easy scanning.

---

## R

### RBF (Replace-By-Fee)
A feature allowing an unconfirmed transaction to be replaced with a new version paying a higher fee.

### Recovery Phrase
See Seed Phrase.

### RPC (Remote Procedure Call)
A protocol for applications to communicate with Bitcoin Core. See JSON-RPC.

---

## S

### Satoshi (sat)
The smallest unit of Bitcoin: 0.00000001 BTC. Named after Bitcoin's creator, Satoshi Nakamoto.

### Satoshi Nakamoto
The pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin who published the whitepaper in 2008 and launched the network in 2009.

### Script
Bitcoin's programming language used to define spending conditions for transactions.

### Secure Element
A tamper-resistant hardware chip that protects sensitive data (like private keys) from physical attacks.

### Seed Phrase
A sequence of 12 or 24 words that encodes your wallet's master seed. The backup that can restore your entire wallet. See [Seed Phrases](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed).

### SegWit (Segregated Witness)
A 2017 Bitcoin upgrade that separates transaction signatures ("witness" data) from transaction data, enabling more efficient transactions and fixing transaction malleability.

### Self-Custody
Holding your own Bitcoin private keys, rather than trusting a third party. See [What is self-custody](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/fundamentals/what-is-self-custody/).

### Signature
Cryptographic proof that a transaction was authorized by the private key owner.

### Signing Device
A hardware wallet or other device used to sign Bitcoin transactions. See [Hardware Wallet Setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet).

### Single-Sig
A standard wallet where one private key controls the funds. Contrast with multisig.

### SOIC8
A type of chip package commonly used for BIOS flash chips. Relevant for [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot) flashing.

### Software Wallet
An application (mobile or desktop) that manages Bitcoin keys on a general-purpose device. See [Software Wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/software-wallets).

### SPV (Simplified Payment Verification)
A method for lightweight wallets to verify transactions without downloading the full blockchain.

---

## T

### Taproot
A 2021 Bitcoin upgrade enabling more efficient and private complex transactions using Schnorr signatures. Addresses start with `bc1p`.

### Testnet
A separate Bitcoin network for testing, using worthless coins. Developers use testnet to experiment without risking real Bitcoin.

### Timelock
A restriction that prevents Bitcoin from being spent until a certain time or block height.

### Tor (The Onion Router)
Privacy network that anonymizes internet traffic. Can be used with Bitcoin nodes and wallets for enhanced privacy.

### Transaction
A signed message that transfers Bitcoin from one or more inputs to one or more outputs.

### Transaction ID (TXID)
A unique identifier for a Bitcoin transaction, generated by hashing the transaction data.

---

## U

### UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output)
A Bitcoin amount that has been received but not yet spent. Your wallet balance is the sum of your UTXOs. See [UTXOs Explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/transactions/utxos).

### UTXO Set
The collection of all unspent transaction outputs in the Bitcoin network. What every Bitcoin node tracks.

---

## V

### Vanity Address
A Bitcoin address containing a custom pattern (like `1Love...`). Generated by repeatedly creating addresses until a match is found.

### vByte (Virtual Byte)
The unit used to measure transaction size for fee calculation. Accounts for SegWit's different weighting of witness data.

### Verification
The process of independently confirming that data (like a transaction or software download) is valid and unmodified.

---

## W

### Wallet
Software or hardware that manages Bitcoin private keys and enables sending/receiving Bitcoin.

### Wallet Descriptor
See Descriptor.

### Watch-Only Wallet
A wallet that can monitor addresses and create unsigned transactions but cannot sign (spend) because it doesn't have the private keys.

### Whitepaper
The original Bitcoin paper published by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008: "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System."

### Witness
In SegWit transactions, the signature data that proves ownership. Separated from the main transaction for efficiency.

---

## X

### xprv (Extended Private Key)
A master private key that can derive all other private keys and addresses in an HD wallet. Must be kept secret like a seed phrase. See [Extended Private Keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xprv).

### xpub (Extended Public Key)
A master public key that can derive all public keys and addresses in an HD wallet. Can be shared to generate receive addresses without exposing private keys. See [Extended Public Keys](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub).

---

## Numbers & Symbols

### 2-of-3
A common multisig configuration requiring any 2 of 3 keys to spend funds. See [Multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig).

### 21 Million
The maximum supply of Bitcoin that will ever exist, enforced by Bitcoin's consensus rules.

### 51% Attack
A theoretical attack where an entity controlling more than half the network's hash rate could double-spend or censor transactions.


---

# Bitcoin Address Types Explained

> Understand the different Bitcoin address types: Legacy, SegWit, Native SegWit, and Taproot. Learn which to use and why it matters for fees and compatibility.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/address-types/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Bitcoin has four address types in common use, told apart by their first characters: legacy addresses start with `1`, nested segwit with `3`, native segwit with `bc1q` and Taproot with `bc1p`. They differ in fees and features, not in security, and you can send from any type to any other. Use native segwit (`bc1q`) by default: it is cheap to spend from and every current wallet and exchange supports it. Taproot (`bc1p`) is the newer alternative, with the most to gain in multisig and complex setups.

The four look like this:

- `1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa` (starts with 1)
- `3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy` (starts with 3)
- `bc1qar0srrr7xfkvy5l643lydnw9re59gtzzwf5mdq` (starts with bc1q)
- `bc1p5d7rjq7g6rdk2yhzks9smlaqtedr4dekq08ge8ztwac72sfr9rusxg3297` (starts with bc1p)

## What are the four address types?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Type | Prefix | Name | Year | Status |
|------|--------|------|------|--------|
| Legacy | `1...` | P2PKH | 2009 | Outdated |
| Nested segwit | `3...` | P2SH-P2WPKH | 2012 | Transitional |
| Native segwit | `bc1q...` | P2WPKH / Bech32 | 2017 | Recommended |
| Taproot | `bc1p...` | P2TR / Bech32m | 2021 | Newest |

</div>

## What is a legacy address?

A legacy address (P2PKH, pay to public key hash) is the original format from 2009 and starts with `1`. Every wallet and exchange can send to it, but coins held at it cost the most to spend, because a legacy input is about 148 vbytes against 68 for native segwit. Use one only for a service that accepts nothing else.

## What is a nested segwit address?

A nested segwit address (P2SH-P2WPKH) starts with `3` and wraps a segwit script inside the pay-to-script-hash format introduced in 2012, so that services built before segwit could still send to it. The same `3` prefix is used by every P2SH script, including older multisig wallets, so a `3` address alone does not tell you which it is. Its inputs, about 91 vbytes, are cheaper than legacy and dearer than native segwit; there is no reason to choose it today unless a service cannot send to `bc1` addresses.

## What is a native segwit address?

A native segwit address (P2WPKH, encoded in Bech32) starts with `bc1q` and has been in use since 2017. It is all lowercase, so it is easy to read aloud and compact in a QR code, and its checksum catches most typing mistakes. Its inputs are about 68 vbytes. It is the default in almost every current wallet, and the type we recommend.

## What is a Taproot address?

A Taproot address (P2TR, encoded in Bech32m) starts with `bc1p` and has been usable since the Taproot upgrade activated in November 2021. It uses Schnorr signatures, and when the signers of a multisig combine their keys into one (MuSig2), spending looks on chain like an ordinary single-signature payment; a Taproot multisig that spends through its script is still recognisable as multisig. For a simple single-signature payment it saves almost nothing over native segwit, because its smaller input is offset by a larger output. Support for sending to `bc1p` arrived later than for `bc1q`, so check that a service can pay to one before you hand it out.

## How do the fees compare?

The size of an input, and so the fee to spend it, depends on the address type the coin is held at:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Spending from | Input size | Fee, relative to legacy |
|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| Legacy (P2PKH) | 148 vbytes | 100% (baseline) |
| Nested segwit (P2SH-P2WPKH) | 91 vbytes | ~61% |
| Native segwit (P2WPKH) | 68 vbytes | ~46% |
| Taproot (P2TR) | 57 vbytes | ~39% |

</div>

Spending a native segwit input costs about 54% less than a legacy one; for a whole typical payment, with its outputs and overhead, the saving is about 38%. Taproot inputs are the smallest, but Taproot outputs are larger (about 43 vB against 31), so a simple Taproot payment costs about the same as a native segwit one.

## Which should you use?

| Type | Use it when | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Native segwit (`bc1q`) | By default | Low fees, universal support, in use since 2017 |
| Taproot (`bc1p`) | Your wallet and the services you use support it, especially for multisig | A multisig or complex script spent by agreement looks like an ordinary single-signature payment, which helps privacy and saves space |
| Nested segwit (`3`) | Only for an old service that cannot send to `bc1` addresses | A transitional format with higher fees |
| Legacy (`1`) | Only when nothing else is accepted | Roughly twice the input fee of native segwit, for no benefit |

## What do wallets use by default?

Most current wallets support every type and default to native segwit:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Wallet | Default address type |
|--------|---------------------|
| Sparrow | Native segwit (`bc1q`), configurable |
| Electrum | Native segwit (`bc1q`), configurable |
| Trezor Suite | Native segwit (`bc1q`) |
| Ledger Live | Native segwit (`bc1q`) |
| Coldcard | Native segwit (`bc1q`), configurable |
| BlueWallet | Native segwit (`bc1q`) |

</div>

Where the table says configurable, the address type can be changed in the wallet's settings or when creating the wallet.

## Which derivation path goes with each type?

Each address type has its own **derivation path**, the route from your seed phrase to its addresses; see [derivation paths](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/derivation-path/).

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Address type | Derivation path | Standard |
|--------------|-----------------|--------------|
| Legacy | `m/44'/0'/0'` | BIP44 |
| Nested segwit | `m/49'/0'/0'` | BIP49 |
| Native segwit | `m/84'/0'/0'` | BIP84 |
| Taproot | `m/86'/0'/0'` | BIP86 |

</div>

When restoring a wallet you need the same path as the original to see your funds. Most wallets handle it automatically, but if a restored wallet is empty, the path is the first thing to check.

## Common questions

### Can you send between different address types?

Yes. You can send from any address type to any other; to the network it is all bitcoin.

### Why does your wallet show a different address each time?

Wallets give you a new address for every payment, for privacy. Each one is different, but all of them come from your seed phrase and all belong to you.

### What if an exchange will not send to a bc1 address?

A few old services still cannot send to `bc1` addresses. Use a different exchange, withdraw to a nested segwit (`3`) address in your wallet for now, or ask the exchange to add support.

### Does the address type affect security?

Not directly. Every type is secure; the differences are in fees, features and compatibility.

### Why does a recovered wallet show a zero balance?

Usually because it is looking at a different address type or derivation path from the original wallet, not because the funds are gone. Set the restoring wallet to the address type your old addresses used, or try each type in Sparrow or Electrum; [recovery troubleshooting](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/faq/recovery-troubleshooting/) covers the rest.


---

# Coldcard vs Trezor vs Jade vs Passport: 2026 Compared

> Compare Bitcoin hardware wallets after the 2026 Coldcard incident: Trezor Safe 7, BitBox02 Nova, Jade Plus, Passport, SeedSigner, Bitkey, and more.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

For a first Bitcoin hardware wallet in October 2026, the BitBox02 Nova (€175) and the Trezor Safe 5 ($129) are the easiest devices to use safely. For security you can verify yourself rather than take on trust, the Blockstream Jade Plus ($149) signs over QR codes without a cable and is fully open source. Our favourite is the [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/), a stateless signer you build yourself, for anyone comfortable with the assembly; it is not a beginner's device. Coldcard is not recommended after the 2026 entropy incident, and Ledger and Bitkey are not recommended because their critical parts cannot be verified. Which device you buy matters less than three habits: supply your own dice entropy when the seed is created, add a passphrase, and split keys across vendors once the balance is significant.

This comparison weighs devices differently from most. In July 2026, attackers drained about $116 million from wallets whose seeds had been generated on Coldcards running firmware with a five-year-old flaw: the devices were air-gapped and worked as designed, but their seeds were guessable. [What happened and who is affected](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) is the full account. Since then, whether you can check a device's randomness, and how its maker behaves when something goes wrong, count for as much as its screen and chips.

## Quick comparison table

Prices are the makers' own store prices, checked on 26 October 2026: in US dollars, except BitBox, which sells in euros. Bitkey's, marked "Aug", was last confirmed in August 2026.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Wallet | Price | Air-gapped | Open source | Secure element | Your own dice entropy | Best for |
|--------|-------|---------|-------------|----------------|---------------------|----------|
| Trezor Safe 5 | $129 | No | Yes | Yes, EAL6+ | Import only | Beginners |
| Trezor Safe 7 | $249 | No | Yes | Yes, two (including the auditable TROPIC01) | Import only | Transparency with polish |
| BitBox02 Nova | €175 | No | Yes | Yes, EAL6+ | Vendor procedure | Simplicity |
| Jade | $79 | Yes, QR with the optional camera | Yes | No: virtual, "blind oracle" | Vendor procedure | Budget |
| Jade Plus | $149 ($169 metal) | Yes, QR | Yes | No: virtual, "blind oracle" | Vendor procedure | Verifiable security |
| Passport Prime | $565 | Yes, QR, plus encrypted Bluetooth | Yes | Yes | Vendor procedure | Premium air-gap |
| Keystone 3 Pro | $149 | Yes, QR only | Yes | Yes, three chips | On the device | QR air-gap value |
| SeedSigner or Krux | About $50-80 in parts | Yes, stateless QR | Yes | None: stateless | On the device | Building your own |
| Coldcard Mk5 or Q | $219 or $319 | Yes, microSD (and QR on the Q) | Source visible, not open licence | Yes, two | On the device | Not recommended for new purchases |
| Ledger (Nano, Flex, Stax) | $69-399 | No | No: secure element firmware is closed | Yes | Import only | Not recommended |
| Bitkey | $250 (Aug) | No | Partly: source published, not reproducible | Yes, secure enclave | No | Not recommended |

</div>

The Coldcard prices are the store's reduced prices on 26 October 2026; the list prices are $269 and $369. In the dice column, "on the device" means you enter dice rolls on the device itself; "vendor procedure" means the maker documents a way to choose the words yourself and enter them; "import only" means you make the seed with [dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) yourself and restore it onto the device, which works on every device here except Bitkey.

## How should you choose? Practices before devices

The 2026 incident made one thing measurable: the practices around a device protected people better than the device itself. Coldcard owners who had used dice entropy, a strong passphrase or multisig lost nothing; owners who trusted the device's defaults lost everything. Decide on the practices first:

1. Supply your own entropy. A seed you [make yourself with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) and then restore onto the device works with every device we recommend, and it removes the exact failure that cost Coldcard users $116 million. The Keystone 3 Pro and SeedSigner also take dice rolls on the device, and BitBox, Blockstream and Foundation document procedures of their own; the entropy table below lists each.
2. Add a [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) for any balance you would miss. In July 2026 it was the difference between drained and untouched.
3. Use [multisig](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) across vendors for significant holdings, so that no single vendor's mistake can reach your funds.

With those in place, the choice of device comes down to how easy it makes verification (screen size, buttons, QR or USB), how much you trust its supply chain, and how its maker has behaved when things went wrong.

## How do the devices compare in detail?

### Trezor Safe 5

The Trezor Safe 5 is the beginner default: a polished, open-source device with a certified secure chip. Our [Trezor Safe 5 setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/trezor-safe-5/) restores a dice seed on it.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | $129 |
| Screen | 1.54-inch colour touchscreen, Gorilla Glass 3 |
| Connectivity | USB-C |
| Open source | Yes: firmware and hardware designs |
| Secure element | Yes, EAL6+ (Infineon Optiga) |
| Dice entropy | Not on the device as of October 2026: restore a seed you made with [dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/). Trezor Suite's entropy check confirms the device used the computer's randomness too |
| Bitcoin-only firmware | Available |
| Strengths | Polished setup and documentation, good Sparrow support, a secure element under open firmware, a security team with a long disclosure record |
| Weaknesses | No air-gap option (USB only); Trezor Suite nudges you toward its own ecosystem; a shipping provider's breach, disclosed in 2026, leaked customers' shipping details (choose a pickup point where you can) |
| Best for | A first hardware wallet, for amounts that do not yet justify multisig |

### Trezor Safe 7

The Trezor Safe 7 is Trezor's flagship, built around a secure element whose design can be audited.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | $249 |
| Screen | 2.5-inch colour touchscreen |
| Connectivity | USB-C and encrypted Bluetooth |
| Open source | Yes, including the design of the TROPIC01 secure element |
| Secure element | Two: TROPIC01 (auditable) and an EAL6+ Optiga |
| Dice entropy | Not on the device as of October 2026: restore a seed you made with [dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) |
| Bitcoin-only firmware | Available |
| Strengths | Auditable secure chip, a large screen for checking addresses, quantum-resistant firmware signing, a Bitcoin-only variant |
| Weaknesses | Premium price; Bluetooth is a radio you may not want (it can stay off); no QR air-gap mode |
| Best for | People who want the most transparency available with mainstream polish |

The TROPIC01 is the first secure element whose design anyone can audit; until it, a secure element meant accepting a chip whose internals were under non-disclosure agreements. After a year in which a silent firmware flaw cost users nine figures, being able to audit the whole stack is no longer a purist's luxury.

### BitBox02 Nova

The BitBox02 Nova is the Swiss-made BitBox02 with an EAL6+ secure chip and the smoothest backup flow of any device here. Our [BitBox02 Nova setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/bitbox02-nova/) covers BitBox's dice procedure and restoring a dice seed.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | €175 (October 2026); the classic BitBox02 is €149 |
| Screen | Glass OLED with touch sliders |
| Connectivity | USB-C, and Bluetooth for iPhone and iPad |
| Open source | Yes, fully |
| Secure element | Yes, EAL6+, in a two-chip design |
| Dice entropy | BitBox's own diceware procedure (documented for the BitBox02), or restore a seed you made with dice |
| Bitcoin-only edition | Available |
| Strengths | Backup to microSD as well as on paper; the open main chip cross-checks the secure chip; fast, open communication during the 2026 crisis, followed by expanded audits |
| Weaknesses | No air-gap mode; the small screen means more scrolling to check an address; the touch sliders divide opinion |
| Best for | Beginners, and anyone who values a clean, fast workflow; the classic BitBox02 is fine if Bluetooth does not matter to you |

### Blockstream Jade and Jade Plus

The Jade and Jade Plus are the verifiable-security pick: fully open source, able to sign over QR codes, and designed so the device cannot leak key material. Our [Jade Plus setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/jade-plus/) sets one up air-gapped on words chosen with dice.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | Jade $79; Jade Plus $149 in plastic, $169 in metal |
| Screen | Colour LCD (the Plus has a larger screen and a better camera) |
| Connectivity | USB, Bluetooth, and a camera for QR air-gapping |
| Open source | Yes, fully |
| Secure element | No: a virtual "blind oracle" model |
| Dice entropy | Not on the device. Blockstream documents dice methods for choosing the words, and the Jade calculates valid last words; or restore a seed you made with dice. By default it mixes several entropy sources, and wallet apps can add their own |
| Coins | Bitcoin and Liquid |
| Strengths | A real QR air-gap at a low price, anti-exfiltration signing, several entropy sources, an exemplary response to the 2026 incident |
| Weaknesses | No hardware secure element, so the oracle model needs understanding; the camera workflow is slower than USB |
| Best for | Security-focused users on any budget; the Plus's better camera makes it the nicer daily device |

The Jade differs from most devices in two ways that both proved wise in 2026. Its anti-exfiltration signing protocol stops a malicious device from leaking key material through its signatures. And instead of one random number generator it mixes several entropy sources, a design Blockstream documented in detail within hours of the Coldcard news, together with a migration guide for affected users.

The trade-off is the missing secure element. Jade's "blind oracle" splits PIN protection with a Blockstream server, or one you host yourself, that limits how many PIN guesses a thief can make. It is a sound model, but understand it before relying on it.

In April 2026 Blockstream added the Jade Core ($99), which has no camera and therefore no QR air-gap. We have not reviewed it.

### Passport Prime

The Passport Prime is the premium air-gapped device, and the most expensive one here.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | $565 |
| Screen | Large colour touchscreen |
| Connectivity | QR codes, and QuantumLink encrypted Bluetooth |
| Open source | Yes, fully (KeyOS, with sandboxed apps) |
| Secure element | Yes |
| Dice entropy | Supported by drawing seed words yourself and importing them; ships an app for testing the device's entropy |
| Bitcoin-only | Yes, by design |
| Strengths | A verification-first interface, US assembly, sandboxed apps, entropy you can test yourself |
| Weaknesses | Far the most expensive device here; more device than most people need; the extra features (2FA codes, file storage) widen what it has to protect |
| Best for | People who want air-gapped, verification-friendly hardware and will pay for it |

Foundation responded to the 2026 incident faster than almost anyone, confirming its entropy paths the same night, and then shipped an entropy-testing app so owners can check the distribution of the random number generator's output themselves.

### Keystone 3 Pro

The Keystone 3 Pro is a QR-only air-gapped device at a mid-range price.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | $149 (October 2026, sold as a pre-order) |
| Screen | 4-inch colour touchscreen, fingerprint reader |
| Connectivity | QR codes and microSD only |
| Open source | Yes, fully |
| Secure element | Three chips |
| Dice entropy | Dice rolls on the device (firmware 1.2.6 or later); 99 rolls for a 24-word seed |
| Bitcoin-only firmware | Available |
| Strengths | A true air-gap with a big screen for checking addresses, three secure elements, good Sparrow multisig support, erases itself if tampered with |
| Weaknesses | Multi-coin firmware by default (install the Bitcoin-only build); a younger company than Trezor or Blockstream; a battery to keep charged |
| Best for | Air-gapped use without the Passport's price, and as one key in a multisig |

### SeedSigner & Krux (DIY)

SeedSigner and Krux are stateless signers you assemble yourself from commodity parts. SeedSigner is our favourite signing device, and the [SeedSigner section](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/) covers why, how to build one and how to use it; it is not the right choice for most beginners, for the reasons given there.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | SeedSigner about $50-80 in parts; Krux about $30-80 (K210-based devices) |
| Screen | Small LCD (SeedSigner: 1.3-inch, with a camera for QR codes) |
| Connectivity | QR codes only, fully air-gapped |
| Open source | Yes, fully, community-built and reproducible |
| Secure element | None: the device stores nothing, so there is nothing to protect |
| Dice entropy | Required: you bring the entropy |
| Bitcoin-only | Yes, by design |
| Best for | Technical users, multisig quorums, and anyone who has built a [coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/) laptop and enjoyed it |

SeedSigner (built on a Raspberry Pi Zero) and Krux take the 2026 lesson furthest: the device never stores a seed. You bring the seed to each signing session, usually as a [SeedQR](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/using-seedsigner/) or by typing it in, and the device forgets everything when it is switched off. Because you generate the seed yourself ([with dice, and verified](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/)), there is no vendor random number generator to trust, and because the parts are commodity hardware, there is no wallet-specific supply chain to intercept. The cost is convenience: every signing session takes longer, and keeping the seed safe is entirely on you. Start with the [build guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/).

### Coldcard Mk5 & Q

Coldcard is not currently recommended for new purchases. For years it was this site's security pick. Then came the [entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/): a 2021 firmware bug silently replaced hardware randomness with a predictable software generator, about $116 million was stolen from more than 5,200 wallets, and, decisively for us, a developer had warned Coinkite about that exact code in May 2025 and been dismissed. As of October 2026, no compensation has been offered.

The current hardware (Mk5 $219, Q $319 at the store's October 2026 prices) is capable, the fixed firmware has been independently reviewed, and seeds generated with dice rolls were never affected. If you already own one, update the firmware, [check whether your seed needs moving](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/#am-i-affected), and make any new seed with dice. For new buyers, we do not recommend rewarding a vendor whose handling of a credible warning cost its users nine figures, at least until a longer record rebuilds that trust.

### Ledger

Ledger devices (Nano S Plus, Nano X and Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax; $69 to $399 as of October 2026) have strong secure elements and came through 2026 without an entropy incident; the company was quick to point to its certified hardware random number generator. Our concerns are unchanged. The secure element firmware is closed source; the 2023 Ledger Recover service showed the firmware can export seed material, split into shares; and the 2020 customer-data breach exposed buyers to years of phishing. You cannot verify the parts that matter most, and 2026 showed how much silent trust that asks for. Ledger suits people committed to its multi-coin ecosystem; for bitcoin self-custody, the open devices above are stronger choices.

### Bitkey

Bitkey, from Block, uses a different trust model entirely, and one you cannot verify.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Price | $250 (August 2026; the 2026 model with a touchscreen; the original was $150) |
| Screen | Touchscreen for checking transactions on the device (2026 model) |
| Connectivity | Bluetooth, with a companion phone app; no air-gap |
| Open source | Partly: source is published, but it cannot be built, because the fingerprint library is closed |
| Secure element | Yes, a secure enclave, unlocked by fingerprint |
| Dice entropy | No; there is no seed phrase shown to the user at all |
| Bitcoin-only | Yes |

Bitkey ships as a 2-of-3 multisig by default (your phone, the device and a recovery server held by Block), with no seed phrase shown to the user and a fingerprint instead of a PIN. It was untouched by the 2026 incident, since by design no single random number generator failure can spend funds, and its communication that night was among the best.

We still do not recommend it, because you cannot verify it. The published firmware cannot be reproduced by outsiders because the proprietary fingerprint-matching library is missing from the repository; WalletScrutiny rates it "nosource". There is no seed phrase to check, no dice entropy to supply, and most recovery paths run through Block's servers. That is the "trust the vendor" posture that cost Coldcard users nine figures; Block has a clean record, but so did Coinkite until July 2026.

Bitkey's fair niche is someone leaving an exchange who would otherwise never hold their own keys: its 2-of-3 design with an Emergency Exit Kit is far better than custody by an exchange. If you can follow a setup guide, a [BitBox02 Nova or Trezor Safe 5](#recommendations-by-use-case) gives you a portable, [standard BIP39 seed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/) that you can verify and recover anywhere.

## How do their security designs compare?

### Secure elements

| Wallet | Secure element | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| Trezor Safe 5 | One Optiga (EAL6+) | Open firmware around a certified chip |
| Trezor Safe 7 | TROPIC01 and Optiga | TROPIC01's design is auditable, with no non-disclosure agreement |
| BitBox02 Nova | One, EAL6+ | Two-chip design: the open main chip cross-checks the secure element |
| Passport Prime | Yes | Sandboxed KeyOS on top |
| Keystone 3 Pro | Three chips | Erases itself if tampered with |
| Coldcard Mk5 and Q | Two, from different vendors | The secure elements were not the 2026 failure; the firmware was |
| Jade and Jade Plus | Virtual (blind oracle) | A server limits PIN guesses; you can host it yourself |
| SeedSigner and Krux | None | Stateless: nothing stored to protect |
| Ledger | One ST33 | Certified, but the firmware is closed |
| Bitkey | Secure enclave | Firmware not reproducible because of a closed fingerprint library |

### Entropy: who lets you verify?

This table is the lesson of 2026: where the randomness in your seed comes from, and how you can check it. As of October 2026 only a few devices take dice rolls on the device; every device except Bitkey can take a seed you made yourself from dice, by restoring it.

| Wallet | Your own entropy | How to verify |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| SeedSigner and Krux | Dice rolls on the device | Re-derive on a second device; stateless by design |
| Keystone 3 Pro | Dice rolls on the device, firmware 1.2.6 or later | Enter the same rolls in a second tool and compare the words |
| BitBox02 and Nova | BitBox's diceware procedure: dice pick 23 words from a table, the device offers valid last words | You chose the words; documented for the BitBox02 |
| Passport Prime | Draw words yourself and import them; an app tests the device's own generator | You chose the words |
| Jade and Jade Plus | Blockstream's dice methods: dice pick 23 words from a table, the device calculates valid last words; by default several internal sources are mixed | You chose the words; the firmware is open |
| Trezor Safe 5 and 7 | Restore a seed you made with dice; no dice entry on the device | Trezor Suite's entropy check confirms the device mixed in the computer's randomness |
| Coldcard Mk5 and Q | Dice rolls on the device (the dice path was never affected) | Compare against a manual derivation |
| Ledger | Restore a seed you made with dice | Otherwise, trust the certification |
| Bitkey | None (no seed phrase is shown) | Cannot be verified; you trust Block's 2-of-3 design |

Whatever you buy, a device could in theory ignore your dice. The check that catches it is re-deriving the seed from the same rolls independently, which the [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) shows how to do.

### How did each vendor respond in 2026?

When the Coldcard news broke, the speed and honesty of each vendor's response varied enormously, and it is a fair guide to how they will behave next time.

| Vendor | Response to the 2026 incident | Earlier history |
|--------|---------------------|---------|
| Blockstream (Jade) | Entropy design documented the same night, with a migration guide | Clean |
| Foundation (Passport) | Confirmation the same night; entropy-testing app afterwards | Clean |
| Block (Bitkey) | Technical analysis the same night | Clean |
| Trezor | Published statement on 5 August, sustained follow-ups; considering support for user-supplied entropy, with no commitment yet | A third-party shipping provider's data breach (disclosed 2026); glitch attacks on older models, addressed with the secure element |
| BitBox | Statement the next day; announced expanded audits | Clean |
| Keystone | Confirmed it was unaffected | Clean |
| Coinkite (Coldcard) | Fast patch and advisory, but see the [dismissed 2025 warning](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) | The incident itself |
| Ledger | Brief statement about 14 hours later | Ledger Recover controversy (2023), customer-data breach (2020) |

## Recommendations by use case

| Use case | Our pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| First hardware wallet | BitBox02 Nova (Bitcoin-only) or Trezor Safe 5 | Polished, open source, secure element; both restore a seed you made with dice |
| Verifiable security | Jade Plus or Passport Prime, seeded with [dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) | Air-gapped workflows from vendors that treat verification, including of their own randomness, as a feature |
| Budget | Blockstream Jade ($79) | Nothing else at this price is open source, air-gap capable and backed by this response record |
| Building your own, maximum verification | [SeedSigner](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/) (our favourite) or Krux | Stateless, assembled from commodity parts, with the entropy fully in your hands; see the [build guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/) |
| Significant holdings | Multisig across vendors, for example Jade Plus, Keystone 3 Pro and Trezor Safe 5 | Three designs, three supply chains, three firmware teams. Multisig users with a weak Coldcard key lost nothing in July 2026; see the [multisig guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/) |

For most people: start with a BitBox02 Nova or Trezor Safe 5, generate the seed with your own dice, and move to multisig as the holdings grow.

## Where should you buy a hardware wallet?

Buy from the manufacturer's own store, or a reseller listed on the manufacturer's site.

| Wallet | Official store |
|--------|---------------|
| Trezor | [trezor.io](https://trezor.io) |
| BitBox | [bitbox.swiss](https://bitbox.swiss) |
| Jade | [store.blockstream.com](https://store.blockstream.com) |
| Passport | [foundation.xyz](https://foundation.xyz) |
| Keystone | [keyst.one](https://keyst.one) |
| SeedSigner (parts list) | [seedsigner.com](https://seedsigner.com) |
| Krux (build guide) | [selfcustody.github.io/krux](https://selfcustody.github.io/krux/) |
| Coldcard | [coldcard.com](https://coldcard.com) |
| Ledger | [ledger.com](https://ledger.com) |
| Bitkey | [bitkey.world](https://bitkey.world) |

**Danger: Never buy from marketplaces, and never accept a pre-made seed**
Amazon, eBay and other marketplace sellers have been sources of tampered devices. Whatever the vendor, set the device up yourself: a "pre-configured" wallet, or a seed phrase card in the box, is always a scam.

## Common questions

### What is the best Bitcoin hardware wallet in 2026?

There is no single best device, and after the 2026 Coldcard entropy incident the practices matter more than the hardware. For beginners, the Trezor Safe 5 ($129) or the BitBox02 Nova (€175) is the easiest to use safely. For verifiable security on a budget, the Blockstream Jade Plus ($149) signs over QR codes. SeedSigner is our favourite for people comfortable building their own device, though it is not for beginners. Whichever you choose, supply your own dice entropy when the seed is created, add a passphrase, and use multisig across vendors for significant holdings.

### Is Coldcard still safe to use in 2026?

We do not currently recommend Coldcard. A build error meant Coldcards generated seeds with a software pseudo-random generator instead of the hardware random number generator between March 2021 and July 2026, and roughly 1,816 BTC was drained from more than 5,200 addresses. Coinkite shipped fixes quickly once the draining began, but it had dismissed a developer's warning about the same code in May 2025. The devices are safe to use with a seed generated from dice or elsewhere, but we point new buyers to other devices.

### Do you need a secure element in a hardware wallet?

Not necessarily. A secure element resists someone physically extracting the seed from a stolen device, which matters if theft is part of your threat model. Devices without one, such as the Blockstream Jade Plus, use a blind oracle design instead and are fully open source and verifiable. The 2026 Coldcard incident is the reminder that a secure element does not help if the seed was weak to begin with.

### Should you use dice to generate your Bitcoin seed phrase?

Yes, for any amount you would be upset to lose. Every hardware wallet we recommend can take a seed you made from dice, by restoring it, and a few take the rolls directly. Coldcard owners who used dice lost nothing in the 2026 incident, while owners who trusted the device's default lost everything. Dice remove your dependence on the vendor's random number generator being correct.


---

# Bitcoin Wallet Security Incidents, 2013 to 2026

> Every incident since 2013 in which a wallet flaw or vendor breach put self-custodied bitcoin at risk: what failed, who is affected and what to do.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/advisories/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

These are the incidents, from 2013 to 2026, in which a flaw in wallet software, wallet firmware or a wallet maker's systems put self-custodied bitcoin at risk. Five of the eight come down to the same failure: a seed or key made from weak randomness. No update repairs a seed that already exists, so the remedy in each of those five is to move the funds to a new seed made properly, which is why this site recommends [making the seed with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/). The table lists the incidents newest first; each has a section below with the dates and the source.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Disclosed | Incident | What failed | Who is affected | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Aug 2026 | [Coldcard entropy flaw](#what-was-the-coldcard-entropy-flaw) | Firmware seeded new wallets from a predictable software generator | Seeds a Coldcard generated without dice between March 2021 and July 2026 | Move the funds to a new seed |
| 5 Aug 2024 | [Dark Skippy](#what-is-dark-skippy) | Research: tampered firmware can leak a seed through two signatures | No known victims; any device running malicious firmware | Install firmware only from the maker; prefer anti-exfil signing |
| 14 Nov 2023 | [Randstorm](#what-was-randstorm) | Weak browser randomness in BitcoinJS-based wallets | Wallets generated in a web browser from 2011 to 2015 | Move the funds to a new wallet |
| 8 Aug 2023 | [Milk Sad](#what-was-milk-sad) | `bx seed` made seeds from 32 bits of clock time | Seeds made with Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x | Move the funds to a new seed |
| 11 May 2021 | [Cake Wallet](#what-went-wrong-with-cake-wallet-in-2021) | Bitcoin wallets made from insecure randomness | Bitcoin wallets created in Cake Wallet before 4.1.7 | Move the funds to a new wallet |
| 29 Jul 2020 | [Ledger customer data](#what-leaked-from-ledger-in-2020) | Ledger's shop and marketing database | About 1 million email addresses; names, postal addresses and phone numbers of 272,000 customers | Expect phishing; never type a seed phrase anywhere |
| 26 Dec 2018 | [Electrum phishing servers](#what-were-the-electrum-phishing-servers) | Malicious servers showed fake update messages | Electrum users who installed the fake update | Update only from electrum.org |
| 11 Aug 2013 | [Android random numbers](#what-was-the-2013-android-flaw) | Android's secure random number generator | Bitcoin wallets on Android at the time | Retire any key from that period |

</div>

## What was the Coldcard entropy flaw?

The Coldcard entropy flaw was a firmware build error, shipped in March 2021, that made Coldcard hardware wallets generate seeds from a predictable software generator instead of their hardware random number generator. Between 30 July and 4 August 2026 attackers swept about 1,816 BTC from more than 5,200 addresses. Seeds made with the Coldcard's dice option, and seeds imported into it, were not affected. The [Coldcard incident page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) has the timeline, the affected firmware and the migration steps.

## What is Dark Skippy?

Dark Skippy is an attack, published on 5 August 2024 by Lloyd Fournier, Nick Farrow and Robin Linus, in which a signing device running malicious firmware hides its seed in the nonces of the signatures it makes, so that an attacker watching the blockchain can rebuild the seed from as few as two signatures. It needs firmware that has been tampered with, and the researchers reported no use in the wild. The researchers disclosed it privately to about 15 vendors in March 2024. The defences are firmware installed only from the maker and checked against its signing keys, a device nobody else can reach between uses, and anti-exfil signing, which some devices, the Blockstream Jade among them, already use to stop a device choosing its own nonces.

Source: [darkskippy.com](https://darkskippy.com/)

## What was Randstorm?

Randstorm is the name Unciphered gave, on 14 November 2023, to a set of weaknesses in the randomness of wallets generated in web browsers with BitcoinJS and the projects built on it, from 2011 to 2015. BitcoinJS used the JSBN library's `SecureRandom()` until March 2014, and combined with weak `Math.random()` implementations in the browsers of the time, the keys it made were weaker than intended. The effort to attack one varies: Unciphered says wallets generated in 2014 are much harder to break than those from 2012. Its advice is to move any funds in a wallet created that way to a new wallet made with trusted software.

Source: [Unciphered](https://www.unciphered.com/disclosure-of-vulnerable-bitcoin-wallet-library-2/)

## What was Milk Sad?

Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910) was a flaw in the `bx seed` command of Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x, which generated seeds with the Mersenne Twister generator seeded from 32 bits of the system clock, so every seed it made was one of about 4.3 billion. Versions 3.0.0 to 3.6.0 are confirmed exploitable. Attackers drained about 29.65 BTC on 12 July 2023, and the researchers who disclosed the flaw on 8 August 2023 put the total stolen across coins at over $900,000. Any wallet whose seed came from `bx seed` should be treated as public.

Source: [milksad.info](https://milksad.info/disclosure.html)

## What went wrong with Cake Wallet in 2021?

Cake Wallet versions before 4.1.7, released in 2020 and 2021, created Bitcoin wallets from insecure randomness. The wallets have 12-word seeds in Electrum's format, not BIP39, and Cake Wallet's Monero wallets were not affected. The vendor told users on 11 May 2021 to move their funds to a wallet made with a fixed version. In February 2024 the Milk Sad researchers reported about 8,700 known affected wallets, some of which still held bitcoin more than two and a half years after the warning.

Source: [Milk Sad update 6](https://milksad.info/posts/research-update-6/)

## What leaked from Ledger in 2020?

On 29 July 2020 Ledger disclosed that an outsider had accessed its e-commerce and marketing database on 25 June 2020, exposing about 1 million email addresses and, Ledger said then, the names, postal addresses and phone numbers of 9,500 customers. On 20 December 2020 the data was posted publicly, and it held the names, postal addresses and phone numbers of 272,000 customers. No device, key or fund was touched, but the list has fed phishing emails and fake replacement devices sent to customers, and it tells criminals where hardware wallet owners live. If you bought from any wallet maker, assume your address may be known, never type a seed phrase into anything a message asks you to, and read [physical security](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/physical-security/).

Sources: [Ledger, July 2020](https://www.ledger.com/addressing-the-july-2020-e-commerce-and-marketing-data-breach), [CoinDesk, December 2020](https://www.coindesk.com/business/2020/12/21/why-ledger-kept-all-that-customer-data-in-the-first-place)

## What were the Electrum phishing servers?

In December 2018 attackers ran many public Electrum servers that answered a transaction broadcast with an error message telling the user to install an "update", which was malware that stole wallets. Electrum versions before 3.3.3 displayed those messages as they arrived; 3.3.3 fixed it, and the developers' advice was to ignore any server message about updates and download only from electrum.org. Malwarebytes estimated in April 2019 that the campaign had taken over 771 BTC. The lesson outlasts Electrum: install wallet software only from its official site and check the signature.

Sources: [Electrum issue 4968](https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/issues/4968), [Malwarebytes](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2019/04/electrum-bitcoin-wallets-under-siege)

## What was the 2013 Android flaw?

On 11 August 2013 the Bitcoin.org alert warned that the component Android used to generate secure random numbers had critical weaknesses, leaving wallet apps that generated keys on the phone open to theft; its incomplete list named Bitcoin Wallet, Blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium. Apps where a company held the keys were not affected. The fixed apps created new keys and moved the funds to them. A key generated on Android before those updates should not hold bitcoin today.

Source: [Bitcoin.org alert](https://bitcoin.org/en/alert/2013-08-11-android)

## What do these incidents have in common?

Weak randomness is the largest single cause, and it is the one that cannot be fixed afterwards: a seed made weak stays weak whatever firmware runs later. A seed from your own [dice rolls](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) does not depend on any generator, and a [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) adds a secret the device never chose. The rest are about trusting what you install and who knows you hold bitcoin: get wallet software and firmware only from the maker and check them, ignore any message asking for your seed phrase, and treat your name and address on a wallet maker's order list as information that may one day be public. The [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) notes which devices accept dice rolls and use anti-exfil signing.


---

# Run Your Own Bitcoin Node: Complete Setup Guide

> Complete guide to running your own Bitcoin node. Learn why it matters, compare software options, and follow step-by-step setup instructions with Parmanode.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Running your own Bitcoin node means your wallet checks balances and transactions against a copy of the blockchain that you downloaded and verified yourself, instead of asking a stranger's server. A complete setup has three parts: Bitcoin Core, which verifies the chain; an Electrum server, which indexes it; and your wallet, such as Sparrow, pointed at that server. It takes two to four hours of work plus a few days of syncing, on a dedicated small computer or an old laptop with a 2 TB SSD. We recommend [Parmanode](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/) to install it, because it handles the downloads, signature checks and configuration and connects Sparrow for you.

Time: 2-4 hours of active work (plus days of sync time). Cost: $150-350 (Raspberry Pi 5 + 2 TB SSD) or $100-150 (an old PC + 2 TB SSD). Level: Intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026.

## Why run a node?

Without your own node, your wallet asks someone else's computer for your balance, whether a payment is valid and what is happening on the network. That server learns your addresses, your transaction history and when you are online. With your own node:

- Your wallet's queries stay on your own hardware, so nobody else can link your addresses together.
- You verify every block and transaction against the rules yourself, rather than trusting someone else's answer.
- You enforce bitcoin's rules directly, as one of the nodes the network is made of.

[Why run your own node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/why-run-node/) covers the reasons in full.

## What are you building?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![A complete node setup: Bitcoin Core downloads and verifies the full chain, an Electrum server indexes it for fast queries, and Sparrow Wallet connects to your own server instead of a stranger's](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/bitcoin-node/node-stack.svg)

</div>

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Component | What it does |
|-----------|--------------|
| Bitcoin Core | Downloads and independently verifies the whole blockchain, about 770 GB as of September 2026 |
| Electrum server | Indexes the blockchain so your wallet can look up its addresses quickly |
| Your wallet | Connects to your Electrum server instead of public ones |

</div>

## What hardware do you need?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Component | Minimum | Recommended |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| Storage | 2 TB SSD | 2 TB SSD or larger |
| Memory | 4 GB | 8 GB or more |
| Processor | Dual-core | Quad-core |
| Internet | A stable connection | No monthly data cap |

</div>

The blockchain grows by roughly 75 GB a year, and Bitcoin Core plus an Electrum server index no longer fit on a 1 TB drive.

**Warning: Use an SSD, not a hard disk**
On a spinning hard disk the initial sync takes weeks instead of days, and the Electrum server stays slow afterwards. An SSD is not the place to save money.

A dedicated device, such as a Raspberry Pi 5 or an old laptop left running, is the better choice: it uses little power and is always available to your wallet. Your everyday computer also works and needs no extra hardware, but the node only runs while the computer is on and has to catch up after each restart.

## What are the steps?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Step | What you do | Time |
|------|----------------|------|
| 1. [Choose software](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/node-software-options/) | Compare the options and pick one | 15 minutes |
| 2. [Set up Parmanode](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/) | Install and configure the node | 1-2 hours |
| 3. [Electrum server](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/electrum-server/) | Understand and choose an indexer | 15 minutes |
| 4. [Tor](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/) | Add network privacy (optional) | 30 minutes |
| 5. [Connect Sparrow](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/connect-sparrow-wallet/) | Point your wallet at your node | 15 minutes |

</div>

## How long does it take?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Phase | Duration |
|-------|----------|
| Reading and planning | 30-60 minutes |
| Installing the software | 30-60 minutes |
| Bitcoin Core's initial sync | 1-7 days, depending on hardware |
| Electrum server indexing | 12-48 hours |
| Connecting the wallet | 15 minutes |

</div>

The initial sync happens once; after it, the node keeps itself current. Start it and leave it running.

## Why do we recommend Parmanode?

[Parmanode](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/) is a terminal-based installer that handles the fiddly parts (downloading, checking signatures, configuring) while leaving you in control of an ordinary Linux system. It also installs Sparrow already connected to your node, so there are no connection details to copy. If you prefer a graphical interface, the [node software options](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/node-software-options/) page compares the alternatives.

If nodes are new to you, read [what a Bitcoin node is](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/nodes/what-is-node/) and [why privacy matters](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/why-privacy-matters/) first.


---

# Parmanode Setup Guide

> Step-by-step guide to setting up a Bitcoin node with Parmanode. Easy installation for Linux, Mac, and Raspberry Pi with automatic wallet configuration.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Parmanode is an open-source installer, run from the terminal, that sets up a Bitcoin node on an ordinary Linux or Mac computer: one command installs it, typing `rp` opens its menus, and from there it installs Bitcoin Core, an Electrum server such as Fulcrum, and Sparrow Wallet already connected to your node. It downloads each program, checks its PGP signature and SHA256 hash, and configures it, while leaving you with a normal system you can inspect and troubleshoot. Expect an hour or two of work, then one to seven days for Bitcoin Core to sync and another half to two days for the Electrum server to index.

Parmanode was created by Arman the Parman, a bitcoin educator. Unlike Umbrel or Start9 it hides nothing: you run real software on a real system, so you can fix it when something goes wrong and change it when you want to.

## What can Parmanode install?

| Category | Software |
|---|---|
| Node | Bitcoin Core or Bitcoin Knots; the Electrum servers electrs, Fulcrum and Electrum X; Mempool (a block explorer); LND (Lightning); BTCPay Server |
| Wallets | Sparrow, Electrum, Specter Desktop, Green, Trezor Suite, Ledger Live |
| Other | Tor, Tor Browser, JoinMarket, a Nostr relay and more |

Install only what you need. The feature that sets Parmanode apart is that wallets installed through it, such as Sparrow or Electrum, come configured to use your own Electrum server, with no connection details to copy.

## Which systems does it run on?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Platform | Support |
|----------|---------------|
| Linux (Debian and Ubuntu family) | Full support; recommended |
| Mac (Intel and Apple Silicon) | Most features |
| Raspberry Pi | Full support, with the ParmanodL operating system |
| Windows | Not supported; use a Linux virtual machine |

</div>

## What do you need first?

- A computer running Linux (Debian or Ubuntu family) or macOS.
- A 2 TB SSD: the blockchain alone was about 770 GB in September 2026, and the Electrum server index needs more.
- A stable internet connection; the blockchain download is about 770 GB.
- Basic comfort with a terminal.

**Warning: Use an SSD, not a hard disk**
On a spinning hard disk the initial sync takes weeks instead of days, and the node stays slow afterwards.

## Step 1: Install Parmanode

Step 1 installs the installer. Open a terminal (on a Mac, Terminal is in Applications, Utilities) and run:

```bash
curl https://parmanode.com/install.sh | sh
```

The script is short; to read it first, run the command without `| sh`, which prints it instead. On a Mac you may be asked to install the Command Line Developer Tools, which git needs: click Install and wait a few minutes.

## Step 2: Open Parmanode

Step 2 starts it. Type:

```bash
rp
```

Parmanode's menus appear. Each option has a short code in brackets; type the code and press Enter:

```
PARMANODE --> Main Menu --> Install Menu --> Node Install
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Not yet installed...

    (core)        Bitcoin Core/Knots
    (ersd)        electrs (Docker)
    (ex)          Electrum X
    (f)           Fulcrum (an Electrum Server)
    ...

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Type your choice from above options, or: (p) for previous,
(m) for main, (q) to quit.
Then <enter>:
```

## Step 3: Install Bitcoin Core

Step 3 installs the node itself. Go to the install menu, then node install, type `core` and follow the prompts. Parmanode downloads Bitcoin Core, checks its signatures, installs and configures it, and starts the initial sync, which takes one to seven days depending on your hardware and connection and only happens once. The Bitcoin Core menu shows the sync's progress.

## Step 4: Install an Electrum server

Step 4 adds the index your wallet will query. In the node install menu, type `f` for Fulcrum, which is faster but uses more memory, or `ersd` for electrs, which suits computers with 4 GB of memory or less, and follow the prompts. The server cannot index until Bitcoin Core has finished syncing, and indexing then takes another 12 to 48 hours. The [Electrum server page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/electrum-server/) compares the options.

## Step 5: Install Sparrow

Step 5 installs your wallet already connected. Go to the install menu, then wallet install, type `sparrow` and follow the prompts. Sparrow is configured to use your own Electrum server, so when you open it, your balances and transactions are already private and checked by your own node.

## How do you see the connection details?

Parmanode configures its own wallets, but the Electrum server's menu shows the addresses for connecting wallets on other devices:

```
═══════════════════════ Electrs v0.10.3 Menu ══════════════

ELECTRS IS: RUNNING
STATUS:     Bitcoin still sync'ing (external drive)

CONNECT:    127.0.0.1:50001   [From this computer only]
            127.0.0.1:50002:s [From this computer only]
            192.168.0.170:50001:s [From any home network computer]

TOR:        [onion address for remote access]

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

[Connect Sparrow to your node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/connect-sparrow-wallet/) covers connecting another computer.

## How do you update Parmanode?

Parmanode updates itself from its main menu. Updating Parmanode does not update the programs it installed: to move to a newer Bitcoin Core, for example, uninstall it with Parmanode's remove option and install it again, and the updated Parmanode installs the newer version. If the built-in update fails, this forces a refresh:

```bash
curl https://parmanode.com/refresh_parmanode | sh
```

## How do you run it on a Raspberry Pi?

ParmanodL is a complete operating system image for the Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, and the easiest way to build a dedicated node. Download it from parmanode.com directly, by torrent or through its Tor address. It boots with the username `parman` and the password `parmanodl`; change the password at first login. To reach it from another computer:

```bash
ssh parman@parmanodl.local
```

Some Parmanode features open graphical programs such as wallets. To see them over SSH, connect with `ssh -Y parman@parmanodl.local` and make sure X11 forwarding is enabled; a Mac needs an X11 viewer such as XQuartz.

## What else is worth knowing?

- When Parmanode asks for a password, it means your computer's own login (sudo) password, which it needs for tasks such as mounting drives.
- Run it as a normal user, not as root, or it will fail.
- It can run on a rented virtual server, but storing the blockchain there gets expensive unless Bitcoin Core is pruned.
- The code is open source and heavily commented. To learn how it works, open `~/parman_programs/parmanode/` in an editor and follow `run_parmanode.sh`; every command in it is one you could run by hand.

The [Parmanode website](https://parmanode.com), its [source code](https://github.com/ArmanTheParman/parmanode) and [Arman the Parman's articles](https://armantheparman.com) go further.


---

# Node Software Options

> Compare Bitcoin node software options: Parmanode, Umbrel, RaspiBlitz, Start9, and DIY setups. Find the right approach for your skill level and needs.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/node-software-options/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Node software ranges from point-and-click appliances to building every part yourself, and the right choice depends on how much you want to understand your node. We recommend Parmanode: a terminal installer on an ordinary Linux system that handles the downloads, signature checks and configuration, and connects Sparrow for you. Umbrel and Start9 suit people who want a graphical app store; RaspiBlitz suits Lightning users; RaspiBolt and MiniBolt suit people who want to type every command themselves. Any of them is far better than no node.

## Where does each option sit?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Node software on a spectrum from guided to manual: Umbrel's web UI, Start9's app store, Parmanode's terminal wizard, RaspiBlitz's scripts and Raspibolt's fully manual setup; these guides use Parmanode, in the middle](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/bitcoin-node/software-spectrum.svg)

</div>

The guided end is easy to start but hard to troubleshoot when something breaks; the manual end takes longer but leaves you understanding your system.

| Option | Difficulty | Control | What you learn | Suits |
|----------|------------|---------|----------------|----------|
| [Parmanode](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/) | Medium | High | A lot | Learning while doing |
| [Umbrel](https://umbrel.com) | Easy | Low | Little | Beginners who want simplicity |
| [Start9](https://start9.com) | Easy | Medium | Some | Privacy-minded users who want a home server |
| [RaspiBlitz](https://docs.raspiblitz.org) | Medium | High | A good deal | Lightning users |
| [RaspiBolt](https://raspibolt.org) or [MiniBolt](https://minibolt.minibolt.info) | Hard | Complete | The most | People who want to understand every part |

## Parmanode (our recommendation)

Parmanode is a terminal-based installer on a real Linux system that does the tedious parts (downloading, checking PGP signatures and SHA256 hashes, configuring) and installs Sparrow already connected to your node. It installs with one command, works on Linux, macOS and Raspberry Pi, and is open source with well-commented code. It has no web interface and needs basic comfort with a terminal. The [Parmanode guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/parmanode-setup/) walks through it.

## Umbrel

Umbrel is a web interface with an app store: Bitcoin Core, an Electrum server and Lightning each install with a click, on a Raspberry Pi or any Linux computer, and it has an active community. The cost is that it hides the details, so troubleshooting is hard when something breaks, and it runs everything in Docker containers. Since 2023 its code has been published under a non-commercial licence rather than an open-source one.

## Start9

Start9's StartOS (formerly embassyOS) is a personal server operating system for self-hosting in general, not only bitcoin, with a strong privacy focus, health monitoring and alerts. Start9 also sells pre-configured hardware. It costs more if you buy their hardware, and its app selection is smaller than Umbrel's.

## RaspiBlitz

RaspiBlitz began as a Lightning node and grew from there. It is feature-rich, well maintained and long established, with a terminal interface of text menus. The many options can feel overwhelming, and it is aimed mainly at the Raspberry Pi.

## RaspiBolt and MiniBolt

RaspiBolt (for Raspberry Pi) and MiniBolt (for a PC or laptop) are step-by-step guides to building a node by hand: you type every command and write every configuration file. Expect hours to days, and mistakes are easy to make, but you finish with a real understanding of every component.

## Which should you choose?

| Choose | If |
|---|---|
| Parmanode | You want to learn without suffering, are comfortable with a terminal, and want your wallet configured for you |
| Umbrel | You want the easiest setup and a graphical interface, and will trade control for convenience |
| Start9 | Privacy is your priority, you want a general self-hosting platform, and will pay for polished hardware |
| RaspiBlitz | Lightning matters to you and you are comfortable with terminal menus |
| RaspiBolt or MiniBolt | Learning matters more than finishing quickly |

If Parmanode feels too technical, start with Umbrel and move later; if it feels too guided, try RaspiBolt.

## What hardware does node software need?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Component | Minimum | Recommended |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| Device | Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) | Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) or a mini PC |
| Storage | 2 TB SSD | 2 TB SSD or larger |
| Memory | 4 GB | 8 GB or more |
| Internet | A stable connection | No monthly data cap |

</div>

**Warning: Use an SSD**
Every option needs an SSD. A spinning hard disk is too slow for the blockchain: the initial sync takes days longer and the node stays slow afterwards.


---

# Electrum Server Explained

> Understand Electrum servers (Electrs, Fulcrum): what they do, why you need one, and how to choose between options for your Bitcoin node setup.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/electrum-server/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

An Electrum server is software that indexes the blockchain your Bitcoin Core node has verified by address, so that a wallet such as Sparrow can ask "what is the balance and history of these addresses?" and get an answer in milliseconds. Running your own keeps those questions private and answered from data you verified, instead of telling a public server every address you own. We recommend Fulcrum, the fastest; electrs uses less memory and suits a Raspberry Pi with 4 GB. Building the index takes 12 to 48 hours once Bitcoin Core has synced.

## What does an Electrum server do?

Bitcoin Core verifies the chain but is not built to look up arbitrary addresses quickly. The Electrum server sits between it and your wallet, reads every block Core has verified, and builds a database that maps addresses to transactions; the wallet then talks only to the Electrum server.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![An Electrum server sits between Sparrow and Bitcoin Core: the wallet asks for an address balance, the server answers instantly from its index, and the index is built by reading the chain Core has verified](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/bitcoin-node/electrum-query-flow.svg)

</div>

## Why do you need one?

| How the wallet gets its data | Speed | Privacy |
|---|---|---|
| Directly from Bitcoin Core (Sparrow supports this) | Works, but each wallet has to be rescanned from its creation date, and few wallets support it | Private |
| From a public Electrum server | Fast | The server sees every address and transaction |
| From your own Electrum server | Fast | Private: the questions stay on your network |

Your own server is the one arrangement that is both fast and private, and it lets any Electrum-compatible wallet, on any of your devices, use your node.

## Which Electrum server should you run?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Server | Written in | Memory | Indexing | Suits |
|--------|----------|-----------|------------|----------|
| Fulcrum | C++ | 4 GB or more, ideally 8 GB | Faster | Most people |
| electrs | Rust | 2 GB or more | Slower | Computers with little memory |
| ElectrumX | Python | 8 GB or more | Varies | Older setups |

</div>

Fulcrum is the fastest, and once its index is built, queries are near-instant; in Parmanode, type `f` in the node install menu. electrs uses less memory, which suits a 4 GB Raspberry Pi 4, at the cost of slower indexing; in Parmanode, type `ersd` for its Docker version. ElectrumX is the original Python implementation; it still works, but the other two are faster and more efficient for new setups.

## What happens during indexing?

After Bitcoin Core finishes syncing, the server reads the whole blockchain from it and builds its database, which takes 12 to 48 hours depending on your hardware. CPU and disk use are high throughout, and wallets cannot connect until it finishes. It happens once: afterwards the server indexes each new block as it arrives, about every ten minutes.

## What does running your own give you?

- Privacy: your wallet's questions never leave your network, where a public server would see every address you check and every transaction you broadcast.
- Verification: the answers come from your own Bitcoin Core, which checked every block against the rules.
- Reliability: public servers go offline, slow down or shut; yours is there whenever your node is running.
- No logging but your own: a public server may record your activity; yours records only what you configure.

## How do you connect a wallet?

If you installed through Parmanode, the server's menu shows its connection details:

```
CONNECT:    127.0.0.1:50001   [From this computer only]
            127.0.0.1:50002:s [From this computer only - SSL]
            192.168.0.170:50001 [From any home network computer]

TOR:        [onion address for remote access]
```

Port 50001 is the standard, unencrypted Electrum protocol, fine on your own network; port 50002 is encrypted with SSL; the Tor address is for connecting privately from outside your home. Wallets installed through Parmanode are already configured. [Connect Sparrow to your node](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/connect-sparrow-wallet/) covers the rest.

## How much storage does the index need?

Each server's index is extra storage on top of the blockchain: Fulcrum's is the largest, at well over 100 GB, electrs's the smallest, at roughly 50 GB, and ElectrumX's in between, all growing with the chain.
