The blockchain itself was about 770 GB in September 2026 and grows by roughly 75 GB a year, so Bitcoin Core plus any of these servers no longer fits on a 1 TB drive. Use a 2 TB SSD.

## What if something does not work?

| Problem | What to check |
|---|---|
| The wallet gets "connection refused" | That Bitcoin Core has fully synced, that the Electrum server is running (Parmanode's menu shows it) and has finished indexing, and that you are using the right port, 50001 or 50002 |
| Indexing seems stuck | It takes 12 to 48 hours. Check for disk activity, which means it is working, how much memory is free, since too little slows it badly, and that Bitcoin Core has fully synced |
| CPU use is high | Normal while indexing; it drops once the index is built |


---

# Tor Configuration for Bitcoin Nodes

> Configure your Bitcoin node to run over Tor for enhanced privacy. Hide your IP address and enable secure remote access to your node.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/tor/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Tor does two jobs for a Bitcoin node. Routing the node's connections to other Bitcoin nodes through Tor hides your home IP address, so the network cannot see that your address runs a node, which would mark you as a likely bitcoin holder. And publishing your Electrum server as a Tor onion address lets your wallet reach your node from anywhere, with no port forwarding and no VPN. Parmanode installs and configures Tor from its menus; the cost is some extra latency.

## Why does your node's IP address matter?

Every node your node connects to sees its IP address, and an IP address is tied to you through your internet provider's records. With little effort, anyone can learn roughly where you live, that you run a Bitcoin node, and possibly link it with your other online activity. Someone who knows you run a node may assume you hold significant bitcoin, and a Lightning node's channel capacity is public, which gives a minimum estimate of your holdings. That makes you a potential target, including for [physical attacks](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/security/physical-security/).

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Tor serves two jobs for a node: routing node-to-network traffic so other Bitcoin nodes never see your IP or location, and carrying wallet-to-node connections to your onion address so you can reach home from anywhere without port forwarding](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/bitcoin-node/tor-use-cases.svg)

</div>

## How does Tor hide your node from the network?

Configured to use only Tor, your node connects to other nodes through their onion addresses and offers its own, so its peers see an onion address and never your home IP. That stops observers learning that you run a node, locating it, correlating it with your other activity, and your internet provider logging your Bitcoin connections.

In Parmanode, Tor is an option in the menus. In Bitcoin Core's own configuration file, these settings route every connection through Tor and connect only to other nodes on Tor:

```
proxy=127.0.0.1:9050
listen=1
bind=127.0.0.1
onlynet=onion
```

## How do you reach your node when you are away from home?

At home, your wallet reaches your node over your local network, privately and without Tor. Away from home, the node's local address (such as `192.168.1.100`) does not exist on the network you are on. The usual alternatives both have drawbacks: port forwarding exposes your node, and your home IP, to the whole internet, and a VPN back home takes setup and often a subscription.

A **Tor hidden service** solves it: your node publishes an `.onion` address reachable through the Tor network from anywhere, without exposing your home IP or opening a port, and the connection is encrypted end to end.

<div class="doc-diagram">

![Remote access over Tor: a wallet on a traveling phone connects through the Tor network to the hidden service onion address of your node at home; no open ports, no exposed IP and no VPN needed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/bitcoin-node/tor-remote-access.svg)

</div>

## How do you set it up with Parmanode?

Install Tor from Parmanode's other-install menu. Parmanode then shows onion addresses for Bitcoin Core and for your Electrum server; the Electrum server's appears in its status menu:

```
TOR:  abc123...xyz.onion:50001
```

Enter that address in your wallet's server settings to connect from anywhere.

## Can you share your node with family?

Yes: give them your Electrum server's onion address and their wallets can use your node from anywhere. Each connected wallet adds load, though, and a Raspberry Pi handles only a few at once, so do not publish the address.

## What does Tor cost?

Tor adds latency, because traffic passes through several relays. That is acceptable for ordinary node use, but can matter for time-sensitive work such as running a routing Lightning node. A hybrid setup, connecting to peers both over Tor and directly, improves connectivity at the price of privacy, since the direct connections reveal your IP.


---

# Connect Sparrow Wallet to Your Node

> Connect Sparrow Wallet to your own Bitcoin node and Electrum server so transactions stay private and verified by your own infrastructure.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/bitcoin-node/connect-sparrow-wallet/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

If you installed Sparrow through Parmanode, it is already connected to your node: open it, and the connection toggle at the bottom right turns blue, Sparrow's colour for a private Electrum server. Otherwise, open Sparrow's server settings, choose Private Electrum, enter your Electrum server's address and port (50002 with SSL, or 50001), test the connection, and switch it on. Away from home, connect to the server's Tor onion address through a Tor proxy. From then on, your balance checks and broadcasts go only to your own node.

## What if you used Parmanode?

Sparrow installed through Parmanode connects automatically. If the toggle does not turn blue, check that the Electrum server (Fulcrum or electrs) is running, that Bitcoin Core has fully synced, and that the Electrum server has finished its first index.

## Step 1: Open Sparrow's server settings

Step 1 finds the settings for a Sparrow you installed yourself. Open `File`, `Settings` (called `Preferences` on some versions and on macOS), choose `Server` in the sidebar, and pick Private Electrum as the server type.

## Step 2: Enter your server's details

Step 2 points Sparrow at your server.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Field | Value | Notes |
|-------|-------|-------|
| URL | Your server's address | `127.0.0.1` on the node itself; its local IP, such as `192.168.1.100`, elsewhere on your network |
| Port | `50002` with SSL, or `50001` without | 50002 is recommended |
| SSL | On, for port 50002 | |

</div>

Parmanode's Electrum server menu shows these details. Otherwise, find the node's local IP in your router's admin page or by running `ip addr` on the node.

## Step 3: Test the connection

Step 3 checks it works. Click `Test Connection`: a successful test shows the server's version and the current block height. If it fails, see [what if it does not connect](#what-if-it-does-not-connect).

## Step 4: Switch the connection on

Step 4 makes it live. Close the settings and turn on the toggle at the bottom right of the main window. It turns blue for a private Electrum server (green would mean Bitcoin Core directly, yellow a public server).

![Sparrow Wallet's main window with the server toggle at the bottom right showing blue, connected to a private Electrum server](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/node/sparrow.webp)

## How do you connect from outside your home?

### Through Tor (recommended)

If your Electrum server has a Tor onion address:

1. Open Sparrow's server settings.
2. Turn on `Use Proxy`, set to `127.0.0.1:9050` for the Tor service or `127.0.0.1:9150` for Tor Browser.
3. Enter the onion address as the URL, with port `50001` and SSL off; Tor already encrypts the connection.

### Through a VPN

If you have a VPN into your home network, connect to it first and use the node's local address as usual.

## How do you check you are using your own node?

The server shown in Sparrow is your own address or onion address, not a public server; the block height matches your node's; and lookups in a new wallet come back quickly. Your addresses are no longer going to strangers' servers.

## Can other wallets use the same server?

Yes. One Electrum server can serve many wallets:

| Wallet | Where to set the server |
|---|---|
| Electrum | `Tools`, `Network`, `Server` |
| BlueWallet | `Settings`, `Network`, `Electrum Server`; use the onion address away from home |
| Nunchuk | `Settings`, `Network Settings` |

## What if it does not connect?

| Problem | What to check |
|---|---|
| "Connection refused" | Whether the Electrum server is running, whether Bitcoin Core has fully synced, whether indexing (12 to 48 hours) has finished, and which port you used; try both 50001 and 50002 |
| "Connection timed out" | The IP address, whether you are on the same network (local addresses do not work from outside), and whether a firewall on the node blocks the port |
| Connected, but the balance looks wrong | Let the wallet finish syncing, check the server has finished indexing, and try a rescan from the wallet's settings |
| Tor does not connect | Whether Tor is running on your computer, the onion address, and the port (usually 50001, without SSL) |


---

# Libreboot Installation Guide

> Install Libreboot on a ThinkPad with a Raspberry Pi Pico: open-source coreboot firmware that strips and disables Intel's ME on your Bitcoin computer.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Libreboot is free, open-source boot firmware for computers, built on coreboot, that replaces the laptop's proprietary BIOS or UEFI. This guide installs it on a Lenovo ThinkPad (the X230, T420, T430, T440p, T480s, T530 or W530) using a Raspberry Pi Pico as an external programmer: build Libreboot and the Pico's firmware from source, clip the Pico onto the laptop's flash chip, back up the original firmware, and write the new image. It takes three to five hours and about $15 to $30 of parts, and gives a [Bitcoin computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/) or [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/) firmware whose source you can read.

![A ThinkPad T480s booting Libreboot: the purple GRUB menu with the leaping-deer logo on screen](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/t480s.webp)

Time: 3-5 hours. Cost: $15-30 (Raspberry Pi Pico + SOIC8 clip + jumper wires). Level: Advanced. Reviewed: 26 Oct 2026. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: A supported ThinkPad, a Raspberry Pi Pico H, a Pomona SOIC-8 clip, jumper wires.

## What does Libreboot change, and what doesn't it?

Libreboot replaces the vendor firmware that starts the computer with open-source code, and it reduces, but does not eliminate, Intel's proprietary code. Since 2022 it follows what it calls a binary blob reduction policy: a board gets the vendor code it cannot boot without, and nothing more.

| | Lenovo firmware | Libreboot |
|---|---|---|
| Firmware source | Closed | Open (coreboot, plus Libreboot's build system) |
| Intel Management Engine (ME) | Fully enabled | Cut down with me_cleaner and disabled; it cannot be removed entirely on these machines |
| Intel Boot Guard (T480s) | Enforced: only Lenovo-signed firmware runs | Disabled with deguard |
| Other vendor code | Built in | Only what the board needs to boot, such as CPU microcode and memory set-up code on some models |
| Boot menu | Lenovo's | EDK2 (UEFI), with SeaBIOS and GRUB available |

The **Intel Management Engine** is a separate processor inside Intel chipsets, running its own closed firmware with access to memory and the network, that operates independently of the operating system. On every ThinkPad in this guide the CPU will not run without part of its firmware, so Libreboot cannot remove it. It uses me_cleaner to strip the ME firmware to the minimum needed to start the machine and to switch it off after that. The ME is removed completely only on older boards such as the ThinkPad X200 and T400. None of the laptops here use AMD processors, so AMD's equivalent (the PSP) does not arise.

What this buys a Bitcoin computer is firmware you can audit and rebuild yourself, a much smaller body of closed code running before your operating system, and no vendor update channel that could change it underneath you. It does not make the hardware free of all closed code, and Libreboot's own documentation says so.

## Which laptops does this guide cover?

As of Libreboot 26.10 (October 2026):

| Laptop | Libreboot target | Flash chips | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| ThinkPad X230 | `lenovo_thinkpad_x230_12mb` | Two (4 MB and 8 MB) | Chips are under the palm rest |
| ThinkPad T420 | `lenovo_thinkpad_t420_8mb` | One (8 MB) | Full disassembly needed |
| ThinkPad T430 | `lenovo_thinkpad_t430_12mb` | Two (4 MB and 8 MB) | Full disassembly needed |
| ThinkPad T440p | `lenovo_thinkpad_t440p_12mb` | Two (4 MB and 8 MB) | Chips reachable from the back |
| ThinkPad T480s | `lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb` | One (16 MB), plus a separate Thunderbolt chip | Update Lenovo's firmware first; see [requirements](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/requirements/) |
| ThinkPad T530 | `lenovo_thinkpad_t530_12mb` | Two (4 MB and 8 MB) | Needs the chip-select workaround in [connection](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/) |
| ThinkPad W530 | `lenovo_thinkpad_w530_12mb` | Two (4 MB and 8 MB) | As the T530 |

The T480s is the most capable: NVMe storage and up to 24 GB of memory. The T480, T580, X280 and X220 are also supported by Libreboot, with similar steps; check [libreboot.org](https://libreboot.org/docs/install/) for their specifics.

## What changed in Libreboot 26.10?

Libreboot 26.10 "Ominous Olive", released on 15 October 2026, made EDK2, an open-source UEFI implementation, the default payload on most boards, with SeaBIOS and GRUB still available. Board targets now carry the vendor's name (`lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb` rather than `t480s_16mb`), and image names start with `uefi_` or `bios_`. The build and ROM pages of this guide use the 26.10 names. If you are updating a machine flashed with an older release, see [update Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/update-bios/).

## What are the steps?

| Step | Page | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Requirements](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/requirements/) | Get the laptop, a Raspberry Pi Pico H, a SOIC-8 clip and cables |
| 2 | [Build Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/build/) | Install dependencies and get the build system |
| 3 | [Build ROMs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/roms/) | Build the firmware image for your laptop |
| 4 | [Build flashprog](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/build-flashprog/) | Build the program that reads and writes the chip |
| 5 | [Build serprog](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/build-serprog/) | Turn the Pico into an SPI programmer |
| 6 | [Connect the Pico](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/) | Wire the Pico to the clip and the clip to the chip |
| 7 | [Flash the BIOS](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/flashing-bios/) | Back up the original firmware, then write Libreboot |

Help is available in the #libreboot channel on Libera IRC. If your laptop is not supported by Libreboot, the [coreboot guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/) covers a route that supports more devices, at the cost of more vendor code.


---

# Libreboot Hardware Requirements

> Hardware list for flashing Libreboot: supported laptops, Raspberry Pi Pico H programmer, Pomona SOIC8 clip, and required cables.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/requirements/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Flashing Libreboot externally needs five things: a supported ThinkPad, a Raspberry Pi Pico H to act as the programmer, a Pomona 5250 SOIC-8 clip, short female-to-female jumper wires, and a micro USB cable that carries data. Together the flashing parts cost about $15 to $30. This guide is written for ThinkPads whose firmware sits on SOIC-8 (8-pin) chips.

## Which laptop?

The models this guide covers, with their Libreboot targets and chip layouts, are listed on the [Libreboot overview](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/#which-laptops-does-this-guide-cover): the X230, T420, T430, T440p, T480s, T530 and W530. The ThinkPad T480s is the newest and most capable of them, with NVMe storage and up to 24 GB of memory.

### What the T480s needs first

Libreboot's [T480 and T480s instructions](https://libreboot.org/docs/install/t480.html) add three requirements the older models do not have:

1. Update Lenovo's own UEFI and embedded controller firmware to the version Libreboot specifies before installing, and change the settings it lists (Thunderbolt BIOS Assist off, Secure Boot off, and others).
2. Remove both the internal battery and the CMOS coin cell before flashing; on the T480s the battery has to come out completely.
3. Deal with the Thunderbolt firmware chip. Early T480 and T480s firmware writes debug logs to the Thunderbolt controller's own flash chip until it fills, after which Thunderbolt and fast charging stop working. Libreboot documents an external re-flash of that chip, done before Libreboot itself and in a strict order; follow their page exactly if your machine needs it.

## Raspberry Pi Pico H

The Raspberry Pi Pico H is a Pico with its header pins already soldered on, and it is the programmer Libreboot recommends: it runs at 3.3 V logic, so it cannot damage these chips with 5 V signals, and it costs a few dollars. Use the original Pico (RP2040). Libreboot removed support for the Pico 2 because of stability problems, and the Pico W works but needs extra vendor firmware for its unused Wi-Fi chip.

![A Raspberry Pi Pico H board with pre-soldered header pins](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/pico.webp)

## Pomona 5250 SOIC-8 clip

The Pomona 5250 is the clip that grips the 8-pin chip while it is still soldered to the board. Cheaper clips exist, but they slip, and a clip that loses contact mid-write is the most common way to end up with a corrupt chip.

![A blue Pomona 5250 SOIC-8 test clip](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/pomona.webp)

## Female-to-female jumper wires, 10 cm

Short wires connect the Pico to the clip. Keep them to about 10 cm: longer wires pick up interference at SPI speeds and cause read and write errors.

![A multicoloured ribbon of short female-to-female Dupont jumper wires](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/dupont.webp)

## Micro USB cable that carries data

The cable connects the Pico to the computer running the flashing software. Many micro USB cables carry power only; if the Pico does not appear as a device when plugged in with BOOTSEL held, try another cable.

![A black micro USB to USB-A cable](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/usb.webp)


---

# Build Libreboot

> Build a Libreboot ROM from source on Linux: install dependencies, clone the lbmk repository, and run a multi-threaded compile.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/build/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Libreboot is built with its own build system, lbmk, on a Linux computer: install git, set a git identity (lbmk refuses to run without one), clone lbmk from Codeberg, and let it install the rest of its dependencies for your distribution. This page prepares the build system; [build ROMs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/roms/) builds the image for your laptop. Commands are for Libreboot 26.10 (October 2026).

## Step 1: Install git and set a git identity

Step 1 installs git and gives it a name and email. lbmk uses git to download and patch coreboot, and git refuses to commit patches without a name and email. Any values work; they never leave your machine.

```bash
sudo apt install git python-is-python3
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

## Step 2: Clone lbmk

Step 2 downloads lbmk, the Libreboot build system, from Libreboot's Codeberg repository and moves into its directory:

```bash
git clone https://codeberg.org/libreboot/lbmk.git
cd lbmk
```

## Step 3: Install the build dependencies

Step 3 has lbmk install the packages your distribution needs. Run the one line that matches yours (the names are files in `config/dependencies/`, so check there if yours is not listed):

```bash
sudo ./mk dependencies debian
sudo ./mk dependencies ubuntu
sudo ./mk dependencies fedora41
sudo ./mk dependencies arch
```

## Step 4: Use every CPU core

Step 4 makes the build use every CPU core: lbmk builds on one thread by default, and setting `XBMK_THREADS` to the number of cores your computer has makes the build several times faster:

```bash
export XBMK_THREADS=$(nproc)
```

`nproc` prints the number of available cores, so this uses all of them. The setting lasts until you close the terminal.

When you build a ROM from source, lbmk downloads the vendor files your laptop needs (such as the Intel ME image, which it then cuts down with me_cleaner) and inserts them during the build. Pre-built release images from libreboot.org ship without them, which is why those need an extra `./mk inject` step that building from source does not.


---

# Build Libreboot ROM Images

> Generate Libreboot ROM images for your specific laptop model. Compile custom BIOS firmware using the lbmk build system, ready to flash.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/roms/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A Libreboot ROM is the firmware image written to the laptop's flash chip. Build it with `./mk -b coreboot` followed by your laptop's target name, then pick the right image from `bin/<target>/`: as of Libreboot 26.10 the recommended one starts with `uefi_edk2_grub_seabios_`, which boots like a normal UEFI computer and still offers GRUB and SeaBIOS.

## Step 1: Find your laptop's target

Step 1 finds the lbmk target name for your laptop. List every board lbmk can build:

```bash
./mk -b coreboot list
```

The ThinkPads in this guide are `lenovo_thinkpad_x230_12mb`, `lenovo_thinkpad_t420_8mb`, `lenovo_thinkpad_t430_12mb`, `lenovo_thinkpad_t440p_12mb`, `lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb`, `lenovo_thinkpad_t530_12mb` and `lenovo_thinkpad_w530_12mb`. The number at the end is the total flash size. Where a model is listed with two sizes (the X230 has `_12mb` and `_16mb` targets), check which chip your board has; on a running Linux system this shows the ROM size the firmware reports:

```bash
sudo dmidecode | grep ROM
```

## Step 2: Build the ROM

Step 2 builds the images for your target. It takes a while the first time, because lbmk downloads and compiles coreboot and its toolchain:

```bash
./mk -b coreboot lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb
```

Replace the target with yours.

## Step 3: Choose the image

Step 3 picks the one image to flash from the set lbmk built, which are in `bin/` under your target's name:

```bash
ls bin/lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb/
```

| Image name starts with | What it boots | Use it if |
|---|---|---|
| `uefi_edk2_grub_seabios_` | EDK2 (UEFI) by default, with GRUB and SeaBIOS in its menu | You want the default; current Linux installers boot from it normally |
| `bios_seabios_` | SeaBIOS, a legacy BIOS | You want the old BIOS-style boot |
| `bios_seagrub_` | SeaBIOS with GRUB first | You want GRUB first; it comes in one file per keyboard layout, so pick yours |

The rest of the name records the graphics set-up (for example `libgfxinit_corebootfb`). Copy the image you chose somewhere easy to reach:

```bash
cp bin/lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb/uefi_edk2_grub_seabios_lenovo_thinkpad_t480s_16mb_*.rom ~/libreboot.rom
```

If more than one file matches, copy the one you want by its full name. The [flashing page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/flashing-bios/) calls this file `libreboot.rom`.


---

# Build Flashprog for Libreboot

> Compile Flashprog from the Libreboot build system. Required tool for reading and writing BIOS chips during Libreboot installation.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/build-flashprog/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

flashprog is the program that reads and writes the flash chip through the Raspberry Pi Pico. It is a fork of flashrom, and lbmk builds the version Libreboot tests against. Build it from the `lbmk` directory:

```bash
./mk -b flashprog
```

lbmk downloads the flashprog source into `src/flashprog/default` and compiles it there (older lbmk versions used `src/flashprog`; `ls src/flashprog` shows which you have). Install it from that directory so that the plain `flashprog` used in the rest of this guide works:

```bash
cd src/flashprog/default
sudo make install
cd ../../..
```

Once the Pico has the serprog firmware on it ([build serprog](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/build-serprog/)), check the two talk to each other, with the Pico plugged in but not yet clipped to anything:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M
```

Several lines starting `serprog:` followed by this means the Pico is working:

```text
No EEPROM/flash device found.
Note: flashprog can never write if the flash chip isn't found automatically.
```

"No flash device found" is expected here, because the clip is not on a chip yet. An error about `/dev/ttyACM0` instead means the Pico is on a different port; `sudo dmesg` shows which.


---

# Prepare a Raspberry Pi Pico for Libreboot Flashing

> Set up a Raspberry Pi Pico H as an SPI programmer for flashing Libreboot: build the serprog firmware and wire the Pico to your laptop's BIOS chip.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To flash Libreboot externally you need an SPI programmer, and a Raspberry Pi Pico H running the open-source serprog firmware is the cheapest reliable one: about $5, and the programmer Libreboot itself recommends. Getting it ready takes two steps: build serprog and copy it onto the Pico, then wire the Pico to a SOIC-8 clip for your laptop's flash chip.

## What are the steps?

1. [Build serprog](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/build-serprog/): compile serprog and copy it onto the Pico
2. [Connect the Pico](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/): wire the Pico to the clip, pin for pin


---

# Build Serprog

> Build serprog firmware for the Raspberry Pi Pico H so it can act as an SPI programmer for flashing Libreboot to a laptop chip.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/build-serprog/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

serprog is open-source firmware that turns a Raspberry Pi Pico into an SPI programmer that flashprog can drive over USB. Build it with lbmk, copy the resulting `.uf2` file onto the Pico while it is in bootloader mode, and check that it reappears as a serial device.

## Step 1: Install the Pico toolchain

Step 1 installs the compiler and libraries for the Pico's ARM processor:

```bash
sudo apt install cmake libusb-1.0-0-dev libmbedtls-dev gcc-arm-none-eabi -y
```

## Step 2: Build the firmware

Step 2 builds the serprog firmware with lbmk. From the `lbmk` directory:

```bash
./mk -b pico-serprog
```

The build takes a few minutes and leaves two files:

- `bin/serprog_pico/serprog_pico.uf2`, for the Pico and Pico H
- `bin/serprog_pico/serprog_pico_w.uf2`, for the Pico W

Use the original Pico (RP2040). Libreboot removed Pico 2 support because of stability problems.

## Step 3: Copy the firmware onto the Pico

1. Hold down the BOOTSEL button on the Pico and plug it into your computer with the USB cable, then let go. Holding BOOTSEL while plugging in starts the Pico's bootloader, and it appears as a USB drive.
2. Copy `serprog_pico.uf2` onto that drive. The Pico restarts with the new firmware and the drive disappears.

To change the firmware later, hold BOOTSEL while plugging in again.

## Step 4: Check the Pico is detected

Step 4 confirms the computer sees the Pico as a serial device. Unplug the Pico, start watching the kernel log, and plug it back in:

```bash
sudo dmesg -wH
```

You should see something like:

```text
[  +0.092782] usb 3-7.2: New USB device found, idVendor=cafe, idProduct=4001, bcdDevice= 1.00
[  +0.000010] usb 3-7.2: New USB device strings: Mfr=1, Product=2, SerialNumber=3
[  +0.000003] usb 3-7.2: Product: pico-serprog (pico)
[  +0.000003] usb 3-7.2: Manufacturer: libreboot.org
[  +0.000002] usb 3-7.2: SerialNumber: E661410403213F31
[  +0.010021] cdc_acm 3-7.2:1.0: ttyACM0: USB ACM device
```

Note the serial port on the last line (`ttyACM0` here). flashprog needs it, and the rest of this guide assumes `/dev/ttyACM0`; use yours if it differs.


---

# Pico-Pomona Clip Connection

> Wire a Raspberry Pi Pico to a Pomona SOIC-8 clip for flashing Libreboot: find pin 1, follow the pin map, and handle the dual-chip T530 and W530 boards.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The Pico connects to the laptop's flash chip through the Pomona clip: six jumper wires run from the Pico to the clip, matching each chip pin to its Pico pin, and the clip then grips the chip on the motherboard. Two pins of the chip stay unconnected. The T530 and W530 need one extra part, which holds the second chip quiet while you work on the first.

## How do you find pin 1 on the chip?

The flash chips on these ThinkPads are SOIC-8 packages: eight legs, four on each side. Pin 1 is marked with a small dot or dimple on the chip's top. From pin 1, count anticlockwise around the chip: pins 1 to 4 down one side, 5 to 8 back up the other.

![Close-up of a SOIC-8 flash chip on a ThinkPad motherboard with its pins numbered 1 to 4 down one side and 5 to 8 up the other](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/soic8.webp)

The X230, T430, T440p, T530 and W530 have two chips side by side (4 MB and 8 MB), and both are flashed, one at a time. The T420 and T480s have one main chip. [Flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/flashing-bios/) covers each case.

## Which Pico pin goes to which chip pin?

| Chip pin | Function | Pico pin |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | CS (chip select) | 7 (GP5) |
| 2 | MISO (data out of the chip) | 6 (GP4) |
| 3 | WP (write protect) | Not connected |
| 4 | GND | 38 (GND) |
| 5 | MOSI (data into the chip) | 5 (GP3) |
| 6 | CLK (clock) | 4 (GP2, labelled SCK) |
| 7 | HOLD | Not connected |
| 8 | VCC | 36 (3V3) |

![Pin map of the Raspberry Pi Pico for serprog: SCK on pin 4, MOSI on pin 5, MISO on pin 6, CS on pin 7, GND on pin 38 and 3V3 on pin 36](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/serprog-pins.webp)

## How do you wire the X230, T420, T430, T440p and T480s?

Wire the clip straight to the Pico following the table; nothing else is needed. The finished wiring looks like this:

![The Pico wired to the blue Pomona clip with six short jumper wires](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/connection.webp)

## What do the T530 and W530 need?

The T530 and W530 have two flash chips on the same SPI bus. They share the data and clock lines, and each has its own chip select (CS) line deciding which one is listening. With the laptop unpowered, the CS line of the chip you are not flashing floats: nothing holds it high or low, so that chip can switch on at random and talk over the one you are reading. The symptoms are read and write errors and dumps that differ every time you read the chip, which shows up as a different `sha1sum` on each read.

The fix is to hold the other chip's CS pin at 3.3 V, which keeps it switched off while you work on the first.

### What extra parts do you need?

- One more female-to-female jumper wire
- A test hook clip ([example](https://www.ebay.com.au/itm/165822939855))
- An AMS1117 3.3 V regulator module ([example](https://www.ebay.com.au/itm/134721404746))
- A plug-in power adapter with selectable output voltage, set to 5 V ([example](https://www.amazon.com.au/dp/B0C16PS3D7))

### How do you connect them?

1. Attach the extra jumper wire to the test hook.
2. Hook it onto the CS pin (pin 1) of the chip you are not flashing.
3. Connect the other end to the 3.3 V output of the AMS1117 module.
4. Connect a GND pin on the Pico to GND on the AMS1117, so the two share a ground.
5. Set the adapter to 5 V and plug it into the AMS1117's input. The AMS1117 is a regulator: it needs about 5 V in to produce a steady 3.3 V out.
6. Clip the Pomona onto the chip you are flashing, wired to the Pico as above.
7. Switch on the adapter. The AMS1117's red LED lights.

The inactive chip is now held off, reads match each other, and you can go on to [flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/flashing-bios/).

<div className="photo-pair">

![The bench setup for the T530 and W530: the Pico wired to the Pomona clip, plus an AMS1117 3.3V regulator board powered from a 5V adapter, with a red test hook on its output lead](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/floating-setup.webp)

![The same setup on a ThinkPad motherboard: the Pomona clip on the chip being flashed and the red test hook holding the other chip's CS# pin at 3.3V](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/floating-clip.webp)

</div>


---

# Flash Libreboot to Your Laptop BIOS

> Flash a Libreboot ROM onto your laptop with an external SPI programmer: locate the chips, split the ROM, detect, and write the new firmware.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/flashing-bios/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Flashing writes the Libreboot image onto the laptop's flash chip with the Pico and the clip: open the laptop to reach the chip, split the image if the board has two chips, check flashprog can see each chip, read the original firmware three times and keep a copy whose reads match, then write Libreboot and confirm it boots. The backup is the step not to skip. If anything goes wrong, it is the only way back to a working laptop.

Before starting, unplug the charger and remove the main battery and the CMOS coin cell. Nothing should power the board except the Pico.

## Step 1: Locate the chip or chips

Step 1 opens the laptop far enough to reach the flash.

| Laptop | Chips | How to reach them |
|---|---|---|
| X230 | Two: 4 MB ("top") and 8 MB ("bottom") | Remove the keyboard and palm rest |
| T420 | One: 8 MB | Full disassembly |
| T430, T530, W530 | Two: 4 MB and 8 MB | Full disassembly |
| T440p | Two: 4 MB and 8 MB | From the back, through the service panel |
| T480s | One: 16 MB, near the memory (the chip near the edge is the Thunderbolt chip) | Remove the bottom cover |

![Two flash chips side by side on a ThinkPad motherboard, the 4 MB and 8 MB halves of a 12 MB firmware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/dual-chip.webp)

Photograph each chip's markings before clipping on. They tell you the chip model if flashprog finds more than one candidate.

## Step 2: Split the image for two-chip boards

Step 2 applies only to the 12 MB boards (X230, T430, T440p, T530 and W530). Their firmware is one 12 MB image stored across two chips, so split it into the first 8 MB, for the 8 MB "bottom" chip, and the last 4 MB, for the 4 MB "top" chip:

```bash
dd if=libreboot.rom of=libreboot_bottom.rom bs=1M count=8
dd if=libreboot.rom of=libreboot_top.rom bs=1M skip=8
```

The T420 and T480s have one chip and take the whole `libreboot.rom` as it is.

## Step 3: Detect the chip

Step 3 confirms flashprog can talk to the chip through the clip. Clip the Pomona firmly onto the chip (the top chip first, on two-chip boards), then plug the Pico into the computer you are flashing from.

![Two ThinkPads on a desk: one runs the flashing commands, the other is opened up with the Pico and clip attached to its flash chip](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/plug.webp)

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M
```

If flashprog reports several possible chips, pick the one matching your photo and name it with `-c` in every command from here on:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E"
```

`MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E` and, below, `EN25Q64` are the chips on our boards; yours may differ, so use the names flashprog gives you. If it finds nothing, reseat the clip and check the wiring against the [pin table](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/#which-pico-pin-goes-to-which-chip-pin).

## Step 4: Back up the factory firmware

Step 4 reads each chip three times and keeps the dump only if all three reads match, because a loose clip can return a corrupt read that looks normal. For the top chip:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E" -r factory_top.bin
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E" -r factory_top2.bin
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E" -r factory_top3.bin
sha1sum factory_top*.bin
```

All three hashes must be identical, for example:

```text
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory_top.bin
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory_top2.bin
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory_top3.bin
```

If they differ, reseat the clip and read again until three reads agree. Then keep one copy, on more than one drive:

```bash
rm factory_top2.bin factory_top3.bin
```

On two-chip boards, move the clip to the bottom chip and repeat with its chip name and `factory_bottom` file names:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "EN25Q64" -r factory_bottom.bin
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "EN25Q64" -r factory_bottom2.bin
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "EN25Q64" -r factory_bottom3.bin
sha1sum factory_bottom*.bin
rm factory_bottom2.bin factory_bottom3.bin
```

On one-chip boards, read the single chip the same way, as `factory.bin`.

## Step 5: Write Libreboot

Step 5 writes the new firmware. flashprog erases the chip, writes the image and reads it back to verify it, and finishes with `Verifying flash... VERIFIED.` when the chip matches the file. For the top chip:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E" -w libreboot_top.rom
```

Then move the clip to the bottom chip:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "EN25Q64" -w libreboot_bottom.rom
```

On one-chip boards, write `libreboot.rom` to the single chip. If a write does not end in `VERIFIED`, do not power the laptop; check the clip and run the same write again.

For an independent check, read the chip back and compare it with the file:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "MX25L3206E/MX25L3208E" -r flashed_top.bin
sha1sum libreboot_top.rom flashed_top.bin
```

The two hashes must match.

## Step 6: Boot it

Step 6 confirms the laptop starts. Unclip, reconnect the battery or charger, and power on before putting the laptop back together: you should see Libreboot's boot menu. If it does not start, write your factory backup back to the chip with the same `-w` command and the `factory_*.bin` files, and the laptop returns to its original firmware.


---

# Update Libreboot Firmware

> Update an existing Libreboot install from inside Linux without opening the laptop: relax /dev/mem access, back up the chip, write the new ROM and verify it.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/update-bios/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Once Libreboot is installed, newer releases can be written from Linux on the laptop itself, without opening it: build the new image as in [build ROMs](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/roms/), allow flashprog to reach the flash chip (which may need the `iomem=relaxed` kernel option), read the current chip three times and keep a matching backup, then write the new image with `flashprog -p internal` and check it before rebooting. If you instead download a pre-built release from libreboot.org, it ships without the vendor files your board needs; insert them first with `./mk inject`, following Libreboot's instructions for your board.

## Step 1: Let flashprog reach the chip

Step 1 checks that the kernel lets flashprog access the flash. Run:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p internal
```

If it reports the chip without errors, go to step 2. If it reports an error about `/dev/mem`, restart with the `iomem=relaxed` kernel option. Open GRUB's settings:

```bash
sudo nano /etc/default/grub
```

add `iomem=relaxed` to the line starting `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`:

```bash
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash iomem=relaxed"
```

then save, update GRUB and reboot:

```bash
sudo update-grub
sudo reboot
```

Some kernels are built with `CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM`, which blocks this access even then; Libreboot's documentation covers that case. Remove `iomem=relaxed` again once the update is done, because it loosens a protection the kernel normally enforces.

## Step 2: Check the chip size

Step 2 confirms the image you built matches the chip. The output of `sudo flashprog -p internal` includes the flash chip and its size; it should match the size in your board target's name (for example 12 MB for `lenovo_thinkpad_x230_12mb`).

## Step 3: Back up what is on the chip now

Step 3 reads the current firmware three times and keeps it only if the reads match:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p internal:laptop=force_I_want_a_brick,boardmismatch=force -r dump.bin
sudo flashprog -p internal:laptop=force_I_want_a_brick,boardmismatch=force -r dump2.bin
sudo flashprog -p internal:laptop=force_I_want_a_brick,boardmismatch=force -r dump3.bin
sha1sum dump*.bin
```

All three hashes must be the same. Keep `dump.bin` somewhere other than this laptop and delete the other two:

```bash
rm dump2.bin dump3.bin
```

## Step 4: Write the new image

Step 4 writes the update:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p internal:laptop=force_I_want_a_brick,boardmismatch=force -w libreboot.rom
```

`laptop=force_I_want_a_brick` and `boardmismatch=force` switch off safety checks that otherwise refuse to flash laptops or boards flashprog does not recognise; with the correct image for your machine, Libreboot's documentation describes them as safe. To use as few overrides as possible, try plain `-p internal` first, then `-p internal:boardmismatch=force`, and add `laptop=force_I_want_a_brick` only if needed.

flashprog verifies the write and prints `VERIFIED` (or reports that the chip already matched) on success.

## Step 5: Check the result before rebooting

Step 5 reads the chip back and compares it with the image:

```bash
sudo flashprog -p internal:laptop=force_I_want_a_brick,boardmismatch=force -r new_dump.bin
sha1sum libreboot.rom new_dump.bin
rm new_dump.bin
```

If the two hashes match, reboot into the updated firmware. If they do not, do not reboot: write the image again, or write `dump.bin` back, until a read matches.


---

# Coreboot Installation Guide

> Install Coreboot open-source firmware for a fast, secure, and transparent boot process. Perfect for Bitcoin nodes and security-focused setups.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Coreboot is open-source firmware that replaces a laptop's proprietary BIOS or UEFI: it starts the hardware and hands over to a payload such as SeaBIOS or GRUB, which boots your operating system. This guide installs it on Ivy Bridge ThinkPads (the X230, T430, T430s, T530 and W530), either internally from Linux after downgrading and unlocking the stock BIOS, or externally with a Raspberry Pi Pico clipped to the flash chip, which also lets you neutralise the Intel Management Engine with me_cleaner. It supports more hardware than [Libreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/), at the cost of more vendor code left in place.

![A ThinkPad T430s running Coreboot with the SeaBIOS payload, its boot menu listing the DVD drive and the internal SSD](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/coreboot/t430s.webp)

Time: 2-4 hours. Cost: $0 (internal flash) or $15-30 (external flash hardware). Level: Advanced. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: Supported laptop, Linux system for building.

## Why use coreboot?

Most computers run proprietary BIOS or UEFI firmware that nobody outside the vendor can inspect. Coreboot replaces it with open source:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Benefit | What it means |
|---------|-------------|
| Open source | The boot code can be audited and rebuilt |
| Minimal | It initialises only what is needed, then hands over |
| Fast | Boots quicker than the stock firmware |
| Wide support | Runs on more machines than Libreboot |

</div>

What it does not do is remove all closed code. On these ThinkPads the Intel Management Engine firmware stays in the flash chip; the [external flashing guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/) neutralises it with me_cleaner, which strips most of it and disables the rest. Some boards also need other vendor code, such as CPU microcode.

## How does coreboot start a computer?

Coreboot runs in stages: a tiny bootblock, then romstage, which sets up memory, then ramstage, which initialises the rest of the hardware, and finally the payload you chose (GRUB, SeaBIOS or a Linux kernel), which boots the operating system. Doing only what is necessary keeps it small, fast and easier to audit.

## Which route should you take?

| Route | When | Pages |
|---|---|---|
| Internal flashing | Your Ivy Bridge ThinkPad's BIOS can be downgraded and unlocked; no disassembly or programmer | [Downgrade](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/downgrading-bios/), [unlock](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/unlocking-bios/), [flash](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/) |
| External flashing | You want to neutralise the Intel ME, the board does not allow internal flashing, or an internal flash failed | [External flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/) |

Both start from the [requirements](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/requirements/) and [building coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/build/). Once it is installed, use the laptop as a [Bitcoin computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/advanced/bitcoin-computer/) or an [air-gapped computer](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/).


---

# Coreboot Hardware Requirements

> What you need to install Coreboot on a ThinkPad: a supported model, a Linux machine and, for external flashing, a Raspberry Pi Pico plus a clip or pogo pins.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/requirements/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

To install coreboot you need a supported laptop, a Linux system to run the tools, the coreboot source and flashrom, the program that reads and writes flash chips. Flashing internally also needs CHIPSEC and, possibly, a USB stick to downgrade the BIOS; flashing externally needs an SPI programmer such as a Raspberry Pi Pico, with a Pomona clip or a pogo-pin adapter depending on the chip.

## What do you need to flash internally?

Internal flashing works on these Ivy Bridge ThinkPads:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

|Model|
|-|
|X230|
|X230T|
|T430|
|T430s|
|T530|
|W530|

</div>

You also need CHIPSEC, a security tool that checks whether the BIOS can be flashed internally, and possibly a USB stick, to boot Lenovo's BIOS updater if you need to [downgrade](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/downgrading-bios/).

## What do you need to flash externally?

An SPI programmer, such as a Raspberry Pi Pico, wired with jumper cables to a Pomona clip for chips in an 8-pin SOIC package, or to a pogo-pin adapter for WSON chips, which a clip cannot grip.

<div className="photo-pair">

![A Raspberry Pi Pico wired with six coloured Dupont cables to a blue Pomona SOIC-8 test clip, the setup for chips in an 8-pin SOIC package](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/connection.webp)

![The same Raspberry Pi Pico wired instead to a pogo-pin adapter, used for WSON chips that a clip cannot grip](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/coreboot/connection.webp)

</div>


---

# Build Coreboot

> Build Coreboot from source on Linux: install the dependencies, clone the source tree, build the cross-compiler toolchain, configure your ThinkPad and compile.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/build/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Building coreboot from source takes five steps on a Linux computer: install the build dependencies, download the coreboot source, build its cross-compiler toolchain (the slowest part), configure the build for your mainboard and payload, and compile it into a ROM image to flash.

## Step 1: Install the build tools and libraries

Step 1 installs the development tools and libraries coreboot needs to compile.
The packages you need depend on your Linux distribution. Run the command that matches your system:

Debian-based distros (e.g., Ubuntu, Linux Mint):

```bash
sudo apt install -y python-is-python3 bison build-essential curl flex git gnat libncurses-dev libssl-dev libcmocka-dev zlib1g-dev pkgconf libpci-dev flashrom coreboot-utils
```

Arch-based distros (e.g., Manjaro, EndeavourOS):

```bash
sudo pacman -S base-devel curl git gcc-ada ncurses zlib
```

Red Hat-based distros (e.g., Fedora, CentOS, RHEL):

```bash
sudo dnf install git make gcc-gnat flex bison xz bzip2 gcc g++ ncurses-devel wget zlib-devel patch
```

If any package is missing, Coreboot may fail to build, so make sure the installation finishes without errors.

## Step 2: Download the coreboot source

Step 2 downloads the coreboot source from the official repository and moves into its directory:

```bash
git clone https://review.coreboot.org/coreboot
cd coreboot
```

This will give you the latest development version of Coreboot.
If you want to build a specific version, you can check out the corresponding branch or tag after cloning.

## Step 3: Build the coreboot toolchain

Step 3 builds coreboot's own cross-compiler toolchain, which keeps builds reproducible and working on every supported board.
You must build this toolchain before compiling Coreboot itself.

First, see which toolchains are available:

```bash
make help_toolchain
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
*** Toolchain targets ***
  crossgcc        - Build coreboot cross-compilers for all platforms
  crossgcc-clean  - Remove all built coreboot cross-compilers
  iasl            - Build coreboot IASL compiler (built by all cross targets)
  clang           - Build coreboot clang compiler
  nasm            - Build coreboot nasm
  test-toolchain  - Reports if toolchain components are out of date
  crossgcc-ARCH   - Build cross-compiler for specific architecture
  ARCH can be "i386", "x64", "arm", "aarch64", "riscv", "ppc64", "nds32le"
  Use "make [target] CPUS=#" to build toolchain using multiple cores
  Use "make [target] DEST=some/path" to install toolchain there
  Use "make [target] BUILDGCC_OPTIONS="-m" to get packages from coreboot mirror"
```

</details>

Choose the one that matches your target architecture.
For most x86 systems, including laptops like the ThinkPad T430s, use the i386 toolchain.

Examples:

```bash
make crossgcc-i386 CPUS=$(nproc)       # build i386 toolchain
make crossgcc-aarch64 CPUS=$(nproc)    # build Aarch64 toolchain
make crossgcc-riscv CPUS=$(nproc)      # build RISC-V toolchain
```

**Important notes:**

- The `i386` toolchain works for all x86 and x86_64 boards.
- You can try building with your system’s compiler, but this often causes build errors. The Coreboot toolchain is strongly recommended.

## Step 4: Configure the build

Step 4 configures coreboot for your computer, here a Lenovo ThinkPad T430s. The configuration decides how coreboot initialises the hardware and which payload, the software it hands over to after startup, it runs.

Run the interactive configuration menu:

```bash
make menuconfig
```

This menu lets you select various options such as the motherboard, ROM chip size, and payload.

### Motherboard

Navigate in the menu:

```text
Mainboard  --->  
    Mainboard vendor (Lenovo)
    Mainboard model (ThinkPad T430s)
    ROM chip size (16384 KB (16 MB))
< Exit >
```

**Note**
Make sure the ROM chip size matches your actual hardware. Using the wrong size may result in a non-working firmware.

### Payload

A payload in Coreboot is a small program that Coreboot loads after it finishes initializing the hardware. Common payloads include:
- **SeaBIOS**: provides a legacy BIOS environment to boot traditional operating systems.
- **GRUB2**: a modern bootloader capable of booting Linux, Windows, and other systems, with more features than SeaBIOS.

Next, select your preferred payload.

#### SeaBIOS

SeaBIOS provides a traditional BIOS interface, making it a simple choice for booting legacy operating systems or when you want a classic BIOS like experience.

```text
Payload  --->
    Payload to add (SeaBIOS)
    SeaBIOS version (1.16.3)
< Exit >
< Exit >
< Yes >
```

#### GRUB2

GRUB2 is a modern, flexible bootloader that can boot Linux, Windows, and other systems. It is more powerful than SeaBIOS but requires some extra configuration.

Install the required dependencies for building the GRUB2 payload:
```bash
sudo apt install automake autoconf autopoint libfreetype6-dev unifont fonts-unifont unifont-bin gawk
```

In the configuration menu:

```text
Payload  --->
     Payload to add (GRUB2)
     GRUB version (2.12)
     Extra modules to include in GRUB image (NEW)
  [*]Include GRUB2 runtime config file into ROM image (NEW)
< Exit >
< Exit >
< Yes >
```
Add GRUB2 Extra Modules.

Modules extend GRUB’s capabilities, for example supporting USB, LVM, encryption, or different filesystems. For a typical laptop, include:

```text
cryptodisk nativedisk ehci ohci usb usbms usbserial_pl2303 usbserial_ftdi usbserial_usbdebug jpeg all_video hashsum regexp linux part_msdos part_gpt lvm luks gcry_md5 gcry_sha1 gcry_sha256 gcry_sha512 gcry_rsa gcry_rijndael gcry_des search search_fs_file search_fs_uuid configfile probe
```

These modules ensure that GRUB can boot from internal disks, USB sticks, handle encrypted drives, and support multiple filesystems.

Create a basic `grub.cfg` to define the boot behavior and include it in the “Include GRUB2 runtime config file into ROM image” option.

<details>
<summary>grub.cfg</summary>

```text
# Coreboot GRUB2: auto-boot with ESC menu and user instructions

set timeout=2
set timeout_style=hidden
set default=0

# Show instructions
echo "Press ESC to access the boot menu."
echo "Otherwise, the system will boot from the hard drive automatically."

### Primary entry: Boot internal disk ###
menuentry "Boot first disk" {
    echo "Booting from the hard drive..."
    search --no-floppy --set=root --file /grub/grub.cfg
    configfile /grub/grub.cfg
}

### Secondary entry: Boot from USB via ESC ###
menuentry "Boot USB" {
    search --no-floppy --removable --file /boot/grub/grub.cfg --set=root
    configfile /grub/grub.cfg
}
```

</details>

#### Save the configuration to a file (optional)

```bash
make savedefconfig
cat defconfig
```

For SeaBIOS, your configuration might include:

```text
CONFIG_VENDOR_LENOVO=y
CONFIG_BOARD_LENOVO_T430S=y
```

For GRUB2, it might look like:

```text
CONFIG_VENDOR_LENOVO=y
CONFIG_BOARD_LENOVO_T430S=y
CONFIG_PAYLOAD_GRUB2=y
CONFIG_GRUB2_EXTRA_MODULES="cryptodisk nativedisk ehci ohci usb usbms usbserial_pl2303 usbserial_ftdi usbserial_usbdebug jpeg all_video hashsum regexp linux part_msdos part_gpt lvm luks gcry_md5 gcry_sha1 gcry_sha256 gcry_sha512 gcry_rsa gcry_rijndael gcry_des search search_fs_file search_fs_uuid configfile probe"
CONFIG_GRUB2_INCLUDE_RUNTIME_CONFIG_FILE=y
```

The exact lines depend on the coreboot version, so more or fewer lines than these is normal.

## Step 5: Build coreboot

Step 5 compiles the coreboot image:

```bash
make
```

If the build completes successfully, you will see a message like:

```text
Built lenovo/t430s (ThinkPad T430s)
```

The compiled ROM file will be located at `build/coreboot.rom`.

If you want to start fresh and remove all compiled files, run:

```bash
make distclean
```

This will reset the build environment so you can reconfigure and rebuild from scratch.

You now have a coreboot ROM to flash, [internally](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/) or [externally](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/).


---

# Internal Coreboot Flashing

> Flash Coreboot from inside a running system: downgrade your stock BIOS, unlock the Intel Flash Descriptor, and write the new firmware safely.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Internal flashing replaces the laptop's stock BIOS with coreboot from inside a running Linux system, without opening the laptop or using an external programmer. It works only on machines whose BIOS region can be unlocked: you install a BIOS version old enough to have the relevant vulnerabilities, use CHIPSEC and a sleep-and-resume trick to remove the write protection, then write and verify the coreboot image. It is faster than external flashing, but it cannot touch the Intel ME region.

## What are the steps?

1. [Downgrade the stock BIOS](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/downgrading-bios/) to a version that still allows internal flashing.
2. [Unlock the BIOS region](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/unlocking-bios/) with CHIPSEC.
3. [Flash coreboot](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/) and verify the result.

If your laptop does not support internal flashing, or you want to neutralise the Intel ME, use [external flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/) instead.


---

# Downgrading BIOS

> Downgrade your laptop's stock BIOS to a version with an unlocked Intel ME region, a prerequisite for internal Coreboot flashing.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/downgrading-bios/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Internal flashing relies on vulnerabilities in older Lenovo BIOS versions, which later updates patched, so a ThinkPad running a newer BIOS has to be downgraded first: download Lenovo's BIOS update ISO for the version in the table below, change its boot script so it allows installing an older version, write it to a USB stick, and boot from it to flash the older BIOS.

## Which BIOS versions still allow internal flashing?

The table lists, for each model, the newest BIOS version that still allows internal flashing. If your BIOS is newer, downgrade to that version or an earlier one before installing coreboot.

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Model | Newest BIOS that can be flashed internally |
|-|-|
| X230 | 2.60 |
| X230T | 2.58 |
| T430 | 2.64 |
| T430s | 2.59 |
| T530 | 2.60 |
| W530 | 2.58 |

</div>

## Why is a downgrade possible?

Lenovo describes its BIOS as having security rollback prevention: once updated, it cannot go back to an older version. The check is made by Lenovo's flashing tools (the Windows utility and the bootable CD), not by the BIOS itself, so running the flashing program (`winflash.exe` or `dosflash.exe`) directly skips it. That takes a small change to the bootable CD image Lenovo publishes.

## Step 1: Download the BIOS ISO

Step 1 downloads Lenovo's bootable BIOS update image for the version in the table. This guide uses a T430s on a BIOS newer than 2.59 as the example. Open the [Lenovo support page for the T430s](https://support.lenovo.com/us/en/downloads/ds029724-bios-update-utility-bootable-cd-for-windows-10-81-8-7-64-bit-81-8-7-32-bit-xp-thinkpad-t430s-t430si), find the "Release (BIOS Bootable)" column, and download `g7uj13us.iso`, which contains BIOS 2.59 (an older version also works). For another model, use that model's support page and the version in the table.

## Step 2: Extract and mount the boot image

Step 2 extracts the El Torito boot image from the ISO and mounts it so its files can be edited. `geteltorito` comes with the `genisoimage` package on Debian and Ubuntu.

```bash
geteltorito -o ./bios.img g7uj13us.iso
sudo mount -t vfat ./bios.img /mnt -o loop,offset=16384
ls /mnt
ls /mnt/FLASH
```

Inside `FLASH` is one directory named after the BIOS build. The commands below show `G1ET93WW`, from a T430 image; use the name you see. List it and look for a `.FL1` file, something like `$01D2000.FL1`:

```bash
ls /mnt/FLASH/G1ET93WW
```

## Step 3: Make the boot script run the flasher directly

Step 3 edits `AUTOEXEC.BAT` so the image starts `dosflash.exe` itself instead of Lenovo's wrapper, which is what enforces the rollback block:

```bash
sudo nano /mnt/AUTOEXEC.BAT
```

The file looks like this:

```bash
@ECHO OFF
PROMPT $p$g
cd c:\flash
command.com
```

Replace the last line, `command.com`, with this, adjusting the path to your `.FL1` file:

```bash
dosflash.exe /sd /file G1ET93WW\$01D2000.FL1
```

Save the file and unmount the image:

```bash
sudo umount /mnt
```

## Step 4: Write the image to a USB drive

Step 4 writes the modified image to a USB drive. Replace `/dev/sdX` with your USB device, and check it with `lsblk` first: `dd` overwrites whatever disk you name.

```bash
sudo dd if=./bios.img of=/dev/sdX bs=1M
```

## Step 5: Flash the older BIOS

Step 5 boots the laptop from the USB drive, which flashes the older BIOS automatically:

1. Reboot and press `F1` to enter the BIOS settings. In the Startup tab, set Startup Mode to Legacy (or Both, Legacy first), then save and reboot with `F10`.
2. Connect AC power. Do not flash on battery: if power is lost during the flash, recovering the laptop needs an external programmer.
3. Press `F12` during startup and choose the USB drive. Flashing starts on its own, and the laptop may reboot several times; do not interrupt it.
4. When it has finished, enter the BIOS settings again and set Startup Mode back to UEFI (or Both, UEFI first). The S3 boot script flaw used on the [next page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/unlocking-bios/) is in the UEFI firmware, so the laptop has to boot in UEFI mode.
5. Boot your operating system and check that `/sys/firmware/efi` exists, which confirms it booted in UEFI mode.


---

# Unlocking BIOS

> Unlock the Intel Flash Descriptor BIOS region with CHIPSEC so Coreboot can be flashed internally without an external SPI programmer.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/unlocking-bios/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The stock BIOS write-protects its own flash region, so before coreboot can be flashed internally those protections must be removed. On the older BIOS versions this guide uses, two flaws make that possible: the SMM_BWP and BLE protections are not enabled, and the S3 boot script, which restores settings after sleep, can be patched. Install CHIPSEC, check the current lock status, dump and patch the boot script, put the laptop to sleep and wake it so the patched script runs, remove the protected ranges, and verify the region is writable.

## Why can older ThinkPad BIOS versions be unlocked?

Two flaws in older factory BIOS versions for these ThinkPads make internal flashing possible without an external programmer.

The first is that two write protections are left off. In BIOS versions released before 2014, SMM_BWP and BLE are both disabled, so the operating system can write to the BIOS without triggering extra security checks. Our testing on several T430 and X230 BIOS versions found that SMM_BWP is set to 1 only from the update whose changelog says:

```text
(New) Improved the UEFI BIOS security feature.
```

That update blocks ordinary internal flashing, which is why the [downgrade](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/downgrading-bios/) comes first.

The second is the S3 boot script flaw. The instructions the firmware runs when the laptop resumes from sleep (the S3 state) could be modified from the running system, and modifying them can stop the firmware from re-locking the flash configuration (the FLOCKDN bit) on resume. Lenovo's [S3 boot script advisory](https://support.lenovo.com/eg/ru/product_security/s3_boot_protect) covers the fix.

## Which registers protect the BIOS flash?

Intel platforms of this generation protect the BIOS flash with three mechanisms:

| Protection | Where it lives | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| SMM_BWP (SMM BIOS Write Protect) | BIOS_CNTL register, LPC bridge PCI config offset `0xDC` | At 1, the BIOS can be written only from System Management Mode. Once set, it cannot be cleared |
| BLE (BIOS Lock Enable) | BIOS_CNTL | At 1, any attempt to set BIOSWE triggers a System Management Interrupt. Once set, it cannot be cleared |
| BIOSWE (BIOS Write Enable) | BIOS_CNTL | Whether the BIOS is writable. Always read/write |
| PR0-PR4 (SPI Protected Ranges) | SPI registers `SPIBAR + 0x74` to `SPIBAR + 0x84` | Each defines an address range; its WP bit blocks writes to that range |
| FLOCKDN (Flash Configuration Lock-Down) | HSFS register, `SPIBAR + 0x04` | At 1, the PR0-PR4 registers cannot be changed until the next hardware reset |

Internal flashing needs two things: BIOS_CNTL must allow writes (SMM_BWP and BLE at 0, so BIOSWE can be set to 1), and no protected range may cover the region being written (WP at 0 on PR0-PR4). FLOCKDN decides whether the second can be fixed: while it is 1, the protected ranges stay as the firmware set them.

## How does the S3 boot script get around the lock?

FLOCKDN can only be cleared by a hardware reset, and the firmware sets it again on every boot. Resuming from S3 sleep (suspend to RAM) is also such a reset, and on resume the chipset restores its settings by running the S3 boot script, a list of register writes kept in RAM. Editing that script before suspending changes what the firmware does on resume: if the write that sets FLOCKDN is changed to leave it at 0, the protected ranges can be cleared after waking, and the BIOS region becomes writable.

## Step 1: Install CHIPSEC

Step 1 installs [CHIPSEC](https://chipsec.github.io/), Intel's open-source framework for inspecting platform firmware security, which reads and writes the registers above. Install the build dependencies, clone the repository and build its driver:

```bash
sudo apt install build-essential python3-dev python3 python-is-python3 gcc linux-headers-$(uname -r) nasm
git clone https://github.com/chipsec/chipsec.git
cd chipsec
python setup.py build_ext -i
```

## Step 2: Check whether the flash configuration is locked

Step 2 reads the HSFS register (`SPIBAR + 0x04`) to see whether FLOCKDN is set:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_main.py -m common.spi_lock
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
[x][ =======================================================================
[x][ Module: SPI Flash Controller Configuration Locks
[x][ =======================================================================
[*] HSFS = 0xE009 << Hardware Sequencing Flash Status Register (SPIBAR + 0x4)
    [00] FDONE            = 1 << Flash Cycle Done
    [01] FCERR            = 0 << Flash Cycle Error
    [02] AEL              = 0 << Access Error Log
    [03] BERASE           = 1 << Block/Sector Erase Size
    [05] SCIP             = 0 << SPI cycle in progress
    [13] FDOPSS           = 1 << Flash Descriptor Override Pin-Strap Status
    [14] FDV              = 1 << Flash Descriptor Valid
    [15] FLOCKDN          = 1 << Flash Configuration Lock-Down
```

</details>

`FLOCKDN = 1` means the SPI configuration is locked: the protected ranges cannot be changed until the next hardware reset. That is the normal state, and Steps 4 to 7 work around it.

## Step 3: Check BIOS_CNTL and the protected ranges

Step 3 reads BIOS_CNTL and the five protected range registers:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_main.py -m common.bios_wp
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
 [x][ =======================================================================
 [x][ Module: BIOS Region Write Protection
 [x][ =======================================================================
 [*] BC = 0x 8 << BIOS Control (b:d.f 00:31.0 + 0xDC)
     [00] BIOSWE           = 0 << BIOS Write Enable
     [01] BLE              = 0 << BIOS Lock Enable
     [02] SRC              = 2 << SPI Read Configuration
     [04] TSS              = 0 << Top Swap Status
     [05] SMM_BWP          = 0 << SMM BIOS Write Protection
 [-] BIOS region write protection is disabled!

 [*] BIOS Region: Base = 0x00500000, Limit = 0x00BFFFFF
 SPI Protected Ranges
 ------------------------------------------------------------
 PRx (offset) | Value    | Base     | Limit    | WP? | RP?
 ------------------------------------------------------------
 PR0 (74)     | 00000000 | 00000000 | 00000000 | 0   | 0
 PR1 (78)     | 8BFF0B40 | 00B40000 | 00BFFFFF | 1   | 0
 PR2 (7C)     | 8B100B10 | 00B10000 | 00B10FFF | 1   | 0
 PR3 (80)     | 8ADE0AD0 | 00AD0000 | 00ADEFFF | 1   | 0
 PR4 (84)     | 8AAF0800 | 00800000 | 00AAFFFF | 1   | 0
```

</details>

On an older BIOS, `SMM_BWP = 0` and `BLE = 0`, which is what this method needs. The protected ranges PR1 to PR4 have `WP = 1`, so large parts of the BIOS region are still write-protected even though BIOS_CNTL looks permissive. Note the value of each protected range, which Step 8 needs, and the BIOS region's Base and Limit, which the [verification after flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/#verify-the-flashed-image) needs.

To see the raw register space instead, which also shows the SPIBAR base address (here `0xFED1F800`) and HSFS at offset `0x04`:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_util.py mmio dump SPIBAR
```

```text
[mmio] MMIO register range [0x00000000FED1F800:0x00000000FED1F800+00000200]:
+00000000: 0BFF0500
+00000004: 0004E009
...
```

## Step 4: Find the S3 boot script entry that sets FLOCKDN

Step 4 dumps the S3 boot script and finds the entry that writes to HSFS, which is `SPIBAR + 0x04`: with SPIBAR at `0xFED1F800`, that is `0xFED1F804`.

```bash
sudo python chipsec_util.py uefi s3bootscript
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
Entry at offset 0x2B8F (len = 0x17, header len = 0x0):
 Data:
 02 00 17 02 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 04 f8 d1 fe 00 |
 00 00 00 09 e0 04 00                            |
 Decoded:
   Opcode : S3_BOOTSCRIPT_MEM_WRITE (0x0002)
   Width  : 0x02 (4 bytes)
   Address: 0xFED1F804
   Count  : 0x1
   Values : 0x0004E009
```

</details>

The value `0x0004E009` written to that address sets `FLOCKDN = 1` on every resume.

## Step 5: Back up the BIOS region

Step 5 dumps the BIOS region three times and compares the dumps, so you have a backup you can trust before changing anything:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p internal -r bios_backup.rom --ifd -i bios
sudo flashrom -p internal -r bios_backup2.rom --ifd -i bios
sudo flashrom -p internal -r bios_backup3.rom --ifd -i bios
sha1sum bios_backup.rom bios_backup2.rom bios_backup3.rom
```

All three hashes must match:

```text
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  bios_backup.rom
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  bios_backup2.rom
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  bios_backup3.rom
```

If they do, keep `bios_backup.rom` somewhere off the laptop and delete the other two. If they differ, the reads are unreliable: do not go on.

## Step 6: Patch the boot script

Step 6 changes the HSFS write in the boot script from `0xE009` to `0x6009`, which clears bit 15 (FLOCKDN) so the flash configuration stays unlocked after resume. Use the HSFS address you found in Step 4:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_main.py -m tools.uefi.s3script_modify -a replace_op,mmio_wr,0xFED1F804,0x6009,0x2
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
 [*] Modifying S3 boot script entry at address 0x00000000DAF49B8F..
 [mem] 0x00000000DAF49B8F
 [*] Original entry:
  2  0 17  2  0  0  0  1  0  0  0  4 f8 d1 fe  0 |
  0  0  0  9 e0  4  0                            |
 [mem] buffer len = 0x17 to PA = 0x00000000DAF49B8F
  2  0 17  2  0  0  0  1  0  0  0  4 f8 d1 fe  0 |
  0  0  0  9 60  0  0                            |
 [mem] 0x00000000DAF49B8F
 [*] Modified entry:
  2  0 17  2  0  0  0  1  0  0  0  4 f8 d1 fe  0 |
  0  0  0  9 60  0  0                            | 
 [*] After sleep/resume, check the value of register 0xFED1F804 is 0x6009
 [+] PASSED: The script has been modified. Go to sleep..
```

</details>

The "Modified entry" at the end of the output shows the new value, `60` in place of `e0`.

## Step 7: Sleep and resume to apply the patch

Step 7 puts the laptop into S3 sleep (suspend) and wakes it, so the firmware runs the patched script. After waking, check FLOCKDN again:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_main.py -m common.spi_lock
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
...
[x][ =======================================================================
[x][ Module: SPI Flash Controller Configuration Locks
[x][ =======================================================================
[*] HSFS = 0x6008 << Hardware Sequencing Flash Status Register (SPIBAR + 0x4)
    [00] FDONE            = 0 << Flash Cycle Done
    [01] FCERR            = 0 << Flash Cycle Error
    [02] AEL              = 0 << Access Error Log
    [03] BERASE           = 1 << Block/Sector Erase Size
    [05] SCIP             = 0 << SPI cycle in progress
    [13] FDOPSS           = 1 << Flash Descriptor Override Pin-Strap Status
    [14] FDV              = 1 << Flash Descriptor Valid
    [15] FLOCKDN          = 0 << Flash Configuration Lock-Down
[-] SPI Flash Controller configuration is not locked
[-] FAILED: SPI Flash Controller not locked correctly.
```

</details>

`[15] FLOCKDN = 0` means the flash configuration is unlocked. CHIPSEC reports this as FAILED because, from a security point of view, an unlocked controller is a failure; here it is the result you want.

## Step 8: Remove write protection from the protected ranges

Step 8 writes each protected range back with its WP bit (bit 31) cleared. The values below are this machine's ranges from Step 3 with the top bit removed (`0x8AAF0800` becomes `0x0AAF0800`); use the values your own Step 3 output printed.

```bash
sudo python chipsec_util.py mmio write SPIBAR 0x74 0x4 0x0AAF0800
sudo python chipsec_util.py mmio write SPIBAR 0x78 0x4 0x0ADE0AD0
sudo python chipsec_util.py mmio write SPIBAR 0x7C 0x4 0x0B100B10
sudo python chipsec_util.py mmio write SPIBAR 0x80 0x4 0x0BFF0B40
```

## Step 9: Verify the BIOS region is writable

Step 9 reads BIOS_CNTL and the protected ranges again:

```bash
sudo python chipsec_main.py -m common.bios_wp
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
[x][ =======================================================================
[x][ Module: BIOS Region Write Protection
[x][ =======================================================================
[*] BC = 0x 9 << BIOS Control (b:d.f 00:31.0 + 0xDC)
    [00] BIOSWE           = 1 << BIOS Write Enable
    [01] BLE              = 0 << BIOS Lock Enable
    [02] SRC              = 2 << SPI Read Configuration
    [04] TSS              = 0 << Top Swap Status
    [05] SMM_BWP          = 0 << SMM BIOS Write Protection
[-] BIOS region write protection is disabled!

[*] BIOS Region: Base = 0x00500000, Limit = 0x00BFFFFF
SPI Protected Ranges
------------------------------------------------------------
PRx (offset) | Value    | Base     | Limit    | WP? | RP?
------------------------------------------------------------
PR0 (74)     | 0AAF0800 | 00800000 | 00AAF000 | 0   | 0
PR1 (78)     | 0ADE0AD0 | 00AD0000 | 00ADE000 | 0   | 0
PR2 (7C)     | 0B100B10 | 00B10000 | 00B10000 | 0   | 0
PR3 (80)     | 0BFF0B40 | 00B40000 | 00BFF000 | 0   | 0
PR4 (84)     | 00000000 | 00000000 | 00000000 | 0   | 0
```

</details>

If every `WP?` value is 0, the BIOS region is writable and you can go on to [flash coreboot internally](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/). The unlock lasts until the next reboot, which sets FLOCKDN again.

**Danger: Write only the BIOS region**
The flash descriptor and ME regions are still locked. Flash with `--ifd -i bios` so flashrom writes the BIOS region alone; a full-chip write fails partway through and can leave the laptop unable to boot.


---

# Flash Coreboot to Your Laptop BIOS

> Flash Coreboot from inside a running system after the BIOS region is unlocked. Includes safety checks and verification of the flashed image.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

With the BIOS region unlocked, flashing coreboot internally takes three steps: back up the current BIOS region, write the coreboot image to it with flashrom, and verify the result before rebooting. If something goes wrong the laptop may not boot, and recovering it needs an external programmer, so make the backup first.

Internal flashing cannot neutralise the Intel ME, because the ME region is locked and cannot be read or written from the running system. To neutralise it, use an external programmer to dump, modify and rewrite the whole firmware image, as [external flashing](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/) describes.

## Step 1: Back up the existing BIOS region

Step 1 reads the current BIOS region to a file, your recovery point if you need to restore the original firmware:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p internal -r factory.rom --ifd -i bios
```

This backs up the BIOS region only. The descriptor and Intel ME regions are locked and left out, so `factory.rom` is not a full image of the chip; a full one needs an external programmer.

## Step 2: Flash coreboot

Step 2 writes the coreboot image to the BIOS region alone:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p internal -w coreboot.rom --ifd -i bios -N
```

`--ifd -i bios` tells flashrom to use the layout in the flash descriptor and write only the BIOS region. `-N` limits flashrom's own verification to that region, because the locked ME region cannot be read back.

## Step 3: Verify the flashed image

Step 3 reads the BIOS region back from the chip and compares it with the image you wrote, so you know the chip holds exactly what you intended before you reboot:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p internal -r flashed.bin --ifd -i bios
```

Then compare the two in any of three ways, each at a different level.

### Compare the bytes
