The byte comparison checks the raw BIOS region. `coreboot.rom` is a full image of the chip, so first cut the BIOS region out of both files. The offsets below come from the BIOS region in the CHIPSEC output on the [unlocking page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/unlocking-bios/), Base `0x00500000` and Limit `0x00BFFFFF`: `skip` is the base (5 MB) and `count` the region's size (7 MB). Use the Base and Limit your own machine printed.

```bash
dd if=coreboot.rom of=coreboot_bios.rom bs=1 skip=5242880 count=7340032
dd if=flashed.bin of=flashed_bios.bin bs=1 skip=5242880 count=7340032
cmp -l coreboot_bios.rom flashed_bios.bin | head -n 20
```

If `cmp` prints nothing, the BIOS region was flashed correctly.

### Compare the build information

The build information check compares the `build_info` file that coreboot stores in its file system (CBFS):

```bash
cbfstool coreboot.rom extract -n build_info -f build_info_expected.txt
cbfstool flashed.bin extract -n build_info -f build_info_actual.txt
diff -u build_info_expected.txt build_info_actual.txt
```

If `diff` prints nothing, the two match.

### Compare the CBFS contents

The CBFS check compares the list of files inside the image, with their offsets, types and sizes. Print the layout of the image you built:

```bash
cbfstool coreboot.rom print
```

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
FMAP REGION: COREBOOT
Name                           Offset     Type           Size   Comp
cbfs_master_header             0x0        cbfs header        32 none
cpu_microcode_blob.bin         0x80       microcode       26624 none
fallback/romstage              0x68c0     stage           92312 none
fallback/ramstage              0x1d1c0    stage          120593 LZMA (255636 decompressed)
config                         0x3a940    raw              3332 LZMA (10602 decompressed)
revision                       0x3b680    raw               774 none
build_info                     0x3b9c0    raw               105 none
fallback/dsdt.aml              0x3ba80    raw             14537 none
vbt.bin                        0x3f380    raw              1409 LZMA (4459 decompressed)
cmos_layout.bin                0x3f940    cmos_layout      2060 none
fallback/postcar               0x40180    stage           23488 none
fallback/payload               0x45dc0    simple elf     473556 none
(empty)                        0xb97c0    null           202212 none
bootblock                      0xeadc0    bootblock       20480 none
```

</details>

Then save the layout of both images and compare them:

```bash
cbfstool coreboot.rom print > cbfs_expected.txt
cbfstool flashed.bin print > cbfs_actual.txt
diff -u cbfs_expected.txt cbfs_actual.txt
```

If all three comparisons match, coreboot has been written correctly and the laptop can be rebooted.


---

# External Flashing

> Flash Coreboot with an external SPI programmer: detect the chip, back up the factory BIOS, neutralise Intel ME, write the image and confirm ME is disabled.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/external-flashing/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

External flashing writes coreboot with a programmer, such as a Raspberry Pi Pico, clipped onto the laptop's flash chip, and it is the only route that can neutralise the Intel Management Engine: detect the chip, back up the whole factory image, run me_cleaner on its ME region and flash the result, flash coreboot to the BIOS region, and check with intelmetool that the ME is disabled.

External flashing is needed in three cases. The stock firmware locks the ME region against internal access, so neutralising the ME takes an external flash the first time. If an internal flash fails and the laptop no longer boots, an external programmer is the only way to restore it. And some boards do not allow internal flashing at all.

## Step 1: Detect the chip

Step 1 connects the programmer to the laptop's flash chip and checks that flashrom can identify the chip. With the laptop switched off and its battery removed:

1. Flash the Raspberry Pi Pico with serprog, as the [Libreboot serprog guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/build-serprog/) describes.
2. Wire the Pico with Dupont cables to a Pomona clip for a SOIC chip (first photo) or a pogo-pin adapter for a WSON chip (second photo), following the [Libreboot wiring guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/libreboot/raspberry-pico/connection/).
3. Attach the clip firmly to the chip, so every pin makes contact.
4. Plug the Pico into the computer you are flashing from with a USB cable.

<div className="photo-pair">

![A Raspberry Pi Pico wired with six coloured Dupont cables to a blue Pomona SOIC-8 test clip, the setup for chips in an 8-pin SOIC package](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/libreboot/connection.webp)

![The same Raspberry Pi Pico wired instead to a pogo-pin adapter, used for WSON chips that a clip cannot grip](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/coreboot/connection.webp)

</div>

Then detect the chip:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M
```

If flashrom reports several possible chip types, identify the right one from the markings on the chip and run the command again with its name:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V"
```

Once flashrom names one chip, go on to the backup.

## Step 2: Back up the factory BIOS

Step 2 reads the whole chip three times and compares the reads, so you have a factory image you can trust. If you are recovering from a failed internal flash, skip this step: an image that does not boot is not worth keeping.

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -r factory.bin
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -r factory2.bin
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -r factory3.bin
```

Compare the three reads:

```bash
sha1sum factory.bin factory2.bin factory3.bin
```

All three hashes must match:

```text
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory.bin
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory2.bin
6cf9bfc90df1ed01336872cd159a00c101d0a7b0  factory3.bin
```

If they do, keep `factory.bin` somewhere safe and delete the other two. If they differ, reseat the clip and read again.

```bash
rm factory2.bin factory3.bin
```

## Step 3: Neutralise the Intel ME

Step 3 checks the factory image and runs me_cleaner on its ME region. First confirm the image has the expected layout with `ifdtool`, from the coreboot source tree:

```bash
cd coreboot/util/ifdtool
make
./ifdtool -d factory.bin
```

It prints a long description of the flash descriptor, including the ME region:

<summary>Output</summary>

```text
  GbE Region Write Access:           enabled
  Intel ME Region Write Access:      enabled
  Host CPU/BIOS Region Write Access: disabled
  Flash Descriptor Write Access:     disabled
  Platform Data Region Read Access:  disabled
  GbE Region Read Access:            enabled
  Intel ME Region Read Access:       enabled
  Host CPU/BIOS Region Read Access:  disabled
  Flash Descriptor Read Access:      enabled
  Requester ID:                      0x0000

FLMSTR3:   0x08080118 (GbE)
  Platform Data Region Write Access: disabled
  GbE Region Write Access:           enabled
  Intel ME Region Write Access:      disabled
  Host CPU/BIOS Region Write Access: disabled
  Flash Descriptor Write Access:     disabled
  Platform Data Region Read Access:  disabled
  GbE Region Read Access:            enabled
  Intel ME Region Read Access:       disabled
  Host CPU/BIOS Region Read Access:  disabled
  Flash Descriptor Read Access:      disabled
  Requester ID:                      0x0118

Found Processor Strap Section
????:      0x00000000
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
????:      0xffffffff
```

</details>

Then check that the ME firmware in the image is valid with [me_cleaner](https://github.com/corna/me_cleaner), which ships in the coreboot tree at `util/me_cleaner`:

```bash
python me_cleaner.py -c factory.bin
```

The output should look like this:

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
Full image detected
The ME/TXE region goes from 0x3000 to 0x500000
Found FPT header at 0x3010
Found 23 partition(s)
Found FTPR header: FTPR partition spans from 0x180000 to 0x24a000
ME/TXE firmware version 8.1.40.1416
Public key match: Intel ME, firmware versions 7.x.x.x, 8.x.x.x
The AltMeDisable bit is NOT SET
Checking the FTPR RSA signature... VALID
```

</details>

Then neutralise the ME. `-S` also sets the AltMeDisable bit, which asks the ME to switch itself off after hardware initialisation, and `-O` writes the result to a new file, leaving `factory.bin` untouched:

```bash
python me_cleaner.py -S -O factory_me_neutralized.bin factory.bin
```

The output should look like this:

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
Full image detected
The ME/TXE region goes from 0x3000 to 0x500000
Found FPT header at 0x3010
Found 23 partition(s)
Found FTPR header: FTPR partition spans from 0x180000 to 0x24a000
ME/TXE firmware version 8.1.40.1416
Public key match: Intel ME, firmware versions 7.x.x.x, 8.x.x.x
The AltMeDisable bit is NOT SET
Reading partitions list...
 ???? (0x000003c0 - 0x000000400, 0x00000040 total bytes): removed
 FOVD (0x00000400 - 0x000001000, 0x00000c00 total bytes): removed
 MDES (0x00001000 - 0x000002000, 0x00001000 total bytes): removed
 FCRS (0x00002000 - 0x000003000, 0x00001000 total bytes): removed
 EFFS (0x00003000 - 0x0000df000, 0x000dc000 total bytes): removed
 BIAL (NVRAM partition, no data, 0x0000add0 total bytes): nothing to remove

Removing partition entries in FPT...
Removing EFFS presence flag...
Correcting checksum (0x2f)...
Reading FTPR modules list...
 UPDATE           (LZMA   , 0x1cc507 - 0x1cc6c5       ): removed
 ROMP             (Huffman, fragmented data, ~2 KiB   ): NOT removed, essential

 POLICY           (Huffman, fragmented data, ~91 KiB  ): removed

The ME minimum size should be 1667072 bytes (0x197000 bytes)
The ME region can be reduced up to:
 00003000:00199fff me
Setting the AltMeDisable bit in PCHSTRP10 to disable Intel ME...
Checking the FTPR RSA signature... VALID
Done! Good luck!
```

</details>

## Step 4: Flash the neutralised image

Step 4 writes the whole neutralised image back to the chip:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -w factory_me_neutralized.bin
```

Read the chip back and compare it with the file you wrote:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -r flashed.bin
```

```bash
sha1sum factory_me_neutralized.bin flashed.bin
```

The two hashes must match:

```text
4b9f06ccd2ce11dad757e337829a450a05df7929  factory_me_neutralized.bin
4b9f06ccd2ce11dad757e337829a450a05df7929  flashed.bin
```

If they do, delete `flashed.bin`. If they differ, write the image again before going on.

```bash
rm flashed.bin
```

## Step 5: Flash the coreboot BIOS region

Step 5 writes coreboot to the BIOS region of the chip. Skip it if you have already flashed coreboot internally. Remove the CMOS battery first: some laptops keep settings that protect the SPI chip in CMOS or the embedded controller. Then disable the chip's write protection:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" --wp-disable
```

flashrom confirms it:

```text
Disabled hardware protection
```

Write only the BIOS region of your coreboot image, leaving the descriptor and the neutralised ME as they are:

```bash
sudo flashrom -p serprog:dev=/dev/ttyACM0,spispeed=16M -c "W25Q128.V" -w coreboot.rom --ifd -i bios -N
```

Then [verify the flashed BIOS region](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/coreboot/internal/flashing-bios/#verify-the-flashed-image), reading it back with this same programmer in place of `-p internal`.

## Step 6: Verify the Intel ME is neutralised

Step 6 boots the laptop and checks the ME's state with `intelmetool`, from the coreboot source tree:

```bash
cd coreboot/util/intelmetool
make
sudo ./intelmetool -m
```

On a neutralised ME the output looks like this:

<details>
<summary>Output</summary>

```text
Bad news, you have a `QM77 Express Chipset LPC Controller` so you have ME hardware on board and you can't control or disable it, continuing...

MEI found: [8086:1e3a] 7 Series/C216 Chipset Family MEI Controller #1

ME Status   : 0x1c020191
ME Status 2 : 0x120a0150

ME: FW Partition Table      : OK
ME: Bringup Loader Failure  : NO
ME: Firmware Init Complete  : NO
ME: Manufacturing Mode      : YES
ME: Boot Options Present    : NO
ME: Update In Progress      : NO
ME: Current Working State   : Initializing
ME: Current Operation State : Bring up
ME: Current Operation Mode  : Debug
ME: Error Code              : No Error
ME: Progress Phase          : BUP Phase
ME: Power Management Event  : Clean global reset
ME: Progress Phase State    : Check to see if straps say ME DISABLED

ME: Extend SHA-256: f9acfe9c2b5b199d321a1580417f5c4334d710175ad70bdaf4350eb1bef276fe

ME: failed to become ready
ME: failed to become ready
ME: GET FW VERSION message failed
```

</details>

In this output, Intel ME remains in the initializing state and fails to become fully ready. This is what a neutralised ME looks like: the hardware is present, but the ME firmware is disabled and cannot initialize.

# Build a Nostr Signing Device (NSD)

> Build your own Nostr Signing Device to keep your private key secure. Hardware-based signing for Nostr using LILYGO T-Display and Horse extension.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

A Nostr signing device is a small piece of hardware, here a LILYGO T-Display board running LNbits' open-source firmware, that holds your Nostr private key and signs your posts itself, so the key never sits in a browser or app where malware could copy it. A browser extension called Horse passes signing requests from a Nostr client to the device. It applies the rule this site teaches for bitcoin keys (keep them offline and isolated) to your Nostr identity, and it is a bonus project: an hour or two and about $15 of parts.

Time: 1-2 hours. Cost: $10-15 (LILYGO T-Display). Level: Intermediate. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: LILYGO T-Display, USB cable, Chrome-based browser.

## Why use a hardware signing device for Nostr?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Without a signing device | With one |
|-------------|----------|
| The private key is stored in a browser or app | The private key is stored on the device |
| Exposed to malware and keyloggers | Out of reach of the computer |
| Can be copied | Never leaves the device |

</div>

## How does it work?

<div class="doc-diagram">

![The NSD chain: the T-Display device holds the Nostr key and signs, the Horse browser extension bridges it to the browser, and the Nostr client only ever sees signatures, never the key](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/diagrams/nostr-signing-device/nsd-chain.svg)

</div>

The LILYGO T-Display is the signing hardware, the Horse extension connects it to the browser, and the Nostr client (Coracle, for example) is where you read and post. The client only ever sees signatures.

## What do you need?

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Part | What it is for | Where to get it |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| LILYGO T-Display 1.14 | The signing hardware | [AliExpress](https://www.aliexpress.com/item/33048962331.html) |
| USB cable | Connecting and flashing the board | Usually included |
| Arduino IDE | Building and uploading the firmware | Free download |
| Horse extension | The bridge between the browser and the device | Built from source, for Chromium |

</div>

## What are the steps?

| Step | Page |
|---|---|
| 1 | [Install the Arduino IDE](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/arduino-ide/) |
| 2 | [Add ESP32 board support](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/esp32-module/) |
| 3 | [Flash the signing device firmware](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/setup/) |
| 4 | [Build the Horse extension](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/horse-extension/) |
| 5 | [Connect to a Nostr client](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/client-connect/) |


---

# Arduino IDE Setup for NSD

> Install and configure Arduino IDE to flash your Nostr Signing Device. Download the legacy version and set up ESP32 board support.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/arduino-ide/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The signing device's firmware is built and uploaded with the Arduino IDE. This guide uses the legacy Arduino IDE 1.8.19 on Linux: download it, extract it, run its install script, and add it to your panel.

## Step 1: Download the Arduino IDE

Step 1 gets the installer. From the [Arduino website](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software/), download the [legacy Arduino IDE 1.8.19](https://downloads.arduino.cc/arduino-1.8.19-linux64.tar.xz).

## Step 2: Extract and install it

Step 2 unpacks and installs it. In a terminal:

```bash
tar -xvf arduino-1.8.19-linux64.tar.xz
cd arduino-1.8.19
sudo sh install.sh
```

The script ends with:

```bash
Adding desktop shortcut, menu item and file associations for Arduino IDE...
.
.
done!
```

## Step 3: Add it to your panel

Step 3 makes it easy to open. On Linux Mint, open the menu, type `Arduino`, right-click the Arduino icon and choose `Add to Panel`.


---

# ESP32 Board Support Setup

> Add ESP32 board support to Arduino IDE so you can compile and flash firmware for the LILYGO T-Display module used by the Nostr Signing Device.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/esp32-module/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The T-Display is an ESP32 board, so the Arduino IDE needs Espressif's ESP32 board package before it can build for it: add the package's address in the preferences, install the package from the board manager, and select the board. The steps follow [Espressif's installation guide](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/arduino-esp32/en/latest/installing.html#before-installing).

## Step 1: Add the ESP32 board address

Step 1 tells the IDE where to find the package. Open the Arduino IDE, go to `File`, `Preferences`, and in the `Additional Boards Manager URLs` field add:

```bash
https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json
```

## Step 2: Install the ESP32 platform

Step 2 downloads it. Open `Tools`, `Board`, `Board Manager`, search for `esp32`, and install the result named esp32 by Espressif Systems. It takes a while.

## Step 3: Select the board

Step 3 chooses the target. Go to `Tools`, `Board`, `ESP32 Arduino` and select TTGO LoRa32-OLED, then restart the Arduino IDE.


---

# Prepare the NSD Firmware

> Clone the NSD repository and flash the firmware to your LILYGO device. Step-by-step instructions to prepare your Nostr Signing Device.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/setup/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Flashing the signing device means downloading LNbits' nostr-signing-device code, copying its libraries into Arduino's, and uploading its `snsd.ino` sketch to the board from the Arduino IDE. When it works, the board shows the LNbits welcome screen.

## Step 1: Get the code and its libraries

Step 1 downloads the firmware and the libraries it needs:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lnbits/nostr-signing-device.git
cd nostr-signing-device/libraries
cp -r . ~/Arduino/libraries
```

The `~/Arduino/libraries` folder should be empty if you have just installed Arduino.

## Step 2: Upload the firmware

Step 2 puts it on the board. Plug the device in by USB, then in the Arduino IDE:

1. Choose the device's serial port under `Tools`, `Port` (for example `/dev/ttyACM0`).
2. Open `snsd.ino` from the `nostr-signing-device/snsd/` folder with `File`, `Open`.
3. Click the Upload button, the right-facing arrow in the toolbar.

## Step 3: Check it started

Step 3 confirms it worked. If the upload finishes without errors, the display shows the LNbits welcome screen.

![The LILYGO T-Display board plugged in by USB, showing the LNbits logo on its screen](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/nsd/nsd.webp)


---

# Install Horse Browser Extension

> Install the Horse Chromium browser extension to connect your Nostr Signing Device to web clients and sign Nostr events from your browser.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/horse-extension/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Horse is LNbits' browser extension that passes signing requests from Nostr websites to the signing device. It works only in Chromium-based browsers and is built from source: clone it, install its dependencies, build it, and load it as an unpacked extension.

## Step 1: Build the extension

Step 1 builds it from source, which needs git and Node.js:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lnbits/horse.git
cd horse
npm install --force
npm run build
```

The `--force` flag is needed for the dependencies to install.

## Step 2: Load it in the browser

Step 2 installs it:

1. Open Chromium and go to `chrome://extensions/`.
2. Turn on `Developer mode`, top right.
3. Click `Load unpacked`, top left, and select the `horse/extension` folder.

Horse then appears among your extensions.

![The Horse 0.0.2 extension in Chromium's extensions page, described as "Hardware Remote Signer of Events"](https://selfcustodylabs.com/img/nsd/horse.webp)


---

# Connect NSD to Nostr Clients

> Connect your Nostr Signing Device to clients like Coracle and NoStrudel. Final step to start using your hardware-secured Nostr identity.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/nostr-signing-device/client-connect/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

The last step is logging in to a Nostr web client that can use the browser extension, so that every post and reaction is signed on the device. We have tested the device and the Horse extension with [Coracle](https://coracle.social/) and [noStrudel](https://nostrudel.ninja/). Other clients, Snort among them, have shown errors whose cause we have not found yet, so stick to those two for now.

Many popular web clients, [Primal](https://primal.net/) for example, do not support external signers and ask for your private key (`nsec`) to log in instead, which defeats the purpose of a signing device. Never paste your `nsec` into one.

Once logged in, add your preferred relays. From then on, every action you take (posting, reacting, following) asks the device to sign it before it is sent to the network.


---

# SeedSigner: Our Favourite Bitcoin Signing Device

> Why SeedSigner is the Self Custody Labs favourite signing solution: stateless, air-gapped, fully verifiable, and built by you from commodity parts.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

SeedSigner is a Bitcoin signing device you build yourself from about $50 of off-the-shelf Raspberry Pi parts. It is the Self Custody Labs favourite signing solution, and this section explains why, how to [build one](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/), and how to [use it](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/using-seedsigner/).

Time: 1-2 hours build, plus practice. Cost: $50-80 in parts. Level: Intermediate to advanced. Updated: 26 Oct 2026. You need: comfort with basic command-line verification and DIY assembly.

**Warning: Not for everyone**
Our favourite does not mean our recommendation for most people. SeedSigner adds layers of complication that a beginner should not take on: you assemble the hardware, verify and flash the software, and manage your seed backup entirely on your own. If you are setting up self-custody for the first time, start with the [hardware wallet setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/) and a device from our [comparison page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/). Come back when the workflow below sounds appealing rather than intimidating.

## Why is SeedSigner our favourite?

The [2026 Coldcard entropy incident](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) reshaped how this site evaluates signing devices: what matters is not what a vendor promises, but what you can verify yourself. SeedSigner is the most complete answer to that standard we know of.

**Stateless by design.** SeedSigner never stores your seed. The seed exists in RAM only during a signing session and vanishes at power-off. There is no flash memory to extract, no PIN to brute-force, and nothing for a thief to find on the device.

**No vendor RNG to trust.** You supply the entropy yourself, typically with [dice rolls](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/), and you can re-derive the resulting seed independently to prove the device honored your input. The exact failure that cost Coldcard users $116M is structurally impossible: there is no vendor seed generation to silently go wrong.

**No wallet-specific supply chain.** A hardware wallet ships to you from one vendor and can be intercepted or backdoored in transit. SeedSigner is assembled from generic Raspberry Pi components that were never labeled "bitcoin device" anywhere in their supply chain, running software you verify and flash yourself.

**Fully open and community-built.** Every line of code is open source, the project is maintained by a community rather than a company with a sales target, and releases are signed so you can verify what you flash. The current release (v0.8.7, July 2026) supports taproot, multisig, message signing, and 22 languages.

**True QR air gap.** The device communicates with your wallet software exclusively through QR codes in both directions. No USB, no Bluetooth, no SD card shuffling. The recommended Raspberry Pi Zero v1.3 has no WiFi or Bluetooth hardware at all.

## What are the trade-offs?

Each is the other side of a strength:

| Trade-off | What it means for you |
|-----------|----------------------|
| No secure element | The device runs a general-purpose Linux stack; its security comes from statelessness and the air gap, not a hardened chip |
| You are the backup | The device stores nothing, so your [seed backup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/seed/) (steel plate, SeedQR) is the single thing keeping your funds recoverable |
| Slower sessions | Loading the seed and scanning animated QR codes takes minutes, not seconds; this is a vault workflow, not a daily spender |
| Camera exposure | The SeedQR workflow puts your seed in front of a camera; do it in a private space away from windows, webcams, and phones |
| DIY responsibility | A mistake in verification or assembly is yours to catch; nobody ships you a warranty |

For a deeper look at how SeedSigner compares to a full air-gapped computer, see [air-gapped wallets](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/air-gapped-wallets/).

## Where does SeedSigner fit best?

- **As a multisig key.** SeedSigner is an outstanding quorum member in a [multisig setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/): a key with no vendor, no supply chain, and no stored state diversifies beautifully against your other devices.
- **As the vault for patient savings.** The slow, deliberate workflow is a feature when you sign a few times a year.
- **As a learning instrument.** Nothing teaches how Bitcoin signing actually works like holding the entire process in your own hands.

Ready? Start with the [build guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/).


---

# Build Your Own SeedSigner

> Source the Raspberry Pi parts, verify and flash SeedSigner OS, and assemble an air-gapped Bitcoin signing device for about $50 in parts.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/build-guide/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Building a SeedSigner takes about $50 of parts (a Raspberry Pi Zero v1.3, a WaveShare 1.3-inch LCD HAT, a Pi Zero camera and a microSD card) and an hour or two: buy the parts, download SeedSigner OS and verify its signature, flash it to the card, assemble the device, and run a few checks before trusting it with funds. None of the steps is hard, but several reward care.

Building it yourself is the point, not a way to save money: generic parts mean there is no bitcoin-specific supply chain to intercept, and flashing software you verified yourself means there is no vendor to take on trust. If you buy a pre-assembled unit instead (such as a SeedSigner+ kit), you bring a supply chain back, so buy only from a reputable builder, and still flash and verify the OS image yourself.

## Step 1: Buy the parts

Step 1 buys the parts, about $40 to $70 in total at the prices below:

<div class="fixed-width-table">

| Part | Notes | Approx. price |
|------|-------|---------------|
| Raspberry Pi Zero v1.3 | The recommended board: it has **no WiFi or Bluetooth hardware at all** | $10-15 |
| WaveShare 1.3" LCD HAT | 240x240 screen with joystick and buttons | $15-20 |
| Pi Zero camera module (OV5647) | Must include a Zero-sized ribbon cable | $10-15 |
| MicroSD card (4GB+) | Any decent brand; the OS is tiny | $5-8 |
| Case (optional) | Community designs exist to 3D print, or buy one | $0-15 |

</div>

SeedSigner OS also runs on the Pi Zero W, Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 2B, Pi 3B, and Pi 4B. The Zero v1.3 remains our recommendation because its air gap is physical: there is no radio to switch off and nothing to misconfigure. If you use a board with WiFi/Bluetooth (like the faster Zero 2 W), understand that you are trusting software to keep the radios off; SeedSigner OS never enables them, but absent hardware beats disabled hardware.

Buy the parts from general electronics retailers (the official [seedsigner.com](https://seedsigner.com) site maintains a current parts list with links). Spreading purchases across ordinary retailers is exactly what makes the supply-chain story boring, which is what you want.

## Step 2: Download and verify SeedSigner OS

Step 2 downloads SeedSigner OS and checks it is the image the project signed. Never flash an image you have not verified: this is the one step where skipping ahead defeats the purpose of the whole device.

1. Download the latest release image from the official GitHub repository ([github.com/SeedSigner/seedsigner/releases](https://github.com/SeedSigner/seedsigner/releases), v0.8.7 as of October 2026). Pick the file matching your board, e.g. `seedsigner_os.0.8.7.pi0.img` for the Pi Zero v1.3.
2. Download the accompanying SHA256 hash file and its GPG signature from the same release page.
3. Import the SeedSigner release signing key and check its fingerprint against at least one independent source (the project website, a maintainer's profile):

```bash
gpg --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com --recv-keys <seedsigner-release-key-id>
gpg --fingerprint <seedsigner-release-key-id>
```

4. Verify the signature and the image hash:

```bash
gpg --verify seedsigner_os.0.8.7.sha256.sig seedsigner_os.0.8.7.sha256
sha256sum --check seedsigner_os.0.8.7.sha256 --ignore-missing
```

Both commands must succeed: a good signature from the key you checked, and an `OK` for your image file. If either fails, stop and re-download from the official repository.

SeedSigner OS builds are reproducible: with the project's build system you can compile the image from source on your own machine and get a byte-identical result. You do not have to go that far, but the fact that anyone can is what keeps the published images honest.

## Step 3: Flash the microSD card

Step 3 writes the verified image to the microSD card. Use any flashing tool you trust; with plain `dd` on Linux (double-check the target device name with `lsblk` first; `dd` overwrites without asking):

```bash
sudo dd if=seedsigner_os.0.8.7.pi0.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync
```

Raspberry Pi Imager or balenaEtcher work too; if you use Raspberry Pi Imager, choose "Use custom image" and do not let it apply any OS customization.

## Step 4: Assemble the device

Step 4 puts the four parts together; no tools are needed unless your Pi Zero has no header:

1. Connect the camera. Lift the retaining clip on the Pi Zero's camera connector, insert the ribbon cable with the contacts facing the board, and press the clip closed. The Zero's connector is smaller than a full-size Pi's, which is why the Zero-specific ribbon matters.
2. Seat the LCD HAT: press the WaveShare HAT onto the Pi's 40-pin GPIO header. If your Pi Zero came without a soldered header, you will need to solder one (or buy the "WH" variant with the header pre-installed).
3. Insert the flashed microSD card and close up the case if you have one.
4. Power it from any USB power source: a phone charger or a power bank is fine. SeedSigner has no battery and needs none; power off between sessions is the security model working as intended.

First boot takes under a minute and lands on the SeedSigner home screen. The device never needs, and never asks for, a network connection.

## Step 5: Check it before trusting it with funds

Step 5 tests the device with a throwaway seed before it guards real money:

- Power-cycle the device and confirm it remembers nothing: no seeds should survive a reboot.
- Generate a throwaway test seed, load it into a hot wallet, and run one full sign-and-broadcast cycle on a small amount you can afford to lose.
- Practice the full [usage workflow](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/using-seedsigner/), including restoring your backup, before trusting it with savings. The [backup verification guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/) applies here in full.


---

# Using SeedSigner: Seeds, SeedQR, and Signing

> Generate a seed with dice on your SeedSigner, back it up as a SeedQR, and sign transactions with Sparrow over an air-gapped QR workflow.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/seedsigner/using-seedsigner/
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

Using a SeedSigner comes down to four steps and an option: generate a seed from your own dice rolls, back it up as words and as a SeedQR, connect Sparrow on your computer as a watch-only wallet, and sign transactions by passing QR codes between Sparrow and the device; it can also be one key of a multisig. The device stores nothing, so every session starts by loading your seed.

**Danger: The device stores nothing; you store everything**
SeedSigner is stateless. Every seed you use exists only while the device is powered, which means your physical backup is the only durable copy of your keys. Treat the backup steps below as the main event, not an afterthought.

## Step 1: Generate a seed with dice

From the home screen, choose **Tools → New seed → Dice rolls**, then roll a physical die 99 times (for 24 words) or 50 times (for 12), entering each roll. Two habits make this trustworthy:

1. **Use a casino-grade die or several ordinary dice mixed**, rolled with a cup. The point is entropy nobody else influenced; see [our randomness guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) for why this matters more than any device feature after 2026.
2. **Verify the derivation.** Write down the rolls, then re-derive the seed from the same rolls on a second device or offline tool and confirm the words match. This single check proves no device in the chain invented its own "randomness". The comparison page's [entropy table](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/#entropy-who-lets-you-verify) shows how rare that verifiability is.

Add a [passphrase](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/passphrase/) if the funds warrant it; SeedSigner supports entering one at load time, and it is never part of the stored backup.

## Step 2: Back it up as words and a SeedQR

Record the seed words on paper first, then transfer to steel for anything long-term. Then let SeedSigner render the seed as a **SeedQR**: a compact QR encoding of the seed words you can etch or punch into metal.

The payoff comes at every future session: instead of typing 24 words on a joystick, you point the camera at your SeedQR and the seed loads in seconds. The cost is that anyone who photographs that QR has your seed.

**SeedQR handling rules:**

- Scan and display it only in a private room, away from windows, webcams, and phones.
- Store it with the same physical security as the written words; it *is* the words.
- If the wallet has a passphrase, the SeedQR alone stays insufficient to spend, which is a good reason to use one.

Before depositing anything, run the [backup verification drill](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/): wipe (power-cycle) the device, restore purely from your backup, and confirm the wallet derives the same addresses.

## Step 3: Connect Sparrow as a watch-only wallet

Sparrow Wallet on your desktop tracks balances and builds transactions; SeedSigner only signs. To pair them:

1. On SeedSigner: load your seed, then **Export xpub** and choose the script type (native segwit for a first wallet).
2. In Sparrow: **File → New Wallet**, keystore type **Airgapped Hardware Wallet → SeedSigner**, and scan the animated QR from the device's screen with your webcam (or import the xpub file if you prefer).
3. Sparrow now knows your [xpub](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/xpub/), so it can watch funds and generate receive addresses, but it holds no key material.

Verify a receive address on both screens before first use: display the address QR in Sparrow, scan it with SeedSigner's **Address Explorer**, and confirm the device agrees the address belongs to your seed.

## Step 4: Sign a transaction

The signing loop is the same every time:

1. **Build** the transaction in Sparrow and click through to the QR display; Sparrow shows the unsigned transaction (PSBT) as an animated QR.
2. **Scan** it with SeedSigner's camera (seed loaded).
3. **Review on the device screen**: amount, destination address, fee, and change. The device screen is the truth; if it disagrees with Sparrow, trust the device and investigate.
4. **Approve**, and SeedSigner displays the signed PSBT as an animated QR.
5. **Scan back** into Sparrow with your webcam and broadcast.

Nothing but QR codes crossed the gap in either direction. When you power off, the device forgets the seed and the whole session.

## How does SeedSigner work in a multisig?

SeedSigner shines as one key in a [multisig quorum](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/): it contributes a key with no vendor, no supply chain, and no stored state, which is exactly the diversity multisig is for. Register the multisig descriptor on the device (SeedSigner can persist it to the microSD as a non-secret convenience, or verify it each session) so the device can confirm change addresses really belong to your quorum. The [multisig hardware setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/) walks through the full configuration.

SeedSigner also signs plain text messages (**Tools → Sign message**, via QR), useful for proving address ownership without moving funds.


---

# Our CoinJoin recommendation is now JoinMarket NG

> On 22 August 2026 we rewrote the CoinJoin guide for the tools that survived 2024 to 2026: JoinMarket NG with Jam recommended, Wasabi and Whirlpool covered.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/notes/coinjoin-recommendation/
Published: 2026-10-26
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

On 22 August 2026 we rewrote our [CoinJoin page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) and added a [hands-on CoinJoin tutorial](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin-tutorial/). We now recommend one tool, JoinMarket NG with the Jam interface, because it has no coordinator that can be seized or shut down. Before the rewrite, the page offered Wasabi, Whirlpool through Sparrow, and the original JoinMarket as three equal choices, and all three entries had gone out of date.

## What had gone out of date?

| What the page said | What was true by August 2026 |
|---|---|
| Use Whirlpool through Sparrow Wallet | US authorities seized Samourai Wallet's coordinator in April 2024, and Sparrow removed its Whirlpool integration in June 2024 |
| Wasabi charges a 0.3% coordinator fee | zkSNACKs shut down its coordinator in June 2024; Wasabi now connects to independent coordinators, and since version 2.2 has no built-in coordinator fee |
| JoinMarket, linked to its original repository | That repository was archived in April 2026; development continues as JoinMarket NG |

## Why recommend only one?

2024 showed what coordinator risk means in practice: the day Samourai's servers were seized, every Whirlpool user stopped mixing. JoinMarket NG is a peer-to-peer market with no company in the middle, so there is nothing to seize. It requires your own Bitcoin node, which the rest of this site already recommends, and Jam makes it usable without the command line.

The other tools are still covered. Wasabi is the simpler alternative. Ashigaru, a community fork of Samourai, launched a new Whirlpool coordinator in June 2025; we describe it without recommending it.

## Why are theory and practice now separate pages?

The [CoinJoin page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin/) explains how mixing works, what it protects and what it does not, and compares the tools. The [tutorial](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/privacy/coinjoin-tutorial/) is the procedure: your own node, a temporary hot wallet protected by a passphrase, JoinMarket NG and Jam, and sweeping the mixed coins out to cold storage when you are done. A reader who only wants to understand CoinJoin no longer has to scroll past installation steps, and a reader following the steps no longer has to skip the theory.


---

# Why we stopped recommending Coldcard

> On 21 August 2026 we took Coldcard out of every recommendation on the site after its entropy flaw, and made dice the default way to create a seed.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/notes/coldcard-no-longer-recommended/
Published: 2026-10-26
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

On 21 August 2026 we removed Coldcard from every place on this site that recommended a hardware wallet, and made a seed rolled with dice the default instead of a seed generated by the device. Coldcard is still in the [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/), with a warning, and the instructions for people who already own one are still here; we no longer suggest buying one.

## What happened?

Between 30 July and 4 August 2026, attackers drained about 1,816 BTC from more than 5,200 addresses whose seeds had been generated on Coldcards. A firmware build error present since March 2021 had made the devices generate seeds from a predictable software generator instead of their hardware random number generator. The [incident page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/coldcard-entropy-incident/) has the timeline, the cause, and what to do if a Coldcard made your seed; this note covers only what the incident changed here.

## What did we change?

| Before 21 August 2026 | After |
|---|---|
| Coldcard was the security pick on the comparison and in the setup chooser | Listed with a warning, in no recommendation slot |
| A seed generated by the device was the default; dice were an extra for the careful | Dice first; the device's random number generator is the fallback |
| "Air-gapped" and "open source" read as guarantees | Both carry their limits: the drained devices were air-gapped, and the bug sat in public code for five years |
| The comparison listed the 2024 lineup | Redone for the August 2026 lineup, with three new criteria: dice entropy, whether the entropy can be verified, and how the vendor handled a crisis |

Sixteen other pages that pointed at Coldcard or the old lineup were updated the same day, and each now links to the incident page rather than retelling it.

## Why stop recommending it, rather than wait for the fix?

Every hardware wallet maker ships bugs, and Coinkite shipped fixed firmware the day after the first theft. The decision rests on two other facts. The flaw silently produced weak seeds for five years in a device whose reputation rested on security, and a developer had warned Coinkite about that code in May 2025 and been dismissed. Recommending a device is a claim that its maker can be trusted with the one step nobody else can check, seed generation, and as of October 2026 we cannot make that claim for Coldcard.

## What does it mean for you?

The change that matters most is the second row of the table. A seed made from dice you rolled yourself does not depend on any manufacturer's random number generator, which is why Coldcard seeds made with the dice option were not affected. The [dice seed guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) shows how to make one, and the [comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) shows which devices let you add your own dice rolls.


---

# Correction: which hardware wallets take dice rolls

> We said every device we recommend takes your own dice rolls. The Trezor Safe cannot, and most others take them off the device. What is true in October 2026.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/notes/correction-device-dice-entry/
Published: 2026-10-26
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

From August to October 2026 several pages on this site said that every hardware wallet we recommend can mix your own dice rolls into seed creation. That was wrong for the Trezor Safe 5 and 7, which as of October 2026 have no dice path at all, and loose for most of the rest: only the Keystone 3 Pro, SeedSigner and Krux take dice rolls on the device, while BitBox, Blockstream and Foundation document ways to choose the words with dice and enter them. Every recommended device can still use a seed you made yourself from dice, by restoring it, so the advice to supply your own randomness stands; what changes is how you do it on each device.

## What is true as of October 2026?

| Device | Your own dice entropy |
|---|---|
| Keystone 3 Pro | Dice rolls on the device, firmware 1.2.6 or later |
| SeedSigner and Krux | Dice rolls on the device |
| BitBox02 | BitBox's own diceware procedure: dice pick the words from a printed table, and the device offers valid last words |
| Passport Prime | Draw the words yourself and import them, as Foundation's documentation describes |
| Trezor Safe 5 and 7 | No dice entry. Make the seed with dice and restore it. Trezor said on 5 August 2026 that it is considering user-supplied entropy, without committing to it |
| Jade and Jade Plus | Blockstream's own dice methods: dice pick the words from its table, and the device calculates valid last words. By default the Jade also mixes several entropy sources |

We found the error while researching device setup guides, by reading each maker's documentation rather than our own earlier summary of it.

## What changed on the site?

The [hardware wallet comparison](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/reference/hardware-wallet-comparison/) now says, for each device, whether dice go in on the device, through a maker's procedure, or by restoring a seed you made, and its entropy table says how you can check each. The [dice guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/), the [hardware wallet setup guide](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/hardware-wallet/), [hardware wallets explained](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/hardware-wallets/) and the [multisig hardware setup](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/wallets/multisig/hardware-setup/) say the same.

## What if you followed the old advice?

If you set up a Trezor or a Jade looking for a dice option on the device and did not find one, the device generated the seed itself from its own sources. Neither maker's generator is known to be flawed, and both said in August 2026 that their devices were not affected by the Coldcard bug. If you want the seed to rest on your own dice instead, [make one with dice](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/learn/keys/random/) (on a Jade, Blockstream's dice method does the same and the device supplies the last word), restore it onto the device as a new wallet, test it with [backup verification](https://selfcustodylabs.com/docs/wallet-setup/backup-verification/), and then move the funds across.


---

# What changed in the October 2026 rebuild

> In October 2026 we rebuilt the site: every guide rewritten and dated, a design that matches our diagrams, private search, and lighter pages that load faster.

Source: https://selfcustodylabs.com/notes/site-rebuild-2026/
Published: 2026-10-26
Last updated: 2026-10-26
Publisher: Self Custody Labs (https://selfcustodylabs.com)

---

In October 2026 we rebuilt Self Custody Labs: how it looks, how it is built, and the text of every guide. No page moved, so every link to the site still works. This note lists what changed.

## What changed in the guides?

All 97 pages were edited for facts and for voice.

On facts, claims that go out of date now carry the date they were checked: prices, firmware versions, release numbers and recommendations. Pages that had drifted were corrected. The firmware pages, for example, said Libreboot removes the Intel Management Engine; on the ThinkPads they cover it neutralises it, which is different, and the Libreboot guide now follows the current release.

On voice, the pages had collected filler: boxes listing what you were about to learn, summary sections that repeated the page, emoji in headings, and bold at the start of every bullet. That is gone, and the build now fails if it comes back. Each page opens with the answer to the question in its title, and its headings are the questions people ask.

Hands-on guides now show a facts line under the opening paragraph: time, cost, difficulty and when the guide last changed, plus the date we last re-checked it against current sources where we have. A guide is marked verified only when we have done it on real hardware.

## What does the site look like now?

The design follows our own diagrams and preview cards: dark paper, hairline rules, monospaced labels, amber only for the thing being explained, and photographs of the actual hardware. Pages print cleanly, with every collapsed section opened, so the dice and multisig guides can be worked from on paper, away from a computer.

## Are the pages faster?

Yes. Search now uses Pagefind, which loads a few small pieces of the index for each search instead of one 3.4 MB file, and your query never leaves the browser. The site's fonts now load, from this domain, photographs are resized and stripped of camera metadata, and the interface libraries the old homepage needed are gone.

## What did not change?

The [positions on the about page](https://selfcustodylabs.com/about/) are the same, and so is the independence: no affiliate links, no sponsors, and no money from the companies we write about. These field notes are new: dated posts about changes like this one, with an [RSS feed](https://selfcustodylabs.com/notes/rss.xml).
